chapters.title: No. 1 — General Introduction (Hamilton)
paragraphs: After plain experience of the ineffectiveness of the existing federal government, you are called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks to its own importance, for its consequences reach nothing less than the existence of the UNION, the safety and welfare of the parts that compose it, and the fate of an empire that is in many respects the most interesting in the world. It has often been remarked that it seems to have been reserved for the people of this country, by their conduct and example, to decide an important question: whether societies of men are truly capable of establishing good government through reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend on accident and force for their political constitutions. If there is any truth in this remark, the crisis we have now reached may rightly be regarded as the era in which that decision is to be made. A wrong choice of the part we shall act may, in this view, deserve to be considered the general misfortune of mankind.

This thought adds the motives of philanthropy to those of patriotism, and heightens the concern that every thoughtful and good person must feel about the outcome. It will be fortunate if our choice is guided by a sound estimate of our true interests, undisturbed and unbiased by considerations unconnected with the public good. But this is more to be ardently wished than seriously expected. The plan offered for our deliberation affects too many particular interests and makes changes in too many local institutions for its discussion not to involve a variety of matters foreign to its merits, and of views, passions and prejudices that do little to help the discovery of truth.

Among the most formidable obstacles the new Constitution will have to meet, we can readily pick out two. The first is the obvious interest of a certain class of men in every State to resist any change that might risk a reduction of the power, pay, and standing of the offices they hold under the State establishments. The second is the corrupted ambition of another class of men, who will either hope to raise themselves through the confusions of their country, or will flatter themselves with better prospects of advancement from the division of the empire into several separate confederacies than from its union under one government.

It is not my design, however, to dwell on observations of this kind. I am well aware that it would be dishonest to write off the opposition of any set of men as selfish or ambitious merely because their situations might expose them to suspicion. Fairness obliges us to admit that even such men may act from upright intentions. And there can be no doubt that much of the opposition that has appeared, or may yet appear, will come from sources that are at least blameless, if not respectable: the honest errors of minds led astray by preconceived jealousies and fears. The causes that give a false bias to the judgment are so numerous and so powerful that on many occasions we see wise and good men on the wrong side, as well as the right side, of questions of the first importance to society. This fact, if properly attended to, should teach moderation to those who are most firmly persuaded that they are right in any controversy. There is a further reason for caution. We cannot always be sure that those who advocate the truth are moved by purer principles than their opponents. Ambition, greed, personal animosity, party opposition, and many other motives no more praiseworthy than these are apt to work on those who support the right side of a question as well as on those who oppose it. Even without such reasons for moderation, nothing could be more ill-judged than the intolerant spirit that has at all times marked political parties. For in politics, as in religion, it is equally absurd to try to make converts by fire and sword. Heresies in either can rarely be cured by persecution.

And yet, however just these views will be admitted to be, we already have enough signs that this great national debate will go as all earlier ones have gone. A torrent of angry and malicious passions will be let loose. Judging from the conduct of the opposing parties, we must conclude that each hopes to prove its opinions right, and to win more converts, by the loudness of its declamations and the bitterness of its invective. An enlightened zeal for the energy and effectiveness of government will be branded as the offspring of a temperament that loves despotic power and is hostile to the principles of liberty. An over-scrupulous jealousy of danger to the rights of the people, which is more often a fault of the head than of the heart, will be painted as mere pretense and artifice, the stale bait of popularity-seeking at the expense of the public good. On the one side, it will be forgotten that jealousy usually goes with love, and that the noble enthusiasm of liberty is apt to be infected with a spirit of narrow and illiberal distrust. On the other side, it will be just as readily forgotten that the vigor of government is essential to the security of liberty. It will be forgotten that, to a sound and well-informed judgment, their interests can never be separated. And it will be forgotten that a dangerous ambition more often lurks behind the specious mask of zeal for the rights of the people than behind the forbidding appearance of zeal for the firmness and effectiveness of government. History will teach us that the former has proved a much more certain road to despotism than the latter. Of those men who have overturned the liberties of republics, the greatest number began their careers by paying servile court to the people: they began as demagogues and ended as tyrants.

In these observations, my fellow-citizens, I have meant to put you on your guard against every attempt, from whatever quarter, to sway your decision on a matter of the utmost importance to your welfare by any impressions other than those that come from the evidence of truth. You will no doubt also have gathered, from the general drift of what I have said, that it comes from a source not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I own to you that, having given it careful consideration, I am clearly of the opinion that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not claim a reserve that I do not feel. I will not entertain you with a show of deliberation when I have already decided. I frankly tell you my convictions, and I will freely lay before you the reasons on which they rest. A consciousness of good intentions disdains ambiguity. I shall not, however, multiply professions on this point. My motives must stay in the keeping of my own breast. My arguments will be open to all, and may be judged by all. They shall at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth.
I propose, in a series of papers, to discuss the following interesting subjects:

THE USEFULNESS OF THE UNION TO YOUR POLITICAL PROSPERITY. THE INSUFFICIENCY OF THE PRESENT CONFEDERATION TO PRESERVE THAT UNION. THE NECESSITY OF A GOVERNMENT AT LEAST EQUALLY ENERGETIC WITH THE ONE PROPOSED, TO ATTAIN THIS OBJECT. THE CONFORMITY OF THE PROPOSED CONSTITUTION TO THE TRUE PRINCIPLES OF REPUBLICAN GOVERNMENT. ITS RESEMBLANCE TO YOUR OWN STATE CONSTITUTION. And lastly, THE ADDITIONAL SECURITY WHICH ITS ADOPTION WILL GIVE TO THE PRESERVATION OF THAT KIND OF GOVERNMENT, TO LIBERTY, AND TO PROPERTY.
As this discussion proceeds, I shall endeavor to give a satisfactory answer to every objection that has appeared and that may seem to have any claim to your attention.

It may perhaps be thought needless to offer arguments to prove the usefulness of the UNION. It is a point, no doubt, deeply engraved on the hearts of the great body of the people in every State, and one that, it might be imagined, has no opponents. But the fact is that we already hear it whispered in the private circles of those who oppose the new Constitution that the thirteen States are too large for any general system, and that we must of necessity resort to separate confederacies of distinct portions of the whole.(1) This doctrine will in all probability be gradually spread until it has enough followers to support an open avowal of it. For nothing can be more evident, to those who are able to take a broad view of the subject, than that the alternative is between adopting the new Constitution and breaking up the Union. It will therefore be useful to begin by examining the advantages of that Union, and the certain evils and probable dangers to which every State would be exposed by its dissolution. This shall accordingly be the subject of my next address.
1. The same idea, following the arguments out to their consequences, is put forward in several of the recent publications against the new Constitution.

chapters.title: No. 2 — Concerning Dangers from Foreign Force and Influence (Jay)
paragraphs: The people of America are now called on to decide a question whose consequences must prove among the most important that ever engaged their attention. When they reflect on this, it will be evident that they ought to take a view of it that is both very comprehensive and very serious.

Nothing is more certain than that government is indispensably necessary. It is equally undeniable that, whenever and however government is set up, the people must give up some of their natural rights to give it the powers it needs. It is therefore well worth considering which would serve the interest of the people of America better. They could be, for all general purposes, one nation under one federal government. Or they could divide themselves into separate confederacies and give the head of each the same kind of powers that they are now advised to place in one national government.

Until lately it was a received and uncontradicted opinion that the prosperity of the people of America depended on their staying firmly united, and the wishes, prayers, and efforts of our best and wisest citizens have always been directed to that goal. But politicians have now appeared who insist that this opinion is mistaken. They say that instead of looking for safety and happiness in union, we ought to seek them in dividing the States into distinct confederacies or sovereignties. However extraordinary this new doctrine may seem, it has its advocates, and some who formerly opposed it strongly are now among them. Whatever arguments or inducements have brought about this change in the views and declarations of these gentlemen, it would certainly be unwise for the people at large to adopt these new political tenets without being fully convinced that they rest on truth and sound policy.

It has often given me pleasure to observe that independent America was not made up of detached and distant territories. One connected, fertile, wide-spreading country was the portion of our western sons of liberty. Providence has blessed it in a special way with a variety of soils and products, and has watered it with countless streams for the delight and convenience of its inhabitants. A succession of navigable waters forms a kind of chain around its borders, as if to bind it together. The noblest rivers in the world, running at convenient distances, give the people highways for easily sending friendly aid to one another and for carrying and exchanging their various goods.

With equal pleasure I have as often noticed that Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people. They descend from the same ancestors, speak the same language, profess the same religion, and are attached to the same principles of government. Their manners and customs are very similar. By their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side through a long and bloody war, they have nobly won general liberty and independence.

This country and this people seem to have been made for each other. It appears to have been the design of Providence that an inheritance so suitable and convenient for a band of brothers, joined together by the strongest ties, should never be split into a number of unsociable, jealous, and alien sovereignties.

Similar views have until now prevailed among all ranks and denominations of men among us. For all general purposes we have always been one people, with every citizen everywhere enjoying the same national rights, privileges, and protection. As a nation we have made peace and war. As a nation we have defeated our common enemies. As a nation we have formed alliances, made treaties, and entered into various compacts and conventions with foreign states.

A strong sense of the value and blessings of union led the people, very early, to set up a federal government to preserve and perpetuate it. They formed it almost as soon as they had a political existence. They formed it even while their homes were in flames, while many of their citizens were bleeding, and while the progress of hostility and devastation left little room for the calm and mature inquiry and reflection that must always come before the formation of a wise and well-balanced government for a free people. It is no wonder that a government set up in times so unfavorable should be found, when tried, to be greatly deficient and inadequate to its purpose.

This intelligent people saw these defects and regretted them. They remained as attached to union as they were devoted to liberty. They saw that the first was in immediate danger and the second in more distant danger. They were persuaded that ample security for both could be found only in a more wisely framed national government. So, as with one voice, they convened the recent convention at Philadelphia to take that important subject under consideration.

This convention was made up of men who had the confidence of the people. Many of them had become highly distinguished for patriotism, virtue and wisdom in times that tried the minds and hearts of men. They undertook the difficult task. In the gentle season of peace, with minds free of other subjects, they spent many months in calm, uninterrupted, daily consultation. In the end, without having been overawed by power or swayed by any passion except love of country, they presented and recommended to the people the plan produced by their joint and very unanimous counsels.

Grant that this plan is only RECOMMENDED, not imposed, which is the fact. Yet remember that it is recommended neither to BLIND approval nor to BLIND rejection. It is recommended to that calm and fair consideration which the size and importance of the subject demand, and which it certainly ought to receive. But (as the preceding number remarked) it is more to be wished than expected that it will be so considered and examined. Experience on a former occasion teaches us not to be too hopeful about this. It is not yet forgotten that well-founded fears of imminent danger led the people of America to form the memorable Congress of 1774. That body recommended certain measures to its constituents, and events proved its wisdom. Yet we remember how soon the press began to swarm with pamphlets and weekly papers against those very measures. Many officers of government who obeyed the dictates of personal interest worked tirelessly to persuade the people to reject the advice of that patriotic Congress. So did others, whether from a mistaken estimate of consequences, or the undue influence of former attachments, or an ambition that aimed at objects that did not match the public good. Many were indeed deceived and misled, but the great majority of the people reasoned and decided wisely, and they are glad to reflect that they did.

They considered that the Congress was made up of many wise and experienced men. They considered that, having come together from different parts of the country, those men brought with them a variety of useful information and shared it with one another. They considered that, in the time they spent together inquiring into and discussing the true interests of their country, they must have gained very accurate knowledge of them. And they considered that those men each had a personal stake in the public liberty and prosperity, so that it was no less their inclination than their duty to recommend only such measures as, after the most mature deliberation, they really thought prudent and advisable.

These and similar considerations led the people to rely greatly on the judgment and integrity of the Congress, and they took its advice despite the various arts and efforts used to deter them. The people at large had reason to trust the men of that Congress, though few of them had been fully tested or generally known. They now have still greater reason to respect the judgment and advice of the convention. For it is well known that some of the most distinguished members of that Congress were also members of this convention. They have since been tested and rightly approved for patriotism and ability, and they have grown old in acquiring political knowledge. They carried their accumulated knowledge and experience into the convention.

It is worth remarking that not only the first Congress but every Congress since, and the recent convention as well, have always agreed with the people in thinking that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan the convention has advised them to adopt. With what propriety, then, or for what good purposes, do some men at this particular time try to belittle the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought rightly on this subject. I am persuaded that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I shall endeavor to develop and explain in some of the following papers. Those who promote the idea of putting a number of distinct confederacies in the place of the convention's plan seem clearly to foresee that rejecting the plan would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That certainly would be the case. I sincerely wish that every good citizen may foresee as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."

chapters.title: No. 3 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence) (Jay)
paragraphs: It is not a new observation that a people who are intelligent and well-informed, as the Americans are, seldom adopt a mistaken opinion about their interests and hold to it steadily for many years. That consideration naturally creates great respect for the view that the people of America have long and uniformly held: that it matters greatly for them to stay firmly united under one federal government, given enough power for all general and national purposes.
The more closely I examine the reasons that seem to have given rise to this opinion, the more convinced I am that they are compelling and conclusive.

A wise and free people must give their attention to many things, and providing for their SAFETY seems to come first. The SAFETY of the people doubtless depends on a great variety of circumstances and considerations, and so leaves wide room for anyone who wishes to define it precisely and comprehensively.

For now I mean to consider it only as it concerns the preservation of peace and tranquillity. This includes security against dangers from FOREIGN ARMS AND INFLUENCE and against dangers of the LIKE KIND that arise from domestic causes. The former comes first in order, so it is proper to discuss it first. Let us therefore examine whether the people are right in thinking that a cordial Union, under an effective national government, gives them the best security that can be devised against HOSTILITIES from abroad.

The number of wars that have happened, or will happen, in the world will always be found proportionate to the number and weight of the causes, whether REAL or PRETENDED, that PROVOKE or INVITE them. If this remark is just, it is useful to ask whether UNITED AMERICA is likely to give as many JUST causes of war as DISUNITED America would. If it turns out that United America will probably give the fewest, it follows that in this respect the Union does the most to keep the people at peace with other nations.

The JUST causes of war come, for the most part, from one of two sources: violation of treaties or direct violence. America has already made treaties with no fewer than six foreign nations, and all of them except Prussia are maritime powers, and so able to annoy and injure us. She also carries on extensive commerce with Portugal, Spain, and Britain, and with the last two she must also reckon with the fact that they are her neighbors.

It is of high importance to the peace of America that she observe the laws of nations toward all these powers. To me it is evident that one national government would do this more perfectly and punctually than thirteen separate States, or three or four distinct confederacies, could.

First, once an effective national government is established, the best men in the country will not only be willing to serve but will generally be the ones chosen to run it. Town or country influence, or some other narrow influence, may put men into State assemblies, senates, courts of justice, or executive departments. But offices under the national government will require a wider and more extensive reputation for talents and other qualifications. This is especially so because the national government will have the widest field to choose from and will never suffer the shortage of suitable persons that is not uncommon in some of the States. It will follow that the administration, the political counsels, and the judicial decisions of the national government will be wiser, more systematic, and more judicious than those of the individual States. They will therefore be more satisfactory to other nations, and more SAFE for us.

Second, under the national government, treaties and parts of treaties, like the laws of nations, will always be interpreted in one sense and carried out in the same way. But rulings on the same points and questions will not always agree or be consistent across thirteen States, or three or four confederacies. This will be so because of the variety of independent courts and judges appointed by different and independent governments, and also because of the differing local laws and interests that may affect and influence them. The wisdom of the convention in placing such questions under the jurisdiction and judgment of courts appointed by, and answerable only to, one national government cannot be praised too highly.

Third, the prospect of present loss or gain may often tempt the governing party in one or two States to depart from good faith and justice. But those temptations do not reach the other States and so have little or no influence on the national government. The temptation will therefore be fruitless, and good faith and justice will be preserved. The case of the treaty of peace with Britain adds great weight to this reasoning.

Fourth, even if the governing party in a State were disposed to resist such temptations, they may, and commonly do, result from circumstances peculiar to the State, and may affect a great number of its inhabitants. The governing party may then be unable, even if willing, to prevent the injustice that is planned or to punish those who commit it. But the national government is not affected by those local circumstances. It will not be led to commit the wrong itself, and it will not lack the power or the will to prevent or punish the wrong when others commit it.

So far, therefore, as violations of treaties and of the laws of nations, whether intended or accidental, give JUST causes of war, they are less to be feared under one general government than under several lesser ones. In that respect the former does the most to favor the SAFETY of the people.

Now consider those just causes of war that come from direct and unlawful violence. It seems to me equally clear that one good national government gives far more security against dangers of that sort than can be had from any other source.

The reason is that such violence is more often caused by the passions and interests of a part than of the whole: of one or two States rather than of the Union. Not one Indian war has yet been caused by aggressions of the present federal government, feeble as it is. But there are several instances of Indian hostilities provoked by the improper conduct of individual States, which were unable or unwilling to restrain or punish offenses and so gave occasion for the slaughter of many innocent inhabitants.

Spanish and British territories border on some States and not on others, and this naturally confines the causes of quarrel mainly to the States along the border. If any States are to provoke war with these nations by direct violence, they will be the bordering ones, acting on sudden irritation and a quick sense of apparent interest or injury. Nothing can prevent that danger so effectively as a national government, whose wisdom and prudence will not be clouded by the passions of the parties directly concerned.

But the national government will not only give fewer just causes of war. It will also be better placed to settle them peacefully. It will be more temperate and cool, and in that respect, as in others, better able to act with deliberation than the offending State. The pride of states, like the pride of men, naturally leads them to justify everything they do, and it stands in the way of their admitting, correcting, or repairing their errors and offenses. The national government will not be affected by this pride in such cases. It will proceed with moderation and fairness to consider and decide on the best means of freeing them from the difficulties that threaten them.

Besides, it is well known that a strong united nation can often offer acknowledgments, explanations, and compensation that are accepted as satisfactory, when the very same offers would be rejected as unsatisfactory coming from a State or confederacy of little consideration or power.

In 1685 the state of Genoa, having offended Louis XIV, tried to appease him. He demanded that they send their Doge, or chief executive, accompanied by four of their senators, to FRANCE, to ask his pardon and receive his terms. For the sake of peace they had to submit. Would he ever have demanded or accepted the same humiliation from Spain, or Britain, or any other POWERFUL nation?

chapters.title: No. 4 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence) (Jay)
paragraphs: My last paper gave several reasons why union would best protect the safety of the people against the danger of JUST causes of war given to other nations. Those reasons show that a national government would give such causes more rarely, and would also settle them more easily, than either the State governments or the proposed little confederacies could.

But the safety of the people of America against dangers from FOREIGN force depends on more than their avoiding JUST causes of war. It also depends on their placing and keeping themselves in a position that does not INVITE hostility or insult. I hardly need point out that there are PRETENDED causes of war as well as just ones.

It is only too true, however shameful to human nature, that nations in general will make war whenever they see something to gain by it. Absolute monarchs will often make war when their nations stand to gain nothing, for purely personal ends: a thirst for military glory, revenge for a personal insult, ambition, or private agreements to advance or support their own families or partisans. These motives and many others touch only the mind of the sovereign, and they often lead him into wars that justice does not sanction and his people neither want nor benefit from. These inducements are more common in absolute monarchies, but they deserve our attention. Apart from them, however, there are others that move nations as often as kings, and some of them, as we shall see, grow out of our own situation and circumstances.

We are rivals of France and Britain in the fisheries. We can supply their markets more cheaply than they can supply themselves, whatever they do to prevent it with bounties on their own fish or duties on foreign fish.

We are rivals of those two and of most other European nations in navigation and the carrying trade. We deceive ourselves if we suppose that any of them will be glad to see that trade flourish. Our carrying trade cannot grow without taking something from theirs, so it is in their interest, and will be their policy, to hold it back rather than help it.

In the trade to China and India we compete with more than one nation. That trade lets us share advantages they had almost monopolized, and it lets us supply ourselves with goods we used to buy from them.

Any nation that holds territory on or near this continent will be displeased to see our commerce expand in our own ships. The cheapness and excellence of our products, our closeness, and the enterprise and skill of our merchants and sailors will give us a larger share of what those territories offer than their sovereigns wish or find consistent with their policy.

Spain finds it convenient to shut the Mississippi to us on one side, and Britain shuts us out of the Saint Lawrence on the other. Neither will allow the other waters that lie between them and us to become channels of mutual contact and trade.

The people of America know that inducements to war may arise from these circumstances, as well as from others not so obvious at present. They know too that, whenever those inducements find a fit time and opportunity to act, pretenses to color and justify them will not be lacking. They are therefore wise to regard union and a good national government as necessary to put and keep them in SUCH A SITUATION that war is discouraged and held down instead of being INVITED. That situation consists in the best possible state of defense, and it depends necessarily on the government, the arms, and the resources of the country.

The safety of the whole is the interest of the whole, and it cannot be provided for without government, whether one government, a few, or many. Let us ask, then, whether one good government is not better equipped for this purpose than any other number.

One government can gather and use the talents and experience of the ablest men, wherever in the Union they may be found. It can act on uniform principles of policy. It can bring the several parts and members into harmony, make them alike, and protect them, and it can extend the benefit of its foresight and precautions to each. In making treaties, it will look to the interest of the whole, and to the particular interests of the parts as bound up with that of the whole. It can bring the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any one part, and it can do so more easily and quickly than State governments or separate confederacies, which lack concert and unity of system. It can put the militia under one plan of discipline and place their officers in a proper line of subordination to the chief executive. In effect it will thus join them into one corps, and make them more effective than if they were split into thirteen, or three or four, distinct and independent companies.

What would the militia of Britain amount to if the English militia took orders from the government of England, the Scottish militia from the government of Scotland, and the Welsh militia from the government of Wales? Suppose an invasion. Would those three governments, if they agreed at all, be able to act against the enemy with all their forces as effectively as the single government of Great Britain?

We have heard much about the fleets of Britain, and the time may come, if we are wise, when the fleets of America may draw attention. But suppose one national government had not regulated British navigation so as to make it a nursery for seamen. Suppose one national government had not called forth all the national means and materials for building fleets. Then British prowess and British thunder would never have been celebrated. Let England have its navigation and fleet, and Scotland its own, and Wales its own, and Ireland its own. Let those four constituent parts of the British empire live under four independent governments, and it is easy to see how soon each would shrink into comparative insignificance.

Apply these facts to our own case. Suppose America left divided into thirteen independent governments, or, if you like, three or four. What armies could they raise and pay? What fleets could they ever hope to have? If one were attacked, would the others rush to its aid and spend their blood and money in its defense? Would there be no danger that they would be flattered into neutrality by its deceptively attractive promises? Or that they would be seduced by too great a love of peace into refusing to risk their tranquillity and present safety for the sake of neighbors whom they have perhaps been jealous of, and whose importance they are content to see reduced? Such conduct would not be wise, but it would be natural. The history of the states of Greece, and of other countries, is full of such instances, and it is not unlikely that what has so often happened would happen again in similar circumstances.

But suppose they were willing to help the invaded State or confederacy. How, when, and in what proportion should they send men and money? Who would command the allied armies, and from which of the allies would he take his orders? Who would settle the terms of peace, and, if disputes arose, what umpire would decide between them and force them to comply? Such a situation would bring endless difficulties and problems. One government, in contrast, would watch over the general and common interests and would combine and direct the powers and resources of the whole. It would be free of all these embarrassments, and it would do far more for the safety of the people.

But whatever our situation may be, whether firmly united under one national government or split into a number of confederacies, foreign nations will certainly see it exactly as it is and will treat us accordingly. Suppose they see an effective and well-administered national government, a prudently regulated trade, a properly organized and disciplined militia, carefully managed resources and finances, restored credit, and a people free, contented, and united. They will then be much more inclined to seek our friendship than to provoke our resentment. Suppose, on the other hand, they find us without an effective government, with each State doing right or wrong as its rulers find convenient. Or suppose they find us split into three or four independent and probably quarreling republics or confederacies, one leaning to Britain, another to France, and a third to Spain, and perhaps played against one another by the three. What a poor, pitiful figure America will make in their eyes! How exposed she would be, not only to their contempt but to their outrage! And how soon dearly bought experience would proclaim that when a people or a family divides in this way, it never fails to divide against itself.

chapters.title: No. 5 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence) (Jay)
paragraphs: Queen Anne, in her letter of the 1st of July, 1706, to the Scottish Parliament, makes some observations on the importance of the UNION then being formed between England and Scotland, and they deserve our attention. I shall give the public one or two extracts from it: "An entire and perfect union will be the solid foundation of lasting peace: It will secure your religion, liberty, and property; remove the animosities amongst yourselves, and the jealousies and differences betwixt our two kingdoms. It must increase your strength, riches, and trade; and by this union the whole island, being joined in affection and free from all apprehensions of different interest, will be ENABLED TO RESIST ALL ITS ENEMIES." "We most earnestly recommend to you calmness and unanimity in this great and weighty affair, that the union may be brought to a happy conclusion, being the only EFFECTUAL way to secure our present and future happiness, and disappoint the designs of our and your enemies, who will doubtless, on this occasion, USE THEIR UTMOST ENDEAVORS TO PREVENT OR DELAY THIS UNION."

The preceding paper observed that weakness and divisions at home would invite dangers from abroad, and that nothing would protect us from those dangers better than union, strength, and good government among ourselves. There is much to say on this subject, and it cannot easily be exhausted.

In general we know the history of Great Britain better than that of any other country, and it teaches many useful lessons. We can profit from their experience without paying what it cost them. Common sense says that the people of such an island should be one nation. Yet for ages they were divided into three, and those three were almost constantly caught up in quarrels and wars with one another. Their true interest with respect to the nations of the Continent was in fact the same. Even so, the arts, policy and practices of those nations kept their mutual jealousies burning without pause. For a long series of years they were far more of a nuisance and a trouble to each other than a help and support.

Suppose the people of America divided themselves into three or four nations. Would not the same thing happen? Would not similar jealousies arise and be nursed in the same way? They would not be "joined in affection" and free from all apprehension of different "interests." Envy and jealousy would soon destroy confidence and affection. The separate interests of each confederacy, rather than the general interests of all America, would be the only objects of their policy and pursuits. Like most other BORDERING nations, they would therefore always be either caught up in disputes and war or living in constant fear of them.

Even the most sanguine advocates of three or four confederacies cannot reasonably suppose that those confederacies would stay equal in strength for long, even if they could be made equal at the start. But grant that this is possible. What human contrivance can keep the equality in place? There are local circumstances that tend to produce and increase power in one part and to hinder its growth in another. And we must also consider the effects of the superior policy and good management that would probably distinguish the government of one above the rest, and that would destroy their relative equality in strength and consideration. For we cannot presume that each of these confederacies would show the same degree of sound policy, prudence, and foresight, year after year, over a long period.

Suppose that any one of these nations or confederacies rose on the scale of political importance far above her neighbors. This might happen from various causes, and happen it would. From that moment her neighbors would look on her with envy and with fear. Both passions would lead them to approve, if not to promote, whatever promised to reduce her importance, and would keep them from measures that might advance, or even secure, her prosperity. It would not take long for her to notice these unfriendly dispositions. She would soon begin to lose confidence in her neighbors, and to feel a disposition just as unfavorable toward them. Distrust naturally creates distrust, and nothing changes good will and kind conduct faster than envious jealousies and unfair accusations, whether spoken or merely implied.

The North is generally the region of strength, and many local circumstances make it likely that the most northern of the proposed confederacies would, before very long, be clearly more formidable than any of the others. As soon as that became evident, the NORTHERN HIVE would stir in the more southern parts of America the same ideas and feelings that it once stirred in the southern parts of Europe. It does not seem a rash guess, either, that its young swarms might often be tempted to gather honey in the more blooming fields and milder air of their luxurious and softer neighbors.

Anyone who studies the history of similar divisions and confederacies will find ample reason to fear that those now in view would be neighbors only in the sense of being borderers. They would neither love nor trust one another. They would instead fall prey to discord, jealousy, and mutual injuries. In short, they would put us exactly where some nations doubtless wish to see us, namely, FORMIDABLE ONLY TO EACH OTHER.

When did the independent states into which Britain and Spain were once divided join in such an alliance, or combine their forces against a foreign enemy? The proposed confederacies will be DISTINCT NATIONS. Each would have its own commerce with foreigners to regulate by its own treaties. Their products and commodities differ and suit different markets, so those treaties would be essentially different. Different commercial concerns must create different interests and, naturally, different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations. It might therefore happen, and probably would, that the foreign nation the SOUTHERN confederacy was at war with would be the very one with which the NORTHERN confederacy was most anxious to keep peace and friendship. An alliance so contrary to their immediate interest would not be easy to form. If it were formed, it would not be kept and fulfilled in perfect good faith.

It is far more probable, in fact, that in America as in Europe, neighboring nations would be driven by opposite interests and unfriendly passions and would often be found on different sides. Given our distance from Europe, it would be more natural for these confederacies to fear danger from one another than from distant nations. Each would therefore be more eager to guard against the others with the help of foreign alliances than to guard against foreign dangers with alliances among themselves. And here let us remember how much easier it is to let foreign fleets into our ports and foreign armies into our country than to persuade or force them to leave. How many conquests did the Romans and others make while posing as allies, and what changes did they introduce, in the same character, into the governments of those they pretended to protect?
Let fair-minded people decide, then, whether splitting America into any number of independent sovereignties would protect us from the hostilities and the improper meddling of foreign nations.

chapters.title: No. 6 — Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The last three numbers of this series were given to listing the dangers we should face, in a state of disunion, from the arms and arts of foreign nations. I shall now go on to describe dangers of a different and perhaps still more alarming kind. These are the dangers that will in all probability flow from dissensions between the States themselves, and from domestic factions and convulsions. They have already been touched on lightly in some places, but they deserve a fuller and more particular investigation.

Only a man far gone in Utopian speculation could seriously doubt that, if these States were wholly disunited, or united only in partial confederacies, the subdivisions into which they might fall would often be at violent odds with one another. To argue that there would be no motives for such contests, and so no contests, would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious. To expect harmony to continue among a number of independent, unconnected sovereignties in the same neighborhood would be to ignore the uniform course of human events and to defy the accumulated experience of ages.

The causes of hostility among nations are innumerable. Some operate generally, and almost constantly, on whole societies. These are the love of power, or the desire for pre-eminence and dominion, and the jealousy of power, or the desire for equality and safety. Others have a narrower but equally active influence within their own spheres. Such are the rivalries and competitions of commerce between commercial nations. And there are others, no less numerous than the first two kinds, that arise entirely from private passions: the attachments, enmities, interests, hopes, and fears of leading individuals in the communities to which they belong. Men of this class, whether favorites of a king or of a people, have in too many instances abused the confidence placed in them. Under the pretext of some public motive, they have not hesitated to sacrifice the national tranquillity to personal advantage or personal gratification.

The celebrated Pericles, to satisfy the resentment of a prostitute,(1) attacked, defeated, and destroyed the city of the SAMMIANS, at the cost of much of the blood and treasure of his countrymen. The same man was the original author of that famous and fatal war that the Grecian annals call the PELOPONNESIAN war. Perhaps he was driven by private spite against the MEGARENSIANS,(2) another nation of Greece. Perhaps he wanted to avoid a prosecution that threatened him as an accomplice in the supposed theft of the sculptor Phidias.(3) Perhaps he wanted to be rid of the accusations being prepared against him for squandering the funds of the state to buy popularity.(4) Or perhaps it was a combination of all these causes. After various turns of fortune, interruptions, and renewals, that war ended in the ruin of the Athenian commonwealth.

The ambitious cardinal who was prime minister to Henry VIII let his vanity aspire to the triple crown.(5) He hoped to win that splendid prize through the influence of the Emperor Charles V. To secure the favor and support of this enterprising and powerful monarch, he pushed England into a war with France. This went against the plainest dictates of policy and risked the safety and independence of the kingdom he guided by his counsels, and of Europe in general. For if there ever was a sovereign who seemed likely to realize the project of universal monarchy, it was the Emperor Charles V, and Wolsey was both the instrument and the dupe of his intrigues.

The influence that the bigotry of one woman,(6) the petulance of another,(7) and the cabals of a third(8) had on the policy, the ferments, and the pacifications of a considerable part of Europe in their time has been discussed too often not to be generally known.

It would be an unnecessary waste of time to multiply examples of the part that personal considerations play in producing great national events, foreign or domestic, according to the direction they take. Those with only a superficial acquaintance with the sources of such examples will recall a variety of them for themselves. Those with a tolerable knowledge of human nature do not need such lights to form their own opinion of how real and how far-reaching that influence is. Perhaps, however, a reference to a case that has recently happened among ourselves may properly be made to illustrate the general principle. If Shays had not been a DESPERATE DEBTOR, it is much to be doubted whether Massachusetts would have been plunged into a civil war.

But despite the agreeing testimony of experience on this point, there are still visionary or designing men who stand ready to defend the paradox of perpetual peace between the States, though they be broken apart and estranged from one another. The character of republics, they say, is peaceful. The spirit of commerce, they say, tends to soften the manners of men and to extinguish those inflammable humors that have so often burst into war. Commercial republics like ours, they say, will never be inclined to exhaust themselves in ruinous contests with each other. They will be governed by mutual interest and will cultivate a spirit of mutual friendship and harmony.

We may ask these projectors in politics: is it not the true interest of all nations to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit? If it is, have they in fact pursued it? Has it not, on the contrary, always been found that momentary passions and immediate interest control human conduct more actively and more imperiously than general or remote considerations of policy, utility, or justice? Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies? Are not the former run by MEN as well as the latter? Do not aversions, preferences, rivalries, and desires for unjust gains affect nations as well as kings? Are not popular assemblies often subject to impulses of rage, resentment, jealousy, greed, and other irregular and violent tendencies? Is it not well known that their decisions are often governed by a few individuals in whom they place confidence, and so are likely to be colored by the passions and views of those individuals? Has commerce so far done anything more than change the objects of war? Is the love of wealth any less domineering and enterprising a passion than the love of power or glory? Since commerce became the prevailing system of nations, have there not been as many wars founded on commercial motives as were once caused by greed for territory or dominion? Has not the spirit of commerce, in many instances, supplied new incentives to the appetite for both? Let experience, the least fallible guide of human opinions, be appealed to for the answer.

Sparta, Athens, Rome, and Carthage were all republics, and two of them, Athens and Carthage, were of the commercial kind. Yet they fought wars, offensive and defensive, as often as the neighboring monarchies of their times. Sparta was little better than a well-regulated camp, and Rome never had enough of carnage and conquest.

Carthage was a commercial republic, yet she was the aggressor in the very war that ended in her destruction. Hannibal had carried her arms into the heart of Italy and to the gates of Rome. Only then did Scipio defeat him in the territories of Carthage, and in turn conquer the commonwealth.

Venice, in later times, took part more than once in wars of ambition. Finally she became an object of concern to the other Italian states, and Pope Julius II managed to form against her that formidable league,(9) which dealt a deadly blow to the power and pride of this haughty republic.

The provinces of Holland took a leading and conspicuous part in the wars of Europe until they were overwhelmed by debts and taxes. They fought furious contests with England for dominion of the sea, and they were among the most persevering and implacable opponents of Louis XIV.

In the government of Britain, the representatives of the people make up one branch of the national legislature. Commerce has been the predominant pursuit of that country for ages. Few nations, nevertheless, have gone to war more often, and in numerous instances the wars of that kingdom have come from the people.

There have been, if I may put it so, almost as many popular wars as royal wars. On various occasions the cries of the nation and the importunities of their representatives have dragged their monarchs into war, or kept them in it, against their inclinations and sometimes against the real interests of the State. Consider the memorable struggle for superiority between the rival houses of AUSTRIA and BOURBON, which kept Europe in a flame for so long. It is well known that the English antipathy against the French, backing the ambition, or rather the greed, of a favorite leader,(10) prolonged that war beyond the limits set by sound policy and, for a considerable time, against the views of the court.

The wars of these last two nations have in great measure grown out of commercial considerations: the desire to supplant, and the fear of being supplanted, whether in particular branches of trade or in the general advantages of trade and navigation. Sometimes there was also the more blameworthy desire to share in the commerce of other nations without their consent.

The last war but one between Britain and Spain sprang from the attempts of British merchants to carry on an illicit trade with the Spanish Main. These unjustifiable practices on their side produced severity on the Spanish side toward British subjects, and that severity was no more justifiable, because it went beyond the bounds of just retaliation and could be charged with inhumanity and cruelty. Many of the English taken on the Spanish coast were sent to dig in the mines of Potosi. By the usual progress of a spirit of resentment, the innocent were soon confounded with the guilty in indiscriminate punishment. The complaints of the merchants kindled a violent flame throughout the nation. It soon broke out in the House of Commons and was passed from that body to the ministry. Letters of reprisal were granted, and war followed. Its consequences overthrew all the alliances that had been formed only twenty years before, with sanguine expectations of the most beneficial fruits.

This summary shows what has happened in other countries whose situations most resembled our own. What reason can we have, after it, to trust those reveries that would lead us to expect peace and cordiality among the members of the present confederacy once they are separated? Have we not already seen enough of the fallacy and extravagance of those idle theories that have amused us with promises of an exemption from the imperfections, weaknesses, and evils that attend society in every form? Is it not time to wake from the deceitful dream of a golden age, and to adopt as a practical maxim for guiding our political conduct that we, like the other inhabitants of the globe, are still far from the happy empire of perfect wisdom and perfect virtue?

Let the extreme depression to which our national dignity and credit have sunk speak. Let the problems felt everywhere from a lax and ill-managed administration of government speak. Let the revolt of a part of the State of North Carolina, the recent menacing disturbances in Pennsylvania, and the actual insurrections and rebellions in Massachusetts speak—!

The general sense of mankind is so far from agreeing with the tenets of those who try to lull our apprehensions of discord and hostility between the States, in the event of disunion, that long observation of the progress of society has made it a sort of axiom in politics that nearness of situation makes nations natural enemies. An intelligent writer says on this subject, to this effect: "NEIGHBORING NATIONS (says he) are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC, and their constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions, extinguishing that secret jealousy which disposes all states to aggrandize themselves at the expense of their neighbors."(11) This passage points out the EVIL and at the same time suggests the REMEDY.
1. Aspasia, vide "Plutarch's Life of Pericles."
4. Ibid. Phidias was supposed to have stolen some public gold, with the connivance of Pericles, for the embellishment of the statue of Minerva.
5. Worn by the popes.
6. Madame de Maintenon.
7. Duchess of Marlborough.
8. Madame de Pompadour.
9. The League of Cambray, comprehending the Emperor, the King of France, the King of Aragon, and most of the Italian princes and states.
10. The Duke of Marlborough.

chapters.title: No. 7 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: People sometimes ask, with an air of seeming triumph, what inducements the States could have to make war on each other if they were disunited. A full answer would be: precisely the same inducements that have at different times drenched all the nations of the world in blood. But, unfortunately for us, the question has a more specific answer. Some causes of difference are right before our eyes. Even under the restraints of a federal constitution, we have had enough experience of how they tend to work to judge what might be expected if those restraints were removed.

Territorial disputes have always been among the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. Perhaps the greatest share of the wars that have desolated the earth sprang from this origin. This cause would exist among us in full force. We have a vast tract of unsettled territory within the boundaries of the United States. Several of the States still have discordant and undecided claims against each other, and the dissolution of the Union would lay a foundation for similar claims among them all. It is well known that they have already had serious and heated discussion over the rights to the lands that were ungranted at the time of the Revolution, and that usually went by the name of crown lands. The States within whose colonial boundaries those lands lay have claimed them as their property. The other States have argued that the rights of the crown in this matter passed to the Union. They argue this especially for all that part of the Western territory which, by actual possession or through the submission of the Indian proprietors, was under the jurisdiction of the king of Great Britain until it was given up in the treaty of peace. This, it has been said, was in any event an acquisition to the Confederacy by compact with a foreign power. Congress has prudently tried to calm this controversy by persuading the States to make cessions to the United States for the benefit of the whole. This has been accomplished far enough to give a decided prospect, if the Union continues, of a friendly end to the dispute. A breakup of the Confederacy, however, would revive the dispute and would create others on the same subject. At present a large part of the vacant Western territory is the common property of the Union, by cession at least, if not by any earlier right. If the Union were ended, the States that made the cession on a principle of federal compromise would be apt to claim the lands back as a reversion once the motive for the grant had ceased. The other States would no doubt insist on a proportion, by right of representation. Their argument would be that a grant, once made, could not be revoked, and that the justice of sharing in territory won or secured by the joint efforts of the Confederacy remained as strong as ever. Suppose, against probability, that all the States admitted that each had a right to a share of this common stock. There would still be a difficulty to overcome in finding a proper rule of apportionment. Different States would put forward different principles for the purpose, and since these would touch the opposing interests of the parties, they might not easily be settled peacefully.

In the wide field of Western territory, then, we see an ample theater for hostile claims, with no umpire or common judge to step between the contending parties. If we reason from the past to the future, we have good ground to fear that the sword would sometimes be appealed to as the arbiter of their differences. The dispute between Connecticut and Pennsylvania over the land at Wyoming warns us not to be sanguine about settling such differences easily. The articles of confederation required the parties to submit the matter to the decision of a federal court. They did so, and the court decided in favor of Pennsylvania. But Connecticut gave strong signs of dissatisfaction with that decision. She did not appear entirely resigned to it until negotiation and management found something like an equivalent for the loss she believed she had suffered. Nothing said here is meant to cast the slightest censure on the conduct of that State. She no doubt sincerely believed the decision had wronged her, and States, like individuals, accept decisions against their interest with great reluctance.

Those who had a chance to see the inside of the transactions that accompanied the controversy between this State and the district of Vermont can vouch for the opposition we met, from States with no stake in the claim as well as from those that had one. They can attest the danger to the peace of the Confederacy that might have arisen had this State tried to assert its rights by force. Two motives weighed most in that opposition. One was jealousy of our future power. The other was the interest of certain influential individuals in the neighboring States who had obtained grants of lands under the actual government of that district. Even the States that put forward claims contradicting ours seemed more anxious to dismember this State than to establish their own pretensions. These were New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. New Jersey and Rhode Island showed a warm zeal for the independence of Vermont on every occasion. Maryland shared the same views deeply until she was alarmed by signs of a connection between Canada and that State. These were small States, and they looked with an unfriendly eye on the prospect of our growing greatness. Reviewing these transactions, we can trace some of the causes that would be likely to embroil the States with each other if it should be their unhappy destiny to become disunited.

The competitions of commerce would be another fruitful source of contention. The States in less favorable positions would want to escape the disadvantages of their location and to share the advantages of their more fortunate neighbors. Each State, or separate confederacy, would pursue a commercial policy of its own. This would create distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, which would breed discontent. We have been used to dealing with one another on equal privileges since the earliest settlement of the country, and that habit would sharpen these causes of discontent beyond what they would naturally be. WE SHOULD BE READY TO CALL INJURIES THOSE THINGS WHICH WERE IN REALITY THE JUSTIFIABLE ACTS OF INDEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTIES CONSULTING A DISTINCT INTEREST. The spirit of enterprise that characterizes the commercial part of America has never missed an occasion to show itself. It is not at all likely that this unbridled spirit would show much respect for those regulations of trade by which particular States might try to secure exclusive benefits for their own citizens. Violations of these regulations on one side, and efforts to prevent and repel them on the other, would naturally lead to outrages, and these to reprisals and wars.

The chances that some States would have to make others tributary to them by commercial regulations would be resented by the tributary States, who would submit impatiently. The relative situation of New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey offers an example. New York, because she needs revenue, must lay duties on her imports. A great part of these duties must be paid by the inhabitants of the two other States, as consumers of what we import. New York would be neither willing nor able to give up this advantage. Her citizens would not agree that a duty paid by them should be refunded for the citizens of her neighbors. And even without this obstacle, it would not be practicable to tell our own customers apart in our own markets. Would Connecticut and New Jersey long submit to being taxed by New York for her exclusive benefit? Would we be allowed for long to enjoy in quiet and peace a metropolis whose possession gave us an advantage so odious to our neighbors and, in their opinion, so oppressive? Could we keep it against the heavy weight of Connecticut on one side and the cooperating pressure of New Jersey on the other? Only recklessness will answer these questions in the affirmative.

The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. Dividing it at the start, and paying it off step by step afterward, would both produce ill-humor and animosity. How could they possibly agree on a rule of apportionment that satisfied everyone? Hardly any rule that can be proposed is entirely free from real objections. As usual, the opposing interests of the parties would exaggerate these objections. The States even hold different views about the general principle of paying off the public debt. Some are less impressed with the importance of national credit, or their citizens have little or no immediate interest in the question. They feel indifference, if not repugnance, to paying the domestic debt at all. These States would be inclined to magnify the difficulties of dividing it. Others have a numerous body of citizens who are creditors of the public, out of proportion to the State's share of the total national debt. They would press hard for some fair and effective provision. The delays of the first group would stir the resentment of the second. Meanwhile, real differences of opinion and pretended delays would put off the settlement of a rule. The citizens of the States concerned would clamor, and foreign powers would press for satisfaction of their just demands. The peace of the States would be exposed to a double risk: invasion from outside and contention within.

Suppose the difficulties of agreeing on a rule were overcome and the apportionment made. There would still be great reason to suppose that, in practice, the rule agreed on would be found to bear harder on some States than on others. Those that suffered by it would naturally seek relief from the burden. The others would just as naturally be unwilling to revise it, since a revision was likely to end by increasing their own burdens. Their refusal would be too plausible a pretext for the complaining States to withhold their contributions, and they would seize on it eagerly. The failure of those States to meet their engagements would be a ground for bitter discussion and altercation. Even if the rule adopted should in practice bear out the equality of its principle, some States would still fall behind in their payments from a variety of other causes. These include a real shortage of resources, mismanagement of their finances, accidental disorders in the management of the government, and, besides all the rest, the reluctance with which men commonly part with money for purposes that have outlived the emergencies that produced them and that compete with the supply of immediate wants. Failures to pay, from whatever causes, would produce complaints, recriminations, and quarrels. There is perhaps nothing more likely to disturb the tranquillity of nations than being bound to mutual contributions for a common object that does not yield an equal and simultaneous benefit. For it is an observation as true as it is trite that there is nothing men disagree about so readily as the payment of money.

Laws in violation of private contracts may be considered another probable source of hostility, since they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them. We have no authority to expect that a more liberal or more equitable spirit would guide the legislation of the individual States in the future, if no further checks restrained them, than we have seen in too many instances, to the disgrace of their separate codes. We have seen how the outrages committed by the Legislature of Rhode Island excited a disposition to retaliate in Connecticut. We reasonably infer that in similar cases, under other circumstances, a war, not of PARCHMENT but of the sword, would punish such atrocious breaches of moral obligation and social justice.

The probability that different States or confederacies would form incompatible alliances with different foreign nations, and the effects of this situation on the peace of the whole, have been sufficiently set out in some earlier papers. The view they have given of this part of the subject leads to this conclusion: if America were not connected at all, or only by the feeble tie of a simple league, offensive and defensive, such clashing alliances would gradually entangle her in all the harmful labyrinths of European politics and wars. The destructive contentions of the parts into which she was divided would likely make her a prey to the artifices and machinations of powers that were equally the enemies of them all. Divide et impera(1) must be the motto of every nation that either hates or fears us.(2)
1. Divide and command.

2. In order that the whole subject of these papers may as soon as possible be laid before the public, it is proposed to publish them four times a week—on Tuesday in the New York Packet and on Thursday in the Daily Advertiser.

chapters.title: No. 8 — The Consequences of Hostilities Between the States (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Let us take it as an established truth, then, that in case of disunion the individual States, or such combinations of them as might be formed out of the wreck of the general Confederacy, would be subject to those swings between peace and war, friendship and enmity, which have been the lot of all neighboring nations not united under one government. On that assumption, let us look briefly at some of the consequences that such a situation would bring.

War between the States, in the first period of their separate existence, would bring far greater suffering than it commonly does in those countries where regular military establishments have long been in place. The disciplined armies always kept on foot in continental Europe have a threatening aspect toward liberty and economy. Nevertheless they have had one signal advantage: they have made sudden conquests impracticable and have prevented the rapid devastation that used to mark the progress of war before they were introduced. The art of fortification has served the same ends. The nations of Europe are ringed with chains of fortified places, which obstruct invasion at every point. Whole campaigns are wasted in reducing two or three frontier garrisons in order to gain entry into an enemy's country. Similar obstacles meet an invader at every step, exhausting his strength and slowing his progress. Formerly an invading army would penetrate into the heart of a neighboring country almost as soon as word of its approach could arrive. Now a comparatively small force of disciplined troops, acting on the defensive and aided by fortified posts, can impede and finally defeat the enterprises of a much larger one. The history of war in that part of the world is no longer a history of nations subdued and empires overturned. It is a history of towns taken and retaken; of battles that decide nothing; of retreats more beneficial than victories; of much effort and little gain.

In this country the scene would be entirely reversed. Jealousy of military establishments would put them off as long as possible. The lack of fortifications, leaving the frontiers of one State open to another, would make invasions easy. The populous States would overrun their less populous neighbors with little difficulty. Conquests would be as easy to make as they would be hard to hold. War, therefore, would be irregular and predatory. PLUNDER and devastation always march in the train of irregular troops. The sufferings of individuals would make the principal figure in the events that characterized our military exploits.

This picture is not too highly colored, though I admit it would not long remain accurate. Safety from external danger is the most powerful director of national conduct. Even the ardent love of liberty will, after a time, give way to its dictates. The violent destruction of life and property that comes with war, and the continual effort and alarm of a state of continual danger, will compel even the nations most attached to liberty to seek repose and security in institutions that tend to destroy their civil and political rights. To be safer, they at length become willing to run the risk of being less free.

The institutions I chiefly have in mind are STANDING ARMIES and the accompanying apparatus of military establishments. It is said that standing armies are not provided against in the new Constitution, and it is therefore inferred that they may exist under it.(1) By the very terms of that argument, however, their existence is at most doubtful and uncertain. But standing armies, it may be answered, must inevitably result from a dissolution of the Confederacy. Frequent war and constant apprehension, which require a state of equally constant preparation, will infallibly produce them. The weaker States or confederacies would turn to them first, to put themselves on an equality with their more powerful neighbors. They would try to make up for inferior population and resources with a more regular and effective system of defense: disciplined troops and fortifications. At the same time they would be forced to strengthen the executive arm of government, and in doing so their constitutions would move progressively toward monarchy. It is in the nature of war to increase the executive at the expense of the legislative authority.

The expedients just mentioned would soon give the States or confederacies that used them a superiority over their neighbors. Small states, or states of less natural strength, under vigorous governments and with the help of disciplined armies, have often triumphed over large states, or states of greater natural strength, that lacked these advantages. Neither the pride nor the safety of the more important States or confederacies would let them submit for long to this mortifying and artificial superiority. They would quickly turn to means like those by which it had been achieved, in order to regain their lost pre-eminence. Thus we should see established in every part of this country, in a short time, the same engines of despotism that have been the scourge of the Old World. This, at least, would be the natural course of things, and our reasonings will be the more likely to be sound in proportion as they conform to that standard.

These conclusions are not vague inferences from supposed or speculative defects in a Constitution that places all power in the hands of the people or of their representatives and delegates. They are sound conclusions, drawn from the natural and necessary course of human affairs.

It may perhaps be asked, as an objection to this, why standing armies did not spring up out of the contentions that so often distracted the ancient republics of Greece. Different answers, equally satisfactory, may be given to this question. The industrious habits of the people of the present day, absorbed in the pursuit of gain and devoted to the improvement of agriculture and commerce, are incompatible with the condition of a nation of soldiers, which was the true condition of the people of those republics. The means of revenue have been greatly multiplied by the increase of gold and silver and of the industrial arts. The science of finance, which is the offspring of modern times, has joined with the habits of nations to produce an entire revolution in the system of war. Together they have made disciplined armies, distinct from the body of the citizens, the inseparable companions of frequent hostility.

There is also a wide difference between military establishments in a country that its situation seldom exposes to invasion within its borders and those in a country that is often subject to such invasions and always fears them. The rulers of the former can have no good pretext, even if they are so inclined, for keeping on foot armies as numerous as must necessarily be maintained in the latter. In the first case these armies are rarely, if ever, called into action for internal defense, so the people are in no danger of being broken to military subordination. The laws are not accustomed to relaxations in favor of military necessities. The civil state remains in full vigor, neither corrupted nor confused with the principles or tendencies of the other state. The smallness of the army makes the natural strength of the community more than a match for it. The citizens, not accustomed to look to the military power for protection or to submit to its oppressions, neither love nor fear the soldiery. They regard them with a spirit of jealous acquiescence in a necessary evil, and stand ready to resist a power that they suppose may be used to the prejudice of their rights.

Under such circumstances the army may usefully aid the public official in suppressing a small faction, or an occasional mob or insurrection. But it will be unable to enforce encroachments against the united efforts of the great body of the people.

In a country in the situation last described, the opposite of all this happens. The perpetual threat of danger obliges the government to be always prepared to repel it, and its armies must be numerous enough for instant defense. The continual need for their services raises the importance of the soldier and lowers the condition of the citizen in proportion. The military state becomes elevated above the civil. The inhabitants of territories that are often the theater of war are unavoidably subjected to frequent infringements of their rights, which weaken their sense of those rights. By degrees the people come to regard the soldiery not only as their protectors but as their superiors. The step from this disposition to regarding them as masters is neither distant nor difficult. But it is very difficult to bring a people under such impressions to make a bold or effective resistance to usurpations backed by military power.

The kingdom of Great Britain falls within the first description. Its situation as an island, and a powerful navy, guard it in great measure against the possibility of foreign invasion and remove the need for a numerous army within the kingdom. A force sufficient to hold out against a sudden landing until the militia could have time to rally and assemble is all that has been thought necessary. No motive of national policy has demanded, nor would public opinion have tolerated, a larger number of troops on its domestic establishment. For a long time there has been little room for the operation of the other causes that I have listed as consequences of internal war. This peculiarly fortunate situation has contributed in great degree to preserve the liberty that the country enjoys to this day, in spite of its prevalent venality and corruption. If, on the contrary, Britain had been situated on the continent and had been compelled by that situation, as she would have been, to make her military establishments at home as large as those of the other great powers of Europe, she would in all probability, like them, be a victim today to the absolute power of a single man. It is possible, though not easy, that the people of that island may be enslaved from other causes. But it cannot be by the prowess of an army as small as the one usually kept up within the kingdom.

If we are wise enough to preserve the Union, we may for ages enjoy an advantage similar to that of an island situation. Europe is at a great distance from us. Her colonies in our vicinity will probably continue to be too far out of proportion to us in strength to be able to give us any dangerous annoyance. Extensive military establishments cannot, in this position, be necessary to our security.
