They still, in short, seem to cherish with blind devotion the political monster of an imperium in imperio. For this reason a full account of the principal defects of the Confederation is necessary. It will show that the evils we suffer do not come from minor or partial imperfections. They come from fundamental errors in the structure of the building, and these cannot be corrected without changing the first principles and main pillars of the fabric.

The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS, in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE CAPACITIES, as distinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist. This principle does not run through all the powers delegated to the Union, but it pervades and governs those on which the effectiveness of the rest depends. Except for the rule of appointment, the United States has unlimited discretion to make requisitions, or formal requests, for men and money. But it has no authority to raise either through regulations that reach the individual citizens of America. The consequence is that in theory the resolutions of the United States on these subjects are laws, constitutionally binding on the members of the Union, but in practice they are mere recommendations that the States may observe or disregard as they please.

It is a singular instance of the capriciousness of the human mind that, after all that experience has taught us on this point, some men still object to the new Constitution because it departs from a principle that has proved the bane of the old one. That principle is plainly incompatible, in itself, with the very idea of GOVERNMENT. If it is to be carried out at all, it must put the violent and bloody agency of the sword in place of the mild influence of the civil authority.

There is nothing absurd or impracticable in a league or alliance between independent nations for certain defined purposes. Such a league would be set out in a treaty that precisely states the purposes and regulates every detail of time, place, circumstance, and quantity, leaves nothing to later discretion, and relies for its execution on the good faith of the parties. Compacts of this kind exist among all civilized nations. They are subject to the usual ups and downs of peace and war, of observance and non-observance, as the interests or passions of the contracting powers dictate. In the early part of this century Europe was seized by an epidemic rage for compacts of this kind, and the politicians of the day fondly hoped they would bring benefits that were never realized. To establish the balance of power and the peace of that part of the world, every resource of negotiation was exhausted, and triple and quadruple alliances were formed. Scarcely had they been formed when they were broken. They taught mankind an instructive but painful lesson: very little dependence can be placed on treaties that have no sanction beyond the obligations of good faith, and that set general considerations of peace and justice against the pull of any immediate interest or passion.

Suppose the individual States of this country are willing to stand in a similar relation to each other and to give up the project of a general DISCRETIONARY SUPERINTENDENCE. The scheme would then indeed be harmful, and it would bring on all the harms listed under the first head. But it would have the merit of being at least consistent and practicable. We would abandon every view toward a confederate government and arrive at a simple alliance, offensive and defensive. We would be placed in a situation where we would be alternately friends and enemies of each other, as our mutual jealousies and rivalries, fed by the intrigues of foreign nations, should direct.

But suppose we are unwilling to be placed in this perilous situation, and still hold to the design of a national government, which is the same as a superintending power under the direction of a common council. Then we must resolve to build into our plan the ingredients that can be considered the characteristic difference between a league and a government. We must extend the authority of the Union to the persons of the citizens, who are the only proper objects of government.

Government implies the power of making laws. It is essential to the idea of a law that it carry a sanction, in other words a penalty or punishment for disobedience. If no penalty is attached to disobedience, the resolutions or commands that pretend to be laws will in fact be nothing more than advice or recommendation. This penalty, whatever it may be, can be inflicted in only two ways: through the courts and ministers of justice, or through military force. That is, it is either the COERCION of the civil authority or the COERCION of arms. The first kind can evidently apply only to individual men. The last kind must of necessity be used against bodies politic, or communities, or States. It is evident that no process of a court can, in the last resort, enforce the observance of the laws against them. Sentences may be pronounced against them for violations of their duty, but those sentences can be carried out only by the sword. In an association where the general authority is confined to the collective bodies of the communities that compose it, every breach of the laws must involve a state of war, and military execution must become the only instrument of civil obedience. Such a state of things surely cannot deserve the name of government, and no prudent man would choose to entrust his happiness to it.

There was a time when we were told not to expect the States to breach the regulations of the federal authority. A sense of common interest, we were told, would govern the conduct of the individual members and produce full compliance with all the constitutional requisitions of the Union. Today this language would sound as wild as a great part of what we now hear from the same quarter will sound once further lessons from experience, that best oracle of wisdom, have reached us. At every time it betrayed ignorance of the true springs of human conduct, and it contradicted the original reasons for establishing civil power. Why was government instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not follow the dictates of reason and justice unless they are constrained. Has it been found that bodies of men act with more rectitude or greater disinterestedness than individuals do? All careful observers of human conduct have inferred the opposite, and the inference rests on obvious reasons. Regard for reputation has less effect when the disgrace of a bad action is shared among many than when it falls on one person alone. A spirit of faction tends to mix its poison into the deliberations of every body of men. It will often carry the persons who make up such a body into improprieties and excesses that they would blush at in a private capacity.

On top of all this, sovereign power by its nature is impatient of control. It disposes those who hold it to look with an evil eye on every outside attempt to restrain or direct its operations. This spirit explains why, in every political association formed on the principle of uniting a number of lesser sovereignties in a common interest, there is a kind of eccentric tendency in the subordinate or inferior orbs. Each makes a perpetual effort to fly off from the common center. This tendency is not hard to account for. It begins in the love of power. Power that is controlled or limited is almost always the rival and enemy of the power that controls or limits it. This simple proposition shows how little reason there is to expect that the persons entrusted with the affairs of the individual members of a confederacy will at all times be ready to carry out the resolutions or decrees of the general authority with perfect good humor and an unbiased regard for the public welfare. The reverse follows from the make-up of human nature.

If, therefore, the measures of the Confederacy cannot be carried out without the intervention of the particular administrations, there is little prospect that they will be carried out at all. The rulers of the individual members will undertake to judge the propriety of the measures themselves, whether or not they have a constitutional right to. They will ask whether what is proposed or required suits their immediate interests or aims, and what momentary conveniences or problems would come with adopting it. All this will be done in a spirit of interested and suspicious scrutiny. It will be done without the knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state that a right judgment requires, and with a strong preference for local objects that can hardly fail to mislead the decision. The same process must be repeated in every member of which the body is made up. The carrying out of plans framed by the councils of the whole will always depend on the discretion of the ill-informed and prejudiced opinion of each part. Consider those who have watched the proceedings of popular assemblies and seen how hard it often is, even when no outside pressure of circumstances exists, to bring them to harmonious resolutions on important points. They will readily see how impossible it must be to induce a number of such assemblies, deliberating at a distance from each other, at different times, and under different impressions, to cooperate for long in the same views and pursuits.

In our case, the Confederation requires the concurrence of thirteen distinct sovereign wills for the complete execution of every important measure that proceeds from the Union. It has turned out as might have been foreseen. The measures of the Union have not been carried out. The delinquencies of the States have matured step by step to an extreme that has at last stopped all the wheels of the national government and brought them to a dreadful standstill. Congress now scarcely has the means to keep up the forms of administration until the States can find time to agree on a more substantial replacement for the present shadow of a federal government. Things did not reach this desperate extreme at once. The causes I have named at first produced only unequal and disproportionate degrees of compliance with the requisitions of the Union. The greater deficiencies of some States gave the complying States, or the least delinquent, a pretext in their example and a temptation in their own interest. Why should we do more in proportion than those embarked with us on the same political voyage? Why should we agree to bear more than our proper share of the common burden? Human selfishness could not withstand such suggestions, and even speculative men, who looked ahead to remote consequences, could not combat them without hesitation. Each State, yielding to the persuasive voice of immediate interest or convenience, has in turn withdrawn its support, until the frail and tottering edifice seems ready to fall on our heads and crush us beneath its ruins.
1. "I mean for the Union."

chapters.title: No. 16 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: We have tested the principle of legislation for States, or communities, in their political capacities by our own experiment, and the result shows where it leads. The fate of every other confederate government we know of shows the same thing, in exact proportion to how far the principle prevailed in each. These confirmations deserve a separate and careful examination. For now I will merely observe that, of all the confederacies of antiquity that history has handed down to us, the Lycian and Achaean leagues appear, as far as traces of them survive, to have been the freest from the fetters of this mistaken principle. They were accordingly the ones that political writers have most deservedly and most generously praised.

This objectionable principle may be called, as truly as emphatically, the parent of anarchy. We have seen that delinquencies in the members of the Union are its natural and necessary offspring, that the only constitutional remedy when they occur is force, and that the immediate result of using force is civil war.

It remains to ask how far so odious an engine of government, applied to us, could even achieve its end. Suppose there were no large army constantly at the disposal of the national government. Then it would either be unable to use force at all, or, if it did use it, the result would be a war between parts of the Confederacy over infractions of a league. In such a war the strongest combination would be the most likely to win, whether it was made up of those who supported the general authority or of those who resisted it. It would rarely happen that the delinquency to be corrected was confined to a single member. If more than one had neglected their duty, their similar situation would lead them to unite in common defense. Apart from this motive of sympathy, suppose a large and influential State were the offender. It would commonly have enough weight with its neighbors to win some of them over as allies. Specious arguments of danger to the common liberty could easily be contrived, and plausible excuses for the offender's failures could readily be invented. These would alarm the fears, inflame the passions, and win the good will even of States that were not guilty of any violation or omission of duty. This would be the more likely because the delinquencies of the larger members might sometimes be expected to come from the ambitious calculation of their rulers, who wanted to be rid of all outside control over their plans for personal aggrandizement. To carry out those plans better, it is to be presumed that they would first tamper with leading individuals in the neighboring States. If allies could not be found at home, they would turn to foreign powers, who would seldom be unwilling to encourage the dissensions of a Confederacy whose firm union they had so much reason to fear. Once the sword is drawn, the passions of men observe no bounds of moderation. Wounded pride and irritated resentment would tend to drive the States against which the arms of the Union were used to any extreme needed to avenge the insult or to avoid the disgrace of submission. The first war of this kind would probably end in the dissolution of the Union.

We may regard this as the violent death of the Confederacy. Its more natural death is the one we now seem about to suffer, unless the federal system is quickly renewed in a more substantial form. Given the character of this country, it is not likely that the complying States would often be inclined to support the authority of the Union by making war on the non-complying States. They would always be readier to take the milder course of putting themselves on an equal footing with the delinquent members by following their example. In this way the guilt of all would become the security of all. Our past experience has shown this spirit at work in its full light. There would in fact be an insuperable difficulty in deciding when force could properly be used. Take money contributions, the most usual source of delinquency. It would often be impossible to decide whether a State had failed to pay because it was unwilling or because it was unable. The plea of inability would always be at hand. The case would have to be flagrant indeed for the falseness of that plea to be detected with enough certainty to justify the harsh expedient of compulsion. It is easy to see that this problem alone, each time it arose, would open a wide field for factional views, bias, and oppression in whatever majority happened to prevail in the national council.

It hardly takes any effort to prove that the States should not prefer a national Constitution that could be kept in motion only by a large army continually on foot to carry out the ordinary requisitions or decrees of the government. Yet that is the plain alternative for those who want to deny it the power of reaching individuals. Such a scheme, if it could work at all, would instantly degenerate into a military despotism. But it will be found impracticable in every light. The resources of the Union would not be equal to maintaining an army large enough to hold the larger States to their duty, and the means to raise such an army in the first place would never be provided. Consider the population and strength of several of these States singly at the present moment, and look ahead to what they will become even half a century from now. Whoever does so will at once dismiss as idle and visionary any scheme that aims to regulate their movements by laws operating on them in their collective capacities, and executed by a coercion applicable to them in the same capacities. A project of this kind is little less romantic than the monster-taming spirit attributed to the fabled heroes and demigods of antiquity.

Even in confederacies made up of members smaller than many of our counties, the principle of legislation for sovereign States, backed by military coercion, has never been found effective. It has rarely been tried except against the weaker members. In most instances, attempts to coerce the refractory and disobedient have been the signal for bloody wars in which one half of the confederacy raised its banners against the other half.

An intelligent mind must draw this clear conclusion from these observations. If a federal government capable of regulating the common concerns and preserving the general tranquillity can be built at all, it must be founded, as to the objects committed to its care, on the reverse of the principle that the opponents of the proposed Constitution contend for. It must carry its agency to the persons of the citizens. It must need no intermediate legislations, but must itself be empowered to use the arm of the ordinary public official to carry out its own resolutions. The majesty of the national authority must be displayed through the courts of justice. The government of the Union, like that of each State, must be able to address itself directly to the hopes and fears of individuals, and to enlist in its support the passions that have the strongest hold on the human heart. In short, it must have all the means, and the right to use all the methods, of carrying out the powers entrusted to it that the governments of the particular States have and use.

Perhaps it will be objected to this reasoning that if any State were disaffected toward the authority of the Union, it could at any time obstruct the execution of the Union's laws. That would bring the matter to the same issue of force, whose necessity is held against the opposite scheme.

This objection loses its plausibility the moment we notice the essential difference between mere NON-COMPLIANCE and DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE. If a measure of the Union needs the intervention of the State legislatures to take effect, they have only NOT TO ACT, or TO ACT EVASIVELY, and the measure is defeated. This neglect of duty may be disguised under affected but insubstantial provisions, so that it does not appear and so does not alarm the people for the safety of the Constitution. The State leaders may even claim credit for their sly invasions of it, on the ground of some temporary convenience, exemption, or advantage.

But suppose the execution of the laws of the national government did not require the intervention of the State legislatures, and the laws took effect directly on the citizens themselves. Then the particular governments could not interrupt their progress without an open and violent exercise of unconstitutional power. No omissions or evasions would do. The States would be obliged to act, and to act in a way that left no doubt they had encroached on the national rights. An experiment of this nature would always be hazardous in the face of a constitution at all able to defend itself, and of a people enlightened enough to tell a legal exercise of authority from an illegal usurpation. To succeed, it would require not merely a factional majority in the legislature but the concurrence of the courts of justice and of the body of the people. If the judges were not part of a conspiracy with the legislature, they would pronounce the resolutions of such a majority contrary to the supreme law of the land, unconstitutional, and void. If the people were not infected with the spirit of their State representatives, they would act as the natural guardians of the Constitution. They would throw their weight into the national scale and give it a decided advantage in the contest. Such attempts would not often be made lightly or rashly, because they could seldom be made without danger to their authors, except when the federal authority was being used tyrannically.

Suppose instead that opposition to the national government arose from the disorderly conduct of refractory or seditious individuals. It could be overcome by the same means that are used every day against the same evil under the State governments. The civil authorities are equally ministers of the law of the land, whatever its source, and they would doubtless be as ready to protect national regulations as local ones from the inroads of private license. Consider the partial commotions and insurrections that sometimes disturb society, arising from the intrigues of an inconsiderable faction or from sudden or occasional ill humors that do not infect the great body of the community. The general government could command more extensive resources for putting down disturbances of that kind than any single member could. Then there are the mortal feuds that at certain junctures spread a conflagration through a whole nation or a very large part of it. They may come from weighty causes of discontent given by the government, or from the contagion of some violent popular fit. They do not fall within any ordinary rules of calculation. When they happen, they commonly amount to revolutions and dismemberments of empire. No form of government can always avoid or control them. It is vain to hope to guard against events too mighty for human foresight or precaution, and it would be idle to object to a government because it could not perform impossibilities.

chapters.title: No. 17 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: An objection of a different kind from the one stated and answered in my last address may perhaps also be raised against the principle of legislation for the individual citizens of America. It may be said that the principle would tend to make the government of the Union too powerful, and let it swallow up the residual authorities that it might be thought proper to leave with the States for local purposes. I give the love of power all the room that any reasonable man could ask. Even so, I confess I cannot see what temptation the persons entrusted with administering the general government could ever feel to strip the States of authorities of that kind. Regulating the mere domestic police of a State seems to me to hold out little to attract ambition. Commerce, finance, negotiation, and war seem to cover every object that has charms for minds ruled by that passion, and all the powers needed for those objects ought, in the first instance, to be placed in the national depository. Administering private justice between citizens of the same State, supervising agriculture, and the other concerns of a similar nature are all things properly provided for by local legislation. They can never be desirable cares for a general jurisdiction. It is therefore unlikely that the federal councils would be inclined to usurp the powers connected with them. Trying to exercise those powers would be as troublesome as it would be useless, and for that reason possessing them would add nothing to the dignity, the importance, or the splendor of the national government.

But grant, for the sake of argument, that mere wantonness and lust of domination would be enough to produce that inclination. Even so, we may safely affirm that the will of the constituent body of the national representatives, in other words the people of the individual States, would hold so extravagant an appetite in check. It will always be far easier for the State governments to encroach on the national authorities than for the national government to encroach on the State authorities. The proof of this proposition rests on the greater influence the State governments will generally have over the people, provided they administer their affairs with uprightness and prudence. This fact also teaches us that all federal constitutions have an inherent and intrinsic weakness, and that we cannot take too much care in organizing them to give them all the force compatible with the principles of liberty.

The State governments would have the greater influence partly because the national government is spread out, but chiefly because of the nature of the objects that the State administrations would attend to.

It is a known fact about human nature that its affections are generally weak in proportion to the distance or diffuseness of their object. A man is more attached to his family than to his neighborhood, and to his neighborhood than to the community at large. By the same principle, the people of each State would tend to feel a stronger bias toward their local governments than toward the government of the Union. The one exception would be if a much better administration of the Union's government overcame the force of that principle.
This strong propensity of the human heart would find powerful allies in the objects of State regulation.

The State governments will necessarily supervise a variety of smaller interests, which will form so many rivulets of influence running through every part of society. To list them would take a detail too tedious and uninteresting to be worth the instruction it might give.

There is one transcendent advantage belonging to the province of the State governments that by itself puts the matter in a clear and satisfactory light. I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. Of all things, this is the most powerful, the most universal, and the most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment. Justice is the immediate and visible guardian of life and property. Its benefits and its terrors are constantly at work before the public eye. It regulates all those personal interests and familiar concerns to which individuals are most immediately alive. For these reasons it does more than anything else to impress on the minds of the people affection, esteem, and reverence toward the government. This great cement of society will flow almost entirely through the channels of the particular governments. Quite apart from all other causes of influence, it would give them so decided a hold over their respective citizens that they would always be a complete counterpoise to the power of the Union and, not infrequently, dangerous rivals to it.

The operations of the national government, by contrast, come less directly under the eyes of the mass of citizens. Its benefits will be noticed and attended to chiefly by speculative men. Since it deals with more general interests, it will be less likely to come home to the feelings of the people, and to the same degree less likely to inspire a habitual sense of obligation and an active feeling of attachment.
The experience of all the federal constitutions we know of, and of all others bearing the least resemblance to them, has borne out the reasoning on this point abundantly.

The ancient feudal systems were not, strictly speaking, confederacies, but they shared the nature of that kind of association. There was a common head, chieftain, or sovereign, whose authority reached over the whole nation. There were also a number of subordinate vassals, or feudatories, who were allotted large portions of land. Under them were numerous trains of INFERIOR vassals or retainers, who occupied and farmed that land on the tenure of fealty or obedience to the persons from whom they held it. Each principal vassal was a kind of sovereign within his own domains. The result was continual opposition to the sovereign's authority and frequent wars among the great barons, or chief feudatories, themselves. The power of the head of the nation was commonly too weak either to keep the public peace or to protect the people against the oppressions of their immediate lords. Historians emphatically call this period of European history the times of feudal anarchy.

A sovereign of vigorous and warlike temper and superior abilities would gain a personal weight and influence that served, for a time, in place of a more regular authority. In general, however, the power of the barons triumphed over that of the prince. In many instances his dominion was thrown off entirely and the great fiefs were set up as independent principalities or States. In the instances where the monarch finally prevailed over his vassals, his success was chiefly owing to the vassals' tyranny over their dependents. The barons, or nobles, were equally the enemies of the sovereign and the oppressors of the common people, and were dreaded and detested by both. At length mutual danger and mutual interest brought about a union between the two that was fatal to the power of the aristocracy. If the nobles had instead kept the fidelity and devotion of their retainers and followers by acting with mercy and justice, their contests with the prince must almost always have ended in their favor, and in the reduction or overthrow of the royal authority.

This assertion is not founded merely on speculation or conjecture. Among other illustrations of its truth that might be cited, Scotland furnishes a compelling example. The spirit of clanship was introduced into that kingdom at an early date and bound the nobles and their dependents together by ties equal to those of kinship. This made the aristocracy a constant overmatch for the power of the monarch. It remained so until the union with England subdued its fierce and ungovernable spirit and brought it within the rules of subordination that a more rational and more energetic system of civil government had earlier established in the latter kingdom.

The separate governments in a confederacy may fittingly be compared to the feudal baronies. They have this advantage on their side. For the reasons already explained, they will generally have the confidence and good will of the people. With so important a support, they will be able to oppose effectively all encroachments by the national government. It will be well if they are not able to counteract its legitimate and necessary authority. The points of similarity are the rivalry of power that applies to both, and the CONCENTRATION of large portions of the community's strength in particular DEPOSITORIES. In the one case these are at the disposal of individuals; in the other, at the disposal of political bodies.

A concise review of the events that have attended confederate governments will further illustrate this important doctrine. Inattention to it has been the great source of our political mistakes and has aimed our jealousy at the wrong target. This review will be the subject of some ensuing papers.

chapters.title: No. 18 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) For the New York Packet. Friday, (Hamilton & Madison)
paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The most considerable of the confederacies of antiquity was that of the Grecian republics, joined together under the Amphictyonic Council. By the best accounts we have of this celebrated institution, it closely resembled the present Confederation of the American States, and the resemblance is very instructive.

The members kept the character of independent and sovereign states, and each had an equal vote in the federal council. The council had general authority to propose and decide whatever it judged necessary for the common welfare of Greece. It could declare and wage war, decide all controversies between the members in the last resort, fine the aggressing party, turn the whole force of the confederacy against the disobedient, and admit new members. The Amphictyons were the guardians of religion and of the immense riches that belonged to the temple of Delphos. There they had the right of jurisdiction in controversies between the inhabitants and those who came to consult the oracle. To give the federal powers further effectiveness, the Amphictyons swore an oath to defend and protect the united cities mutually, to punish anyone who violated the oath, and to take vengeance on sacrilegious despoilers of the temple.

In theory, and on paper, this array of powers seems amply sufficient for all general purposes. In several important respects it goes beyond the powers listed in the Articles of Confederation. The Amphictyons controlled the superstition of the times, which was one of the principal engines by which government was then maintained. They also had a declared authority to use coercion against refractory cities, and an oath bound them to use it when the occasion required.

The experiment, nevertheless, turned out very differently from the theory. As in the present Congress, the powers were administered by deputies appointed wholly by the cities in their political capacities, and they were exercised over the cities in those same capacities. From this came the weakness, the disorders, and finally the destruction of the confederacy. The more powerful members, instead of being held in awe and subordination, tyrannized in turn over all the rest. Athens, as we learn from Demosthenes, was the arbiter of Greece for seventy-three years. The Lacedaemonians governed it next, for twenty-nine years. At a later time, after the battle of Leuctra, the Thebans had their turn at domination.
Plutarch tells us it happened all too often that the deputies of the strongest cities overawed and corrupted those of the weaker ones, and that judgment went to the most powerful party.

Even in the midst of defensive and dangerous wars with Persia and Macedon, the members never acted together. More or fewer of them were always the dupes or the hirelings of the common enemy. The intervals between foreign wars were filled with domestic upheavals, convulsions, and carnage.

After the war with Xerxes ended, the Lacedaemonians, it appears, demanded that a number of the cities be expelled from the confederacy for the unfaithful part they had played. The Athenians saw that the Lacedaemonians would lose fewer partisans by this measure than they themselves would, and would become masters of the public deliberations. They therefore opposed the attempt vigorously and defeated it. This piece of history proves at once the ineffectiveness of the union, the ambition and jealousy of its most powerful members, and the dependent and degraded condition of the rest. By the theory of their system the smaller members were entitled to revolve in equal pride and majesty around the common center. In fact they had become satellites of the orbs of primary magnitude.

The Abbe Milot says that if the Greeks had been as wise as they were courageous, experience would have taught them the need of a closer union. They would have used the peace that followed their success against the Persian arms to make that reform. Instead of this obvious policy, Athens and Sparta, puffed up with the victories and glory they had won, became first rivals and then enemies. They did each other infinitely more harm than they had suffered from Xerxes. Their mutual jealousies, fears, hatreds, and injuries ended in the celebrated Peloponnesian war, which in turn ended in the ruin and slavery of the Athenians who had started it.

A weak government that is not at war is always agitated by internal dissensions, and these never fail to bring fresh calamities from abroad. The Phocians had plowed up some consecrated ground belonging to the temple of Apollo. In keeping with the superstition of the age, the Amphictyonic Council fined the sacrilegious offenders. The Phocians, supported by Athens and Sparta, refused to submit to the decree. The Thebans, with some of the other cities, undertook to maintain the authority of the Amphictyons and to avenge the violated god. Because the Thebans were the weaker party, they invited the assistance of Philip of Macedon, who had secretly stirred up the quarrel. Philip gladly seized the chance to carry out the designs against the liberties of Greece that he had long planned. By his intrigues and bribes he won over the popular leaders of several cities. Through their influence and votes he gained admission to the Amphictyonic Council. And through his arts and his arms he made himself master of the confederacy.

These were the consequences of the fallacious principle on which this interesting establishment was founded. A judicious observer, writing on the fate of Greece, says that if she had been united by a stricter confederation and had held to her union, she would never have worn the chains of Macedon. She might even have proved a barrier to the vast projects of Rome.
The Achaean league, as it is called, was another society of Grecian republics, and it gives us valuable instruction.

Here the Union was far closer, and the organization much wiser, than in the previous case. It will therefore appear that, though the league did not escape a similar catastrophe, it by no means deserved it as much.

The cities that made up this league kept their municipal jurisdiction, appointed their own officers, and enjoyed perfect equality. The senate, in which they were represented, held the sole and exclusive right of peace and war, of sending and receiving ambassadors, of entering into treaties and alliances, and of appointing a chief executive, called the praetor, who commanded their armies. With the advice and consent of ten of the senators, the praetor not only administered the government while the senate was in recess but also had a great share in its deliberations when it was in session. Under the original constitution two praetors shared the administration, but after a trial a single one was preferred.

It appears that all the cities had the same laws and customs, the same weights and measures, and the same money. How far this came from the authority of the federal council, however, is left uncertain. We are told only that the cities were in a manner compelled to accept the same laws and usages. When Philopoemen brought Lacedaemon into the league, the institutions and laws of Lycurgus were abolished and those of the Achaeans adopted. The Amphictyonic confederacy, of which she had been a member, had left her in full exercise of her government and her legislation. This circumstance alone proves a very important difference in the character of the two systems.

It is much to be regretted that such imperfect records survive of this curious political structure. If we could determine its internal structure and regular operation, it would probably throw more light on the science of federal government than any of the similar experiments known to us.

All the historians who notice Achaean affairs seem to attest one important fact. After the league was renewed by Aratus, as before it was dissolved by the arts of Macedon, its government was administered with infinitely more moderation and justice, and its people showed less violence and sedition, than could be found in any of the cities that exercised SINGLY all the prerogatives of sovereignty. The Abbe Mably, in his observations on Greece, says that the popular government, so tempestuous elsewhere, caused no disorders among the members of the Achaean republic, BECAUSE IT WAS THERE TEMPERED BY THE GENERAL AUTHORITY AND LAWS OF THE CONFEDERACY.

We must not conclude too hastily, however, that faction did not to some degree agitate the particular cities, much less that proper subordination and harmony reigned in the general system. The ups and downs and the fate of the republic show the contrary clearly enough.

While the Amphictyonic confederacy lasted, the Achaean confederacy, which included only the less important cities, made little figure on the stage of Greece. When the former fell victim to Macedon, the latter was spared by the policy of Philip and Alexander. Under the successors of these princes, however, a different policy prevailed. The arts of division were practiced among the Achaeans. Each city was seduced into a separate interest, and the union was dissolved. Some of the cities fell under the tyranny of Macedonian garrisons, others under that of usurpers who rose out of their own confusion. Shame and oppression soon awakened their love of liberty. A few cities reunited, and others followed their example as chances arose to get rid of their tyrants. The league soon took in almost the whole Peloponnesus. Macedon saw its progress but was kept by internal dissensions from stopping it. All Greece caught the enthusiasm and seemed ready to unite in one confederacy. Then the jealousy and envy that Sparta and Athens felt at the rising glory of the Achaeans threw a fatal damper on the enterprise. Fear of the Macedonian power led the league to court the alliance of the Kings of Egypt and Syria, who as successors of Alexander were rivals of the king of Macedon. Cleomenes, king of Sparta, defeated this policy. His ambition led him to make an unprovoked attack on his neighbors the Achaeans, and as an enemy of Macedon he had enough influence with the Egyptian and Syrian princes to make them break their engagements with the league.

The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes or begging aid from Macedon, their former oppressor. They chose the latter. The contests of the Greeks always gave that powerful neighbor a welcome chance to meddle in their affairs. A Macedonian army quickly appeared and Cleomenes was defeated. The Achaeans soon learned, as so often happens, that a victorious and powerful ally is only another name for a master. All that their most abject compliance could win from him was toleration of the exercise of their laws. Philip, now on the throne of Macedon, soon provoked fresh combinations among the Greeks by his tyrannies. The Achaeans were weakened by internal dissensions and by the revolt of Messene, one of their members. Even so, joined by the AEtolians and Athenians, they raised the standard of opposition. Finding themselves unequal to the undertaking even with this support, they once more resorted to the dangerous expedient of bringing in foreign arms. The Romans, to whom the invitation was made, eagerly accepted it. Philip was conquered and Macedon subdued. A new crisis followed for the league. Dissensions broke out among its members, and the Romans encouraged them. Callicrates and other popular leaders became paid instruments for luring their countrymen astray. To feed discord and disorder more effectively, the Romans had already proclaimed universal liberty(1) throughout Greece, to the astonishment of those who trusted their sincerity. With the same treacherous aims, they now drew the members away from the league by appealing to their pride over the violation it committed on their sovereignty. By these arts this union, the last hope of Greece, the last hope of ancient liberty, was torn to pieces. Such weakness and distraction were introduced that the arms of Rome found little difficulty in completing the ruin their arts had begun. The Achaeans were cut to pieces, and Achaia was loaded with chains, under which it groans to this hour.

I have thought it not superfluous to give the outlines of this important portion of history, both because it teaches more than one lesson and because it adds to the outline of the Achaean constitution. It emphatically illustrates the tendency of federal bodies to produce anarchy among the members rather than tyranny in the head.
1. This was only a more plausible-sounding name for the independence of the members from the federal head.

chapters.title: No. 19 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton & Madison)
paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The ancient confederacies I described in my last paper do not exhaust what experience can teach us on this subject. Some institutions that exist today rest on a similar principle and deserve careful study. The first to come to mind is the Germanic body.

In the early centuries of Christianity, seven separate nations lived in Germany, and they had no common chief. One of them, the Franks, conquered the Gauls and founded the kingdom that still bears their name. In the ninth century the warlike monarch Charlemagne sent his victorious armies in every direction, and Germany became part of his vast dominions. After his empire was broken up under his sons, this portion became a separate, independent empire. Charlemagne and his immediate descendants held the substance of imperial power, along with its emblems and dignity. But the chief vassals, whose fiefs had become hereditary and who sat in the national diets that Charlemagne had left in place, gradually shook off imperial control and rose to sovereign jurisdiction and independence. Imperial sovereignty was too weak to restrain such powerful dependents, or to keep the empire united and at peace. The princes and states waged the most furious private wars on one another, with every kind of calamity in their train. The imperial authority could not keep public order and declined step by step, until it was almost extinct in the anarchy that shook the long interval between the death of the last emperor of the Suabian line and the accession of the first emperor of the Austrian line. In the eleventh century the emperors held full sovereignty; by the fifteenth they had little more than the symbols and trappings of power.

From this feudal system, which itself has many of the important features of a confederacy, there grew the federal system that makes up the Germanic empire. Its powers are divided among three bodies. One is a diet, which represents the member states of the confederacy. Another is the emperor, the chief executive, who has a negative on the decrees of the diet. The third consists of the imperial chamber and the aulic council, two courts with supreme jurisdiction over controversies that concern the empire or that arise among its members.

The diet holds the general power to legislate for the empire. It may make war and peace, form alliances, assess quotas of troops and money, build fortresses, regulate coin, and admit new members. It may also place disobedient members under the ban of the empire, which strips the offender of his sovereign rights and forfeits his possessions. The members of the confederacy are expressly forbidden to make compacts that harm the empire; to impose tolls and duties on trade among themselves without the consent of the emperor and diet; to change the value of money; to wrong one another; or to give aid or refuge to disturbers of the public peace. Those who violate any of these restrictions are declared under the ban. The members of the diet, in their capacity as members, are in all cases subject to judgment by the emperor and diet, and in their private capacities by the aulic council and imperial chamber.

The emperor's prerogatives are many. The most important are these: he alone may bring proposals before the diet; he may negative its resolutions; he names ambassadors, confers dignities and titles, fills vacant electorates, and founds universities; he grants privileges, provided they do not injure the states of the empire; he receives and applies the public revenues; and in general he watches over the public safety. In certain cases the electors act as his council. As emperor he holds no territory within the empire and receives no revenue for his support. But the revenue and dominions he holds in other capacities make him one of the most powerful princes in Europe.

Seeing such an array of constitutional powers in the representatives and the head of this confederacy, one would naturally suppose that it must be an exception to the general character of similar systems. The reality is quite the opposite. The empire rests on a fundamental principle: it is a community of sovereigns, the diet represents sovereigns, and the laws are addressed to sovereigns. That principle makes the empire a body without strength, unable to govern its own members, unprotected against outside dangers, and in constant internal turmoil.

The history of Germany is one of wars between the emperor and the princes and states, and of wars among the princes and states themselves. It is a record of the strong running wild and the weak being oppressed; of foreign intrusions and foreign intrigues; of requisitions for men and money that were ignored or only partly met; of efforts to enforce them that either came to nothing or brought slaughter and desolation, in which the innocent suffered with the guilty. It is a record of general feebleness, confusion, and misery.

In the sixteenth century the emperor, with one part of the empire behind him, was seen fighting the other princes and states. In one of these conflicts the emperor himself was routed and very nearly captured by the elector of Saxony. The late king of Prussia was more than once set against his imperial sovereign, and usually got the better of him. Quarrels and wars among the members themselves have been so frequent that the German annals are full of bloody pages describing them. Before the peace of Westphalia, Germany was ravaged by a thirty years' war. The emperor and half the empire stood on one side, and Sweden and the other half on the opposite side. Peace was in the end negotiated, and dictated, by foreign powers, and its articles, to which foreign powers are parties, became a fundamental part of the Germanic constitution.

Suppose the nation is, in some emergency, more united than usual by the need to defend itself. Its situation is still wretched. Military preparations must first go through so many tedious debates, caused by the jealousies, pride, separate aims, and conflicting claims of sovereign bodies, that the enemy is already in the field before the diet can settle on its arrangements, and is retiring to winter quarters before the federal troops are ready to take the field.

The small body of national troops judged necessary in peacetime is badly kept up and poorly paid. It is infected with local prejudices and supported by uneven and disproportionate contributions to the treasury.

Because it was impossible to keep order and administer justice among these sovereign subjects, a new scheme was tried. The empire was divided into nine or ten circles or districts, each was given an internal organization, and each was charged with the military enforcement of the laws against delinquent and stubborn members. This experiment has only shown more fully the radical vice of the constitution. Every circle is a small portrait of the deformities of this political monster. The circles either fail to carry out their commissions, or they carry them out with all the devastation and carnage of civil war. Sometimes entire circles fall into default, and then they add to the very harm they were set up to cure.

We can judge how this scheme of military coercion works from an instance reported by Thuanus. In Donawerth, a free and imperial city in the circle of Suabia, the Abbe de St. Croix held certain immunities that had been reserved to him. When he exercised them on some public occasions, the townspeople committed outrages against him. As a result the city was placed under the ban of the empire, and the Duke of Bavaria, although he was director of a different circle, secured an appointment to enforce it. He soon appeared before the city with ten thousand troops. He saw a good opportunity, as he had secretly planned from the start, to revive an old claim, on the pretext that his ancestors had allowed the place to be detached from his territory.(1) He took possession of it in his own name, disarmed and punished the inhabitants, and joined the city once more to his domains.

Someone may ask what has kept this disjointed machine from collapsing altogether for so long. The answer is plain. Most of the members are weak and do not want to expose themselves to the mercy of foreign powers. Most of the principal members, too, are weak compared with the formidable powers around them. The emperor draws great weight and influence from his own separate, hereditary dominions, and he has an interest in preserving a system tied to his family pride and making him the first prince of Europe. These causes sustain a feeble and precarious Union—while the repellent quality that goes with the nature of sovereignty, and that grows stronger with time, blocks any reform based on proper consolidation. And even if this obstacle could be overcome, we should not imagine that the neighboring powers would allow a revolution that gave the empire the force and preeminence it is entitled to. Foreign nations have long regarded themselves as having a stake in the changes that events bring to this constitution, and on various occasions they have shown that their policy is to perpetuate its anarchy and weakness.

If more direct examples were needed, Poland, as a government over local sovereigns, could fairly be mentioned. No proof could show more strikingly the calamities that flow from such institutions. Unfit for self-government and for self-defense alike, Poland has long been at the mercy of its powerful neighbors, who recently had the mercy to relieve it of a third of its people and territory.
The tie among the Swiss cantons hardly amounts to a confederacy, although it is sometimes cited as an example of how stable such institutions can be.
They have no common treasury; no common troops, even in war; no common coin; no common court; and no other common mark of sovereignty.

What holds them together is the peculiar lie of their land; their individual weakness and insignificance; fear of powerful neighbors, to one of which they were once subject; the few causes of quarrel among a people with such simple and uniform manners; their joint interest in their dependent possessions; the mutual aid they need to put down insurrections and rebellions, which is expressly promised and often called for and given; and the need for some regular and permanent way of settling disputes among the cantons. The provision is that the parties to a dispute each choose four judges from the neutral cantons, and if these disagree, they choose an umpire. This tribunal, bound by an oath of impartiality, pronounces a final sentence, which all the cantons are obliged to enforce. We can gauge how well this arrangement works from a clause in their treaty of 1683 with Victor Amadeus of Savoy, in which he binds himself to step in as mediator in disputes between the cantons and, if necessary, to use force against the party that defies the ruling.

As far as their peculiar case can be compared with that of the United States, it confirms the principle I am trying to establish. Whatever effect the union may have had in ordinary cases, it failed the moment a difference arose that was strong enough to test it. The controversies over religion, which on three occasions set off violent and bloody conflicts, may be said in fact to have split the league. The Protestant and Catholic cantons have held separate diets since then, where all the most important business is settled, and they have left the general diet with little to do except look after the jointly held bailiwicks.

That separation had another consequence worth noting. It led to opposing alliances with foreign powers: Berne, at the head of the Protestant association, allied with the United Provinces, and Luzerne, at the head of the Catholic association, allied with France.
1. Pfeffel, "Nouvel Abrég. Chronol. de l'Hist., etc., d'Allemagne," says the pretext was to indemnify himself for the expense of the expedition.

chapters.title: No. 20 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton & Madison)
paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The United Netherlands form a confederacy of republics, or rather of aristocracies, with a very remarkable structure. Yet they confirm every lesson we have drawn from the confederacies already reviewed.

The union consists of seven sovereign states, equal in rank, and each state or province is in turn made up of equal and independent cities. On every important question, not only the provinces but the cities as well must be unanimous.

The States-General represent the sovereignty of the Union. They usually number about fifty deputies, appointed by the provinces. Their terms differ: some deputies sit for life, others for six years, three years, or one, and two provinces keep their deputies in office only during pleasure.

The States-General may enter into treaties and alliances, make war and peace, raise armies and equip fleets, fix quotas, and demand contributions. In all these matters, however, they need unanimity and the approval of those they represent. They may also appoint and receive ambassadors, carry out treaties and alliances already made, arrange for the collection of duties on imports and exports, regulate the mint (subject to the rights of the provinces), and govern the dependent territories as sovereigns. The provinces may not, without general consent, make foreign treaties, set up imposts that harm other provinces, or charge their neighbors higher duties than they charge their own subjects. A council of state, a chamber of accounts, and five colleges of admiralty support and strengthen the federal administration.

The union's chief executive is the stadtholder, who is now a hereditary prince. His main weight and influence in the republic rest on several things: this independent title; his large inherited estates; his family ties with some of the chief potentates of Europe; and, more than all of these, perhaps, the fact that he is stadtholder in the individual provinces as well as for the union. In that provincial role he appoints town officials under certain regulations, carries out provincial decrees, presides in the provincial courts whenever he chooses, and holds the power of pardon in every province.
Even as stadtholder of the union, though, he has considerable prerogatives.

In his political capacity he may settle disputes between the provinces when other methods fail, attend the deliberations of the States-General and their special conferences, receive foreign ambassadors, and maintain agents for his own affairs at foreign courts.

In his military capacity he commands the federal troops, provides for garrisons, and generally manages military affairs. He makes every appointment from colonel down to ensign, and fills the governorships and posts of fortified towns.

In his naval capacity he is admiral-general. He oversees and directs everything that concerns the naval forces and other naval affairs, presides over the admiralties in person or through a deputy, appoints lieutenant-admirals and other officers, and sets up councils of war, whose sentences are not carried out until he approves them.
His revenue, apart from his private income, comes to three hundred thousand florins. The standing army under his command numbers about forty thousand men.

That is the celebrated Belgic confederacy as it is set down on parchment. What features has practice stamped upon it? A feeble government; discord among the provinces; foreign influence and indignities; an uncertain existence in peace, and special calamities in war.
Grotius observed long ago that only his countrymen's hatred of the house of Austria saved them from being ruined by the vices of their constitution.

Another respected writer says that the union of Utrecht places in the States-General an authority that seems enough to ensure harmony, but that the jealousy in each province makes the practice very different from the theory.

Another says that the same instrument requires each province to levy certain contributions, but that this article never could be carried out and probably never will be, because the inland provinces, having little commerce, cannot pay an equal quota.

On contributions, the usual practice is to set the articles of the constitution aside. The danger of delay forces the consenting provinces to supply their quotas without waiting for the rest, and then to recover the money from the others through deputations, which are frequent, or by whatever other means they can. The great wealth and influence of the province of Holland let her achieve both ends.

More than once the deficiencies have finally had to be collected at the point of the bayonet. That can be done, though it is dreadful, in a confederacy where one member exceeds all the others in strength and several are too small to think of resisting. It is utterly impossible in a confederacy whose members include several that are equal to each other in strength and resources, and each equal by itself to a vigorous and lasting defense.

Sir William Temple, who was himself a foreign minister, says that foreign ministers get around matters taken ad referendum by tampering with the provinces and cities. In 1726 the treaty of Hanover was held up in this way for a whole year. Instances of the same kind are numerous and notorious.

In critical emergencies the States-General are often forced to go beyond their constitutional limits. In 1688 they concluded a treaty on their own authority, at the risk of their heads. The treaty of Westphalia, in 1648, which formally and finally recognized their independence, was concluded without the consent of Zealand. Even in the recent treaty of peace with Great Britain, the constitutional principle of unanimity was set aside. A weak constitution must end one of two ways: in dissolution, for want of proper powers, or in the usurpation of the powers needed for the public safety. Whether the usurpation, once begun, will stop at the beneficial point or go on to the dangerous extreme depends on the chance events of the moment. Tyranny has perhaps more often grown out of assumptions of power that a defective constitution made necessary in pressing emergencies than out of the full exercise of the greatest constitutional authorities.

Calamities have come from the stadtholdership, and yet it has been supposed that without his influence in the individual provinces, the causes of anarchy so plain in the confederacy would long ago have dissolved it. "Under such a government," says the Abbe Mably, "the Union could never have subsisted, if the provinces had not a spring within themselves, capable of quickening their tardiness, and compelling them to the same way of thinking. This spring is the stadtholder." Sir William Temple observes "that in the intermissions of the stadtholdership, Holland, by her riches and her authority, which drew the others into a sort of dependence, supplied the place."

Other circumstances, too, have held back the tendency to anarchy and dissolution. The surrounding powers make union to a certain degree an absolute necessity, and at the same time their intrigues feed the constitutional vices that keep the republic, to some degree, always at their mercy.

True patriots have long grieved over the fatal tendency of these vices. They have made no fewer than four regular attempts to find a remedy, by means of EXTRAORDINARY ASSEMBLIES called together for that special purpose. Each time their praiseworthy zeal has found it impossible to UNITE THE PUBLIC COUNCILS in reforming the known, the acknowledged, the fatal evils of the existing constitution. Let us pause for a moment, my fellow-citizens, over this sad and cautionary lesson of history. With the tear we shed for the calamities that conflicting opinions and selfish passions have brought on mankind, let us join a prayer of thanks to Heaven for the fortunate harmony that has marked the consultations about our political happiness.
A plan was also conceived to set up a general tax to be administered by the federal authority. This too had its opponents and failed.

This unhappy people now appear to be in the crisis of their destiny, suffering from popular convulsions, from dissensions among the states, and from actual invasion by foreign arms. All nations have their eyes fixed on this awful spectacle. The first wish that humanity prompts is that this severe trial may result in such a revolution in their government as will establish their union and make it the parent of tranquillity, freedom and happiness. The next is that the asylum in which, we trust, these blessings will soon be secured in this country may receive them and console them for the catastrophe of their own.

I offer no apology for having dwelt so long on these federal precedents. Experience is the oracle of truth, and when its answers are unambiguous, they ought to be conclusive and sacred. The important truth that it declares without ambiguity in the present case is this: a sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities as opposed to individuals, is a solecism in theory, and in practice it destroys the order and ends of civil government. It puts VIOLENCE in the place of LAW, or the destructive COERCION of the SWORD in the place of the mild and beneficial COERCION of the MAGISTRACY.

chapters.title: No. 21 — Other Defects of the Present Confederation (Hamilton)
paragraphs: In the last three numbers I surveyed the main circumstances and events that revealed the character and fate of other confederate governments. I shall now go on to list the most important of the defects that have so far disappointed our hopes in the system we ourselves have established. To judge soundly and safely what the remedy should be, we must be thoroughly acquainted with how far the disease extends and how malignant it is.

The next most glaring defect of the existing Confederation is its complete lack of any SANCTION for its laws. The United States, as now constituted, have no power to compel obedience to their resolutions or to punish disobedience, whether by fines, by suspending or stripping privileges, or by any other constitutional means. No authority to use force against delinquent members has been expressly delegated to them. If such a right were attributed to the federal head as following from the nature of the social compact among the States, it could only be by inference and construction, and in the teeth of the part of the second article that declares, "that each State shall retain every power, jurisdiction, and right, not EXPRESSLY delegated to the United States in Congress assembled." There is surely a striking absurdity in supposing that no such right exists. But we are left with a dilemma. We must either accept that supposition, preposterous as it seems, or contradict or explain away a provision that has lately been a constant theme of praise from the opponents of the new Constitution, and whose absence from that plan has drawn much plausible comment and harsh criticism. If we are unwilling to weaken the force of this applauded provision, we must conclude that the United States present the extraordinary spectacle of a government without even the shadow of constitutional power to enforce its own laws. The examples I have cited will show that on this point the American Confederacy stands apart from every other institution of a similar kind, and presents a new and unexampled phenomenon in the political world.

The absence of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another major imperfection in the federal plan. Nothing of this kind is declared in the articles that make it up. To imply a tacit guaranty from considerations of usefulness would be a still more flagrant departure from the clause I have mentioned than to imply a tacit power of coercion on the same grounds. The lack of a guaranty, though its consequences might endanger the Union, does not strike as directly at its existence as the lack of a constitutional sanction for its laws.

Without a guaranty, we must give up any help the Union could offer against the domestic dangers that may sometimes threaten the existence of the State constitutions. Usurpation may raise its head in any State and trample on the liberties of the people, while the national government could lawfully do nothing more than watch its encroachments with indignation and regret. A successful faction may build a tyranny on the ruins of order and law, and the Union could not constitutionally give any help to the friends and supporters of the government. The stormy situation from which Massachusetts has barely emerged shows that dangers of this kind are not merely theoretical. Who can say what the outcome of her recent convulsions might have been if the malcontents had been led by a Caesar or a Cromwell? Who can predict what effect a despotism established in Massachusetts would have on the liberties of New Hampshire or Rhode Island, of Connecticut or New York?

Excessive pride in the importance of the State has led some minds to object to the principle of a guaranty in the federal government, on the ground that it would be an officious interference in the domestic concerns of the members. A scruple of this kind would deprive us of one of the principal advantages we expect from union, and it can only come from misunderstanding the nature of the provision. It could be no obstacle to reforms of a State constitution made by a majority of the people in a lawful and peaceable way. That right would remain undiminished. The guaranty could only work against changes brought about by violence. For preventing calamities of this kind, we cannot provide too many checks. The peace of society and the stability of government depend entirely on how effective the precautions taken on this point are. Where the whole power of the government is in the hands of the people, there is less pretext for violent remedies for the partial or occasional disorders of the State. The natural cure for poor administration, in a popular or representative constitution, is a change of men. A guaranty by the national authority would be aimed as much against the usurpations of rulers as against the ferment and outrages of faction and sedition among the people.

The principle of fixing the States' contributions to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation. I have already pointed out that it is incompatible with an adequate supply for the national emergencies, and the trial it has had has shown this plainly enough. I speak of it now only from the standpoint of equality among the States. Anyone who has studied the circumstances that produce and make up national wealth must be satisfied that there is no common standard or barometer by which its degree can be determined. Neither the value of lands nor the number of people, both of which have been proposed in turn as the rule for the States' contributions, has any claim to be a just measure. Compare the wealth of the United Netherlands with that of Russia or Germany, or even France. Then compare the total value of the lands and the total population of that small district with the total value of the lands and the total population of the immense regions of any of those three countries. We shall see at once that neither of these two measures bears any proportion to the relative wealth of those nations. A similar comparison among several of the American States would give a similar result. Set Virginia beside North Carolina, Pennsylvania beside Connecticut, or Maryland beside New Jersey, and we shall be convinced that the ability of these States to produce revenue has little or no relation to their relative holdings of land or their relative populations. The same point can be illustrated in the same way by comparing counties within a single State. No one acquainted with the State of New York will doubt that the active wealth of King's County stands in a much greater proportion to that of Montgomery than it would appear to do if we took either the total value of the lands or the total number of people as the measure!

The wealth of nations depends on an endless variety of causes: location, soil, climate, the nature of the products, the nature of the government, the character of the citizens, the degree of knowledge they possess, the state of commerce, of the arts, of industry. These circumstances, and many more that are too complex, too minute, or too accidental to list one by one, produce differences in the relative opulence and riches of different countries that are hardly conceivable. The plain consequence is that there can be no common measure of national wealth, and therefore no general or fixed rule by which a state's ability to pay taxes can be determined. The attempt to regulate the contributions of the members of a confederacy by any such rule is bound to produce glaring inequality and extreme oppression.

In America this inequality would by itself be enough to bring about the eventual destruction of the Union, if any way could be found to force compliance with its requisitions. The suffering States would not long agree to stay united on a principle that shares the public burdens so unequally, and that was bound to impoverish and oppress the citizens of some States, while those of others would hardly notice the small share of the weight they were asked to bear. Yet this is an evil that cannot be separated from the principle of quotas and requisitions.

There is no way of steering clear of this problem except by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way. Imposts, excises, and in general all duties on articles of consumption may be compared to a fluid that will in time find its level with the means of paying them. In some degree, each citizen's contribution will be a matter of his own choice and can be adjusted to his resources. The rich may be extravagant, the poor can be frugal, and private oppression can always be avoided by a judicious choice of the objects suitable for such taxes. If duties on particular objects should create inequalities in some States, these will in all probability be offset by corresponding inequalities in other States from duties on other objects. In the course of time and events, a balance will be established everywhere, as far as that can be achieved in so complicated a subject. Or, if inequalities should still remain, they would not be so great, so uniform in their operation, or so odious in appearance as those that must arise from quotas on any scale that could possibly be devised.

A signal advantage of taxes on articles of consumption is that by their own nature they carry a safeguard against excess. They set their own limit, which cannot be passed without defeating the very purpose, which is to increase the revenue. Applied to this subject, the saying is as true as it is witty that "in political arithmetic, two and two do not always make four." If duties are too high, they reduce consumption, people evade the collection, and the yield to the treasury is smaller than when the duties are kept within proper and moderate bounds. This forms a complete barrier against any serious oppression of the citizens by taxes of this class, and is itself a natural limit on the power to impose them.

Taxes of this kind usually fall under the name of indirect taxes, and for a long time they must make up the chief part of the revenue raised in this country. Direct taxes, which relate mainly to land and buildings, may admit of a rule of apportionment. Either the value of land or the number of the people may serve as the standard. The condition of agriculture and the size of a country's population have been regarded as closely connected. And as a rule for the purpose intended, numbers deserve the preference for their simplicity and certainty. In every country, getting a valuation of the land is a herculean task. In a country only partly settled and still improving, the difficulties grow almost to the point of impossibility. The cost of an accurate valuation is, in all situations, a formidable objection. In a branch of taxation where the nature of things sets no limits to the government's discretion, establishing a fixed rule that does not conflict with the purpose may bring fewer drawbacks than leaving that discretion wholly unrestrained.

chapters.title: No. 22 — The Same Subject Continued (Other Defects of the Present Confederation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Besides the defects already listed in the existing federal system, there are others of equal importance, and together they make it altogether unfit for managing the affairs of the Union.

All parties admit that the lack of a power to regulate commerce is one of these. I anticipated the usefulness of such a power under the first head of our inquiries, and for that reason, and because everyone is convinced of it, little needs to be added here. Even at the most superficial glance it is evident that no object, whether for the interests of trade or of finance, more strongly calls for federal oversight. The lack of it has already blocked the making of beneficial treaties with foreign powers and has caused dissatisfaction among the States. No nation that understands the nature of our political association would be foolish enough to make agreements with the United States in which it gave up privileges of any importance to itself, when it knew that the Union's commitments could be broken at any moment by its members, and when experience showed that it could enjoy every advantage it wanted in our markets without granting us anything in return except what its momentary convenience might suggest. It is no wonder, then, that Mr. Jenkinson, when he brought into the House of Commons a bill to regulate the temporary dealings between the two countries, began by declaring that similar provisions in earlier bills had served every purpose for the commerce of Great Britain, and that it would be prudent to stay with the plan until it became clear whether the American government was likely to gain greater stability.(1)

Several States have tried, through separate prohibitions, restrictions, and exclusions, to influence the conduct of that kingdom in this respect. But the lack of concert, which comes from the lack of a general authority and from the clashing and dissimilar views of the States, has so far defeated every such experiment, and will keep defeating them as long as the same obstacles to uniform measures remain.

The meddling and unneighborly regulations of some States, contrary to the true spirit of the Union, have in different instances given other States just cause for offense and complaint. It is to be feared that if a national control does not restrain such examples, they will multiply and spread until they become as serious a source of animosity and discord as they are a harmful obstacle to trade between the different parts of the Confederacy. "The commerce of the German empire(2) is in continual trammels from the multiplicity of the duties which the several princes and states exact upon the merchandises passing through their territories, by means of which the fine streams and navigable rivers with which Germany is so happily watered are rendered almost useless." The character of the people of this country might never allow this description to apply to us strictly.
