Still, from the gradual clashes of State regulations we may reasonably expect that the citizens of each State would in the end come to be regarded and treated by the others as no better than foreigners and aliens.

On the plainest reading of the articles of the Confederation, the power of raising armies is merely a power to make requisitions on the States for quotas of men. In the recent war, this practice was found full of obstacles to a vigorous and economical system of defense. It gave rise to a competition among the States that turned into a kind of auction for men. To supply the quotas required of them, they outbid each other until the bounties grew to an enormous and unsupportable size. The hope that they would rise still further gave those inclined to serve a reason to put off enlisting, and made them unwilling to sign on for any considerable period. The results were slow and scanty levies of men in the most critical emergencies of our affairs; short enlistments at an unparalleled expense; and continual shifts in the troops, which ruined their discipline and often exposed the public safety to the perilous crisis of a disbanded army. Hence also came the oppressive expedients for raising men that were used on several occasions, and which nothing but enthusiasm for liberty would have led the people to endure.

This method of raising troops is no more friendly to economy and vigor than it is to an equal distribution of the burden. The States near the seat of war, moved by the need to preserve themselves, made efforts to supply their quotas that even exceeded their abilities, while those far from danger were for the most part as slack in their exertions as the others were diligent. In this case, unlike the case of money contributions, the immediate weight of this inequality was not eased by the hope of a final settling of accounts. The States that did not pay their share of money could at least be charged with their deficiencies, but no account could be made of the deficiencies in the supply of men. We shall not see much reason to regret the lack of that hope, however, when we consider how little prospect there is that the most delinquent States will ever be able to make up their failures in money. The system of quotas and requisitions, whether applied to men or to money, is in every view a system of weakness in the Union and of inequality and injustice among the members.

Equal suffrage among the States is another part of the Confederation that deserves objection. Every notion of proportion and every rule of fair representation argues against a principle that puts Rhode Island on an equal footing in the scale of power with Massachusetts, Connecticut, or New York, and gives Delaware the same voice in national deliberations as Pennsylvania, Virginia, or North Carolina. It contradicts the fundamental maxim of republican government, which requires that the sense of the majority should prevail. Sophistry may reply that sovereigns are equal, and that a majority of the votes of the States will be a majority of confederated America. But this kind of logical sleight of hand will never overcome the plain suggestions of justice and common sense. It may happen that this majority of States is a small minority of the people of America;(3) and two thirds of the people of America could not long be persuaded, on the strength of artificial distinctions and syllogistic subtleties, to submit their interests to the management and disposal of one third. The larger States would after a while revolt against receiving the law from the smaller. To accept such a deprivation of their due importance in the political scale would be not merely to be insensible to the love of power but even to give up the desire for equality. It is neither reasonable to expect the first nor just to require the last. The smaller States, considering how peculiarly their safety and welfare depend on union, ought readily to give up a pretension that, if it is not relinquished, would prove fatal to the union's survival.

It may be objected that the most important resolutions need the consent not of seven but of nine States, or two thirds of the whole number, and from this it may be inferred that nine States would always include a majority of the Union. But this does not remove the impropriety of an equal vote between States of the most unequal size and population. Nor is the inference accurate as a matter of fact, for we can name nine States that contain less than a majority of the people;(4) and it is constitutionally possible for these nine to carry the vote. Besides, there are matters of considerable moment that a bare majority can decide, and there are others, about which doubts have been raised, that would reach interests of the first magnitude if they were interpreted in favor of the sufficiency of a vote of seven States. In addition, the number of States will probably increase, and no provision has been made for a proportional increase in the ratio of votes.

But this is not all. What at first sight may seem a remedy is in reality a poison. To give a minority a negative on the majority (which is always the case where more than a majority is required for a decision) is in its tendency to subject the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser. Because a few States failed to attend, Congress has often been in the situation of a Polish diet, where a single VOTE has been enough to stop all its movements. A sixtieth part of the Union, which is about the proportion of Delaware and Rhode Island, has several times been able to put a complete bar on its operations. This is one of those refinements that in practice has an effect the reverse of what theory expects of it. The demand for unanimity in public bodies, or for something approaching it, rests on the supposition that it would add to security. But what it really does is to embarrass the administration, to destroy the energy of the government, and to put the pleasure, caprice, or artifices of an insignificant, turbulent, or corrupt junto in place of the regular deliberations and decisions of a respectable majority. In those emergencies of a nation when the goodness or badness, the weakness or strength, of its government matters most, there is commonly a necessity for action. The public business must go forward in some way. If a stubborn minority can control the opinion of a majority about the best way to conduct it, then the majority, in order that something may be done, must conform to the views of the minority. In this way the sense of the smaller number will overrule that of the greater and set the tone of the national proceedings. The result is tedious delays, continual negotiation and intrigue, and contemptible compromises of the public good. And yet in such a system it is even fortunate when such compromises can be made, for on some occasions things will not allow of accommodation, and then the measures of government must be harmfully suspended or fatally defeated. Often the government is kept in a state of inaction by the impossibility of obtaining the agreement of the necessary number of votes. Its situation must always savor of weakness and sometimes border on anarchy.

It is not hard to see that a principle of this kind gives more scope to foreign corruption, as well as to domestic faction, than the principle that lets the sense of the majority decide, though the opposite has been assumed. The mistake has come from not paying due attention to the harms that may result from obstructing the progress of government at certain critical times. When the Constitution requires the agreement of a large number for any national act, we tend to rest satisfied that all is safe, because nothing improper is likely TO BE DONE. But we forget how much good may be prevented, and how much ill may be produced, by the power to hinder the doing of what may be necessary, and to keep affairs in the same unfavorable position in which they happen to stand at particular times.

Suppose, for instance, that we were at war, together with one foreign nation, against another. Suppose the necessity of our situation called for peace, and the interest or ambition of our ally led him to want to continue the war, with aims that might justify us in making separate terms. In such a situation, this ally of ours would plainly find it much easier, by his bribes and intrigues, to keep the government from making peace where two thirds of all the votes were required for that purpose than where a simple majority would be enough. In the first case he would have to corrupt a smaller number, and in the other a greater. On the same principle, it would be much easier for a foreign power with which we were at war to confuse our councils and hinder our exertions. And in matters of trade we may suffer similar problems. A nation with which we might have a commercial treaty could much more easily prevent our forming a connection with her competitor in trade, even if such a connection would be ever so beneficial to ourselves.

Evils of this kind should not be regarded as imaginary. One of the weak sides of republics, among their many advantages, is that they open too easy an entrance to foreign corruption. A hereditary monarch, though often willing to sacrifice his subjects to his ambition, has so great a personal stake in the government and in the nation's glory abroad that it is not easy for a foreign power to offer him an equivalent for what he would give up by betraying the state. The world has accordingly seen few examples of this kind of royal prostitution, though it has seen plenty of every other kind.

In republics, persons raised from the mass of the community by the votes of their fellow-citizens to positions of great eminence and power may find rewards for betraying their trust. To any but minds animated and guided by superior virtue, these rewards may seem to exceed the share of interest they have in the common stock and to outweigh the obligations of duty. This is why history gives us so many humiliating examples of the prevalence of foreign corruption in republican governments. How much this contributed to the ruin of the ancient commonwealths has already been described. It is well known that the deputies of the United Provinces have in various instances been bought by the emissaries of neighboring kingdoms. The Earl of Chesterfield (if my memory serves me right), in a letter to his court, hinted that the success of an important negotiation depended on his obtaining a major's commission for one of those deputies. And in Sweden the parties were bought in turn by France and England so openly and notoriously that it aroused universal disgust in the nation. It was a principal cause of the transformation, in a single day, without tumult, violence, or opposition, of the most limited monarchy in Europe into one of the most absolute and uncontrolled.

One circumstance that crowns the defects of the Confederation remains to be mentioned: the lack of a judicial power. Laws are a dead letter without courts to explain and define their true meaning and operation. The treaties of the United States, to have any force at all, must be considered part of the law of the land. Their true meaning, so far as individuals are concerned, must be settled, like all other laws, by judicial decisions. To make these decisions uniform, they ought to be submitted, in the last resort, to one SUPREME COURT. And this court ought to be established under the same authority that makes the treaties themselves. Both of these ingredients are indispensable. If each State has a court of final jurisdiction, there may be as many different final decisions on the same point as there are courts. Men's opinions differ endlessly. We often see not only different courts but the judges of the same court disagreeing with each other. To avoid the confusion that would inevitably follow from the contradictory decisions of a number of independent courts, all nations have found it necessary to establish one court above the rest, with general oversight, and with authority to settle and declare in the last resort a uniform rule of civil justice.

The need is greater still where the government is built in such a compound way that the laws of the whole are in danger of being overridden by the laws of the parts. In that situation, if the individual courts hold the right of final jurisdiction, we must expect contradictions from differences of opinion, and we have much to fear from the bias of local views and prejudices and from the clash of local regulations. Every time such a clash occurred, there would be reason to dread that the particular laws would be preferred to the general laws, for nothing is more natural to men in office than to show special deference to the authority to which they owe their official existence.

Under the present Constitution, the treaties of the United States are open to violation by thirteen different legislatures and as many different courts of final jurisdiction acting under those legislatures' authority. The good faith, the reputation, and the peace of the whole Union are thus continually at the mercy of the prejudices, passions, and interests of each member of which it is composed. Can foreign nations possibly respect or trust such a government? Can the people of America possibly consent any longer to trust their honor, their happiness, and their safety to so precarious a foundation?

In this review of the Confederation I have confined myself to showing its most material defects. I have passed over the imperfections in its details, through which even a great part of the power meant to be conferred on it has been largely nullified. By this time it must be evident to all thoughtful men who can rid themselves of the prepossessions of preconceived opinions that it is a system so radically vicious and unsound that it admits of no amendment short of an entire change in its leading features and character.

The organization of Congress is itself utterly unsuited to exercising the powers that must be placed in the Union. A single assembly may be a proper holder for the slender, or rather fettered, authorities that have so far been delegated to the federal head. But it would contradict all the principles of good government to entrust it with the additional powers that even the moderate and more reasonable opponents of the proposed Constitution admit ought to reside in the United States. Suppose that plan is not adopted, and suppose the necessity of the Union can withstand the ambitious aims of those who may entertain grand schemes of personal aggrandizement from its dissolution. The probability would then be that we should fall upon the project of giving supplementary powers to Congress as it is now constituted. Then one of two things would happen. Either the machine, from the inherent feebleness of its structure, will crumble to pieces in spite of our ill-judged efforts to prop it up; or, by successive increases of its force and energy as necessity may prompt, we shall finally gather into a single body all the most important prerogatives of sovereignty, and so leave our posterity one of the most execrable forms of government that human folly ever contrived. We should thus create in reality the very tyranny that the opponents of the new Constitution either are, or pretend to be, anxious to avert.

The existing federal system has been weakened not a little by the fact that the PEOPLE never ratified it. It rests on nothing firmer than the consent of the individual legislatures. As a result, it has been exposed to frequent and intricate questions about the validity of its powers, and in some instances it has produced the monstrous doctrine of a right of legislative repeal. Because it owes its ratification to the law of a State, some have argued that the same authority could repeal the law by which it was ratified. To maintain that a PARTY to a COMPACT may revoke that COMPACT is a gross heresy, yet the doctrine has found respectable advocates. That such a question can even be raised proves that we must lay the foundations of our national government deeper than the mere sanction of delegated authority. The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE. The streams of national power ought to flow directly from that pure, original fountain of all legitimate authority.
1. This, as nearly as I can recollect, was the sense of his speech on introducing the last bill.
2. Encyclopedia, article "Empire."
3. New Hampshire, Rhode Island, New Jersey, Delaware, Georgia, South Carolina, and Maryland are a majority of the whole number of the States, but they do not contain one third of the people.
4. Add New York and Connecticut to the foregoing seven, and they will be less than a majority.

chapters.title: No. 23 — The Necessity of a Government as Energetic as the One Proposed to the Preservation of the Union (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The point we have now reached for examination is the necessity, for the preservation of the Union, of a Constitution at least as energetic as the one proposed.

This inquiry will naturally divide into three branches: the objects the federal government must provide for; the amount of power needed to accomplish those objects; and the persons on whom that power ought to operate. How that power should be distributed and organized will more properly claim our attention under the next head.

The principal purposes that union must serve are these: the common defense of the members; the preservation of the public peace, against internal convulsions as well as external attacks; the regulation of commerce with other nations and among the States; and the oversight of our dealings, political and commercial, with foreign countries.

Defending the members in common requires the following authorities: to raise armies; to build and equip fleets; to prescribe the rules that govern both; to direct their operations; and to provide for their upkeep. These powers should be unlimited, BECAUSE IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO FORESEE OR DEFINE THE EXTENT AND VARIETY OF NATIONAL EXIGENCIES, OR THE CORRESPONDENT EXTENT AND VARIETY OF THE MEANS WHICH MAY BE NECESSARY TO SATISFY THEM. There is no end to the circumstances that endanger the safety of nations, and so it would be unwise to put constitutional shackles on the power entrusted with that safety. This power should reach as far as every possible combination of such circumstances, and should be directed by the same councils that are appointed to preside over the common defense.

This is one of those truths that carry their own evidence with them to a sound and unprejudiced mind. Argument and reasoning may obscure it but cannot make it plainer. It rests on axioms as simple as they are universal: the MEANS ought to be proportioned to the END, and the persons from whose action the attainment of any END is expected ought to possess the MEANS by which it is to be attained.

Whether there ought to be a federal government entrusted with the common defense is, at the outset, an open question for discussion. But the moment it is decided in the affirmative, it follows that this government ought to be given all the powers required to carry out its trust completely. Unless it can be shown that the circumstances that may affect the public safety can be confined within certain definite limits, and unless the opposite of this position can be fairly and reasonably disputed, we must admit as a necessary consequence that there can be no limit on the authority that is to provide for the defense and protection of the community, in any matter essential to its effectiveness, that is, in any matter essential to the FORMATION, DIRECTION, or SUPPORT of the NATIONAL FORCES.

The present Confederation has proved defective, but its framers appear to have fully recognized this principle, though they did not make proper or adequate provision for exercising it. Congress has unlimited discretion to make requisitions for men and money, to govern the army and navy, and to direct their operations. Because its requisitions are made constitutionally binding on the States, which are in fact under the most solemn obligation to furnish the supplies required of them, the intention was evidently that the United States should command whatever resources they judged necessary for the "common defense and general welfare." It was assumed that a sense of their true interests and a regard for the dictates of good faith would be sufficient pledges that the members would punctually perform their duty to the federal head.

The experiment has shown, however, that this expectation was ill-founded and illusory. The observations made under the last head will, I believe, have been enough to convince the impartial and discerning that the first principles of the system must be changed entirely. If we are in earnest about giving the Union energy and durability, we must abandon the vain project of legislating for the States in their collective capacities. We must extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America. We must discard the deceptive scheme of quotas and requisitions as equally impracticable and unjust. The result of all this is that the Union ought to be given full power to levy troops, to build and equip fleets, and to raise the revenues needed to form and support an army and navy, in the customary and ordinary ways practiced in other governments.

Suppose the circumstances of our country call for a compound government instead of a simple one, a confederate government instead of a single one. The essential point left to settle will then be to distinguish, as far as possible, the OBJECTS that belong to the different provinces or departments of power, giving each the fullest authority to fulfill the objects committed to its charge. Shall the Union be made the guardian of the common safety? Are fleets, armies, and revenues necessary for this purpose? Then the government of the Union must be empowered to pass all laws and make all regulations that relate to them. The same must hold for commerce, and for every other matter to which its jurisdiction is allowed to extend. Is the administration of justice between citizens of the same State the proper department of the local governments? Then they must hold all the authorities connected with this object, and with every other that may be assigned to their particular care and direction. Not to give each, in every case, a degree of power matching its end would violate the most obvious rules of prudence and propriety, and would rashly entrust the great interests of the nation to hands that are disabled from managing them with vigor and success.

Who is more likely to make suitable provision for the public defense than the body to which the guardianship of the public safety is entrusted? As the center of information, it will best understand the extent and urgency of the dangers that threaten. As the representative of the WHOLE, it will feel itself most deeply interested in the preservation of every part. From the responsibility that goes with its assigned duty, it will be most keenly impressed with the necessity of proper exertions. And by extending its authority throughout the States, it alone can establish uniformity and concert in the plans and measures by which the common safety is to be secured. Is there not a manifest inconsistency in laying on the federal government the care of the general defense, while leaving in the State governments the EFFECTIVE powers by which it is to be provided for? Is not lack of cooperation the certain consequence of such a system? And will not weakness, disorder, an unfair distribution of the burdens and calamities of war, and an unnecessary and intolerable increase of expense be its natural and unavoidable companions? Have we not had unmistakable experience of its effects in the course of the revolution we have just accomplished?

Every view we may take of the subject, as fair inquirers after truth, will convince us that it is both unwise and dangerous to deny the federal government unconfined authority over all the objects entrusted to its management. It will indeed deserve the most vigilant and careful attention of the people to see that it is shaped in such a way that it can safely be given the requisite powers. If any plan that has been, or may be, offered for our consideration should not, on dispassionate inspection, be found to answer this description, it ought to be rejected. A government whose constitution makes it unfit to be trusted with all the powers that a free people ought to delegate to any government would be an unsafe and improper keeper of the NATIONAL INTERESTS. Wherever THESE can properly be confided, the accompanying powers may safely go with them. This is the true result of all sound reasoning on the subject. And the opponents of the plan put forward by the Convention ought to have confined themselves to showing that the internal structure of the proposed government was such as to make it unworthy of the people's confidence. They ought not to have wandered into inflammatory declamations and meaningless quibbles about the extent of the powers. The POWERS are not too extensive for the OBJECTS of federal administration, or, in other words, for the management of our NATIONAL INTERESTS; nor can any satisfactory argument be framed to show that they are chargeable with such an excess. Suppose it is true, as some of the writers on the other side have hinted, that the difficulty arises from the nature of the thing, and that the size of the country will not allow us to form a government in which such ample powers can safely be placed. That would prove that we ought to narrow our views and resort to the expedient of separate confederacies, which will move within more practicable spheres. For the absurdity must continually stare us in the face of confiding to a government the direction of the most essential national interests without daring to trust it with the authorities indispensable to their proper and effective management. Let us not try to reconcile contradictions, but firmly embrace a rational alternative.

I trust, however, that the impracticability of one general system cannot be shown. I am greatly mistaken if anything of weight has yet been advanced to that effect, and I flatter myself that the observations made in the course of these papers have placed the opposite position in as clear a light as any matter still in the womb of time and experience can be made to appear. At all events, this much must be evident: the very difficulty drawn from the extent of the country is the strongest argument in favor of an energetic government, for any other can certainly never preserve the Union of so large an empire. If we adopt the tenets of those who oppose the proposed Constitution as the standard of our political creed, we cannot fail to bear out the gloomy doctrines that predict the impracticability of a national system reaching across the entire limits of the present Confederacy.

chapters.title: No. 24 — The Powers Necessary to the Common Defense Further Considered (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Of all the powers proposed to be given to the federal government for creating and directing the national forces, I have met with only one specific objection. If I understand it correctly, it is that proper provision has not been made against standing armies in time of peace. I shall now try to show that this objection rests on weak and unsubstantial foundations.

It has indeed been put forward in the vaguest and most general form, supported only by bold assertions, with no appearance of argument and not even the backing of theoretical opinion. It contradicts the practice of other free nations and the general sense of America, as expressed in most of the existing constitutions. The correctness of this remark will be plain the moment we recall that the objection turns on a supposed need to restrain the LEGISLATIVE authority of the nation in the matter of military establishments. That principle is unheard of except in one or two of our State constitutions, and all the rest reject it.

Suppose a stranger to our politics were to read our newspapers at the present moment without having examined the plan reported by the Convention. He would naturally be led to one of two conclusions: either that the plan contained a positive command that standing armies be kept up in time of peace, or that it gave the EXECUTIVE the whole power of levying troops, without making his discretion subject in any way to the control of the legislature.

If he then went on to read the plan itself, he would be surprised to find that neither was the case. He would find that the whole power of raising armies was placed in the LEGISLATURE, not in the EXECUTIVE; that this legislature was to be a popular body, made up of representatives of the people elected at regular intervals; and that, instead of the provision in favor of standing armies he had imagined, there was on this subject an important limit even on the legislature's discretion. This is the clause that forbids appropriating money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years. On a closer look, this precaution will prove to be a great and real security against keeping up troops without evident necessity.

Disappointed in his first guess, the person I have imagined would be inclined to carry his conjectures a little further. He would naturally say to himself that all this vehement and passionate declamation cannot be without some plausible pretext. It must be, he would reason, that this people, so jealous of their liberties, have inserted the most precise and rigid precautions on this point in all the earlier models of the constitutions they have established, and that the omission of these precautions from the new plan has given rise to all this alarm and clamor.

Suppose that, with this impression, he went on to review the individual State constitutions. How great would be his disappointment to find that TWO ONLY of them(1) contained a ban on standing armies in time of peace, and that the other eleven had either kept a profound silence on the subject or had expressly admitted the right of the Legislature to authorize their existence.

Still, he would be persuaded that there must be some plausible foundation for the cry raised on this subject. While any source of information remained unexplored, he could never imagine that it was nothing more than an experiment on the public's credulity, prompted either by a deliberate intention to deceive or by an excess of zeal too intemperate to be honest. It would probably occur to him that he might find the precautions he was looking for in the original compact between the States. Here, at last, he would expect to find the answer to the puzzle. No doubt, he would tell himself, the existing Confederation must contain the most explicit provisions against military establishments in time of peace, and a departure from this model on a favorite point has produced the discontent that seems to move these political champions.

Suppose he now applied himself to a careful and critical study of the Articles of Confederation. His astonishment would not only grow but would take on a touch of indignation, at the unexpected discovery that the Articles do not contain the prohibition he looked for. With jealous caution they had restricted the authority of the State legislatures in this respect, but they had not imposed a single restraint on that of the United States. If he happened to be a man of quick feeling or ardent temper, he could no longer refrain from regarding these clamors as the dishonest tricks of a sinister and unprincipled opposition to a plan that ought at least to receive a fair and open-minded examination from all sincere lovers of their country. How else, he would ask, could the authors of these clamors have been tempted to utter such loud censures on the plan about a point on which it seems to have conformed to the general sense of America, as declared in its different forms of government, and on which it has even added a new and powerful safeguard unknown to any of them? If, on the contrary, he happened to be a man of calm and dispassionate feelings, he would sigh over the frailty of human nature and lament that, in a matter so important to the happiness of millions, the true merits of the question should be confused and entangled by expedients so unfriendly to an impartial and correct judgment. Even such a man could hardly keep from remarking that conduct of this kind has too much the appearance of an intention to mislead the people by alarming their passions, rather than to convince them by arguments addressed to their understanding.

But however little this objection is supported even by precedents among ourselves, it may be worthwhile to take a closer look at its intrinsic merits. A close examination will show that restraints on the legislature's discretion over military establishments in time of peace would be improper to impose and, if imposed, would be unlikely to be observed, given the necessities of society.

Though a wide ocean separates the United States from Europe, there are various considerations that warn us against excessive confidence or security. On one side of us, stretching far to our rear, are growing settlements under the dominion of Britain. On the other side, extending to meet the British settlements, are colonies and establishments under the dominion of Spain. This situation, together with the nearness of the West India Islands belonging to these two powers, creates between them a common interest in regard to their American possessions and in relation to us. The savage tribes on our Western frontier ought to be regarded as our natural enemies and their natural allies, because they have most to fear from us and most to hope from them. Improvements in the art of navigation have, in making communication easier, made distant nations in great measure neighbors. Britain and Spain are among the principal maritime powers of Europe. A future agreement of aims between these nations ought not to be regarded as improbable. The growing distance of the blood relationship is every day weakening the force of the family compact between France and Spain, and politicians have always, with great reason, considered ties of blood to be feeble and uncertain links of political connection. Taken together, these circumstances warn us not to be too sanguine in thinking ourselves entirely out of the reach of danger.

Before the Revolution, and ever since the peace, there has been a constant necessity for keeping small garrisons on our Western frontier. No one can doubt that these will continue to be indispensable, if only against the ravages and plundering of the Indians. These garrisons must be supplied either by occasional detachments from the militia or by permanent corps in the pay of the government. The first is impracticable, and if it were practicable it would be harmful. The militia would not long submit, if at all, to being dragged from their occupations and families to perform that most disagreeable duty in times of profound peace. And if they could be persuaded or compelled to do it, the greater expense of frequent rotation of service, together with the loss of labor and the disruption of the productive pursuits of individuals, would be conclusive objections to the scheme. It would be as burdensome and injurious to the public as it would be ruinous to private citizens. The second resource, permanent corps in the pay of the government, amounts to a standing army in time of peace: a small one, indeed, but no less real for being small. Here is a simple view of the subject, and it shows us at once how improper a constitutional ban on such establishments would be, and how necessary it is to leave the matter to the discretion and prudence of the legislature.

As our strength increases, it is probable, indeed it may be said to be certain, that Britain and Spain will enlarge their military establishments in our neighborhood. If we are unwilling to be exposed, naked and defenseless, to their insults and encroachments, we shall find it advisable to increase our frontier garrisons in some proportion to the force that could harass our Western settlements. There are, and will be, particular posts whose possession will include command of large districts of territory and will make future invasions of the rest easier. It may be added that some of those posts will be keys to the trade with the Indian nations. Can anyone think it would be wise to leave such posts in a condition to be seized at any moment by one or the other of two neighboring and formidable powers? To act in that way would be to abandon all the usual maxims of prudence and policy.

If we mean to be a commercial people, or even to be secure on our Atlantic side, we must try to have a navy as soon as possible. For this purpose there must be dock-yards and arsenals, and for the defense of these, fortifications and probably garrisons. When a nation has become so powerful by sea that it can protect its dock-yards with its fleets, this removes the need for garrisons for that purpose. But where naval establishments are in their infancy, moderate garrisons will in all likelihood prove an indispensable security against landings aimed at destroying the arsenals and dock-yards, and sometimes the fleet itself.

1 This account of the matter is taken from the printed collection of State constitutions. Pennsylvania and North Carolina are the two that contain the ban, in these words: "As standing armies in time of peace are dangerous to liberty, THEY OUGHT NOT to be kept up." This is, in truth, rather a CAUTION than a PROHIBITION. New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Delaware, and Maryland have, in each of their bills of rights, a clause to this effect: "Standing armies are dangerous to liberty, and ought not to be raised or kept up WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF THE LEGISLATURE"; which is a formal admission of the authority of the Legislature. New York has no bill of rights, and her constitution says not a word about the matter. No bills of rights appear attached to the constitutions of the other States, except those just mentioned, and their constitutions are equally silent. I am told, however, that one or two States have bills of rights that do not appear in this collection, but that those also recognize the right of the legislative authority in this respect.

chapters.title: No. 25 — The Same Subject Continued (The Powers Necessary to the Common Defense Further Considered) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It may perhaps be argued that the objects listed in the preceding number ought to be provided for by the State governments, under the direction of the Union. But this would in reality invert the first principle of our political association, since in practice it would transfer the care of the common defense from the federal head to the individual members. Such a scheme would be oppressive to some States, dangerous to all, and ruinous to the Confederacy.

The territories of Britain, Spain, and the Indian nations in our neighborhood do not border on particular States but encircle the Union from Maine to Georgia. The danger, though in different degrees, is therefore common. And the means of guarding against it ought, in the same way, to be the business of common councils and of a common treasury. It happens that some States, because of their location, are more directly exposed. New York is one of these. Under a plan of separate provisions, New York would have to bear the whole weight of the establishments needed for her own immediate safety and for the indirect or ultimate protection of her neighbors. This would be neither fair to New York nor safe for the other States. Various problems would attend such a system. The States that happened to be assigned the support of the necessary establishments would be as little able as willing, for a considerable time to come, to bear the burden of adequate provision. The security of all would thus be subject to the stinginess, improvidence, or inability of a part. Suppose the resources of that part grew more abundant and extensive, and its provisions were enlarged in proportion. The other States would quickly take alarm at seeing the whole military force of the Union in the hands of two or three of its members, and those probably among the most powerful. Each would choose to have some counterweight, and pretexts could easily be contrived. In this situation, military establishments fed by mutual jealousy would tend to swell beyond their natural or proper size, and, being at the separate disposal of the members, they would be instruments for cutting down or destroying the national authority.

Reasons have already been given for supposing that the State governments will all too naturally tend to rivalry with that of the Union, a rivalry founded on the love of power, and that in any contest between the federal head and one of its members the people will be most inclined to side with their local government. Suppose that, on top of this immense advantage, the ambition of the members were stimulated by their separate and independent possession of military forces. That would give them too strong a temptation, and too great a facility, to make attempts on the constitutional authority of the Union and finally to overthrow it. On the other hand, the liberty of the people would be less safe in this state of things than in one that left the national forces in the hands of the national government. To the extent that an army may be considered a dangerous weapon of power, it had better be in the hands the people are most likely to be jealous of than in those they are least likely to be jealous of. For it is a truth, attested by the experience of ages, that the people are always in the most danger when the means of injuring their rights are in the possession of those they suspect least.

The framers of the existing Confederation, fully aware of the danger to the Union from the States' separate possession of military forces, have expressly prohibited them from having either ships or troops without the consent of Congress. The truth is that a federal government and military establishments under State authority are no less at odds with each other than an adequate supply of the federal treasury is with the system of quotas and requisitions.

There are other lights, besides those already noticed, in which the impropriety of restraints on the discretion of the national legislature will be equally plain. The aim of the objection I have mentioned is to rule out standing armies in time of peace. Yet we have never been told how far the prohibition is meant to extend, whether to raising armies as well as to KEEPING THEM UP in a season of tranquillity, or not. If it is confined to the latter, it will have no precise meaning and will not achieve its intended purpose. When armies have once been raised, what shall be called "keeping them up" contrary to the sense of the Constitution? What length of time will be required to establish the violation? Shall it be a week, a month, a year? Or shall we say they may be continued as long as the danger that caused them to be raised continues? This would be to admit that they might be kept up IN TIME OF PEACE, against threatening or impending danger, which would at once depart from the literal meaning of the prohibition and introduce a wide latitude of interpretation. Who shall judge whether the danger continues? This must undoubtedly be left to the national government, and the matter would then come down to this: to provide against apprehended danger, the national government might in the first instance raise troops, and might afterwards keep them on foot as long as it supposed the peace or safety of the community to be in any degree of jeopardy. It is easy to see that so broad a discretion would leave ample room for evading the force of the provision.

The supposed usefulness of a provision of this kind can be founded only on the supposed probability, or at least possibility, of a combination between the executive and the legislative in some scheme of usurpation. Should this ever happen, how easy it would be to fabricate pretexts of approaching danger! Indian hostilities, stirred up by Spain or Britain, would always be at hand. Provocations to produce the desired appearances might even be given to some foreign power, and then soothed again by timely concessions. If we can reasonably suppose such a combination to have been formed, and the enterprise to be justified by a sufficient prospect of success, then the army, once raised, from whatever cause or on whatever pretext, may be used to carry out the plan.

Suppose that, to prevent this consequence, it were resolved to extend the prohibition to the RAISING of armies in time of peace. The United States would then present the most extraordinary spectacle the world has yet seen: a nation made incapable by its Constitution of preparing for defense before it was actually invaded. Since the ceremony of a formal declaration of war has lately fallen into disuse, we would have to wait for the presence of an enemy within our territories as the legal warrant for the government to begin levying men for the protection of the State. We must receive the blow before we could even prepare to return it. All that kind of policy by which nations anticipate distant danger and meet the gathering storm must be avoided, as contrary to the true maxims of a free government. We must expose our property and liberty to the mercy of foreign invaders, and invite them by our weakness to seize a naked and defenseless prey, because we are afraid that rulers created by our choice and dependent on our will might endanger that liberty by abusing the means necessary to its preservation.

At this point I expect we will be told that the country's natural bulwark is its militia, and that the militia would always be enough for the national defense. In substance, this doctrine nearly cost us our independence, and it cost the United States millions that could have been saved. The lessons of our own experience that forbid relying on the militia in this way are too fresh for us to be taken in by the suggestion. Only a force of the same regular, disciplined kind can successfully carry on the sustained operations of war against a regular and disciplined army. Considerations of economy, no less than of stability and vigor, confirm this. In the recent war the American militia, by their valor on many occasions, raised eternal monuments to their fame. Yet the bravest of them feel and know that the liberty of their country could not have been won by their efforts alone, however great and valuable those efforts were. War, like most other things, is a science, and it is learned and perfected only through diligence, perseverance, time, and practice.

Any policy that does violence to the natural and well-known course of human affairs defeats itself. Pennsylvania offers an example of this right now. Her Bill of Rights declares that standing armies are dangerous to liberty and ought not to be kept up in time of peace. Yet in a time of profound peace, because of local disorders in one or two of her counties, Pennsylvania has resolved to raise a body of troops, and she will in all probability keep them up as long as the public peace appears to be in any danger. Massachusetts offers a lesson on the same subject, though on different ground. That State was compelled to raise troops to put down a domestic insurrection, and she did so without waiting for the approval of Congress that the Articles of Confederation require. She still keeps a corps in pay to prevent the spirit of revolt from reviving. The particular constitution of Massachusetts put no obstacle in the way of this measure. But the case still teaches us that situations are likely to arise under our government, as under those of other nations, in which a military force in time of peace will sometimes be essential to the security of society, and that it is therefore improper in this respect to control the legislature's discretion. Applied to the United States, it also shows how little the rights of a weak government are likely to be respected, even by its own constituents. And it shows us, besides, how poorly matched parchment provisions are against public necessity.

It was a fundamental maxim of the Lacedaemonian commonwealth that the post of admiral should not be given twice to the same person. The Peloponnesian allies, having suffered a severe defeat at sea by the Athenians, demanded Lysander, who had earlier served successfully in that capacity, to command the combined fleets. The Lacedaemonians, to please their allies and yet keep up the appearance of adhering to their ancient institutions, resorted to the flimsy subterfuge of giving Lysander the real power of admiral under the nominal title of vice-admiral. This instance is chosen from a multitude that might be cited to confirm the truth already stated and illustrated by examples from our own country: that nations pay little regard to rules and maxims that by their very nature run counter to the necessities of society. Wise politicians will be cautious about fettering the government with restrictions that cannot be observed. They know that every breach of the fundamental laws, though dictated by necessity, impairs the sacred reverence that rulers ought to feel toward the constitution of a country, and creates a precedent for other breaches where the same plea of necessity does not exist at all, or is less urgent and obvious.

chapters.title: No. 26 — The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It could hardly be expected that, in a popular revolution, men's minds would stop at that happy mean which marks the beneficial boundary between POWER and PRIVILEGE and combines the energy of government with the security of private rights. A failure on this delicate and important point is the great source of the problems we now experience. If we are not careful to avoid repeating the error in our future attempts to correct and improve our system, we may travel from one fantastic project to another and try change after change, yet never be likely to make any material change for the better.

The idea of restraining the legislative authority in the means of providing for the national defense is one of those refinements that owe their origin to a zeal for liberty more ardent than enlightened. We have seen, however, that it has not so far been widely accepted. Even in this country, where it first appeared, Pennsylvania and North Carolina are the only two States that have favored it to any degree, and all the others have refused to give it the least support. They wisely judged that confidence must be placed somewhere, that the necessity of doing so is implied in the very act of delegating power, and that it is better to risk an abuse of that confidence than to hamper the government and endanger the public safety by unwise restrictions on the legislative authority. In this respect the opponents of the proposed Constitution fight against the general decision of America. Instead of being taught by experience to correct any extremes we may have run into before, they seem ready to lead us into others still more dangerous and more extravagant. As if the tone of government had been found too high or too rigid, the doctrines they teach are calculated to lower or relax it by expedients that, on other occasions, have been condemned or avoided. It may be affirmed, without any charge of invective, that if the principles they teach on various points were to prevail so far as to become the popular creed, they would utterly unfit the people of this country for any kind of government whatever. But a danger of this kind is not to be feared. The citizens of America have too much discernment to be argued into anarchy. And I am much mistaken if experience has not produced a deep and solemn conviction in the public mind that greater energy of government is essential to the welfare and prosperity of the community.

It may not be amiss here to remark briefly on the origin and progress of the idea that aims at excluding military establishments in time of peace. In speculative minds it may arise from contemplating the nature and tendency of such institutions, reinforced by events in other ages and countries. But as a national feeling, it must be traced to the habits of thinking we inherit from the nation from which the inhabitants of these States have in general descended.

In England, for a long time after the Norman Conquest, the authority of the monarch was almost unlimited. Inroads were gradually made on the prerogative in favor of liberty, first by the barons and afterward by the people, until the greater part of its most formidable claims died out. But it was not until the revolution of 1688, which raised the Prince of Orange to the throne of Great Britain, that English liberty completely triumphed. As an incident of the undefined power of making war, which was an acknowledged prerogative of the crown, Charles II had, on his own authority, kept a body of 5,000 regular troops on foot in time of peace. James II increased this number to 30,000, who were paid out of his civil list. At the revolution, to abolish the exercise of so dangerous an authority, an article was included in the Bill of Rights then drawn up, that "the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, UNLESS WITH THE CONSENT OF PARLIAMENT, was against law."

In that kingdom, when the pulse of liberty was at its highest pitch, no security against the danger of standing armies was thought necessary beyond a prohibition on raising or keeping them up by the mere authority of the chief executive. The patriots who brought about that memorable revolution were too temperate and too well informed to think of any restraint on the legislative discretion. They knew that a certain number of troops for guards and garrisons was indispensable; that no precise limits could be set to national emergencies; that a power equal to every possible contingency must exist somewhere in the government; and that, when they referred the exercise of that power to the judgment of the legislature, they had reached the furthest point of precaution that was consistent with the safety of the community.

It is remarkable that even in the two States that seem to have contemplated a ban on military establishments in time of peace, the wording used is cautionary rather than prohibitory. It is not said that standing armies SHALL NOT BE kept up, but that they OUGHT NOT to be kept up in time of peace. This ambiguity of wording appears to have resulted from a conflict between jealousy and conviction: between the desire to exclude such establishments at all events and the belief that an absolute exclusion would be unwise and unsafe.

Can it be doubted that such a provision, whenever the state of public affairs was understood to require a departure from it, would be interpreted by the legislature as a mere admonition and made to yield to the necessities, or supposed necessities, of the State? Let the fact already mentioned about Pennsylvania decide. What, then, it may be asked, is the use of such a provision, if it ceases to operate the moment there is an inclination to disregard it?

Let us examine whether there is any comparison, in effectiveness, between the provision I have mentioned and the one in the new Constitution that limits appropriations of money for military purposes to a period of two years. The former, by aiming at too much, is bound to accomplish nothing. The latter steers clear of an imprudent extreme and is perfectly compatible with proper provision for the nation's emergencies, so it will have a beneficial and powerful effect.

By this provision the legislature of the United States will be OBLIGED, at least once in every two years, to deliberate on whether it is proper to keep a military force on foot, to come to a new resolution on the point, and to declare its view of the matter by a formal vote in the face of its constituents. It will not be AT LIBERTY to give the executive department permanent funds for the support of an army, even if it were incautious enough to be willing to place so improper a confidence in it. Since the spirit of party, in different degrees, must be expected to infect all political bodies, there will no doubt be persons in the national legislature ready enough to challenge the measures and accuse the intentions of the majority. The provision for supporting a military force will always be a favorable subject for declamation. Every time the question comes up, the opposition party will rouse the public's attention and draw it to the subject. If the majority should really be disposed to exceed the proper limits, the community will be warned of the danger and will have an opportunity to take measures to guard against it. Apart from parties in the national legislature itself, every time the period of discussion arrives, the State legislatures will have their attention awake to the conduct of the national rulers. They will always be not only vigilant but suspicious and jealous guardians of the citizens' rights against encroachments from the federal government, and if anything improper appears they will be ready enough to sound the alarm to the people, and to be not only the VOICE but, if necessary, the ARM of their discontent.

Schemes to overthrow the liberties of a great community REQUIRE TIME to mature for execution. An army large enough to menace those liberties seriously could be formed only by gradual additions. That would suppose not merely a temporary combination between the legislature and the executive but a continued conspiracy over a period of time. Is it probable that such a combination would exist at all? Is it probable that it would be persisted in and passed along through all the successive changes in a representative body that elections every two years would naturally produce in both houses? Is it to be presumed that every man, the instant he took his seat in the national Senate or House of Representatives, would begin as a traitor to his constituents and to his country? Can it be supposed that there would not be found one man discerning enough to detect so atrocious a conspiracy, or bold or honest enough to inform his constituents of their danger? If such presumptions can fairly be made, there ought at once to be an end of all delegated authority. The people should resolve to take back all the powers they have so far parted with, and to divide themselves into as many States as there are counties, so that they may manage their own concerns in person.

Even if such suppositions could reasonably be made, it would still be impracticable to conceal the design for any length of time. The very act of enlarging the army to so great an extent in time of profound peace would announce it. What plausible reason could be given, in a country so situated, for such vast additions to the military force? It is impossible that the people could be deceived for long, and the destruction of the project and of its projectors would quickly follow the discovery.

It has been said that the provision limiting appropriations for the support of an army to a period of two years would be useless. The argument is that the Executive, once in possession of a force large enough to awe the people into submission, would find in that very force resources enough to do without supplies from acts of the legislature. But the question comes up again: on what pretense could he be put in possession of a force of that size in time of peace? If we suppose it to have been created because of some domestic insurrection or foreign war, then the case falls outside the principles of the objection, which is aimed at the power of keeping up troops in time of peace. Few people will be so visionary as to contend seriously that military forces ought not to be raised to put down a rebellion or resist an invasion. And if the defense of the community in such circumstances should make it necessary to have an army so numerous as to put its liberty at risk, this is one of those calamities for which there is neither prevention nor cure. It cannot be provided against by any possible form of government. It might even result from a simple league, offensive and defensive, if the confederates or allies were ever required to form an army for common defense.

But it is an evil far less likely to befall us in a united state than in a disunited one. Indeed, it may safely be asserted that it is an evil altogether unlikely to befall us in the latter situation. It is not easy to imagine that dangers so formidable could assail the whole Union as to require a force large enough to put our liberties in the least jeopardy, especially if we take into account the aid to be had from the militia, which ought always to be counted on as a valuable and powerful auxiliary. But in a state of disunion, as has been fully shown elsewhere, the opposite supposition would become not only probable but almost unavoidable.

chapters.title: No. 27 — The Same Subject Continued (The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It has been argued, in different forms, that a Constitution of the kind proposed by the Convention cannot operate without the aid of a military force to carry out its laws. Like most other things alleged on that side, however, this rests on mere general assertion, with no precise or intelligible statement of the reasons behind it. As far as I have been able to guess the hidden meaning of the objectors, it seems to start from an assumption that the people will be unwilling to see federal authority exercised in any matter of an internal nature. Setting aside any objection that might be raised to the inaccuracy and vagueness of the distinction between internal and external, let us ask what ground there is for assuming that unwillingness in the people. Unless we assume at the same time that the powers of the general government will be worse administered than those of the State governments, there seems to be no room for presuming ill will, disaffection, or opposition in the people. I believe it may be laid down as a general rule that their confidence in a government, and their obedience to it, will commonly be proportioned to the goodness or badness of its administration. It must be admitted that there are exceptions to this rule, but they depend so entirely on accidental causes that they cannot be considered to have any bearing on the intrinsic merits or demerits of a constitution. These can be judged only by general principles and maxims.

Various reasons have been suggested in the course of these papers for thinking it probable that the general government will be better administered than the individual State governments. The principal ones are these. Enlarging the spheres of election will give the people a wider range of choice. Through the State legislatures, which are select bodies of men and which are to appoint the members of the national Senate, there is reason to expect that this branch will generally be composed with particular care and judgment. These circumstances promise greater knowledge and more extensive information in the national councils. They also promise that those councils will be less likely to be tainted by the spirit of faction, and more out of reach of those occasional ill humors, or temporary prejudices and inclinations, which in smaller societies often contaminate the public councils, bring about injustice and oppression of one part of the community, and breed schemes that, though they gratify a momentary inclination or desire, end in general distress, dissatisfaction, and disgust. Several additional reasons of considerable force to strengthen that probability will occur when we come to examine more critically the internal structure of the edifice we are invited to erect. It will be enough to remark here that, until satisfactory reasons can be given for thinking that the federal government is likely to be administered in a way that makes it odious or contemptible to the people, there can be no reasonable ground for supposing that the laws of the Union will meet any greater obstruction from them, or will need any other methods of enforcement, than the laws of the individual members.

The hope of impunity is a strong incitement to sedition, and the dread of punishment is a proportionately strong discouragement to it. The government of the Union, if it has a proper degree of power, can call to its aid the collective resources of the whole Confederacy. Will it not be more likely to suppress the FORMER feeling and to inspire the LATTER than the government of a single State, which can command only the resources within itself? A turbulent faction in a State may easily suppose itself able to contend with the friends of the government in that State. But it can hardly be so infatuated as to imagine itself a match for the combined efforts of the Union. If this reflection is sound, there is less danger of resistance to the authority of the Confederacy from irregular combinations of individuals than to the authority of a single member.

I will here venture an observation that will be no less just because to some it may seem new. The more the operations of the national authority are mixed into the ordinary exercise of government; the more the citizens are used to meeting it in the common events of their political life; the more familiar it becomes to their sight and feelings; and the further it reaches into those matters that touch the most sensitive chords and set in motion the most active springs of the human heart: the greater will be the probability that it will win the respect and attachment of the community. Man is very much a creature of habit. A thing that rarely strikes his senses will generally have little influence on his mind. A government that is always at a distance and out of sight can hardly be expected to engage the feelings of the people. The inference is that the authority of the Union, and the affections of the citizens toward it, will be strengthened rather than weakened by its extension to what are called matters of internal concern, and that it will have less occasion to resort to force in proportion to the familiarity and breadth of its activity. The more it circulates through those channels and currents in which the passions of mankind naturally flow, the less it will need the violent and dangerous expedients of compulsion.

One thing, at all events, must be plain: a government like the one proposed would stand a much better chance of avoiding the necessity of using force than that kind of league which most of its opponents argue for, whose authority would operate only on the States in their political or collective capacities. It has been shown that in such a Confederacy there can be no sanction for the laws but force; that frequent failures of duty by the members are the natural offspring of the very frame of the government; and that whenever these happen, they can be remedied, if at all, only by war and violence.

The plan reported by the Convention extends the authority of the federal head to the individual citizens of the individual States. It will thereby enable the government to use the ordinary public officials of each State in carrying out its laws. It is easy to see that this will tend to wipe out, in the common mind, any distinction between the sources from which the laws might come. It will give the federal government the same advantage in securing due obedience to its authority that the government of each State enjoys, in addition to the influence on public opinion that will result from the important fact that it has power to call to its assistance and support the resources of the whole Union. It deserves particular attention here that the laws of the Confederacy, as to the ENUMERATED and LEGITIMATE objects of its jurisdiction, will become the SUPREME LAW of the land, and that all officers, legislative, executive, and judicial, in each State will be bound to observe them by the sanctity of an oath. Thus the legislatures, courts, and public officials of the individual members will be incorporated into the operations of the national government AS FAR AS ITS JUST AND CONSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY EXTENDS, and will be made auxiliary to the enforcement of its laws.(1) Anyone who follows out for himself the consequences of this situation will see good ground to expect a regular and peaceable execution of the laws of the Union, if its powers are administered with a common share of prudence. If we choose arbitrarily to suppose the contrary, we may draw any inferences we please from the supposition. It is certainly possible, by an unwise exercise of the authority of the best government that ever was or ever can be established, to provoke and drive the people into the wildest excesses. But suppose the adversaries of the proposed Constitution presume that the national rulers would be insensible to the motives of public good or to the obligations of duty. I would still ask them how the interests of ambition, or the aims of encroachment, can be advanced by such conduct.
1. The sophistry that has been used to show that this will tend to the destruction of the State governments will, in its will, in its proper place, be fully detected.

chapters.title: No. 28 — The Same Subject Continued (The Idea of Restraining the Legislative Authority in Regard to the Common Defense Considered) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It cannot be denied that cases may arise in which the national government is compelled to resort to force. Our own experience has confirmed the lessons taught by the examples of other nations: emergencies of this sort will sometimes arise in all societies, however constituted. Seditions and insurrections are, unhappily, maladies as inseparable from the body politic as tumors and eruptions are from the natural body. The idea of governing at all times by the simple force of law, which we have been told is the only admissible principle of republican government, has no place except in the daydreams of those political doctors whose cleverness scorns the lessons of experience.

Should such emergencies ever arise under the national government, there could be no remedy but force. The means used must be proportioned to the extent of the harm. If it were a slight commotion in a small part of a State, the militia of the rest of the State would be adequate to put it down, and the national presumption is that they would be ready to do their duty. An insurrection, whatever its immediate cause, ultimately endangers all government. Concern for the public peace, if not for the rights of the Union, would lead the citizens to whom the contagion had not spread to oppose the insurgents. And if the general government were found in practice to promote the prosperity and happiness of the people, it would be irrational to believe they would be unwilling to support it.

If, on the contrary, the insurrection should spread through a whole State, or a principal part of it, using a different kind of force might become unavoidable. Massachusetts, it appears, found it necessary to raise troops to suppress the disorders within that State, and Pennsylvania, from mere fear of commotions among a part of her citizens, has thought it proper to take the same measure. Suppose the State of New York had been inclined to re-establish her lost jurisdiction over the inhabitants of Vermont. Could she have hoped to succeed in such an enterprise by the efforts of the militia alone? Would she not have been compelled to raise and maintain a more regular force to carry out her design? If it must then be admitted that the necessity of turning to a force other than the militia, in cases of this extraordinary kind, applies to the State governments themselves, why should the possibility that the national government might be under a like necessity in similar extremities be made an objection to its existence? Is it not surprising that men who profess an attachment to the Union in the abstract should urge as an objection to the proposed Constitution what applies with tenfold weight to the plan they advocate, and what, so far as it has any foundation in truth, is an inevitable consequence of civil society on an enlarged scale? Who would not prefer that possibility to the unceasing agitations and frequent revolutions that are the continual scourges of petty republics?

Let us pursue this examination in another light. Suppose that, in place of one general system, two or three or even four Confederacies were formed. Would not the same difficulty stand in the way of the operations of each of these Confederacies? Would not each of them be exposed to the same accidents, and, when these happened, be obliged to resort to the same expedients for upholding its authority that are objected to in a government for all the States? On this supposition, would the militia be any more ready or more able to support the federal authority than in the case of a general union? All fair-minded and intelligent men must, on due consideration, acknowledge that the principle of the objection applies equally to either case. Whether we have one government for all the States, or different governments for different parcels of them, or even an entire separation of the States, there might sometimes be a necessity to use a force constituted differently from the militia, to preserve the peace of the community and to maintain the just authority of the laws against those violent attacks on them that amount to insurrections and rebellions.

Apart from all other reasoning on the subject, it is a full answer to those who demand a more peremptory provision against military establishments in time of peace to say that the whole power of the proposed government is to be in the hands of the representatives of the people. This is the essential security for the rights and privileges of the people, and after all the only effective one, that can be attained in civil society.(1)

If the representatives of the people betray their constituents, nothing is left but to exercise that original right of self-defense, which stands above every positive form of government. Against usurpation by the national rulers, this right can be exercised with infinitely better prospects of success than against usurpation by the rulers of a single State. In a single State, suppose the persons holding supreme power turn usurpers. The parcels, subdivisions, or districts that make up the State have no separate government of their own, so they can take no regular measures for defense. The citizens must rush to arms in confusion, without concert, without system, and with no resources except their courage and despair. The usurpers, clothed with the forms of legal authority, can too often crush the opposition while it is still in its infancy. The smaller the territory, the harder it is for the people to form a regular or systematic plan of opposition, and the easier it is to defeat their first efforts. Word of their preparations and movements reaches the usurpers faster, and the military force in the usurpers' hands can be sent more quickly against the place where the opposition has begun. In this situation, a peculiar combination of circumstances would be needed to bring success to the popular resistance.

As a state grows larger, the obstacles to usurpation grow and the means of resistance multiply, provided the citizens understand their rights and are ready to defend them. In a large community, the people's natural strength compared with the government's artificial strength is greater than in a small one, so the people are better able to contend with the government's attempts to set up a tyranny. But in a confederacy, it is no exaggeration to say that the people are entirely the masters of their own fate. Power is almost always the rival of power, so the general government will always stand ready to check the usurpations of the state governments, and they will be disposed the same way toward the general government. The people, by throwing their weight into either scale, will without fail make it prevail. If either invades their rights, they can use the other as the instrument of redress. How wise it will be for them to cherish the union and so preserve an advantage that can never be valued too highly!

We may safely accept it as an axiom of our political system that, in every possible contingency, the State governments will give complete security against invasions of the public liberty by the national authority. A select body of men is far less likely than the people at large to be taken in by the pretenses under which projects of usurpation are disguised. The legislatures will have better means of information. They can see the danger from a distance. Since they hold all the organs of civil power and have the confidence of the people, they can at once adopt a regular plan of opposition and bring together all the resources of the community. They can easily communicate with one another in the different States and join their common forces to protect their common liberty.

The great size of the country is a further security. We have already seen how useful it was against the attacks of a foreign power, and it would have exactly the same effect against the enterprises of ambitious rulers in the national councils. Suppose the federal army were able to crush the resistance of one State. The distant States would then be able to make a stand with fresh forces. The army would have to give up what it had gained in one place in order to subdue the opposition in others, and the moment the part it had forced into submission was left to itself, its efforts would begin again and its resistance would revive.

We should remember that the size of the military force must in any case be regulated by the resources of the country. For a long time to come it will not be possible to maintain a large army, and as the means of doing so increase, the population and natural strength of the community will increase in proportion. When will the time come that the federal government can raise and maintain an army capable of setting up a despotism over the great body of the people of an immense empire, who are in a position, through their State governments, to take measures for their own defense with all the speed, regularity, and system of independent nations? The fear may be considered a disease for which no cure can be found in the resources of argument and reasoning.
1. Its full effectiveness will be examined hereafter.

chapters.title: No. 29 — Concerning the Militia (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The power to regulate the militia and to command its services in times of insurrection and invasion comes naturally with the duties of overseeing the common defense and watching over the internal peace of the Confederacy.

It takes no skill in the science of war to see that uniformity in the organization and discipline of the militia would have the most beneficial effects whenever they were called into service for the public defense. It would enable them to carry out the duties of the camp and the field with mutual understanding and coordination, an advantage of particular importance in the operations of an army.
