It would also fit them to reach much sooner the degree of proficiency in military functions that is essential to their usefulness. This desirable uniformity can be achieved only by entrusting the regulation of the militia to the direction of the national authority. It is, therefore, with the most evident propriety that the plan of the Convention proposes to empower the Union "to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia, and for governing such part of them as may be employed in the service of the United States, RESERVING TO THE STATES RESPECTIVELY THE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS, AND THE AUTHORITY OF TRAINING THE MILITIA ACCORDING TO THE DISCIPLINE PRESCRIBED BY CONGRESS."

Of all the grounds taken against the plan of the Convention, none was so little to be expected, or is so indefensible in itself, as the one from which this particular provision has been attacked. If a well-regulated militia is the most natural defense of a free country, it ought certainly to be under the regulation and at the disposal of the body that has been made the guardian of the national security. If standing armies are dangerous to liberty, then an effective power over the militia, held by the body charged with protecting the State, ought as far as possible to remove the inducement and the pretext for such unfriendly institutions. If the federal government can command the help of the militia in those emergencies that call for the military arm in support of the civil authority, it can the better do without a different kind of force. If it cannot make use of the former, it will be obliged to turn to the latter. Making an army unnecessary will be a surer way of preventing its existence than a thousand prohibitions on paper.

To cast odium on the power of calling out the militia to execute the laws of the Union, it has been remarked that the proposed Constitution nowhere provides for calling out the POSSE COMITATUS to assist the public officer in the performance of his duty. From this it has been inferred that military force was intended to be his only auxiliary. There is a striking incoherence in the objections that have appeared, sometimes even from the same quarter, and it is not much calculated to inspire a very favorable opinion of the sincerity or fair dealing of their authors. The same persons who tell us in one breath that the powers of the federal government will be despotic and unlimited inform us in the next that it does not have authority enough even to call out the POSSE COMITATUS. The latter, fortunately, falls as far short of the truth as the former exceeds it. It would be as absurd to doubt that a right to pass all laws NECESSARY AND PROPER to execute its declared powers would include the right to require the assistance of the citizens to the officers entrusted with executing those laws, as it would be to believe that a right to enact laws necessary and proper for imposing and collecting taxes would include the right to change the rules of inheritance and of the transfer of landed property, or to abolish trial by jury in cases relating to it. It is therefore evident that the supposition that the government lacks power to require the aid of the POSSE COMITATUS is entirely without foundation. It follows that the conclusion drawn from it, as applied to the authority of the federal government over the militia, is as unfair as it is illogical. What reason could there be to infer that force was intended to be the sole instrument of authority, merely because there is a power to use it when necessary? What shall we think of the motives that could induce men of sense to reason in this manner? How shall we prevent a conflict between charity and conviction?

By a curious refinement on the spirit of republican jealousy, we are even taught to fear danger from the militia itself in the hands of the federal government. It is observed that select corps may be formed, made up of the young and ardent, who may be made subservient to the aims of arbitrary power. What plan for regulating the militia the national government may follow is impossible to foresee. But I am so far from viewing the matter as those who object to select corps as dangerous do that, if the Constitution were ratified and I were to give my views on a militia establishment to a member of the federal legislature from this State, I should put to him, in substance, the following discourse:

"The project of disciplining all the militia of the United States would be as futile as it would be harmful, if it could be carried out. A tolerable skill in military movements is a matter that takes time and practice. A day, or even a week, will not suffice to attain it. To require the great body of the yeomanry and of the other classes of citizens to be under arms for military exercises and maneuvers as often as might be needed to reach the degree of perfection that would entitle them to be called a well-regulated militia would be a real grievance to the people and a serious public problem and loss. It would take an annual deduction from the productive labor of the country that, calculated on the present numbers of the people, would not fall far short of the whole expense of the civil establishments of all the States. To attempt something that would cut down the mass of labor and industry to so considerable an extent would be unwise, and the experiment, if made, could not succeed, because it would not long be endured. Little more can reasonably be aimed at, with respect to the people at large, than to have them properly armed and equipped; and to see that this is not neglected, it will be necessary to assemble them once or twice in the course of a year.

"But though the scheme of disciplining the whole nation must be given up as harmful or impracticable, it is extremely important that a well-considered plan be adopted as soon as possible for properly establishing the militia. The government should give its attention especially to forming a select corps of moderate size, on principles that will truly fit its members for service in case of need. By limiting the plan in this way, we can have an excellent body of well-trained militia ready to take the field whenever the defense of the State requires it. This will not only lessen the call for military establishments. It also means that if circumstances should ever oblige the government to form an army of any size, that army can never be a threat to the liberties of the people, so long as there is a large body of citizens, little if at all inferior to the army in discipline and the use of arms, who stand ready to defend their own rights and those of their fellow-citizens. This seems to me the only substitute that can be devised for a standing army, and the best possible security against one, should it come into existence."

Thus I should reason on the same subject very differently from the adversaries of the proposed Constitution, drawing arguments for safety from the very sources they represent as full of danger and ruin. But how the national legislature may reason on the point is something that neither they nor I can foresee.

There is something so far-fetched and extravagant in the idea of danger to liberty from the militia that one is at a loss whether to treat it gravely or with mockery: whether to consider it a mere display of skill, like the paradoxes of rhetoricians; a dishonest trick to plant prejudices at any price; or the serious offspring of political fanaticism. Where, in the name of common sense, are our fears to end if we may not trust our sons, our brothers, our neighbors, our fellow-citizens? What shadow of danger can there be from men who mingle every day with the rest of their countrymen and share with them the same feelings, views, habits and interests? What reasonable cause for fear can be drawn from a power in the Union to prescribe regulations for the militia and to command its services when necessary, while the individual States are to have the SOLE AND EXCLUSIVE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS? If it were possible to entertain seriously a jealousy of the militia under any conceivable establishment by the federal government, the fact that the officers are appointed by the States ought at once to put an end to it. There can be no doubt that this fact will always secure the States a preponderating influence over the militia.

In reading many of the publications against the Constitution, a man is likely to imagine that he is reading some badly written tale or romance. Instead of natural and pleasing images, it shows the mind nothing but frightful and distorted shapes—
"Gorgons, hydras, and chimeras dire";
discoloring and disfiguring whatever it represents, and turning everything it touches into a monster.

A sample of this appears in the exaggerated and improbable claims that have been made about the power of calling for the militia's services. The militia of New Hampshire is to be marched to Georgia, that of Georgia to New Hampshire, that of New York to Kentucky, and that of Kentucky to Lake Champlain. Indeed, the debts owed to the French and Dutch are to be paid in militiamen instead of louis d'ors and ducats. At one moment there is to be a large army to crush the liberties of the people. At another, the militia of Virginia are to be dragged five or six hundred miles from their homes to tame the republican stubbornness of Massachusetts, while Massachusetts's militia are to be carried the same distance to subdue the unruly haughtiness of the aristocratic Virginians. Do the people who rave in this fashion imagine that their art or eloquence can make the people of America accept any fancy or absurdity as infallible truth?

If there should be an army to use as the engine of despotism, what need is there of the militia? If there should be no army, where would the militia go, irritated at being called on to undertake a distant and hopeless expedition to rivet the chains of slavery on a part of their countrymen? Would they not head straight for the seat of the tyrants who had planned so foolish as well as so wicked a project, to crush them in their imagined entrenchments of power and to make them an example of the just vengeance of an abused and enraged people? Is this the way usurpers stride to dominion over a numerous and enlightened nation? Do they begin by arousing the detestation of the very instruments of their intended usurpations? Do they usually begin their career with wanton and disgusting acts of power, calculated to serve no end but to draw universal hatred and execration on themselves? Are suppositions of this sort the sober warnings of discerning patriots to a discerning people? Or are they the inflammatory ravings of incendiaries or deranged enthusiasts? Even if we were to suppose the national rulers driven by the most ungovernable ambition, it is impossible to believe that they would use such preposterous means to accomplish their designs.

In times of insurrection or invasion, it would be natural and proper for the militia of a neighboring State to be marched into another to resist a common enemy, or to guard the republic against the violence of faction or sedition. This was frequently done, as to the first object, in the course of the recent war, and this mutual help is indeed a principal end of our political association. If the power of giving it is placed under the direction of the Union, there will be no danger of a sluggish and listless inattention to the dangers of a neighbor until its near approach had added the urgings of self-preservation to the too feeble impulses of duty and sympathy.

chapters.title: No. 30 — Concerning the General Power of Taxation (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I have already observed that the federal government ought to have the power to provide for the support of the national forces. By that proposition I meant to include the cost of raising troops, of building and equipping fleets, and all other expenses connected in any way with military arrangements and operations. But these are not the only objects for which the Union must necessarily be empowered to raise revenue. Its power must also cover the support of the national civil list, the payment of the national debts already contracted or yet to be contracted, and, in general, all those matters that will call for payments out of the national treasury. The conclusion is that a general power of taxation, in one form or another, must be built into the structure of the government.

Money is rightly considered the vital principle of the body politic: it is what sustains the body's life and motion and enables it to perform its most essential functions. A complete power to procure a regular and adequate supply of money, as far as the resources of the community will permit, may therefore be regarded as an indispensable ingredient of every constitution. Where this power is lacking, one of two evils must follow. Either the people must be subjected to continual plunder, as a substitute for a better way of supplying the public wants, or the government must waste away into a fatal atrophy and, in a short time, perish.

In the Ottoman or Turkish empire, the sovereign is in other respects the absolute master of the lives and fortunes of his subjects, yet he has no right to impose a new tax. The consequence is that he permits the pashas, or governors of provinces, to pillage the people without mercy, and then in turn squeezes out of them the sums he needs to meet his own necessities and those of the state. In America, from a like cause, the government of the Union has gradually dwindled into a state of decay that comes close to annihilation. Who can doubt that the happiness of the people in both countries would be advanced if competent authorities, placed in the proper hands, could provide the revenues that the public's necessities might require?

The present Confederation, feeble as it is, was intended to place in the United States an unlimited power to provide for the money needs of the Union. But because it proceeded on an erroneous principle, the power was set up in such a manner as entirely to defeat the intention. Under the articles that make up that compact (as I have already stated), Congress is authorized to determine and call for any sums of money that, in its judgment, are necessary for the service of the United States; and its requisitions, the formal requests it makes to the States for money, are, if they follow the rule of apportionment, binding on the States in every constitutional sense. The States have no right to question the propriety of the demand, and no discretion beyond devising the ways and means of furnishing the sums demanded. But although this is strictly and truly the case, and although the assumption of such a right would be an infringement of the articles of Union, and although it may seldom or never have been openly claimed, in practice the right has been constantly exercised, and would continue to be, as long as the revenues of the Confederacy remain dependent on the intermediate agency of its members. What the consequences of this system have been is known to every man the least familiar with our public affairs, and has been fully shown in different parts of these inquiries. It is this system that has contributed most to reduce us to a situation that gives ample cause both for mortification to ourselves and for triumph to our enemies.

What remedy can there be for this situation, except a change of the system that produced it, a change of the false and deceptive system of quotas and requisitions? What substitute can be imagined for this ignis fatuus in finance, other than permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by the ordinary methods of taxation authorized in every well-ordered constitution of civil government? Ingenious men may argue plausibly on any subject, but no human ingenuity can point out any other expedient to rescue us from the problems and embarrassments that naturally result from an inadequately supplied public treasury.

The more intelligent opponents of the new Constitution admit the force of this reasoning, but they qualify their admission with a distinction between what they call INTERNAL and EXTERNAL taxation. The former they would reserve to the State governments. The latter, which they explain as commercial imposts, or rather duties on imported articles, they declare themselves willing to concede to the federal head. This distinction, however, would violate the maxim of good sense and sound policy that every POWER ought to be in proportion to its OBJECT. It would also leave the general government in a kind of tutelage to the State governments, which is inconsistent with every idea of vigor or effectiveness. Who can pretend that commercial imposts are, or would be, alone equal to the present and future necessities of the Union? Take into account the existing debt, foreign and domestic, under any plan of paying it off that a man moderately impressed with the importance of public justice and public credit could approve, and add the establishments that all parties will acknowledge to be necessary. We could not reasonably flatter ourselves that this resource alone, even on the most improved scale, would suffice for our present necessities. Our future necessities admit of no calculation or limit, and on the principle I have more than once mentioned, the power of providing for them as they arise ought to be equally unconfined. I believe it may be regarded as a position warranted by the history of mankind that, IN THE USUAL PROGRESS OF THINGS, THE NECESSITIES OF A NATION, IN EVERY STAGE OF ITS EXISTENCE, WILL BE FOUND AT LEAST EQUAL TO ITS RESOURCES.

To say that shortfalls may be made up by requisitions upon the States is, on the one hand, to acknowledge that this system cannot be depended upon, and, on the other hand, to depend upon it for everything beyond a certain limit. Those who have carefully studied its vices and deformities, as experience has displayed them or as these papers have described them, must feel an invincible repugnance to trusting the national interests to its operation in any degree. Whenever it is put into action, its inevitable tendency must be to weaken the Union and to sow the seeds of discord and contention between the federal head and its members, and among the members themselves. Can it be expected that shortfalls would be better supplied in this way than the total wants of the Union have so far been supplied in the same way? It should be remembered that if less is required from the States, they will have proportionally less means to meet the demand. If the opinions of those who contend for the distinction I have mentioned were accepted as evidence of truth, one would be led to conclude that there was some known point in the economy of national affairs at which it would be safe to stop and say: Thus far the ends of public happiness will be advanced by supplying the wants of government, and all beyond this is unworthy of our care or anxiety. How is it possible for a government that is half supplied and always in need to fulfill the purposes of its institution, to provide for the security, advance the prosperity, or support the reputation of the commonwealth? How can it ever possess either energy or stability, dignity or credit, confidence at home or respectability abroad? How can its administration be anything other than a succession of expedients, temporizing, impotent and disgraceful? How will it be able to avoid frequently sacrificing its engagements to immediate necessity? How can it undertake or carry out any liberal or large-scale plans for the public good?

Let us consider what the effects of this situation would be in the very first war in which we happened to be engaged. We will suppose, for the sake of argument, that the revenue from the impost duties is enough to provide for the public debt and for a peacetime establishment for the Union. With things so arranged, a war breaks out. What would the government probably do in such an emergency? It has learned from experience that no proper dependence can be placed on the success of requisitions. It is unable, by its own authority, to lay hold of fresh resources. It is urged on by the danger to the nation. Would it not be driven to the expedient of diverting the funds already appropriated from their proper objects to the defense of the State? It is not easy to see how a step of this kind could be avoided; and if it were taken, it is evident that it would destroy public credit at the very moment when credit was becoming essential to the public safety. To imagine that credit might be dispensed with at such a crisis would be the height of infatuation. In the modern system of war, even the wealthiest nations are obliged to have recourse to large loans. A country so little wealthy as ours must feel this necessity much more strongly. But who would lend to a government that opened its overtures for borrowing with an act showing that no reliance could be placed on the steadiness of its measures for paying? The loans it might be able to obtain would be as limited in amount as they were burdensome in their conditions. They would be made on the same principles on which usurers commonly lend to bankrupt and fraudulent debtors: with a sparing hand and at enormous premiums.

It may perhaps be imagined that, because the resources of the country are scanty, the necessity of diverting the established funds in the case I have supposed would exist even if the national government possessed an unrestrained power of taxation. But two considerations should quiet all apprehension on this point. One is that we can be sure the resources of the community, in their full extent, will be brought into use for the benefit of the Union. The other is that whatever shortfalls there may be can be supplied without difficulty by loans.

The power to create new funds, from new objects of taxation, by its own authority, would enable the national government to borrow as far as its necessities might require. Foreigners, as well as the citizens of America, could then reasonably place confidence in its engagements. But to rely on a government that must itself depend on thirteen other governments for the means of fulfilling its contracts would, once its situation is clearly understood, require a degree of credulity not often met with in the money dealings of mankind, and one hardly reconcilable with the usual sharp-sightedness of avarice.

Reflections of this kind may carry little weight with men who hope to see the halcyon scenes of the poetic or fabulous age realized in America. But to those who believe we are likely to experience a common share of the ups and downs and calamities that have fallen to the lot of other nations, they must appear to deserve serious attention. Such men must view the actual situation of their country with painful concern, and must dread the evils that ambition or revenge might all too easily inflict upon it.

chapters.title: No. 31 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: In inquiries of every kind there are certain primary truths, or first principles, on which all later reasoning depends. Such truths carry an internal evidence that wins the mind's assent before any reflection or combining of ideas. When they fail to do so, the cause must lie either in some defect or disorder of the organs of perception, or in the pull of some strong interest, passion or prejudice. The maxims of geometry are of this kind: "the whole is greater than its part; things equal to the same are equal to one another; two straight lines cannot enclose a space; and all right angles are equal to each other." So are these other maxims of ethics and politics: that there cannot be an effect without a cause; that the means ought to be proportioned to the end; that every power ought to be commensurate with its object; that there ought to be no limitation of a power destined to effect a purpose which is itself incapable of limitation. And these two latter sciences contain other truths which, though they cannot claim to rank as axioms, are such direct inferences from axioms, are so obvious in themselves, and agree so well with the natural, unsophisticated dictates of common sense, that they win the assent of a sound and unbiased mind with almost equally irresistible force and conviction.

The objects of geometrical inquiry stand so far removed from the pursuits that stir up the unruly passions of the human heart that people accept without difficulty not only the simpler theorems of the science but even those abstruse paradoxes which, although they may seem capable of demonstration, run against the natural conceptions the mind would form on the subject without the aid of philosophy. The INFINITE DIVISIBILITY of matter, in other words the INFINITE divisibility of a FINITE thing, extending down to the smallest atom, is a point agreed among geometricians. It is no less incomprehensible to common sense than any of those mysteries in religion against which the batteries of infidelity have been so industriously aimed.

In the sciences of morals and politics, however, men are far less easily led. To a certain degree it is right and useful that they should be so, because caution and investigation are a necessary armor against error and imposition. But this resistance can be carried too far, and can degenerate into obstinacy, perverseness or dishonesty. It cannot be claimed that the principles of moral and political knowledge have, in general, the same certainty as those of mathematics. Yet they have much better claims to certainty than the conduct of men in particular situations would lead us to grant. The obscurity lies much more often in the passions and prejudices of the reasoner than in the subject. Too often men do not give their own understandings a fair chance. They yield to some unfortunate bias, and they entangle themselves in words and confound themselves in subtleties.

How else could it happen (if we grant that the objectors are sincere) that positions as clear as those showing the necessity of a general power of taxation in the government of the Union should find any opponents among men of discernment? These positions have been fully stated elsewhere. Still, it may not be improper to restate them here, as an introduction to examining whatever has been offered against them. In substance they are as follows:

A government ought to contain within itself every power needed to accomplish fully the objects committed to its care and to carry out completely the trusts for which it is responsible. It ought to be free of every other control except a regard for the public good and for the sense of the people.

Overseeing the national defense and securing the public peace against foreign or domestic violence involve providing for emergencies and dangers to which no possible limits can be set. The power to make that provision, therefore, ought to know no bounds other than the necessities of the nation and the resources of the community.

Revenue is the essential engine by which the means of meeting the national necessities must be obtained. The power to obtain revenue in its full extent must therefore be included in the power to provide for those necessities.

Theory and practice both show that the power to raise revenue is ineffective when it is exercised over the States in their collective capacities. The federal government must therefore of necessity be given an unqualified power of taxation in the ordinary modes.

If experience did not show otherwise, it would be natural to conclude that the propriety of a general power of taxation in the national government could safely rest on the evidence of these propositions, without further arguments or illustrations. But in fact we find that the opponents of the proposed Constitution, far from accepting the justness or truth of these propositions, seem to direct their principal and most zealous effort against this very part of the plan. It may therefore be satisfactory to analyze the arguments they use against it.

The arguments they have labored over most for this purpose seem in substance to come to this: "It is not true that, because the necessities of the Union may not be capable of limitation, its power of laying taxes ought to be unconfined. Revenue is as necessary for the purposes of the local administrations as for those of the Union, and the former are at least as important as the latter to the happiness of the people. It is therefore as necessary that the State governments should be able to command the means of supplying their wants as that the national government should have the same ability for the wants of the Union. But an indefinite power of taxation in the LATTER might, and probably would in time, deprive the FORMER of the means of providing for their own necessities, and would put them entirely at the mercy of the national legislature. The laws of the Union are to become the supreme law of the land, and the Union is to have power to pass all laws that may be NECESSARY for carrying into execution the authorities with which it is proposed to vest it. The national government might therefore abolish at any time the taxes imposed for State objects, on the pretense that they interfere with its own. It might claim that this was necessary in order to give effect to the national revenues. And thus all the resources of taxation might by degrees become the subjects of federal monopoly, to the entire exclusion and destruction of the State governments."

At times this reasoning seems to rest on the supposition that the national government will usurp power. At other times it seems intended only as a deduction from the constitutional operation of its intended powers. Only in the latter light can it claim any fairness. The moment we launch into conjectures about usurpations by the federal government, we plunge into an unfathomable abyss and place ourselves entirely beyond the reach of reasoning. Imagination may roam at will until it is bewildered among the labyrinths of an enchanted castle, and cannot tell which way to turn to get out of the perplexities it has so rashly entered. Whatever the limits or modifications of the Union's powers, it is easy to imagine an endless train of possible dangers. By indulging an excess of jealousy and timidity, we may bring ourselves to a state of absolute skepticism and irresolution. I repeat here what I have said in substance elsewhere: every observation founded on the danger of usurpation ought to be directed to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers. The State governments, by their original constitutions, are invested with complete sovereignty. What does our security against usurpation from that quarter consist in? Doubtless in the manner of their formation, and in the proper dependence of those who are to administer them on the people. If the proposed structure of the federal government turns out, on impartial examination, to give the same kind of security to a proper extent, then all apprehensions about usurpation ought to be discarded.

We should not forget that the State governments are quite as likely to be disposed to encroach on the rights of the Union as the Union is to encroach on the rights of the State governments. Which side would prevail in such a conflict must depend on the means the contending parties could use to secure success. In republics strength is always on the side of the people, and there are weighty reasons to believe that the State governments will commonly have the most influence over them. The natural conclusion is that such contests will most often end to the disadvantage of the Union, and that the members are more likely to encroach on the federal head than the federal head on the members. But all conjectures of this kind must plainly be extremely vague and fallible. By far the safest course is to set them entirely aside and to confine our attention wholly to the nature and extent of the powers as the Constitution lays them out. Everything beyond this must be left to the prudence and firmness of the people. They will hold the scales in their own hands, and it is to be hoped they will always take care to preserve the constitutional equilibrium between the general and the State governments. On this ground, which is evidently the true one, it will not be difficult to answer the objections that have been made to an indefinite power of taxation in the United States.

chapters.title: No. 32 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I believe the State governments would face no real danger from a power in the Union to control them in levying money. I am persuaded that the sense of the people, the extreme risk of provoking the resentment of the State governments, and a conviction that local administrations are useful and necessary for local purposes would together be a complete barrier against any oppressive use of such a power. Even so, I am willing to grant here, in its full extent, the justness of the reasoning which requires that the individual States have an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise their own revenues for their own wants. Having made this concession, I affirm that under the plan of the Convention the States would keep that authority in the most absolute and unqualified sense, with the sole exception of duties on imports and exports. An attempt by the national government to restrict them in using it would be a violent assumption of power, unwarranted by any article or clause of its Constitution.

A complete consolidation of the States into one national sovereignty would mean the complete subordination of the parts, and whatever powers remained in them would depend entirely on the general will. But the plan of the Convention aims only at a partial union or consolidation. The State governments would therefore plainly keep all the rights of sovereignty they had before, except those that were, by that act, EXCLUSIVELY delegated to the United States. This exclusive delegation, or rather this alienation, of State sovereignty would exist in only three cases. The first is where the Constitution in express terms grants an exclusive authority to the Union. The second is where it grants an authority to the Union in one place and prohibits the States from exercising the like authority in another. The third is where it grants the Union an authority to which a similar authority in the States would be absolutely and totally CONTRADICTORY and REPUGNANT. I use these terms to distinguish this last case from another that might look like it but would in fact be essentially different. I mean the case where exercising a concurrent jurisdiction might now and then produce interferences in the POLICY of some branch of administration, but would not imply any direct contradiction or repugnancy in constitutional authority. These three cases of exclusive jurisdiction in the federal government can be illustrated by the following examples. The last clause but one in the eighth section of the first article provides expressly that Congress shall exercise "EXCLUSIVE LEGISLATION" over the district to be appropriated as the seat of government. This answers to the first case. The first clause of the same section empowers Congress "to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts and excises"; and the second clause of the tenth section of the same article declares that "NO STATE SHALL, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except for the purpose of executing its inspection laws." From these two clauses results an exclusive power in the Union to lay duties on imports and exports, with the one exception mentioned. Another clause, however, which declares that no tax or duty shall be laid on articles exported from any State, narrows this power; with that qualification, it now reaches only the DUTIES ON IMPORTS. This answers to the second case. The third is found in the clause which declares that Congress shall have power "to establish an UNIFORM RULE of naturalization throughout the United States." This must necessarily be exclusive, because if each State had power to prescribe a DISTINCT RULE, there could not be a UNIFORM RULE.

Another case may perhaps be thought to resemble the last, but it is in fact widely different, and it bears directly on the question before us. I mean the power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports. This, I contend, is plainly a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States. Nothing in the granting clause makes that power EXCLUSIVE in the Union. No separate clause or sentence forbids the States to exercise it. Far from it: a plain and conclusive argument to the contrary can be drawn from the restraint laid on the States regarding duties on imports and exports. That restriction admits that, had it not been inserted, the States would have had the power it excludes. It admits further that, as to all other taxes, the authority of the States remains undiminished. On any other view the restriction would be both unnecessary and dangerous. It would be unnecessary because, if granting the Union the power to lay such duties implied the exclusion of the States, or even their subordination in this particular, no such restriction would be needed. It would be dangerous because introducing it leads directly to the conclusion I have mentioned, which could not have been intended if the objectors' reasoning is right: that in every case the restriction did not cover, the States would have a power of taxation concurrent with the Union's. The restriction in question amounts to what lawyers call a NEGATIVE PREGNANT, that is, a NEGATION of one thing and an AFFIRMANCE of another. It denies the States the authority to impose taxes on imports and exports, and it affirms their authority to impose them on all other articles. It would be mere sophistry to argue that the clause meant to exclude the States ABSOLUTELY from taxes of the former kind and to leave them free to lay others SUBJECT TO THE CONTROL of the national legislature. The restraining or prohibitory clause says only that they shall not, WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF CONGRESS, lay such duties. If we understood this in the sense last mentioned, the Constitution would be made to include a formal provision for the sake of a very absurd conclusion: that the States, WITH THE CONSENT of the national legislature, might tax imports and exports, and might tax every other article UNLESS CONTROLLED by that same body. If this was the intention, why not leave the matter in the first place to what is alleged to be the natural operation of the original clause, which confers a general power of taxation on the Union? Clearly this could not have been the intention, and the clause will not bear such a construction.

A supposed repugnancy between the power of taxation in the States and in the Union cannot be supported in the sense that would be needed to exclude the States. It is certainly possible that a State might tax a particular article in a way that would make it INEXPEDIENT for the Union to lay a further tax on the same article. That would not imply a constitutional inability to impose a further tax. How much to impose, and whether it is expedient to increase the tax on either side, would be questions of prudence for both, and no direct contradiction of power would be involved. The particular policy of the national and State systems of finance might now and then fail to coincide exactly and might require each side to hold back for the other. But it is not a mere possibility of inconvenience in exercising powers; it is an immediate constitutional repugnancy that can, by implication, alienate and extinguish a pre-existing right of sovereignty.

The need for a concurrent jurisdiction in certain cases follows from the division of the sovereign power. The rule that the States keep in full vigor every authority they are not explicitly stripped of in favor of the Union is not a mere theoretical consequence of that division. The whole tenor of the instrument containing the articles of the proposed Constitution clearly admits it. We find there that, although general authorities are granted in the affirmative, the most pointed care was taken, wherever it was thought improper for the States to hold the like authorities, to insert negative clauses forbidding the States to exercise them. The tenth section of the first article consists entirely of such provisions. This is a clear indication of the sense of the Convention, and it furnishes a rule of interpretation drawn from the body of the act itself, which justifies the position I have advanced and refutes every hypothesis to the contrary.

chapters.title: No. 33 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The rest of the argument against the Constitution's provisions on taxation is built on the following clause. The last clause of the eighth section of the first article of the plan under consideration authorizes the national legislature "to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution THE POWERS by that Constitution vested in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof." And the second clause of the sixth article declares "that the Constitution and the laws of the United States made IN PURSUANCE THEREOF, and the treaties made by their authority shall be the SUPREME LAW of the land, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

These two clauses have drawn a flood of bitter invective and petulant declamation against the proposed Constitution. They have been held up to the people, in every exaggerated color of misrepresentation, as destructive engines meant to destroy their local governments and wipe out their liberties. They have been called a hideous monster whose devouring jaws would spare neither sex nor age, neither high nor low, neither sacred nor profane. Yet, strange as it may seem after all this clamor, anyone who has not happened to view them in the same light may be assured with perfect confidence that the intended government would operate, constitutionally, in exactly the same way if these clauses were struck out entirely as if they were repeated in every article. They merely declare a truth that would follow by necessary and unavoidable implication from the very act of constituting a federal government and giving it certain specified powers. The proposition is so clear that even moderation itself can hardly listen to the railings so copiously poured out against this part of the plan without feeling its calm disturbed.

What is a power, if not the ability or faculty of doing a thing? What is the ability to do a thing, if not the power of using the MEANS necessary to carry it out? What is a LEGISLATIVE power, if not a power of making LAWS? What are the MEANS of carrying out a LEGISLATIVE power, if not LAWS? What is the power of laying and collecting taxes, if not a LEGISLATIVE POWER, a power of MAKING LAWS to lay and collect taxes? And what are the proper means of carrying out such a power, if not NECESSARY and PROPER laws?

This simple line of inquiry gives us at once a test for judging the true nature of the clause complained of. It brings us to this plain truth: a power to lay and collect taxes must be a power to pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying out that power. And what does the unfortunate and slandered provision do beyond declaring the same truth, namely that the national legislature, to which the power of laying and collecting taxes had already been given, might in carrying out that power pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER to give it effect? I have applied these observations in particular to the power of taxation because it is the subject now before us, and because it is the most important of the authorities proposed to be conferred on the Union. But the same process will lead to the same result for all the other powers declared in the Constitution. It is EXPRESSLY to carry out these powers that the sweeping clause, as it has been affectedly called, authorizes the national legislature to pass all NECESSARY and PROPER laws. If anything is objectionable, the objection must be looked for in the specific powers on which this general declaration rests. The declaration itself may be charged with tautology or redundancy, but it is perfectly harmless.

But SUSPICION may ask why it was introduced, then. The answer is that it could only have been done out of extra caution, to guard against every quibbling refinement by those who might later feel inclined to curtail and evade the legitimate authorities of the Union. The Convention probably foresaw what these papers have chiefly aimed to impress: that the danger most threatening to our political welfare is that the State governments will in the end undermine the foundations of the Union. On so cardinal a point it may therefore have thought it necessary to leave nothing to construction. Whatever moved it to include the clause, the wisdom of the precaution is plain from the outcry raised against it, since that very outcry betrays a readiness to question the great and essential truth which the provision was manifestly meant to declare.

But it may be asked again: who is to judge of the NECESSITY and PROPRIETY of the laws to be passed for carrying out the powers of the Union? My first answer is that this question arises just as fully on the simple grant of those powers as on the declaratory clause. My second is that the national government, like every other, must judge in the first instance of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents in the last. Suppose the federal government should overstep the just bounds of its authority and use its powers tyrannically. The people, whose creature it is, must then appeal to the standard they have set up, and take whatever measures to redress the injury done to the Constitution the emergency may suggest and prudence justify. The propriety of a law, in a constitutional light, must always be decided by the nature of the powers on which it is founded. Suppose that, by some forced construction of its authority (which indeed can hardly be imagined), the federal legislature should try to change the law of descent in some State. Would it not be evident that in making such an attempt it had exceeded its jurisdiction and infringed on that of the State? Suppose again that, on the pretense of interference with its revenues, it should undertake to abolish a land tax imposed by the authority of a State. Would it not be equally evident that this was an invasion of the concurrent jurisdiction in this kind of tax which the Constitution plainly supposes the State governments to have? If any doubt on this point should ever arise, the blame will lie entirely with those reasoners who, in the imprudent zeal of their hostility to the plan of the Convention, have labored to wrap it in a cloud meant to hide the plainest and simplest truths.

But it is said that the laws of the Union are to be the SUPREME LAW of the land. What can be inferred from this? And what would those laws amount to if they were not supreme? Plainly, nothing. A LAW, by the very meaning of the term, includes supremacy. It is a rule that those to whom it is given are bound to obey. This follows from every political association. When individuals enter into a state of society, the laws of that society must be the supreme regulator of their conduct. When a number of political societies enter into a larger political society, the laws that the larger one enacts in accordance with the powers entrusted to it by its constitution must necessarily be supreme over those societies and over the individuals who compose them. Otherwise it would be a mere treaty, dependent on the good faith of the parties, and not a government, which is only another word for POLITICAL POWER AND SUPREMACY. But it does not follow from this doctrine that acts of the larger society which are NOT PURSUANT to its constitutional powers, and which invade the residuary authorities of the smaller societies, will become the supreme law of the land. Such acts will be mere usurpation and will deserve to be treated as such. So we see that the clause declaring the supremacy of the laws of the Union, like the one we have just examined, only declares a truth that flows immediately and necessarily from the institution of a federal government. It will not, I presume, have escaped notice that the clause EXPRESSLY confines this supremacy to laws made PURSUANT TO THE CONSTITUTION. I mention this merely as an instance of the Convention's caution, since the limitation would have been understood even if it had not been stated.

Therefore, a law laying a tax for the use of the United States would be supreme in its nature and could not legally be opposed or controlled. But a law abolishing or preventing the collection of a tax laid by the authority of a State (unless on imports and exports) would not be the supreme law of the land; it would be a usurpation of power not granted by the Constitution. An improper pile-up of taxes on the same object might make collection difficult or uncertain. That would be a problem for both sides, arising not from superior or defective power on either side but from an unwise use of power by one or the other, in a manner equally disadvantageous to both. It is to be hoped and presumed, however, that mutual interest would dictate coordination in this respect and so avoid any serious problem. The inference from the whole is that under the proposed Constitution the individual States would keep an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise revenue, to whatever extent they may need, by every kind of taxation except duties on imports and exports. It will be shown in the next paper that this CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in taxation was the only admissible substitute for the complete subordination of State authority to that of the Union in this branch of power.

chapters.title: No. 34 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I flatter myself that my last number showed clearly that, under the proposed Constitution, the particular States would have COEQUAL authority with the Union in matters of revenue, except for duties on imports. This leaves the States far the greater part of the community's resources, so there can be no pretext for claiming that they would lack means as abundant as could be wished to supply their own wants, free of all outside control. That the field is wide enough will appear more fully when we come to the small share of the public expenses that the State governments will have to provide for.

To argue from abstract principles that this coordinate authority cannot exist is to set supposition and theory against fact and reality. Such reasoning may be proper for showing that a thing OUGHT NOT TO EXIST. It must be wholly rejected when it is used to prove that a thing does not exist, in the face of the fact itself. It is well known that in the Roman republic the legislative authority, in the last resort, rested for ages in two different political bodies. They were not branches of one legislature but distinct and independent legislatures, and in each an opposing interest prevailed: the patrician in one, the plebeian in the other. Many arguments might have been offered to prove that two such seemingly contradictory authorities, each able to ANNUL or REPEAL the acts of the other, were unfit to coexist. But anyone at Rome who tried to disprove their existence would have been thought frantic. It will be readily understood that I am referring to the COMITIA CENTURIATA and the COMITIA TRIBUTA. In the former, where the people voted by centuries, the arrangement gave the patrician interest the advantage. In the latter, where numbers prevailed, the plebeian interest was wholly predominant. And yet these two legislatures existed side by side for ages, and the Roman republic rose to the utmost height of human greatness.

In the case now before us there is no such contradiction as appears in the example I cited, because neither side has power to annul the acts of the other. In practice, too, there is little reason to fear any problem. In a short time the wants of the States will naturally shrink WITHIN A VERY NARROW COMPASS, and in the meantime the United States will in all probability find it convenient to stay entirely away from those objects to which the particular States would be inclined to turn.

To judge the true merits of this question more precisely, it will be well to look at the proportion between the objects that will require a federal provision of revenue and those that will require a State provision. We shall find that the former are altogether unlimited and the latter are held within very moderate bounds. In pursuing this inquiry we must keep in mind that we are not to look only at the present period but forward to a remote future. Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed on a calculation of present necessities alone, but on a combination of these with the probable necessities of ages, following the natural and tried course of human affairs. Nothing, therefore, can be more fallacious than to infer, from an estimate of its immediate necessities, how much power ought to be lodged in the national government. There ought to be a CAPACITY to provide for future contingencies as they arise; and since these are illimitable by nature, it is impossible to limit that capacity safely. It is true, perhaps, that one could compute, accurately enough for the purpose, how much revenue is needed to discharge the Union's existing engagements and to maintain the peacetime establishments that would suffice for some time to come. But would it be wise, or would it not rather be the extreme of folly, to stop at this point? That would leave the government entrusted with the national defense wholly incapable of protecting the community against future breaches of the public peace, whether by foreign war or domestic convulsions. If, on the contrary, we ought to go past this point, where can we stop short of an indefinite power to provide for emergencies as they arise? It is easy to assert, in general terms, that a rational judgment can be formed of a proper provision against probable dangers. But we may safely challenge those who make this assertion to produce their data, and may affirm that those data would prove as vague and uncertain as any that could be offered to establish how long the world will probably last. Observations confined to the mere prospect of internal attacks deserve no weight, though even these admit of no satisfactory calculation. And if we mean to be a commercial people, our policy must include being able one day to defend that commerce. Supporting a navy and naval wars would involve contingencies that must defeat all the efforts of political arithmetic.

Suppose we admit that we ought to try the novel and absurd experiment in politics of tying the government's hands against offensive war founded on reasons of state. Certainly we ought not to disable it from guarding the community against the ambition or enmity of other nations. A cloud has hung over the European world for some time. If it should break into a storm, who can assure us that some of its fury would not be spent on us as it moves? No reasonable man would hastily declare that we are entirely out of its reach. Or suppose the combustible materials that now seem to be gathering should disperse before coming to maturity, or a flame should be kindled that does not reach us. What security have we that our tranquillity will long remain undisturbed from some other cause or quarter? Let us remember that peace or war will not always be left to our choice. However moderate or unambitious we may be, we cannot count on the moderation of others or hope to extinguish their ambition. At the end of the last war, who could have imagined that France and Britain, wearied and exhausted as both were, would so soon look on each other with such hostility? If we judge by the history of mankind, we shall have to conclude that the fiery and destructive passions of war rule the human breast far more powerfully than the mild and beneficent feelings of peace. To model our political systems on speculations of lasting tranquillity is to calculate on the weaker springs of the human character.

What are the chief sources of expense in every government? What has caused the enormous accumulation of debts that weighs on several of the European nations? The answer is plain: wars and rebellions, and the upkeep of the institutions necessary to guard the body politic against these two most deadly diseases of society. The expenses of institutions that concern the mere domestic police of a state, the support of its legislative, executive and judicial departments with their various appendages, and the encouragement of agriculture and manufactures (which will cover almost all the objects of state expenditure) are insignificant beside those that concern the national defense.

In the kingdom of Great Britain, which must pay for all the ostentatious apparatus of monarchy, not more than a fifteenth part of the nation's annual income goes to the class of expenses I last mentioned. The other fourteen fifteenths are swallowed up by interest on the debts contracted to carry on the wars that country has fought, and by the upkeep of fleets and armies. One may observe, on the one hand, that the expenses of pursuing the ambitious enterprises and vainglorious projects of a monarchy are not a proper standard for judging what a republic might need. On the other hand, one ought to remark that there should be an equally great gap between the profusion and extravagance of a wealthy kingdom in its domestic administration and the frugality and economy that become, in this respect, the modest simplicity of republican government. If we balance a proper deduction on one side against the one that is supposed to be made on the other, the proportion may still be considered to hold.

But consider the large debt we ourselves ran up in a single war, and calculate on no more than a common share of the events that disturb the peace of nations. We shall see at once, without any elaborate illustration, that there must always be an immense disproportion between federal and State expenditures. It is true that several of the States, separately, are burdened with considerable debts, an outgrowth of the recent war. But this cannot happen again if the proposed system is adopted. When those debts are paid off, the only call for revenue of any consequence that the State governments will still have is the mere support of their respective civil lists. Adding all contingencies to this, the total in every State ought to come in considerably under two hundred thousand pounds.

In framing a government for posterity as well as for ourselves, we ought, in those provisions meant to be permanent, to calculate on permanent rather than temporary causes of expense. If this principle is just, our attention would be directed to providing the State governments with an annual sum of about two hundred thousand pounds, while the necessities of the Union could admit of no limits, even in imagination. Seen in this way, by what logic can it be maintained that the local governments ought to command, in perpetuity, an EXCLUSIVE source of revenue for any sum beyond two hundred thousand pounds? To extend their power further, in EXCLUSION of the authority of the Union, would be to take the resources of the community out of the hands that needed them for the public welfare and put them into other hands that could have no just or proper occasion for them.

Suppose, then, that the Convention had been inclined to divide the objects of revenue between the Union and its members in PROPORTION to their comparative necessities. What particular fund could have been picked out for the States that would not have been either too much or too little: too little for their present wants, too much for their future wants? Take the dividing line between external and internal taxes. By rough computation, this would leave the States command of two thirds of the community's resources to pay from a tenth to a twentieth part of its expenses, and would leave the Union one third of the resources to pay from nine tenths to nineteen twentieths of its expenses. If we abandon this boundary and are content to leave the States an exclusive power of taxing houses and lands, there would still be a great disproportion between the MEANS and the END: possession of one third of the community's resources to supply, at most, one tenth of its wants. Suppose some fund could have been picked out and set aside that was equal to the object and no greater. It would still have been inadequate to discharge the existing debts of the particular States, and would have left them dependent on the Union for a provision for this purpose.

The preceding train of observations will justify the position laid down elsewhere, that "A CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union." Any separation of the objects of revenue that could have been devised would have sacrificed the great INTERESTS of the Union to the POWER of the individual States. The Convention thought the concurrent jurisdiction preferable to that subordination. It evidently has at least the merit of reconciling an indefinite constitutional power of taxation in the federal government with an adequate and independent power in the States to provide for their own necessities. A few other lights remain in which this important subject of taxation will claim further consideration.

chapters.title: No. 35 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Before we examine any other objections to an indefinite power of taxation in the Union, I shall make one general remark. If the national government's jurisdiction over revenue were restricted to particular objects, an undue share of the public burdens would naturally fall on those objects. Two evils would spring from this: the oppression of particular branches of industry, and an unequal distribution of the taxes, both among the individual States and among the citizens of the same State.

Suppose, as has been argued, that the federal power of taxation were confined to duties on imports. It is evident that the government, unable to command other resources, would often be tempted to push these duties to an injurious excess. Some people imagine that such duties can never be carried too far. The higher they are, it is alleged, the more they will discourage extravagant consumption, produce a favorable balance of trade and promote domestic manufactures. But every extreme is harmful in various ways. Exorbitant duties on imported articles would breed a general spirit of smuggling, which always harms the fair trader and in the end the revenue itself. They tend to make other classes of the community tributary, to an improper degree, to the manufacturing classes, to whom they give a premature monopoly of the markets. They sometimes force industry out of its more natural channels into others where it flows with less advantage. And finally, they oppress the merchant, who is often obliged to pay them himself with no repayment from the consumer. When demand matches the quantity of goods at market, the consumer generally pays the duty. But when the markets happen to be overstocked, a great share falls on the merchant, and sometimes it not only eats up his profits but cuts into his capital. I am inclined to think that the duty is divided between seller and buyer more often than is commonly imagined. It is not always possible to raise the price of a commodity in exact proportion to each additional imposition laid on it. The merchant, especially in a country with a small commercial capital, is often forced to hold prices down so as to sell more quickly.

The maxim that the consumer is the payer holds so much more often than its opposite that it is far more equitable for the duties on imports to go into a common stock than to benefit the importing States alone. But the maxim is not true often enough to make it equitable for those duties to be the only national fund. When the merchant pays them, they work as an additional tax on the importing State, whose citizens pay their share as consumers. In this way they produce inequality among the States, and the inequality would grow as the duties grew. Confining the national revenues to this kind of impost would also produce inequality, from a different cause, between the manufacturing and the non-manufacturing States. The States that can go furthest in supplying their own wants from their own manufactures will not, in proportion to their numbers or wealth, consume as large a share of imported articles as the States that are not so favorably placed. By this means alone, then, they would not contribute to the public treasury in proportion to their abilities. To make them do so, we must have recourse to excises, whose proper objects are particular kinds of manufactures. New York has a deeper interest in these considerations than those of her citizens who argue for limiting the power of the Union to external taxation may realize. New York is an importing State and is not likely soon to become, to any great extent, a manufacturing State. She would therefore suffer in two ways from confining the Union's jurisdiction to commercial imposts.

These observations are meant to show a danger that the import duties might be pushed to an injurious extreme. On that point, as I remarked in another part of these papers, the interest of the revenue itself would be a sufficient guard against such an extreme. I readily admit this would be so as long as other resources were open. But if the avenues to them were closed, HOPE, spurred by necessity, would produce experiments, backed by rigorous precautions and additional penalties. These would have the intended effect for a time, until people had leisure to devise ways around the new precautions. The first success would be apt to inspire false opinions, which might take a long course of later experience to correct. Necessity, especially in politics, often gives rise to false hopes, false reasonings, and a correspondingly mistaken system of measures. But even if this supposed excess should not result from limiting the federal power of taxation, the inequalities I have described would still follow, though not to the same degree, from the other causes I have noted. Let us now return to examining objections.

One objection, which to judge by how often it is repeated seems the one most relied on, is that the House of Representatives is not numerous enough to take in all the different classes of citizens, so as to combine the interests and feelings of every part of the community and to produce a due sympathy between the representative body and its constituents. This argument comes in a very specious and seductive form and is well designed to seize on the prejudices of those it is addressed to. But when we dissect it with attention, it turns out to be made up of nothing but fair-sounding words. The object it seems to aim at is, in the first place, impracticable, and in the sense in which it is urged, unnecessary. I reserve for another place the question whether the representative body is sufficient in numbers. Here I shall content myself with examining the particular use that has been made of the contrary supposition in connection with the subject of our present inquiries.

The idea of actual representation of all classes of the people by persons from each class is altogether visionary. Unless the Constitution expressly provided that each different occupation should send one or more members, the thing would never happen in practice. Mechanics and manufacturers will always be inclined, with few exceptions, to vote for merchants rather than for persons of their own professions or trades. These discerning citizens are well aware that the mechanic and manufacturing arts furnish the materials of mercantile enterprise and industry. Many of them, indeed, are directly connected with the operations of commerce. They know that the merchant is their natural patron and friend. They know that, however much confidence they may rightly have in their own good sense, the merchant can advance their interests more effectively than they can themselves. They are aware that their habits in life have not given them those acquired endowments without which, in a deliberative assembly, the greatest natural abilities are for the most part useless. And they are aware that the influence, weight and superior acquirements of the merchants make them better able to contend with any spirit that might happen to find its way into the public councils unfriendly to the manufacturing and trading interests. These considerations, and many others that might be mentioned, prove, and experience confirms, that artisans and manufacturers will commonly be disposed to give their votes to merchants and to those whom the merchants recommend. We must therefore consider merchants the natural representatives of all these classes of the community.

As for the learned professions, little needs to be said. They truly form no distinct interest in society, and depending on their situation and talents, they will be chosen, without distinction, by each other and by other parts of the community, as the objects of their confidence.

Nothing remains but the landed interest. In a political view, and particularly with respect to taxes, I take this to be perfectly united, from the wealthiest landlord down to the poorest tenant. No tax can be laid on land that will not affect the owner of millions of acres just as it affects the owner of a single acre. Every landholder will therefore share an interest in keeping the taxes on land as low as possible, and common interest can always be counted on as the surest bond of sympathy. But even if we could suppose a difference of interest between the wealthy landholder and the middling farmer, what reason is there to conclude that the first would have a better chance than the last of being sent to the national legislature? If we take fact as our guide and look at our own senate and assembly, we shall find that moderate landowners prevail in both. This is no less true in the senate, which has fewer members, than in the assembly, which has more. Where the qualifications of the electors are the same, whether they have to choose a small number or a large one, their votes will go to those in whom they have most confidence, whether these happen to be men of large fortunes, of moderate property, or of no property at all.

It is said to be necessary that every class of citizens have some of its own number in the representative body, so that its feelings and interests may be better understood and attended to. But we have seen that this will never happen under any arrangement that leaves the votes of the people free. Where they are free, the representative body will be composed of landholders, merchants and men of the learned professions, with too few exceptions to have any influence on the spirit of the government. But where is the danger that these three kinds of men will fail to understand or attend to the interests and feelings of the different classes of citizens? Will not the landholder know and feel whatever will promote or secure the interest of landed property? Will he not, from his own stake in that kind of property, be inclined enough to resist every attempt to harm or burden it? Will not the merchant understand, and be disposed to cultivate as far as is proper, the interests of the mechanic and manufacturing arts, to which his commerce is so closely allied? And will not the man of a learned profession, who will feel neutral toward the rivalries between the different branches of industry, be likely to prove an impartial arbiter between them, ready to promote either so far as it seems to him to serve the general interests of society?

Now take into account the passing moods or dispositions that may happen to prevail in particular parts of society, and to which a wise administration will never be inattentive. Is a man whose situation leads him to wide inquiry and information less likely to judge their nature, extent and foundation competently than a man whose observation does not go beyond the circle of his neighbors and acquaintances? Is it not natural that a man who is a candidate for the favor of the people, and who depends on the votes of his fellow citizens to keep his public honors, should take care to inform himself of their dispositions and inclinations and should be willing to allow them their proper degree of influence on his conduct? This dependence, and the necessity of binding himself and his posterity by the laws to which he gives his assent, are the true and strong chords of sympathy between the representative and the constituent.

Of all the business of government, taxation demands the most extensive information and the most thorough knowledge of the principles of political economy. A man who understands those principles best will be the least likely to turn to oppressive expedients, or to sacrifice some particular class of citizens in order to raise revenue. It could be demonstrated that the most productive system of finance is always the least burdensome. There can be no doubt that anyone who is to exercise the power of taxation judiciously must know the general character, habits and ways of thinking of the people at large, and must know the resources of the country. That is all anyone can reasonably mean by a knowledge of the interests and feelings of the people. In any other sense the claim means nothing, or something absurd. Taking it in that sense, let every considerate citizen judge for himself where the needed qualification is most likely to be found.

chapters.title: No. 36 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The previous number was devoted mainly to one set of observations, and their result, as we have seen, is this. The different interests and views of the various classes of the community will naturally operate in such a way that the representatives of the people, whether they are fewer or more numerous, will be almost entirely landowners, merchants and members of the learned professions. These men will truly represent all those interests and views. Someone may object that other kinds of men have sat in the local legislatures. My answer is that I admit there are exceptions to the rule, but there are too few of them to change the general complexion or character of the government. Strong minds appear in every walk of life and rise above the disadvantages of their situation. They earn the tribute their merit deserves, not only from the classes they belong to but from society as a whole. The door ought to be equally open to everyone. I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we shall see such vigorous plants flourish in the soil of federal legislation as well as of State legislation. But a few cases of this sort do not make the reasoning any less conclusive, since it rests on the general course of things.

The subject could be placed in several other lights, and all would lead to the same result. For instance, one might ask what closer affinity or relation of interest can be imagined between the carpenter and the blacksmith, on the one hand, and the linen manufacturer or stocking weaver, on the other, than between the merchant and any of them. Everyone knows that the different branches of the mechanic or manufacturing arts are often as much rivals as any of the departments of labor and industry are. So unless the representative body were made far larger than any sound idea of order or wisdom in its deliberations would allow, the spirit of this objection, as it seems to be, could never be realized in practice. But I will say no more on a matter that has so far worn too loose a garb for anyone to inspect its real shape or tendency accurately.

Another objection, somewhat more precise, deserves our attention. It is asserted that the national legislature could never use a power of internal taxation to good effect, for two reasons: it would lack sufficient knowledge of local circumstances, and the revenue laws of the Union would interfere with those of the individual States. The claim that proper knowledge would be lacking seems to me to have no foundation at all. Suppose a State legislature is deciding a question about one of its counties that calls for knowledge of local details. How does it get that knowledge? Surely from the members who come from that county. Cannot the national legislature obtain the same knowledge from the representatives of each State? And should we not presume that the men generally sent there will be intelligent enough to pass that information along? What is knowledge of local circumstances, as applied to taxation? Is it a detailed topographical acquaintance with every mountain, river, stream, highway and bypath in each State? Or is it a general acquaintance with the State's situation and resources: the condition of its agriculture, commerce and manufactures, the nature of what it produces and consumes, and the different degrees and kinds of its wealth, property and industry?

Even under the more popular kinds of government, nations in general hand the management of their finances to single men or to small boards. These men work out and prepare the plans of taxation first, and the sovereign or the legislature afterward enacts them into law.

Everywhere, then, inquisitive and enlightened statesmen are thought best qualified to choose wisely the objects suited to revenue. As far as the opinion of mankind can count in this question, that is a clear sign of what kind of knowledge of local circumstances taxation requires.

The taxes meant by the general name of internal taxes can be divided into DIRECT and INDIRECT taxes. The objection is made against both, but its reasoning seems to be aimed only at the first. As for the second, which must be taken to mean duties and excises on articles of consumption, one cannot imagine what difficulties are feared. The knowledge needed about them must plainly be of a sort that the nature of the article itself will suggest, or that any well-informed man, especially one of the mercantile class, can easily supply. Whatever distinguishes an article's situation in one State from its situation in another must be few, simple and easy to grasp. The main thing to attend to would be to avoid articles already reserved for the use of a particular State, and there could be no trouble in finding out the revenue system of each. It could always be learned from their codes of laws, and from the members who represent the individual States.

Applied to real property, meaning houses and lands, the objection appears at first sight to have more force. Yet even here it will not survive a close look. Land taxes are commonly laid in one of two ways. One is by ACTUAL valuations, permanent or periodic.
