The other is by OCCASIONAL assessments, made at the discretion, or according to the best judgment, of certain officers whose duty it is to make them. In either case the EXECUTION of the business is the only part that requires knowledge of local details, and it must fall to discreet persons acting as commissioners or assessors, whether elected by the people or appointed by the government for that purpose. All the law can do is name those persons, or set out how they are to be elected or appointed, fix their numbers and qualifications, and sketch the general outlines of their powers and duties. What is there in all this that the national legislature cannot do as well as a State legislature? The attention of either can reach only general principles. As I have said, local details must be left to those who are to carry out the plan.

There is, however, a simple way of putting this matter that must be entirely satisfactory. The national legislature can use the SYSTEM OF EACH STATE WITHIN THAT STATE. The federal government can adopt and employ, in every part, the method that each State uses to lay and collect this kind of tax.

Remember also that the share of these taxes is not left to the discretion of the national legislature. It is to be fixed by the numbers of each State, as described in the second section of the first article. An actual census, or enumeration of the people, must supply the rule, and this effectively shuts the door on bias and oppression. The abuse of this power of taxation seems to have been guarded against with careful circumspection. Besides the precaution just mentioned, there is a provision that "all duties, imposts, and excises shall be UNIFORM throughout the United States."

Various speakers and writers on the side of the Constitution have rightly pointed out that if the exercise of the power of internal taxation by the Union should prove on experiment to be really inconvenient, the federal government may then give up the use of it and go back to requisitions, the formal requests to the States for money. To this, opponents have triumphantly replied: why not leave out that ambiguous power in the first place and depend on the other resource? Two solid answers can be given. First, if the power turns out to be convenient, it will be preferable because it will be more effective, and no theory can prove, nor anything but experiment, that it cannot be used to advantage. Indeed the opposite seems most probable. Second, simply having such a power in the Constitution will give requisitions a strong influence. When the States know that the Union can act without their help, they will have a powerful motive to make an effort themselves.

Next, the objection that the revenue laws of the Union and of its members will interfere. We have already seen that their authorities cannot clash or conflict. In a legal sense, then, the laws cannot interfere with each other. And it is far from impossible to avoid interference even in the policy of their different systems. An effective means is for each side to keep away from the objects that the other has taken up first. Neither can CONTROL the other, so each will plainly and sensibly see that it has an interest in this mutual restraint. Where there is an IMMEDIATE common interest, we may safely count on its working. Once the particular debts of the States are cleared away and their expenses are held within their natural limits, hardly any possibility of interference will remain. A small land tax will meet the needs of the States, and will be their simplest and most fitting resource.

Many specters have been conjured out of this power of internal taxation to alarm the people. We have heard of double sets of revenue officers, of burdens doubled by double taxation, and of the frightful shapes of odious and oppressive poll taxes. All of these have been played upon with the ingenious dexterity of political sleight of hand.

Take the first point. There are two cases in which there can be no room for double sets of officers. In the first, the right to impose the tax belongs exclusively to the Union, as with duties on imports. In the second, the object has not yet come under any State regulation or provision, which may be true of a variety of objects. In other cases, the United States will probably either stay away entirely from objects already taken up for local purposes, or use State officers and State regulations to collect the additional charge. This will best serve the aims of revenue, since it saves the expense of collection, and it will best avoid giving the State governments and the people any occasion for disgust. At all events, here is a workable way to avoid such a problem, and nothing more is required than to show that the evils predicted do not necessarily follow from the plan.

Next, any argument drawn from a supposed system of influence. It is enough to answer that such a thing ought not to be presumed. But the supposition also admits of a more precise answer. Suppose such a spirit did infest the councils of the Union. The surest road to its goal would be to employ the State officers as much as possible, and to bind them to the Union by adding to their pay. That would turn the tide of State influence into the channels of the national government, instead of making federal influence run in an opposite and hostile current. But all suppositions of this kind are invidious and ought to be kept out of the great question before the people. They serve no purpose except to cast a mist over the truth.

The suggestion of double taxation has a plain answer. The wants of the Union must be supplied one way or another. If they are supplied by the authority of the federal government, they will not be supplied by the State governments. The total amount of taxes the community pays must be the same either way. There is, however, an advantage if the Union makes the provision. The chief resource of commercial imposts, the most convenient branch of revenue, can be prudently developed much further under federal than under State regulation, which will naturally make it less necessary to turn to more inconvenient methods. There is a further advantage. To whatever extent the power of internal taxation really is difficult to exercise, that very difficulty will encourage greater care in choosing and arranging the means. It must naturally make it a fixed point of policy in the national administration to go as far as practicable in making the luxury of the rich pay into the public treasury, so as to lessen the need for impositions that might create dissatisfaction among the poorer and most numerous classes of society. How fortunate when the interest that a government has in preserving its own power coincides with a proper distribution of the public burdens, and tends to protect the least wealthy part of the community from oppression!

As for poll taxes, I confess without hesitation that I disapprove of them. They have prevailed from an early period in those States(1) that have always been the most tenacious of their rights. Even so, I should be sorry to see them introduced under the national government. But does it follow that, because a power to lay them exists, they will actually be laid? Every State in the Union has the power to impose taxes of this kind, and yet in several of them they are unknown in practice. Are the State governments to be stigmatized as tyrannies because they hold this power? If they are not, how can the same power justify such a charge against the national government, or even be urged as an obstacle to adopting it? However unfriendly I am to this kind of imposition, I am still thoroughly convinced that the federal government ought to have the power of resorting to it. Nations face certain emergencies in which expedients that should be avoided in the ordinary state of things become essential to the public welfare. Because such emergencies are possible, the government ought always to have the option of using them. The real scarcity in this country of objects that can be counted on as productive sources of revenue is a reason peculiar to ourselves for not limiting the discretion of the national councils in this respect. There may be critical and tempestuous conjunctures of the State in which a poll tax becomes an invaluable resource. And since I know nothing that exempts this part of the globe from the common calamities that have befallen other parts, I confess my aversion to any scheme that would disarm the government of even one weapon that might, in any possible contingency, be usefully employed for the general defense and security.

(I have now finished examining those of the powers proposed for the United States that bear directly on the energy of the government, and I have tried to answer the principal objections made against them. I have said nothing of the minor authorities, which are either too inconsiderable to have been thought worth the hostility of the opponents of the Constitution, or so obviously proper that they admit of no dispute. The mass of judiciary power, however, might have claimed an investigation under this head. I decided against it because its organization and its extent can be considered more advantageously together, and so I refer it to the next branch of our inquiries.)(E1)

(I have now finished examining those powers proposed for the federal government that relate more particularly to its energy and to its effectiveness in achieving the great and primary objects of union. There are others which I have omitted here, but which will be taken up under the next head of our inquiries, to make the view of the subject more complete. I flatter myself that the progress made so far will have satisfied the fair and judicious part of the community of this: some of the objections most strenuously urged against the Constitution, and most formidable when they first appeared, are not only without substance but, had they influenced the framing of the plan, would have made it unfit for the great ends of public happiness and national prosperity. I flatter myself equally that a further and more critical investigation of the system will recommend it still more to every sincere and disinterested advocate of good government, and will leave men of this character no doubt of the propriety and expediency of adopting it. How fortunate it will be for ourselves, and how much more honorable for human nature, if we have wisdom and virtue enough to set so glorious an example to mankind!)(E1)
1. The New England States.
E1. Two versions of this paragraph appear in different editions.

chapters.title: No. 37 — Concerning the Difficulties of the Convention in Devising a Proper Form of Government. (Madison)
paragraphs: In reviewing the defects of the existing Confederation, and showing that no government with less energy than the one now before the public can remedy them, we naturally had to consider several of that government's most important principles. But the ultimate object of these papers is to determine clearly and fully the merits of this Constitution and the wisdom of adopting it. Our plan cannot be complete, then, unless we survey the work of the Convention more critically and thoroughly. We must examine it from every side, compare all its parts, and calculate its probable effects. If this remaining task is to be carried out in a frame of mind that leads to a just and fair result, I must first indulge in some reflections that fairness itself suggests.

It is a misfortune inseparable from human affairs that public measures are seldom examined in the spirit of moderation that a just estimate of their real tendency to help or hinder the public good requires. That spirit is more likely to be weakened than strengthened by the very occasions that demand an unusual amount of it. Those whom experience has led to notice this will not be surprised that the act of the Convention has met, or has stirred up, attitudes unfriendly to a fair discussion and accurate judgment of its merits, on one side as much as on the other. After all, it recommends so many important changes and innovations, it can be viewed in so many lights and relations, and it touches the springs of so many passions and interests. In some people it has been all too plain from their own publications that they have examined the proposed Constitution not merely with a leaning toward censure but with a settled decision to condemn it. The language of others betrays the opposite decision, or bias, and this makes their opinions of little weight in the question too. In putting these two kinds of people on the same level as to the weight of their opinions, I do not mean to suggest that there may not be a real difference in the purity of their intentions. It is only just to say in favor of the second kind that our situation is universally admitted to be peculiarly critical, and to require absolutely that something be done for our relief. The man who has decided in advance to support what has actually been done may therefore have drawn his bias from the weight of these considerations, as well as from motives of a sinister kind. The man who has decided in advance to oppose it, on the other hand, can have been moved by no excusable motive at all. The intentions of the first may be upright, though they may equally be blameworthy. The aims of the last cannot be upright, and must be blameworthy. But the truth is that these papers are not addressed to people of either description. They ask for the attention only of those who combine a sincere zeal for the happiness of their country with a temperament favorable to judging fairly the means of promoting it.

People of this character will set about examining the plan the Convention submitted without any wish to find faults or to magnify them. They will see that it is only reasonable to remember that a faultless plan was not to be expected. Nor will they merely make allowance for the errors that the Convention, as a body of men, was liable to commit because of human fallibility. They will bear in mind that they themselves are only men too, and ought not to assume infallibility when they rejudge the fallible opinions of others.

They will see just as readily that, apart from these reasons for fairness, many allowances should be made for the difficulties inherent in the very nature of the task that was entrusted to the Convention.

The novelty of the undertaking strikes us at once. These papers have shown that the existing Confederation is founded on false principles, so that we must change this first foundation and with it the structure resting on it. They have shown that the other confederacies which could be consulted as precedents were spoiled by the same erroneous principles, and so can offer no light except that of beacons, which warn of the course to be avoided without pointing out the one to be followed. The most the Convention could do in such a situation was to avoid the errors that the past experience of other countries, and of our own, had revealed, and to provide a convenient way of correcting its own errors as future experience might uncover them.

One very important difficulty the Convention met must have been the task of combining the necessary stability and energy in government with unfailing attention to liberty and to the republican form. If they had not substantially accomplished this part of their task, they would have fulfilled very imperfectly the object of their appointment and the expectation of the public. Yet no one who does not wish to betray his ignorance of the subject will deny that it could not easily be accomplished. Energy in government is essential to security against external and internal danger, and to the prompt and beneficial execution of the laws, both of which enter into the very definition of good government. Stability in government is essential to national character and the advantages that go with it, and also to that repose and confidence in the minds of the people which are among the chief blessings of civil society. A changeable and irregular legislation is no more an evil in itself than it is odious to the people. It may be said with assurance that the people of this country, enlightened as they are about the nature of good government and concerned as the great body of them are in its effects, will never be satisfied until some remedy is applied to the vicissitudes and uncertainties that mark the State administrations. But when we compare these valuable ingredients with the vital principles of liberty, we see at once how hard it is to mix them in their due proportions. The spirit of republican liberty seems to demand, on one side, not only that all power be derived from the people but that those entrusted with it be kept in independence on the people by the short duration of their appointments. It seems to demand also that even during this short period the trust be placed not in a few hands but in a number of them. Stability, on the contrary, requires that the hands in which power is lodged remain the same for a length of time. Frequent elections will bring a frequent change of men, and a frequent change of men will bring a frequent change of measures. Energy in government, meanwhile, requires not only a certain duration of power but that it be exercised by a single hand.
How far the Convention may have succeeded in this part of its work will appear better on a closer view of it. From the brief look taken here, it must be clear that this part was an arduous one.

Equally arduous must have been the task of marking the proper line of partition between the authority of the general government and that of the State governments. Every man will be aware of this difficulty in proportion as he has been accustomed to contemplate and distinguish objects that are extensive and complicated in their nature. Even the faculties of the mind have never yet been distinguished and defined with satisfactory precision, for all the efforts of the most acute and metaphysical philosophers. Sense, perception, judgment, desire, volition, memory and imagination are found to be separated by such delicate shades and minute gradations that their boundaries have eluded the most subtle investigation, and remain a rich source of ingenious discussion and controversy. The boundaries between the great kingdoms of nature, and still more between the various provinces and lesser portions into which they are subdivided, illustrate the same important truth. The most sagacious and laborious naturalists have never yet succeeded in tracing with certainty the line that separates the district of vegetable life from the neighboring region of unorganized matter, or that marks where the first ends and the animal empire begins. There is still greater obscurity in the distinguishing characters by which the objects in each of these great departments of nature have been arranged and sorted.

When we pass from the works of nature to the institutions of man, our hopes and expectations from the efforts of human sagacity must be moderated still further. In nature all the outlines are perfectly accurate, and appear otherwise only because the eye that surveys them is imperfect. In human institutions the obscurity comes as much from the object itself as from the organ that contemplates it. Experience has taught us that no skill in the science of government has yet been able to distinguish and define with sufficient certainty its three great provinces, the legislative, the executive and the judiciary, or even the privileges and powers of the different legislative branches. Questions arise daily in practice that prove the obscurity reigning over these subjects, and that puzzle the greatest adepts in political science.

The experience of ages, with the continued and combined labors of the most enlightened legislatures and jurists, has been equally unsuccessful in describing the several objects and limits of different codes of law and different courts of justice. In Great Britain, where accuracy in such subjects has been pursued more industriously than anywhere else in the world, the precise extent of the common law, the statute law, the maritime law, the ecclesiastical law, the law of corporations and other local laws and customs still remains to be clearly and finally settled. The jurisdiction of her separate courts, general and local, of law, of equity, of admiralty and so on, is no less a source of frequent and intricate disputes, which sufficiently show how indeterminate the limits are that circumscribe them. All new laws, though drafted with the greatest technical skill and passed after the fullest and most mature deliberation, are considered more or less obscure and equivocal until a series of particular discussions and judgments has settled and fixed their meaning. Besides the obscurity that comes from the complexity of objects and the imperfection of the human faculties, the medium through which men's conceptions are conveyed to each other adds a fresh embarrassment. The use of words is to express ideas. Clarity therefore requires not only that the ideas be distinctly formed but that they be expressed in words distinctly and exclusively suited to them. But no language is so copious as to supply words and phrases for every complex idea, or so correct as not to include many words that equivocally denote different ideas. It must follow that, however accurately objects may be distinguished in themselves, and however accurately the distinction may be considered, the definition of them may be made inaccurate by the inaccuracy of the terms in which it is delivered. This unavoidable inaccuracy must be greater or less according to the complexity and novelty of the objects defined. Even when the Almighty himself condescends to address mankind in their own language, his meaning, luminous as it must be, is made dim and doubtful by the cloudy medium through which it is communicated.

Here, then, are three sources of vague and incorrect definitions: the indistinctness of the object, the imperfection of the organ of conception, and the inadequacy of the vehicle of ideas. Any one of them must produce some degree of obscurity. In drawing the boundary between federal and State jurisdictions, the Convention must have felt the full effect of all three.

To the difficulties already mentioned we may add the conflicting claims of the larger and smaller States. We cannot be wrong in supposing that the larger States would contend for a share in the government fully proportioned to their greater wealth and importance, and that the smaller would be no less tenacious of the equality they now enjoy. We may well suppose that neither side would give way entirely to the other, and so the struggle could end only in compromise. It is also extremely probable that, after the ratio of representation had been settled, this very compromise must have produced a fresh struggle between the same parties. Each would try to shape the organization of the government and the distribution of its powers so as to increase the importance of those branches in forming which it had obtained the greatest share of influence. There are features in the Constitution that bear out each of these suppositions. And so far as either of them is well founded, it shows that the Convention must have been compelled to sacrifice theoretical propriety to the force of outside considerations.

Nor could it have been only the large and small States that lined up against each other on various points. Other combinations, arising from differences of local position and policy, must have created further difficulties. Every State may be divided into different districts, and its citizens into different classes, which give birth to contending interests and local jealousies. In the same way the different parts of the United States are distinguished from each other by a variety of circumstances that produce a like effect on a larger scale. And although this variety of interests may have a beneficial influence on the administration of the government once it is formed, for reasons sufficiently explained in an earlier paper, everyone must be aware of the opposite influence that was felt in the task of forming it.

Would it be surprising if, under the pressure of all these difficulties, the Convention had been forced into some departures from that artificial structure and regular symmetry which an abstract view of the subject might lead an ingenious theorist to give to a Constitution planned in his study or in his imagination? The real wonder is that so many difficulties were overcome, and overcome with a unanimity almost as unprecedented as it must have been unexpected. No man of fairness can reflect on this circumstance without sharing the astonishment. No man of pious reflection can fail to see in it a finger of that Almighty hand which has so often and so signally been extended to our relief at the critical stages of the recent revolution.

In an earlier paper we had occasion to notice the repeated and unsuccessful attempts made in the United Netherlands to reform the baneful and notorious vices of their constitution. The history of almost all the great councils and consultations held among mankind to reconcile their discordant opinions, calm their mutual jealousies and adjust their respective interests is a history of factions, contentions and disappointments. It may be ranked among the darkest and most degraded pictures that show the infirmities and depravities of the human character. If a few scattered instances present a brighter aspect, they serve only as exceptions that remind us of the general truth, and by their luster they deepen the gloom of the opposite prospect with which they are contrasted. When we consider the causes of these exceptions and apply them to the particular instance before us, we are necessarily led to two important conclusions. The first is that the Convention must have enjoyed, to a very singular degree, freedom from the pestilential influence of party animosities, the disease most common to deliberative bodies and most likely to contaminate their proceedings. The second conclusion is that all the deputations that made up the Convention were either satisfactorily accommodated by the final act or were brought to agree to it by a deep conviction of the necessity of sacrificing private opinions and particular interests to the public good, and by despair of seeing this necessity lessened by delay or by new experiments.

chapters.title: No. 38 — The Same Subject Continued, and the Incoherence of the Objections to the New Plan Exposed. (Madison)
paragraphs: It is remarkable that in every case ancient history reports in which a government was established by deliberate and common consent, the task of framing it was not given to an assembly of men. It was carried out by some individual citizen of outstanding wisdom and proven integrity.

We learn that Minos was the first founder of the government of Crete, and Zaleucus of that of the Locrians. Theseus first, and then Draco and Solon, set up the government of Athens. Lycurgus was the lawgiver of Sparta. Romulus laid the foundation of the original government of Rome, and two of his elected successors, Numa and Tullius Hostilius, completed the work. When the monarchy was abolished, Brutus put the consular administration in its place. He came forward with a plan for such a reform, which, he claimed, Tullius Hostilius had prepared, and his skill won for it the assent and ratification of the senate and the people. The same holds true of confederate governments. Amphictyon, we are told, was the author of the one that bore his name. The Achaean league was first born through Achaeus and born a second time through Aratus.

In every instance we cannot determine what part these reputed lawgivers played in their respective establishments, or how far they held the lawful authority of the people. In some cases, however, the proceeding was strictly regular. Draco appears to have been entrusted by the people of Athens with unlimited powers to reform their government and laws. And Solon, according to Plutarch, was in a manner compelled by the universal vote of his fellow citizens to take on himself the sole and absolute power of remodeling the constitution. The proceedings under Lycurgus were less regular. But so far as the advocates of a regular reform could prevail, they all looked to the individual efforts of that celebrated patriot and sage, instead of trying to bring about a revolution through a deliberative body of citizens.

Where could it have come from that a people as jealous of their liberty as the Greeks were should abandon caution so far as to place their destiny in the hands of a single citizen? Where could it have come from that the Athenians, who would not allow an army to be commanded by fewer than ten generals, and who needed no other proof of danger to their liberties than the illustrious merit of a fellow citizen, should consider one illustrious citizen a better keeper of their own fortunes and their posterity's than a select body of citizens, from whose joint deliberations more wisdom and more safety might have been expected? These questions cannot be fully answered without supposing that the fear of discord and disunion among a number of counselors outweighed their fear of treachery or incapacity in a single individual. History also tells us of the difficulties these celebrated reformers had to contend with, and of the expedients they were forced to use to put their reforms into effect. Solon, who seems to have followed a more temporizing policy, confessed that he had not given his countrymen the government best suited to their happiness, but the one most tolerable to their prejudices. And Lycurgus, who held more firmly to his object, had to mix some violence with the authority of superstition, and secured his final success by a voluntary renunciation, first of his country and then of his life. These lessons teach us, on the one hand, to admire the improvement America has made on the ancient way of preparing and establishing regular plans of government. On the other hand, they serve no less to warn us of the hazards and difficulties that go with such experiments, and of the great imprudence of multiplying them without need.

Is it an unreasonable conjecture that whatever errors the plan of the Convention contains are such as have resulted from lack of earlier experience in this complicated and difficult subject, rather than from any lack of accuracy or care in investigating it, and consequently are such as will not be found until an actual trial has pointed them out? Many considerations of a general nature make this conjecture probable, and so does the particular case of the Articles of Confederation. Notice that when these articles were submitted to the individual States for ratification, they produced numerous objections and proposed amendments. Not one of them alludes to the great and radical error that actual trial has since uncovered. If we except the observations that New Jersey was led to make by her local situation rather than by any special foresight, it may be doubted whether a single suggestion was weighty enough to justify revising the system. There is nevertheless abundant reason to suppose that, trivial as these objections were, some States would have clung to them with very dangerous inflexibility, had their zeal for their opinions and supposed interests not been stifled by the more powerful feeling of self-preservation. We may remember that one State persisted for several years in refusing her agreement, although the enemy remained the whole time at our gates, or rather in the very bowels of our country. In the end she was brought around by no weaker motive than the fear of being blamed for prolonging the public calamities and endangering the outcome of the contest. Every fair-minded reader will draw the proper reflections from these important facts.

A patient finds his disorder growing worse every day, and that an effective remedy cannot be delayed any longer without extreme danger. After coolly considering his situation and the characters of different physicians, he picks and calls in those he judges most capable of relieving him and most deserving of his confidence. The physicians attend. His case is carefully examined and a consultation is held. They agree unanimously that the symptoms are critical, but that with proper and timely relief the case is so far from desperate that it may even lead to an improvement of his constitution. They are equally unanimous in prescribing the remedy by which this happy effect is to be produced. But no sooner is the prescription made known than a number of people step in. Without denying that the disorder is real or dangerous, they assure the patient that the prescription will be poison to his constitution, and forbid him, on pain of certain death, to use it. Might not the patient reasonably demand, before he ventured to follow this advice, that the authors of it should at least agree among themselves on some other remedy to take its place? And if he found them differing as much from one another as from his first counselors, would he not act prudently in trying the experiment those first counselors unanimously recommended, rather than listening to people who could neither deny the need of a speedy remedy nor agree in proposing one?

America at this moment is such a patient in such a situation. She has been aware of her malady. She has obtained regular and unanimous advice from men of her own careful choosing. And others warn her against following this advice, on pain of the most fatal consequences. Do the advisers deny that her danger is real? No. Do they deny the need of some speedy and powerful remedy? No. Are they agreed, are even any two of them agreed, in their objections to the proposed remedy or in the proper one to put in its place? Let them speak for themselves. This one tells us that the proposed Constitution ought to be rejected because it is not a confederation of the States but a government over individuals. Another admits that it ought to be a government over individuals to a certain extent, but by no means to the extent proposed. A third does not object to a government over individuals, or to the extent proposed, but to the lack of a bill of rights. A fourth agrees that a bill of rights is absolutely necessary, but argues that it ought to declare, not the personal rights of individuals, but the rights reserved to the States in their political capacity. A fifth is of the opinion that a bill of rights of any sort would be superfluous and out of place, and that the plan would be beyond objection but for the fatal power of regulating the times and places of election. An objector in a large State cries out loudly against the unreasonable equality of representation in the Senate. An objector in a small State is equally loud against the dangerous inequality in the House of Representatives. From one quarter we are alarmed at the amazing expense, owing to the number of persons who are to run the new government. From another quarter, and sometimes from the same quarter on another occasion, the cry is that Congress will be only a shadow of a representation, and that the government would be far less objectionable if the number and the expense were doubled. A patriot in a State that does not import or export finds insuperable objections to the power of direct taxation. The patriotic adversary in a State with great exports and imports is no less dissatisfied that the whole burden of taxes may be thrown on consumption. This politician discovers in the Constitution a direct and irresistible tendency to monarchy; that one is equally sure it will end in aristocracy. Another is puzzled to say which of these shapes it will finally take, but sees clearly that it must be one or the other. And a fourth is not lacking who, with no less confidence, affirms that the Constitution is so far from leaning toward either of these dangers that the weight on that side will not be enough to keep it upright and firm against its opposite tendencies. With another class of adversaries to the Constitution the language is that the legislative, executive and judiciary departments are intermixed in such a way as to contradict all ideas of regular government and all the precautions needed in favor of liberty. While this objection circulates in vague and general terms, few lend it their support. Let each one come forward with his own explanation, and scarcely any two are exactly agreed on the subject. In the eyes of one, the vicious part of the organization is the joining of the Senate with the President in the responsible function of appointing to offices, instead of vesting this executive power in the Executive alone. To another, the exclusion of the House of Representatives is equally offensive, since its numbers alone could be a proper security against corruption and bias in exercising such a power. For another, letting the President have any share in a power that must always be a dangerous engine in the hands of the chief executive is an unpardonable violation of the maxims of republican jealousy. According to some, no part of the arrangement is more inadmissible than trying impeachments before the Senate, which is alternately a member of both the legislative and executive departments, when this power so obviously belonged to the judiciary department. "We concur fully," others reply, "in the objection to this part of the plan, but we can never agree that a reference of impeachments to the judiciary authority would be an amendment of the error. Our principal dislike to the organization arises from the extensive powers already lodged in that department." Even among the zealous supporters of a council of state, the most irreconcilable disagreement is found over how it ought to be constituted. One gentleman demands that the council consist of a small number, to be appointed by the most numerous branch of the legislature. Another would prefer a larger number, and regards it as a fundamental condition that the appointment be made by the President himself.

Our argument can give no offense to the writers against the plan of the federal Constitution if we suppose that, as they are the most zealous, so they are also the wisest of those who think the recent Convention unequal to its assigned task, and that a wiser and better plan might and ought to be substituted. Let us suppose further that their country agrees, both with this favorable opinion of their merits and with their unfavorable opinion of the Convention, and so proceeds to form them into a second convention, with full powers and for the express purpose of revising and remolding the work of the first. Suppose the experiment were seriously made, though it takes some effort to view it seriously even as fiction. I leave it to be decided by the sample of opinions just displayed whether, with all their enmity toward their predecessors, they would depart from their example at any single point so widely as in the discord and ferment that would mark their own deliberations. I leave it also to be decided whether the Constitution now before the public would not stand as fair a chance of immortality as Lycurgus gave that of Sparta, by making its change depend on his own return from exile and death, if it were adopted immediately and were to remain in force, not until a BETTER one, but until ANOTHER should be agreed upon by this new assembly of lawgivers.

It is a matter of both wonder and regret that those who raise so many objections against the new Constitution never call to mind the defects of the one that is to be exchanged for it. The former need not be perfect; it is enough that the latter is more imperfect. No man would refuse to give brass for silver or gold because the silver or gold had some alloy in it. No man would refuse to leave a shattered and tottering house for a firm and comfortable building because the building had no porch, or because some of the rooms were a little larger or smaller, or the ceilings a little higher or lower, than he would have planned them. But setting aside illustrations of this sort, is it not plain that most of the main objections urged against the new system apply with tenfold weight against the existing Confederation? Is an unlimited power to raise money dangerous in the hands of the federal government? The present Congress can make requisitions, or formal requests for money, in any amount it pleases, and the States are constitutionally bound to furnish them. It can issue bills of credit as long as it will pay for the paper. It can borrow, abroad and at home, as long as a shilling will be lent. Is an unlimited power to raise troops dangerous? The Confederation gives Congress that power also, and Congress has already begun to use it. Is it improper and unsafe to mix the different powers of government in the same body of men? Congress, a single body of men, is the sole depositary of all the federal powers. Is it especially dangerous to put the keys of the treasury and the command of the army into the same hands? The Confederation places both in the hands of Congress. Is a bill of rights essential to liberty? The Confederation has no bill of rights. Is it an objection to the new Constitution that it empowers the Senate, with the concurrence of the Executive, to make treaties that are to be the laws of the land? The existing Congress, without any such check, can make treaties which it has itself declared, and most of the States have recognized, to be the supreme law of the land. Does the new Constitution permit the importation of slaves for twenty years? Under the old one it is permitted forever.

I shall be told that, however dangerous this mixture of powers may be in theory, it is made harmless by Congress's dependence on the States for the means of putting them into practice. However large the mass of powers may be, I shall be told, in fact it is a lifeless mass. To this I say, first, that the Confederation is then guilty of the still greater folly of declaring certain powers in the federal government absolutely necessary while at the same time making them absolutely worthless. I say, next, that if the Union is to continue and no better government is substituted, effective powers must either be granted to the existing Congress or be assumed by it, and in either case the contrast I have just drawn will hold good. But this is not all. Out of this lifeless mass an unnatural growth of power has already arisen, one that tends to realize every danger that can be feared from a defective construction of the supreme government of the Union. It is no longer a matter of speculation and hope that the Western territory is a mine of vast wealth to the United States. It is not of such a nature as to extricate them from their present distresses, or for some time to come to yield any regular supplies for the public expenses. Yet under proper management it must hereafter be able both to bring about a gradual discharge of the domestic debt and to furnish, for a certain period, liberal contributions to the federal treasury. A very large share of this fund has already been surrendered by individual States, and it may reasonably be expected that the remaining States will not persist in withholding similar proofs of their fairness and generosity. We may calculate, therefore, that a rich and fertile country, of an area equal to the inhabited extent of the United States, will soon become a national stock. Congress has taken over the administration of this stock. It has begun to make it productive. Congress has undertaken to do more. It has proceeded to form new States, to set up temporary governments, to appoint officers for them, and to prescribe the conditions on which such States shall be admitted into the Confederacy. All this has been done, and done without the least color of constitutional authority. Yet no blame has been whispered; no alarm has been sounded. A GREAT and INDEPENDENT fund of revenue is passing into the hands of a SINGLE BODY of men, who can RAISE TROOPS to an INDEFINITE NUMBER, and appropriate money for their support for an INDEFINITE PERIOD OF TIME. And yet there are men who have not only been silent spectators of this prospect but are advocates for the system that presents it, and who at the same time urge against the new system the objections we have heard. Would they not act more consistently if they urged the establishment of the new system as no less necessary to guard the Union against the future powers and resources of a body constructed like the existing Congress than to save it from the dangers threatened by that Assembly's present impotence?

By anything I have said here I do not mean to censure the measures Congress has pursued. I am aware that it could not have done otherwise. The public interest and the necessity of the case laid on it the task of overleaping its constitutional limits. But is not the fact an alarming proof of the danger that results from a government that lacks regular powers equal to its objects? Dissolution or usurpation is the dreadful dilemma to which such a government is continually exposed.

chapters.title: No. 39 — The Conformity of the Plan to Republican Principles (Madison)
paragraphs: With the last paper we finished the observations meant as an introduction to a fair survey of the plan of government reported by the Convention. We now turn to carrying out that part of our undertaking.

The first question to ask is whether the general form and aspect of the government is strictly republican. Clearly no other form could be reconciled with the spirit of the people of America, with the fundamental principles of the Revolution, or with the honorable resolve, shared by every devotee of liberty, to rest all our political experiments on mankind's capacity for self-government. If the plan of the Convention turns out to depart from the republican character, then, its advocates must give it up as no longer defensible.

What, then, distinguishes the republican form? Suppose we looked for the answer not in principles but in the way political writers have applied the term to the constitutions of different States. We would never find a satisfactory one. Holland, where not a particle of the supreme authority comes from the people, has almost universally been called a republic. The same title has been given to Venice, where a small body of hereditary nobles holds absolute power, and exercises it absolutely, over the great body of the people. Poland, a mixture of aristocracy and monarchy in their worst forms, has been dignified with the same name. England has only one republican branch of government, combined with a hereditary aristocracy and a monarchy, yet it has with equal impropriety often been put on the list of republics. These examples are nearly as unlike one another as they are unlike a genuine republic, and they show how extremely loosely the term has been used in political discussions.

Suppose instead we take as our standard the different principles on which different forms of government are founded. We may then define a republic as, or at least give that name to, a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior. It is ESSENTIAL to such a government that it be derived from the great body of the society, and not from an inconsiderable proportion of it or a favored class. If it were otherwise, a handful of tyrannical nobles who exercised their oppressions by delegating their powers could aspire to the rank of republicans and claim the honorable title of republic for their government. It is SUFFICIENT for such a government that those who administer it be appointed by the people, directly or indirectly, and that they hold their appointments by one of the tenures just named. If that were not enough, every government in the United States would lose its republican character, and so would every other popular government that has been or can be well organized or well executed. In every State in the Union, the constitution provides that some officers of government, at least, are appointed only indirectly by the people. In most of them the chief executive himself is appointed in this way. In one, this mode of appointment reaches even one of the co-ordinate branches of the legislature. In all the constitutions, too, the highest offices are held for a fixed period, and in many cases, in both the legislative and executive departments, for a period of years. Most of the constitutions also provide, as the most respected and accepted opinions on the subject recommend, that the members of the judiciary department keep their offices by the firm tenure of good behavior.

Compare the Constitution planned by the Convention with this standard, and we see at once that it meets it in the strictest sense. The House of Representatives is elected directly by the great body of the people, as at least one branch of every State legislature is. The Senate, like the present Congress and the Senate of Maryland, gets its appointment indirectly from the people. The President is derived indirectly from the choice of the people, following the example of most of the States. Even the judges and all the other officers of the Union will be chosen by the people themselves, though by a remote choice, just as in the individual States. The length of the appointments also accords with the republican standard and with the model of the State constitutions. The House of Representatives is elected at fixed intervals, as in all the States, and for two years, as in the State of South Carolina. The Senate is elected for six years, only one year more than the term of the Senate of Maryland and only two more than that of the Senates of New York and Virginia. The President is to stay in office for four years. In New York and Delaware, by comparison, the chief executive is elected for three years, and in South Carolina for two. In the other States the election is annual. In several of the States, moreover, the constitution makes no provision for impeaching the chief executive, and in Delaware and Virginia he cannot be impeached until he is out of office. The President of the United States can be impeached at any time while in office. The judges are to hold their places, as unquestionably they ought, by the tenure of good behavior. The tenure of ministerial offices in general will be settled by law, as the reason of the case and the example of the State constitutions require.

Should any further proof of the republican complexion of this system be wanted, the most decisive is its absolute prohibition of titles of nobility under both the federal and the State governments, together with its express guaranty of the republican form to each of the State governments.

"But it was not sufficient," say the adversaries of the proposed Constitution, "for the convention to adhere to the republican form. They ought, with equal care, to have preserved the FEDERAL form, which regards the Union as a CONFEDERACY of sovereign states; instead of which, they have framed a NATIONAL government, which regards the Union as a CONSOLIDATION of the States." And it is asked by what authority this bold and radical innovation was undertaken. The use that has been made of this objection means we must examine it with some precision.

I will not stop to ask whether the distinction behind the objection is accurate. To judge the force of the objection fairly, we need to do three things. First, we must find out the real character of the government in question. Second, we must ask how far the Convention was authorized to propose such a government. Third, we must ask how far the duty it owed its country could make up for any lack of regular authority.

First. To find out the real character of the government, we can look at it under five relations: to the foundation on which it is to be established, to the sources from which its ordinary powers are drawn, to the operation of those powers, to their extent, and to the authority by which future changes in the government are to be introduced.

Look at the first relation. On the one hand, the Constitution is to be founded on the assent and ratification of the people of America, given by deputies elected for the special purpose. On the other hand, the people are to give this assent and ratification not as individuals who make up one entire nation, but as the people of the distinct and independent States to which they respectively belong. It is to be the assent and ratification of the individual States, derived from the supreme authority in each State, that is, the authority of the people themselves. So the act establishing the Constitution will not be a NATIONAL act but a FEDERAL one.

One consideration alone shows plainly that it will be a federal and not a national act, as the objectors understand these terms. It will be the act of the people as forming so many independent States, not as forming one aggregate nation, because it is to come neither from the decision of a MAJORITY of the people of the Union nor from that of a MAJORITY of the States. It must come from the UNANIMOUS assent of the individual States that are parties to it. It differs from their ordinary assent only in being expressed by the people themselves rather than by the legislative authority. Suppose the people were regarded in this transaction as forming one nation. Then the will of the majority of all the people of the United States would bind the minority, just as the majority in each State must bind the minority there. That majority would be determined either by comparing the individual votes or by taking the will of the majority of the States as evidence of the will of a majority of the people of the United States. Neither rule has been adopted. Each State, in ratifying the Constitution, is treated as a sovereign body, independent of all the others, and bound only by its own voluntary act. In this relation, then, the new Constitution, if it is established, will be a FEDERAL and not a NATIONAL constitution.

The next relation concerns the sources from which the ordinary powers of government are to be derived. The House of Representatives will draw its powers from the people of America, and the people will be represented in the same proportion and on the same principle as in the legislature of a particular State. So far the government is NATIONAL, not FEDERAL. The Senate, on the other hand, will draw its powers from the States as political and coequal societies, and these will be represented in the Senate on the principle of equality, as they now are in the existing Congress. So far the government is FEDERAL, not NATIONAL. The executive power will come from a very compound source. The States, in their political characters, will make the immediate election of the President. The votes allotted to them follow a compound ratio, which treats them partly as distinct and coequal societies and partly as unequal members of one society. The eventual election, in turn, is to be made by that branch of the legislature composed of the national representatives; yet for this one act they are to be arranged in delegations, one for each of so many distinct and coequal bodies politic. Seen from this side, the government has a mixed character, with at least as many FEDERAL as NATIONAL features.

As it concerns the OPERATION OF THE GOVERNMENT, the difference between a federal and a national government is supposed to be this. In a federal government the powers act on the political bodies that make up the Confederacy, in their political capacities. In a national government they act on the individual citizens who make up the nation, in their individual capacities. Tested by this criterion, the Constitution falls under the NATIONAL character, not the FEDERAL, though perhaps not so completely as has been understood. In several cases, and especially in trying controversies to which States may be parties, the States must be regarded and proceeded against only in their collective and political capacities. To that extent the national countenance of the government on this side seems to be disfigured by a few federal features. But this blemish is perhaps unavoidable in any plan. And because the government acts on the people in their individual capacities in its ordinary and most essential proceedings, we may on the whole call it, in this relation, a NATIONAL government.

Yet if the government is national in the OPERATION of its powers, it changes its aspect once more when we look at the EXTENT of its powers. A national government implies not only authority over the individual citizens but an unlimited supremacy over all persons and things, so far as they can be objects of lawful government. Among a people consolidated into one nation, the national legislature holds this supremacy completely. Among communities united only for particular purposes, it is divided between the general legislature and the municipal legislatures. In the first case, all local authorities are subordinate to the supreme one, which may control, direct or abolish them at pleasure. In the second, the local or municipal authorities hold distinct and independent portions of the supremacy. Within their own spheres they are no more subject to the general authority than the general authority is subject to them within its sphere. In this relation, then, the proposed government cannot be called a NATIONAL one. Its jurisdiction reaches only certain enumerated objects, and it leaves the individual States a residuary and inviolable sovereignty over all the rest. It is true that, when a controversy arises over the boundary between the two jurisdictions, the court with the final decision is to be set up under the general government. But that does not alter the principle. The decision is to be made impartially, by the rules of the Constitution, and all the usual and most effective precautions are taken to secure that impartiality. Some such court is clearly essential to prevent an appeal to the sword and a dissolution of the compact. That it ought to be established under the general government rather than the local governments, or to put it more properly that it could be safely established only under the first, is a position that is unlikely to be disputed.

Test the Constitution by its last relation, to the authority by which amendments are made, and we find it neither wholly NATIONAL nor wholly FEDERAL. If it were wholly national, the supreme and ultimate authority would lie with the MAJORITY of the people of the Union, and that authority could at any time alter or abolish the established government, as the majority of any national society can. If it were wholly federal, every State in the Union would have to concur in any alteration that was to bind them all. The mode the plan of the Convention provides is founded on neither principle. By requiring more than a majority, and particularly by counting the proportion by STATES and not by CITIZENS, it moves away from the NATIONAL character toward the FEDERAL. By making the agreement of fewer than all the States enough, it gives up the FEDERAL character again and takes on the NATIONAL.

The proposed Constitution, therefore, is strictly speaking neither a national nor a federal Constitution but a composition of the two. In its foundation it is federal, not national. In the sources from which the ordinary powers of the government are drawn, it is partly federal and partly national. In the way those powers operate, it is national, not federal. In their extent, once more, it is federal, not national. And finally, in the authoritative mode of introducing amendments, it is neither wholly federal nor wholly national.

chapters.title: No. 40 — On the Powers of the Convention to Form a Mixed Government Examined and Sustained For the New York Packet. Friday, January 18, 1788. (Madison)
paragraphs: The SECOND point to be examined is whether the Convention was authorized to frame and propose this mixed Constitution.

To be exact, we should measure the Convention's powers by examining the commissions that its members received from the bodies that sent them. But every one of those commissions pointed back to one of two recommendations: the one from the meeting at Annapolis in September, 1786, or the one from Congress in February, 1787. So it is enough to look at those two acts.

The act from Annapolis recommends the "appointment of commissioners to take into consideration the situation of the United States; to devise SUCH FURTHER PROVISIONS as shall appear to them necessary to render the Constitution of the federal government ADEQUATE TO THE EXIGENCIES OF THE UNION; and to report such an act for that purpose, to the United States in Congress assembled, as when agreed to by them, and afterwards confirmed by the legislature of every State, will effectually provide for the same."

The act of Congress that made the recommendation reads as follows: "WHEREAS, There is provision in the articles of Confederation and perpetual Union, for making alterations therein, by the assent of a Congress of the United States, and of the legislatures of the several States; and whereas experience hath evinced, that there are defects in the present Confederation; as a mean to remedy which, several of the States, and PARTICULARLY THE STATE OF NEW YORK, by express instructions to their delegates in Congress, have suggested a convention for the purposes expressed in the following resolution; and such convention appearing to be the most probable mean of establishing in these States A FIRM NATIONAL GOVERNMENT:

"Resolved, That in the opinion of Congress it is expedient, that on the second Monday of May next a convention of delegates, who shall have been appointed by the several States, be held at Philadelphia, for the sole and express purpose OF REVISING THE ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION, and reporting to Congress and the several legislatures such ALTERATIONS AND PROVISIONS THEREIN, as shall, when agreed to in Congress, and confirmed by the States, render the federal Constitution ADEQUATE TO THE EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT AND THE PRESERVATION OF THE UNION."

The authority under which the Convention acted has to be drawn out of these several statements, compared with each other and read fairly. The members were to frame a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT that would be adequate to the EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT, and OF THE UNION. They were also to recast the articles of Confederation in whatever form would accomplish those purposes.

Two rules of interpretation apply here. Plain reason dictates both, and both rest on legal axioms. The first is that each part of an expression should, where possible, be given some meaning and be made to serve a common end. The second is that when the parts cannot be made to fit together, the less important must yield to the more important. The means should be given up for the sake of the end, not the end for the sake of the means.

Now suppose that the expressions defining the Convention's authority really did conflict beyond reconciling. Suppose the Convention judged that no ALTERATIONS and PROVISIONS made in the ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION could possibly produce a NATIONAL and ADEQUATE GOVERNMENT. Which part of the definition should it have followed, and which should it have set aside? Which part mattered more, and which less? Which was the end, and which the means? Let these questions be answered by the most scrupulous interpreters of delegated powers, and by the most bitter opponents of what the Convention did. Let them say what mattered more to the happiness of the people of America: that the articles of Confederation be set aside, an adequate government be provided and the Union be preserved; or that an adequate government be left out and the articles of Confederation be kept. Let them say whether keeping these articles was the end, with reform of the government as the means of securing it; or whether the end that the articles themselves originally aimed at was a government adequate to the national happiness, to which the articles, being insufficient means, should have been sacrificed.

But must we suppose that these expressions are absolutely irreconcilable? Must we suppose that no ALTERATIONS or PROVISIONS made in the articles of the confederation could possibly shape them into a national and adequate government, the kind of government the Convention has proposed?

Surely no weight will be put on the TITLE here, since changing it could never be taken as using a power that was not granted. ALTERATIONS in the body of the document are expressly authorized, and so are NEW PROVISIONS in it. So the Convention had power to change the title, to add new articles and to alter old ones. Must we then admit that the power was overstepped as long as some of the old articles survive? Anyone who says so should at least draw the line between authorized and usurped innovations. He should show what degree of change falls within ALTERATIONS AND FURTHER PROVISIONS and what degree amounts to a TRANSMUTATION of the government. Will it be said that the alterations should not have touched the substance of the Confederation? The States would never have appointed a convention so solemnly, or described its objects so broadly, if they had not contemplated some SUBSTANTIAL reform. Will it be said that the FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES of the Confederation lay outside the Convention's purview and should not have been changed? I ask, What are these principles? Do they require that the States be treated, in establishing the Constitution, as distinct and independent sovereigns? The proposed Constitution treats them that way. Do they require that the members of the government be appointed by the legislatures and not by the people of the States? One branch of the new government is to be appointed by these legislatures; and under the Confederation the delegates to Congress MAY ALL be appointed directly by the people, and in two States(1) they actually are. Do they require that the government's powers act on the States and not directly on individuals? In some cases, as has been shown, the powers of the new government will act on the States in their collective characters. In some cases, too, the powers of the existing government act directly on individuals. Take cases of capture; of piracy; of the post office; of coins, weights and measures; of trade with the Indians; of claims under grants of land by different States; and above all, of trials by courts-martial in the army and navy, where death may be inflicted without a jury or even a civil magistrate. In all these cases the powers of the Confederation operate directly on the persons and interests of individual citizens. Do these fundamental principles require, in particular, that no tax be levied except through the States as intermediaries? The Confederation itself authorizes a direct tax, to a certain extent, on the post office. Congress has also read the power of coinage as allowing it to draw a tribute directly from that source. But leave these instances aside. Was it not an acknowledged aim of the Convention, and the universal expectation of the people, that the regulation of trade should be placed with the general government in a form that would make it a direct source of general revenue? Had Congress not repeatedly recommended this measure as consistent with the fundamental principles of the Confederation? Had not every State but one, New York herself included, gone far enough along with Congress's plan to accept the PRINCIPLE of the innovation? Finally, do these principles require that the powers of the general government be limited, and that beyond that limit the States keep their sovereignty and independence? We have seen that in the new government, as in the old, the general powers are limited, and that in all cases not listed the States keep their sovereign and independent jurisdiction.

The truth is that the great principles of the Constitution the Convention proposed are better seen as an expansion of principles already found in the articles of Confederation than as something absolutely new. The trouble with the old system is that these principles are so feeble and narrow that they justify every charge of ineffectiveness brought against it, and need to be enlarged so much that the new system looks like a complete transformation of the old.

In one respect it is admitted that the Convention has departed from the terms of its commission. Instead of reporting a plan that needs the confirmation OF THE LEGISLATURES OF ALL THE STATES, it has reported one to be confirmed by the PEOPLE, which can take effect with NINE STATES ONLY. It is worth noting that this objection, though the most plausible, has been pressed the least in the pamphlets and articles that have swarmed out against the Convention. The restraint can only come from an irresistible sense of how absurd it would be to make the fate of twelve States depend on the perverseness or corruption of a thirteenth. It may also come from the example of stubborn opposition given by a MAJORITY of one sixtieth of the people of America to a measure that twelve States, holding fifty-nine sixtieths of the people, had approved and called for. That example is still fresh in the memory, and the indignation, of every citizen who has felt for the wounded honor and prosperity of his country. Since those who have criticized the Convention's powers have more or less dropped this objection, I will set it aside without further comment.
The THIRD point to be examined is how far a sense of duty, arising out of the situation itself, could have made up for any lack of regular authority.

So far we have analyzed and tested the powers of the Convention as strictly, and by the same rules, as if they had been real and final powers to establish a Constitution for the United States. We have seen how they hold up even on that assumption. Now we should remember that the powers were only advisory and recommendatory. The States meant them to be so, and the Convention understood them to be so. The Convention has accordingly planned and proposed a Constitution that will be worth no more than the paper it is written on unless it receives the approval of the people to whom it is addressed. This changes the whole look of the matter, and lets us judge properly the course the Convention took.

Consider the position the Convention was in. We can gather from its proceedings that the members were deeply and unanimously impressed by the crisis, which had led their country, almost with one voice, to try so unusual and solemn an experiment: correcting the errors of the very system that had produced the crisis. They were just as deeply and unanimously convinced that a reform like the one they have proposed was absolutely necessary to accomplish the purposes of their appointment. They could not have been ignorant that the great body of citizens throughout this great empire were waiting with the keenest anxiety for the outcome of their deliberations. They had every reason to believe that the opposite feelings stirred the minds and hearts of every foe, foreign and domestic, of the liberty and prosperity of the United States. They had seen, from the beginning and through the course of the experiment, how readily the PROPOSITION of a single State (Virginia), for a partial amendment of the Confederation, had been taken up and advanced. They had seen the LIBERTY ASSUMED by a VERY FEW deputies from a VERY FEW States, meeting at Annapolis, of recommending a great and critical object that was wholly foreign to their commission, not only justified by public opinion but actually carried out by twelve of the thirteen States. They had seen Congress, many times, take on not only recommendatory but operative powers, and the public approve, on occasions and for objects infinitely less urgent than those that were to govern their own conduct. They must have reflected that in every great change of an established government, forms ought to yield to substance. Rigid adherence to forms in such cases would make the transcendent and precious right of the people to "abolish or alter their governments as to them shall seem most likely to effect their safety and happiness"(2) merely nominal and worthless, since the people cannot move toward their goal spontaneously and all together; and it is therefore essential that such changes be started by some INFORMAL AND UNAUTHORIZED PROPOSITIONS from some patriotic and respectable citizen or group of citizens. They must have recalled that it was through this irregular and self-assumed privilege of proposing to the people plans for their safety and happiness that the States were first united against the danger their ancient government threatened; that committees and congresses were formed to concentrate their efforts and defend their rights; and that CONVENTIONS were ELECTED in THE SEVERAL STATES to establish the constitutions under which they are now governed. Nor could they have forgotten that nobody showed petty, ill-timed scruples or zeal for ordinary forms, except those who wished to hide behind these masks their secret hostility to the substance being fought for. They must have kept in mind that, because the plan they framed and proposed was to be submitted TO THE PEOPLE THEMSELVES, this supreme authority's disapproval would destroy it forever, while its approval would wipe out all earlier errors and irregularities. It might even have occurred to them that, where people are inclined to find fault, neglecting to use the full power vested in them, and still more recommending any measure that their commission did not warrant, would draw as much criticism as recommending, at one stroke, a measure fully equal to the national exigencies.

Suppose the Convention, with all these impressions and in the midst of all these considerations, had not shown a manly confidence in its country, which had singled it out by so particular a confidence, and had not pointed to a system that it judged capable of securing the country's happiness. Suppose it had instead made the cold and sullen decision to disappoint the country's ardent hopes, to sacrifice substance to forms, and to commit the country's dearest interests to the uncertainty of delay and the hazard of events. I would ask any man who can raise his mind to one elevated thought, or stir in his heart one patriotic feeling, what verdict the impartial world, the friends of mankind and every virtuous citizen should have passed on the conduct and character of this assembly. Or if there is a man whose urge to condemn will not be controlled, I would ask what sentence he keeps in reserve for the twelve States that USURPED THE POWER of sending deputies to the Convention, a body wholly unknown to their constitutions; for Congress, which recommended appointing this body, equally unknown to the Confederation; and for the State of New York in particular, which first urged this unauthorized step and then took it.

But to leave the objectors without any pretext, let us grant for a moment that the Convention was neither authorized by its commission nor justified by circumstances in proposing a Constitution to its country. Does it follow that the Constitution must be rejected for that reason alone? According to the noble precept, it is lawful to take good advice even from an enemy. Shall we then set the ignoble example of refusing such advice when our friends offer it? In every case the prudent question is not so much FROM WHOM the advice comes as whether the advice is GOOD.

To sum up what has been argued and proved here: the charge that the Convention exceeded its powers has no foundation, except for one point that the objectors have hardly pressed. Even if the Convention had exceeded its powers, the circumstances it was placed in not only warranted but required it, as the trusted servant of its country, to take the liberty it assumed. And finally, even if it had violated both its powers and its obligations in proposing a Constitution, we should still embrace that Constitution if it is fitted to accomplish the aims and the happiness of the people of America. How far it deserves that description is the subject we are investigating.

chapters.title: No. 41 — General View of the Powers Conferred by The Constitution (Madison)
paragraphs: The Constitution the Convention proposed can be viewed in two general ways. The FIRST looks at the sum or quantity of power it gives the government, including the restraints it places on the States. The SECOND looks at the particular structure of the government and at how this power is divided among its separate branches.

Taking the FIRST view, two important questions arise. 1. Is any part of the powers handed over to the general government unnecessary or improper? 2. Taken all together, are they dangerous to the share of jurisdiction left to the individual States?
Is the aggregate power of the general government greater than ought to have been vested in it? This is the FIRST question.

Anyone who has listened fairly to the arguments against the government's extensive powers must have noticed that their authors have given very little thought to whether these powers are necessary means to a necessary end. They have preferred to dwell on the drawbacks that are bound to be mixed in with every political advantage, and on the possible abuses that go along with any power or trust that can be put to good use. This way of treating the subject cannot fool the good sense of the people of America. It may show off the writer's cleverness; it may open a boundless field for rhetoric and declamation; it may inflame the passions of the unthinking and confirm the prejudices of the misthinking. But cool and fair-minded people will see at once that even the purest human blessings contain some alloy; that we must always choose the GREATER good rather than the PERFECT good, if we cannot choose the lesser evil; and that in every political institution a power to advance the public happiness carries a discretion that may be misused and abused. They will therefore see that whenever power is to be conferred, the first question to settle is whether the power is necessary to the public good. If the answer is yes, the next question is how to guard as effectively as possible against turning the power to the public's harm.

To judge this subject correctly, we should review the several powers conferred on the government of the Union. To do so conveniently, we can sort them into classes by the objects they concern: 1. Security against foreign danger; 2. Regulation of the intercourse with foreign nations; 3. Maintenance of harmony and proper intercourse among the States; 4. Certain miscellaneous objects of general utility; 5. Restraint of the States from certain injurious acts; 6. Provisions for giving due effectiveness to all these powers.
The FIRST class contains the powers of declaring war and granting letters of marque; of providing armies and fleets; of regulating and calling forth the militia; and of levying and borrowing money.

Security against foreign danger is among the first purposes of civil society. It is an avowed and essential purpose of the American Union. The powers needed to achieve it must be entrusted, with real effect, to the federal councils.
