Is the power to declare war necessary? No one will say it is not, so proving that it is would be superfluous. The existing Confederation gives this power in the fullest form.
Is the power to raise armies and equip fleets necessary? It follows from the power just discussed. It follows from the power of self-defense.
But was it necessary to give an INDEFINITE POWER of raising TROOPS as well as providing fleets, and of keeping up both in PEACE as well as in WAR?

The answer to these questions has already been anticipated elsewhere, too fully to allow a lengthy discussion of them here. The answer in fact seems so obvious and conclusive that it hardly justifies a lengthy discussion anywhere. How can anyone decently limit the force needed for defense, when he cannot limit the force of offense? If a federal Constitution could put chains on the ambition of all other nations, or set bounds to their exertions, then it might wisely chain its own government's discretion and set bounds to its exertions for its own safety.

How could readiness for war in time of peace be safely forbidden, unless we could forbid in the same way the preparations and establishments of every hostile nation? The means of security can be regulated only by the means of attack and the danger of it. In fact they will always be set by these standards and by no others. It is useless to put constitutional barriers in the way of the drive for self-preservation. It is worse than useless, because it plants in the Constitution itself necessary usurpations of power, and every precedent among them is a seed of unnecessary and repeated ones. When one nation constantly keeps a disciplined army ready to serve its ambition or revenge, it forces the most peaceable nations within reach of its schemes to take matching precautions. The fifteenth century was the unhappy period when military establishments in peacetime began. Charles VII of France introduced them. All Europe has followed his example or been forced to. If other nations had not followed it, all Europe would long ago have worn the chains of a universal monarch. If every nation except France were to disband its peacetime establishments now, the same thing might happen. The veteran legions of Rome could overpower the undisciplined courage of every other nation, and they made her mistress of the world.

It is just as true, though, that the liberties of Rome became in the end the victim of her military triumphs, and that the liberties of Europe, as far as they ever existed, have with few exceptions been the price paid for her military establishments. A standing force is therefore a dangerous provision, even if it is also a necessary one. On the smallest scale it has its drawbacks. On a large scale its consequences may be fatal. On any scale it is an object of laudable caution and precaution. A wise nation will weigh all these considerations. It will not rashly cut itself off from any resource that may prove essential to its safety, but it will bring all its prudence to bear on lessening both the need to resort to a resource that may be unfavorable to its liberties and the danger of doing so.

The proposed Constitution bears the clearest marks of this prudence. The Union itself, which it joins firmly together and secures, removes every pretext for a military establishment that could be dangerous. America united, with a handful of troops or not a single soldier, presents a more forbidding face to foreign ambition than America disunited with a hundred thousand veterans ready to fight. It was remarked on an earlier occasion that the absence of this pretext saved the liberties of one nation in Europe. Because her island position and her naval resources made her safe from the armies of her neighbors, the rulers of Great Britain have never been able, with real or invented dangers, to trick the public into a large peacetime establishment. The distance of the United States from the powerful nations of the world gives them the same happy security. A dangerous establishment can never be either necessary or plausible as long as they remain a united people. But they must never forget, even for a moment, that they owe this advantage to the Union alone. The day it dissolves will be the start of a new order of things. The fears of the weaker States, or the ambition of the stronger States or Confederacies, will set the same example in the New World that Charles VII set in the Old. The example will be followed here for the same reasons that made everyone imitate it there. Instead of drawing from our situation the precious advantage Great Britain draws from hers, America will look just like the continent of Europe. It will show liberty crushed everywhere between standing armies and perpetual taxes. The fortunes of a disunited America will be even more disastrous than Europe's. In Europe the sources of evil are confined within her own borders. No superior powers from another quarter of the globe intrigue among her rival nations, inflame their mutual animosities and turn them into instruments of foreign ambition, jealousy and revenge. In America, the miseries springing from her internal jealousies, contentions and wars would make up only part of her lot. A large additional share of evils would come from the relation in which Europe stands to this quarter of the earth, a relation no other quarter of the earth has to Europe.

This picture of the consequences of disunion cannot be painted too vividly or shown too often. Every man who loves peace, his country or liberty ought to keep it always before his eyes, so that he may feel in his heart a proper attachment to the Union of America and know the right value of the means of preserving it.

After the effective establishment of the Union, the best precaution against the danger of standing armies is to limit the term for which revenue may be appropriated to their support. The Constitution has wisely added this precaution. I will not repeat the observations that, I flatter myself, have put this subject in a just and satisfactory light. But it may be worth noticing an argument against this part of the Constitution that has been drawn from the policy and practice of Great Britain. It is said that keeping an army in that kingdom requires a vote of the legislature every year, while the American Constitution has stretched this critical period to two years. That is how the comparison is usually put before the public. But is the comparison put fairly? Does the British Constitution limit Parliament's discretion to one year? Does the American Constitution require Congress to make appropriations for two years? On the contrary, the authors of the fallacy cannot be unaware that the British Constitution sets no limit at all on the legislature's discretion, while the American Constitution binds the legislature to two years as the longest permitted term.

If the argument from the British example had been stated truly, it would have gone like this. The term for which supplies may be appropriated to the army, though the British Constitution leaves it unlimited, has nevertheless been limited in practice to a single year by Parliament's own discretion. Now consider Great Britain, where the House of Commons is elected for seven years, where so large a share of its members are chosen by so small a share of the people, where the electors are so corrupted by the representatives and the representatives so corrupted by the Crown. If the representative body there can have the power to make appropriations for the army for an indefinite term, and yet either does not wish to or does not dare to extend the term beyond one year, then ought not suspicion itself to blush when it pretends that the representatives of the United States cannot safely be trusted with discretion over such appropriations, though they are elected FREELY by the WHOLE BODY of the people every SECOND YEAR and the appropriations are expressly limited to the short period of TWO YEARS?

A bad cause seldom fails to give itself away. The way the opposition to the federal government has been conducted is a constant illustration of this truth. But of all the blunders committed, none is more striking than the attempt to bring over to that side the prudent jealousy the people feel toward standing armies. The attempt has fully awakened public attention to that important subject, and has led to inquiries that must end in a thorough and universal conviction of two things. One is that the Constitution has provided the most effective guards against danger from that quarter. The other is that only a Constitution fully adequate to the national defense and the preservation of the Union can save America from having as many standing armies as it is split into States or Confederacies, and from a steady growth of these establishments in each. Such growth would make them as burdensome to the property, and as ominous to the liberties, of the people as any establishment that might become necessary under a united and effective government would be tolerable to the one and safe to the other.

The plain necessity of the power to provide and maintain a navy has shielded that part of the Constitution from the spirit of censure that has spared few other parts. It must indeed be counted among the greatest blessings of America that, since her Union will be the only source of her naval strength, this strength will in turn be a chief source of her security against danger from abroad. In this respect our situation resembles in another way the island advantage of Great Britain. Happily, the batteries best able to repel foreign attempts on our safety are of a kind that a treacherous government can never turn against our liberties.

The inhabitants of the Atlantic frontier all have a deep interest in this provision for naval protection. They have been allowed so far to sleep quietly in their beds; their property has stayed safe from the plundering spirit of lawless adventurers; their seaport towns have not yet had to buy off the terror of burning by giving in to the demands of bold and sudden invaders. These pieces of good fortune are not to be credited to the existing government's ability to protect the people from whom it claims allegiance, but to causes that are passing and deceptive. Except perhaps for Virginia and Maryland, which are especially exposed on their eastern frontiers, no part of the Union ought to feel more anxiety on this subject than New York. Her seacoast is long. A very important district of the State is an island. A large navigable river runs into the State for more than fifty leagues. The great emporium of her commerce, the great reservoir of her wealth, lies every moment at the mercy of events, and may almost be regarded as a hostage for shameful compliance with the orders of a foreign enemy, or even with the greedy demands of pirates and barbarians. If war should result from the uncertain state of European affairs, and all the unruly passions that go with war were let loose on the ocean, it would be truly a miracle if we escaped insults and plundering, not only at sea but along every part of the land bordering on it. In America's present condition, the States most directly exposed to these calamities have nothing to hope for from the phantom of a general government that now exists. And if their own separate resources were equal to fortifying themselves against the danger, the thing to be protected would be nearly eaten up by the cost of protecting it.
The power of regulating and calling forth the militia has already been defended and explained sufficiently.

The power of levying and borrowing money is the sinew of the power to be used for the national defense, and is therefore rightly placed in the same class. This power too has already been examined with close attention, and I trust it has been clearly shown to be necessary, in both the extent and the form the Constitution gives it. I will offer only one further thought to those who argue that the power should have been limited to external taxation, by which they mean taxes on articles imported from other countries. There can be no doubt that this will always be a valuable source of revenue, that for a good while it must be a principal source, and that at this moment it is an essential one. But we may form very mistaken ideas on this subject if our calculations do not keep in mind two things. First, the amount of revenue drawn from foreign commerce must rise and fall with changes in both the amount and the kind of imports. Second, these changes do not match the growth of population, which must be the general measure of the public's needs. As long as agriculture remains the only field of labor, imports of manufactured goods must grow as consumers multiply. As soon as domestic manufactures begin, with hands that agriculture does not need, imported manufactures will fall as the population grows. At a later stage, imports may consist in large part of raw materials that will be worked up into articles for export, and these will need the encouragement of bounties rather than the burden of discouraging duties. A system of government meant to last ought to look ahead to these changes and be able to adapt to them.

Some who have not denied that the power of taxation is necessary have launched a very fierce attack on the Constitution over the language in which it is defined. It has been urged and echoed that the power "to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States," amounts to an unlimited commission to exercise any power that may be claimed necessary for the common defense or general welfare. There could be no stronger proof of how hard up these writers are for objections than their stooping to such a misreading.

If the Constitution had contained no other listing or definition of the powers of Congress than the general expressions just quoted, the authors of the objection might have had some color for it, though it would still have been hard to find a reason for describing an authority to legislate in all possible cases in so awkward a way. A power to destroy the freedom of the press or trial by jury, or even to regulate the order of inheritance or the forms of conveyances, would be a very odd thing to express by the words "to raise money for the general welfare."

But what color can the objection have when a specification of the objects hinted at by these general terms follows right away, separated from them by no more than a semicolon? Different parts of the same document ought to be interpreted so as to give meaning to every part that can bear one. Shall one part of the same sentence then be shut out entirely from any share in the meaning, while the more doubtful and indefinite terms are kept in their full breadth and the clear and precise expressions are denied any meaning at all? Why would the list of particular powers have been inserted, if these and all other powers were meant to be included in the general power before it? Nothing is more natural or common than to use a general phrase first and then to explain and qualify it by listing particulars. But the idea of a list of particulars that neither explains nor qualifies the general meaning, and can have no effect except to confuse and mislead, is an absurdity. We are forced into a dilemma: we must charge it either to the authors of the objection or to the authors of the Constitution, and we must take the liberty of supposing it did not originate with the latter.

The objection is all the more extraordinary because the language the Convention used turns out to be copied from the articles of Confederation. The objects of the Union among the States, as described in article third, are "their common defense, security of their liberties, and mutual and general welfare." The terms of article eighth are closer still: "All charges of war and all other expenses that shall be incurred for the common defense or general welfare, and allowed by the United States in Congress, shall be defrayed out of a common treasury," etc. Similar language appears again in article ninth. Read either of these articles by the rules that would justify the reading given to the new Constitution, and they give the existing Congress a power to legislate in all cases whatsoever. But what would have been thought of that assembly if it had seized on these general expressions, ignored the specifications that fix and limit their meaning, and exercised an unlimited power of providing for the common defense and general welfare? I appeal to the objectors themselves: would they in that case have used the same reasoning to justify Congress that they now use against the Convention? How hard it is for error to escape its own condemnation!

chapters.title: No. 42 — The Powers Conferred by the Constitution Further Considered (Madison)
paragraphs: The SECOND class of powers placed in the general government consists of those that govern dealings with foreign nations. These are: to make treaties; to send and receive ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls; to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations; and to regulate foreign commerce. The last includes a power to prohibit, after the year 1808, the importation of slaves, and to lay in the meantime a duty of ten dollars per head, to discourage such importations.
These powers are an obvious and essential part of federal administration. If we are to be one nation in anything, we should plainly be one in relation to other nations.

The powers to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors are obviously proper and need no defense. Both are already in the articles of Confederation, with only two differences. First, the Convention's plan removes from the treaty power an exception under which treaties could be largely defeated by regulations of the States. Second, a power of appointing and receiving "other public ministers and consuls" is expressly added, and rightly so, to the earlier provision about ambassadors. Taken strictly, as the second of the articles of Confederation seems to require, the term ambassador covers only the highest rank of public ministers. It leaves out the ranks that the United States will most likely prefer wherever foreign embassies are needed. And no stretching of the term can make it cover consuls. Yet Congress has found it useful, and has made a practice of it, to employ the lower ranks of public ministers and to send and receive consuls.

It is true that where commercial treaties provide for each side to appoint consuls whose functions relate to commerce, admitting foreign consuls may fall within the power of making commercial treaties. It is also true that where there are no such treaties, sending American consuls to foreign countries may PERHAPS be covered by the authority given in the ninth article of the Confederation to appoint all civil officers needed to manage the general affairs of the United States. But admitting consuls into the United States where no earlier treaty has so provided seems not to have been provided for anywhere. Filling this gap is one of the smaller ways in which the Convention has improved on the model it had before it. Yet even the smallest provisions matter when they remove the need, or the excuse, for gradual and unnoticed usurpations of power. A list of the cases in which the defects of the Confederation have betrayed or forced Congress into violating its chartered authority would greatly surprise anyone who has not paid attention to the subject. It would also be a considerable argument for the new Constitution, which seems to have attended as carefully to the lesser defects of the old system as to the more obvious and striking ones.

The power to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations, belongs just as properly to the general government, and is a still greater improvement on the articles of Confederation. Those articles make no provision for offenses against the law of nations. As a result, any careless member can embroil the Confederacy with foreign nations. On piracies and felonies, the federal articles go no further than establishing courts to try these offenses. The definition of piracies might perhaps be left to the law of nations without harm, though most municipal codes do contain a legislative definition of them. A definition of felonies on the high seas is clearly needed. Felony is a loosely defined term even in the common law of England, and it has varied meanings in that kingdom's statute law. But neither the common law nor the statute law of England, or of any other nation, ought to be the standard for our proceedings unless our legislature has first adopted it as its own. The meaning of the term as defined in the codes of the individual States would be an impractical guide, just as the English law would be a dishonorable and illegitimate one. It is not exactly the same in any two States, and in each of them it changes with every revision of its criminal laws. For the sake of certainty and uniformity, then, the power to define felonies in this case was in every respect necessary and proper.

The regulation of foreign commerce has been taken up from several points of view in earlier discussion of this subject. It has been discussed too fully to need more proof here that it is properly placed in the federal administration.

It is certainly to be wished that the power to prohibit the importation of slaves had not been postponed until 1808, or rather that it had been allowed to take effect at once. But it is not hard to explain either this restriction on the general government or the way the whole clause is worded. We should count it a great point won for humanity that within twenty years this traffic, which has so long and so loudly reproached the barbarism of modern policy, may be ended forever within these States. In that time the federal government will discourage it considerably, and the few States that continue the unnatural traffic may agree to abolish it entirely, following the example of prohibition set by so great a majority of the Union. How happy it would be for the unfortunate Africans if they had an equal prospect of being redeemed from the oppressions of their European brethren!

Some have tried to turn this clause into an objection to the Constitution. On one side it is portrayed as a criminal tolerance of an illicit practice, and on another as likely to prevent voluntary and beneficial emigration from Europe to America. I mention these misreadings not to answer them, since they deserve no answer, but as samples of the manner and spirit in which some have chosen to carry on their opposition to the proposed government.
The powers in the THIRD class are those that provide for harmony and proper dealings among the States.

The particular restraints placed on the authority of the States, and certain powers of the judicial department, might be included under this head. But the former are set aside for a class of their own, and the latter will be examined in detail when we come to the structure and organization of the government. I will limit myself to a quick review of the remaining powers that fall under this third description. They are: to regulate commerce among the several States and the Indian tribes; to coin money, and to regulate its value and the value of foreign coin; to provide for the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and securities of the United States; to fix the standard of weights and measures; to establish a uniform rule of naturalization and uniform laws of bankruptcy; to prescribe how the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and what effect they shall have in other States; and to establish post offices and post roads.

The existing Confederacy's lack of power to regulate commerce among its members is one of the defects that experience has clearly exposed. To the proofs and remarks that earlier papers have offered on this subject we can add that, without this supplementary provision, the great and essential power of regulating foreign commerce would have been incomplete and ineffective. One very important aim of this power was to relieve the States that import and export through other States from the improper contributions those other States levy on them. If the latter were free to regulate trade between one State and another, we must foresee that they would find ways to burden articles of import and export, while passing through their territory, with duties that would fall on the producers of the exports and the consumers of the imports. Past experience assures us that such a practice would be brought in by future schemes. Both that experience and common knowledge of human affairs assure us that it would feed endless animosities and might well end in serious breaches of the public peace. For those who do not look at the question through passion or self-interest, the desire of the commercial States to collect, in any form, an indirect revenue from their uncommercial neighbors must seem as unwise as it is unfair, because resentment as well as interest would drive the injured party to look for less convenient channels for its foreign trade. But the mild voice of reason, pleading for a broader and lasting interest, is all too often drowned out, in public bodies as well as in individuals, by the clamor of an impatient greed for immediate and excessive gain.

Other examples besides our own have shown the need for an authority overseeing the mutual trade of confederated States. In Switzerland, where the Union is very loose, each canton must let merchandise pass through its territory into other cantons without raising the tolls. In Germany it is a law of the empire that the princes and states may not lay tolls or customs on bridges, rivers or passages without the consent of the emperor and the diet. But a quotation in an earlier paper shows that in this matter, as in many others in that confederacy, practice has not followed the law, and has produced there the harms we have foreseen here. Among the restraints the Union of the Netherlands puts on its members is one that they may not establish imposts disadvantageous to their neighbors without general permission.

It is quite right that the regulation of commerce with the Indian tribes is freed from two limits in the articles of Confederation, which make the provision there obscure and contradictory. There the power is confined to Indians who are not members of any of the States, and it must not violate or infringe the legislative right of any State within its own limits. Which Indians are to count as members of a State has not been settled, and it has often caused perplexity and contention in the federal councils. And how trade with Indians who are not members of a State but live within its legislative jurisdiction can be regulated by an outside authority, without intruding on the State's internal rights of legislation, is simply incomprehensible. This is not the only case where the articles of Confederation have thoughtlessly tried to accomplish impossibilities: to reconcile a partial sovereignty in the Union with complete sovereignty in the States, and to overturn a mathematical axiom by taking away a part and leaving the whole.

All that needs saying about the power to coin money, and to regulate its value and that of foreign coin, is that by providing for foreign coin the Constitution has filled a significant gap in the articles of Confederation. The authority of the existing Congress is limited to regulating coin STRUCK by its own authority or by that of the respective States. It is plain at once that the planned uniformity in the VALUE of the current coin could be destroyed if foreign coin were left to the different regulations of the different States.
Punishing the counterfeiting of public securities, as well as of the current coin, naturally goes to the authority that is to secure the value of both.
The regulation of weights and measures is carried over from the articles of Confederation, and rests on the same considerations as the preceding power to regulate coin.

The differences among the States in the rules of naturalization have long been noted as a fault in our system, and as a basis for intricate and delicate questions. The fourth article of the Confederation declares "that the FREE INHABITANTS of each of these States, paupers, vagabonds, and fugitives from justice, excepted, shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of FREE CITIZENS in the several States; and THE PEOPLE of each State shall, in every other, enjoy all the privileges of trade and commerce," etc. The language here is remarkably confused. It is hard to tell why the terms FREE INHABITANTS are used in one part of the article, FREE CITIZENS in another and PEOPLE in another, or what was meant by adding "all the privileges of trade and commerce" to "all privileges and immunities of free citizens." It seems nearly unavoidable, though, to conclude that those who count as FREE INHABITANTS of a State, even if not citizens of that State, are entitled in every other State to all the privileges of FREE CITIZENS of that other State. That means greater privileges than they may have in their own State. So a particular State may have the power, or rather every State is placed under a necessity, to confer the rights of citizenship in other States, not only on anyone it admits to such rights within itself, but on anyone it allows to become an inhabitant within its jurisdiction. But suppose we accepted an interpretation of the term "inhabitants" that confined the promised privileges to citizens alone. The difficulty would only be reduced, not removed. Each State would still keep the very improper power of naturalizing aliens in every other State. In one State a short residence confers all the rights of citizenship, and in another more important qualifications are required. So an alien who is legally barred from certain rights in the latter State may get around the bar merely by having lived earlier in the former. In this way the law of one State is absurdly made to override the law of another within that other State's own jurisdiction. We owe it to mere chance that we have so far escaped very serious embarrassments over this. By the laws of several States, certain kinds of aliens who had made themselves obnoxious were put under prohibitions that were inconsistent not only with the rights of citizenship but with the privilege of residence. What would have followed if such persons, by residence or otherwise, had acquired the character of citizens under the laws of another State, and had then claimed their rights as citizens, both to residence and to citizenship, in the State that had banned them? Whatever the legal consequences might have been, other consequences would probably have followed that were too serious not to be guarded against. The new Constitution has accordingly, and very properly, made provision against them, and against all other consequences of the Confederation's defect on this point, by authorizing the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.

The power to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy is so closely tied to the regulation of commerce, and will prevent so many frauds where the parties or their property may be located or moved in different States, that its usefulness seems unlikely to be questioned.

The power to prescribe, by general laws, how the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and what effect they shall have in other States, is a clear and valuable improvement on the corresponding clause in the articles of Confederation. The meaning of that clause is extremely vague, and under any reading it will bear it can matter very little. The power established here may become a very convenient instrument of justice. It will be especially useful on the borders of neighboring States, where property that is liable to legal process may be quickly and secretly moved into a foreign jurisdiction at any stage of the proceeding.

The power of establishing post roads must in every view be harmless, and with sound management may perhaps become the source of great public convenience. Nothing that helps the intercourse between the States can be thought unworthy of the public's attention.

chapters.title: No. 43 — The Same Subject Continued (The Powers Conferred by the Constitution Further Considered) (Madison)
paragraphs: The FOURTH class comprises the following miscellaneous powers:
1. A power "to promote the progress of science and useful arts, by securing, for a limited time, to authors and inventors, the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries."

Few will question the usefulness of this power. In Great Britain the courts have solemnly ruled that an author's copyright is a right of common law. The right to useful inventions seems, for equally good reasons, to belong to the inventors. In both cases the public good fully agrees with the claims of individuals. The States cannot separately make effective provision for either, and most of them have already acted ahead of the question, passing laws at Congress's request.

2. "To exercise exclusive legislation, in all cases whatsoever, over such district (not exceeding ten miles square) as may, by cession of particular States and the acceptance of Congress, become the seat of the government of the United States; and to exercise like authority over all places purchased by the consent of the legislatures of the States in which the same shall be, for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings."

The need for complete authority at the seat of government is so plain that it proves itself. Every legislature in the Union, and I might say in the world, exercises such a power by virtue of its general supremacy. Without it, public authority might be insulted and its proceedings interrupted with impunity. Worse, the members of the general government would have to depend, for protection while doing their duty, on the State that contains the seat of government. That might expose the national councils to a charge of being overawed or influenced, which would dishonor the government and displease the other members of the Confederacy. The point carries more weight because public improvements would gradually pile up at the government's permanent home. That would be too great a public pledge to leave in the hands of a single State, and it would create so many obstacles to moving the government that its necessary independence would be curtailed further. The federal district is small enough to satisfy any jealousy of the opposite kind. And every imaginable objection seems to be met, for several reasons. The district is to be set aside for this use with the consent of the State that cedes it. The State will no doubt provide in the compact for the rights and consent of the citizens living there. The inhabitants will find enough in their own interest to become willing parties to the cession. They will have had a voice in electing the government that will exercise authority over them. They will of course be allowed a municipal legislature for local purposes, chosen by their own votes. And the authority of the State legislature, and of the inhabitants of the ceded part of the State, to agree to the cession will come from the whole people of the State, through their adoption of the Constitution.

A like authority over forts, magazines and the like, set up by the general government, is just as plainly necessary. The public money spent on such places, and the public property kept in them, require that they be exempt from the authority of the particular State. Nor would it be proper for places on which the security of the whole Union may depend to be dependent in any degree on one member of it. All objections and scruples are again met by requiring the agreement of the States concerned in every such establishment.
3. "To declare the punishment of treason, but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attained."

Since treason may be committed against the United States, the authority of the United States ought to be able to punish it. But new-fangled and artificial treasons have been the great engines with which violent factions, the natural offspring of free government, have usually taken turns venting their malignity on each other. The Convention has therefore shown great judgment in setting up a barrier against this particular danger. It has put into the Constitution a definition of the crime, fixed the proof required for conviction and forbidden Congress, even when punishing treason, to carry the consequences of guilt beyond the person who committed it.

4. "To admit new States into the Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the junction of two or more States, or parts of States, without the consent of the legislatures of the States concerned, as well as of the Congress."

The articles of Confederation contain no provision on this important subject. Canada was to be admitted as of right when she joined in the measures of the United States, and the other COLONIES, by which were plainly meant the other British colonies, at the discretion of nine States. The compilers of that document seem to have overlooked the eventual creation of NEW STATES. We have seen the problem this omission caused, and the assumption of power it led Congress into. The new system has therefore, and very properly, filled the gap. The general precaution, that no new States be formed without the agreement of the federal authority and of the States concerned, accords with the principles that ought to govern such transactions. The particular precaution against creating new States by splitting a State without its consent calms the jealousy of the larger States, just as the matching precaution against merging States without their consent calms that of the smaller ones.

5. "To dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States," with a proviso that "nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular State."

This is a power of very great importance, and the same kind of considerations that show the propriety of the previous one call for it. The proviso attached to it is proper in itself, and was probably made absolutely necessary by jealousies and disputes over the Western territory that are well enough known to the public.

6. "To guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government; to protect each of them against invasion; and on application of the legislature, or of the executive (when the legislature cannot be convened), against domestic violence."

In a confederacy founded on republican principles and made up of republican members, the superintending government clearly ought to have authority to defend the system against aristocratic or monarchical innovations. The closer such a union is, the more interest the members have in one another's political institutions, and the greater their right to insist that the forms of government under which they entered the compact be SUBSTANTIALLY kept. But a right implies a remedy; and where else could the remedy be placed than where the Constitution places it? Governments of unlike principles and forms have proved less suited to any sort of federal coalition than governments of a similar nature. "As the confederate republic of Germany," says Montesquieu, "consists of free cities and petty states, subject to different princes, experience shows us that it is more imperfect than that of Holland and Switzerland." "Greece was undone," he adds, "as soon as the king of Macedon obtained a seat among the Amphictyons." In the latter case, no doubt, the new member's disproportionate strength, as well as its monarchical form, had a share in bringing about the events. It may possibly be asked what need there could be for such a precaution, and whether it might become a pretext for altering the State governments without the States' own agreement. These questions have ready answers. If the interposition of the general government should not be needed, the provision for such an event will be only a harmless superfluity in the Constitution. But who can say what experiments the caprice of particular States, the ambition of enterprising leaders, or the intrigues and influence of foreign powers may produce? To the second question, the answer is that if the general government steps in under this constitutional authority, it will of course be bound to stay within the authority. But the authority reaches no further than a GUARANTY of a republican form of government, which assumes that a government of the form to be guaranteed already exists. So as long as the States keep their existing republican forms, the federal Constitution guarantees them. Whenever the States choose to put other republican forms in their place, they have a right to do so and to claim the federal guaranty for the new ones. The only restriction on them is that they may not exchange republican for antirepublican Constitutions, a restriction that, it is presumed, will hardly be thought a grievance.

Every society owes its parts protection against invasion. The broad wording used here seems to protect each State not only against foreign hostility but also against ambitious or vengeful schemes by its more powerful neighbors. The history of confederacies, ancient and modern, proves that the weaker members of a union should not be indifferent to the wisdom of this article.

Protection against domestic violence is added just as properly. It has been noted that even among the Swiss cantons, which strictly speaking are not under one government, provision is made for this object. The history of that league shows that mutual aid is often asked for and given, by the most democratic cantons as much as by the others. A recent and well-known event among ourselves has warned us to be ready for emergencies of the same kind.

At first glance it might seem not to fit republican theory to suppose either that a majority lacks the right to overthrow a government or that a minority will have the force to do so; and so it might seem that federal interposition could never be required except when it would be improper. But theoretical reasoning, here as in most other cases, has to be qualified by what practice teaches. Why could illicit combinations for violent purposes not be formed by a majority of a State, especially a small State, just as they could by a majority of a county or district within the same State? And if the State's authority ought to protect the local officials in the second case, ought not the federal authority to support the State authority in the first? Besides, some parts of the State constitutions are so interwoven with the federal Constitution that a violent blow to one cannot be struck without wounding the other. Insurrections in a State will rarely lead to federal interposition unless the number involved bears some proportion to the friends of government. It will be far better for the superintending power to put down the violence in such cases than for the majority to be left to defend its cause in a bloody and stubborn contest. The existence of a right to interpose will generally spare the need to use it.

Is it true that force and right are necessarily on the same side in republican governments? May the smaller party not have such an advantage in money, in military talent and experience, or in secret help from foreign powers that it also wins an appeal to the sword? May a more compact and advantageous position not tip the scale its way against a larger number so situated that it is less able to bring its strength to bear promptly and together? Nothing could be more fanciful than to imagine that in a trial of actual force victory can be calculated by the rules that hold in a census of the inhabitants or that settle the outcome of an election! May it not happen, in short, that the minority of CITIZENS becomes a majority of PERSONS, through the addition of alien residents, a chance crowd of adventurers, or people whom the constitution of the State has not admitted to the right to vote? I pass over an unhappy class of people, numerous in some of the States, who in the calm of regular government are sunk below the level of men, but who in the stormy scenes of civil violence may rise into the human character and give a superiority of strength to any party they may join.

Where it is doubtful on which side justice lies, what better umpires could two violent factions desire, as they rush to arms and tear a State to pieces, than the representatives of confederate States, who are not heated by the local flame? They would combine the impartiality of judges with the affection of friends. How happy it would be if all free governments could enjoy such a remedy for their infirmities, and if an equally effective plan could be established for the universal peace of mankind!

Suppose it is asked what remedy there would be for an insurrection that spreads through all the States and commands a superiority of the entire force, though it has no constitutional right. The answer must be that such a case would lie beyond the reach of human remedies, and fortunately it also lies beyond the reach of human probability. It is recommendation enough for the federal Constitution that it lessens the risk of a calamity for which no possible constitution can supply a cure.

Among the advantages of a confederate republic that Montesquieu lists, an important one is "that should a popular insurrection happen in one of the States, the others are able to quell it. Should abuses creep into one part, they are reformed by those that remain sound."

7. "To consider all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of this Constitution, as being no less valid against the United States, under this Constitution, than under the Confederation."

This can be taken only as a declaratory proposition. Among other reasons, it may have been inserted to reassure the foreign creditors of the United States, who cannot be strangers to the pretended doctrine that a change in the political form of civil society magically dissolves its moral obligations.

Among the lesser criticisms leveled at the Constitution, it has been remarked that the validity of engagements ought to have been asserted in favor of the United States as well as against them. In the spirit that usually marks little critics, this omission has been blown up into a plot against the national rights. The authors of this discovery can be told what hardly anyone else needs telling: engagements are by nature reciprocal, so asserting their validity on one side necessarily implies their validity on the other; and since the article is merely declaratory, establishing the principle in one case is enough for every case. They can be told further that every constitution must confine its precautions to dangers that are not altogether imaginary, and that there is no real danger that the government would DARE, with this constitutional declaration before it or even without it, to cancel debts justly owed to the public on the pretext they condemn here.
8. "To provide for amendments to be ratified by three fourths of the States under two exceptions only."

That experience would suggest useful changes had to be foreseen. A way of making them therefore had to be provided. The way the Convention preferred seems to bear every mark of propriety. It guards equally against two extremes: too much ease, which would make the Constitution too changeable, and too much difficulty, which might make its discovered faults permanent. It also lets the general government and the State governments equally start the amendment of errors, whichever side experience may expose them on. The exception in favor of equal suffrage in the Senate was probably meant as a safeguard for the residuary sovereignty of the States, which that principle of representation in one branch of the legislature implies and secures; and the States particularly attached to that equality probably insisted on it. The other exception must have been admitted on the same grounds that produced the privilege it protects.
9. "The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States, ratifying the same."

This article speaks for itself. Only the express authority of the people could give the Constitution proper validity. Requiring the unanimous ratification of the thirteen States would have put the essential interests of the whole at the mercy of the caprice or corruption of a single member. It would have shown a lack of foresight in the Convention that our own experience would have made inexcusable.

Two very delicate questions present themselves here. 1. On what principle can the Confederation, which stands as a solemn compact among the States, be replaced without the unanimous consent of its parties? 2. What relation is to exist between the nine or more States that ratify the Constitution and the remaining few that do not become parties to it?

The first question is answered at once by turning to the absolute necessity of the case, to the great principle of self-preservation, and to the transcendent law of nature and of nature's God, which declares that the safety and happiness of society are the aims of all political institutions and that all such institutions must be sacrificed to them. PERHAPS an answer can also be found without looking beyond the principles of the compact itself. We have already noted, among the defects of the Confederation, that in many of the States it received no higher sanction than a mere ratification by the legislature. The principle of reciprocity seems to require that its binding force on the other States be brought down to the same level. A compact between independent sovereigns, resting on ordinary acts of legislative authority, can claim no higher validity than a league or treaty between the parties. It is an established doctrine about treaties that all the articles are conditions of one another; that a breach of any one article is a breach of the whole treaty; and that a breach by either party frees the others and authorizes them, if they wish, to declare the compact violated and void. Should it unhappily become necessary to appeal to these delicate truths to justify going ahead without the consent of particular States to dissolving the federal pact, will the complaining parties not find it hard to answer the MULTIPLIED and IMPORTANT infractions that may be thrown back at them? There was a time when we all had to veil the ideas this paragraph sets out. The scene has now changed, and with it the part that the same motives dictate.

The second question is no less delicate, and the pleasing prospect that it will remain merely hypothetical forbids an overcurious discussion of it. It is one of those cases that must be left to provide for itself. In general, it may be observed that although no political relation can exist between the assenting and the dissenting States, the moral relations will remain in force. The claims of justice on both sides will hold and must be met. The rights of humanity must always be respected on both sides. And it is hoped that considerations of common interest, and above all the memory of the dear scenes now past and the hope of a speedy victory over the obstacles to reunion, will not urge in vain MODERATION on one side and PRUDENCE on the other.

chapters.title: No. 44 — Restrictions on the Authority of the Several States (Madison)
paragraphs: A fifth class of provisions favoring the federal authority consists of the following restrictions on the individual States:

1. "No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal; coin money; emit bills of credit; make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts; pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts; or grant any title of nobility."

The ban on treaties, alliances, and confederations is already part of the existing Articles of the Union, and for reasons that need no explanation it is copied into the new Constitution. The ban on letters of marque also comes from the old system, but the new Constitution extends it somewhat. Under the old Articles, the States could grant letters of marque once war had been declared. Under the new Constitution, these licenses must come from the government of the United States, in wartime and before any declaration of war alike. The change is fully justified by the advantage of uniformity in everything that concerns foreign powers, and by the advantage of immediate responsibility to the nation for every act that the nation itself will be answerable for.

The Confederation left the right of coining money in the hands of the States, which this clause now takes from them. They held it alongside Congress, subject to one exception: Congress alone had the right to regulate the alloy and value. Here, too, the new provision improves on the old. So long as the general authority fixed the alloy and value, a right of coinage in the particular States could do nothing except multiply expensive mints and vary the forms and weights of the coins in circulation. That second problem defeats one of the purposes for which the power was first given to the federal head. The first might spare the inconvenience of shipping gold and silver to a central mint for recoinage, but local mints established under the general authority can serve that end just as well.

Every citizen must be pleased that the prohibition now reaches bills of credit, in proportion to his love of justice and his knowledge of the true sources of public prosperity. Since the peace, America has suffered from the pestilent effects of paper money on the confidence needed between man and man, on the confidence needed in the public councils, on the industry and morals of the people, and on the character of republican government. These losses are an enormous debt, chargeable against the States that adopted this unwise measure, and it must long remain unpaid. Or rather, they are an accumulated guilt that can be expiated only by one thing: a voluntary sacrifice, on the altar of justice, of the very power that has been the instrument of it. Beyond these persuasive considerations, we may observe that the same reasons that show the necessity of denying the States the power of regulating coin prove equally that they should not be free to put a paper medium in the place of coin. If every State had a right to regulate the value of its coin, there might be as many currencies as there are States, and dealings among them would be obstructed. Its value could be altered retroactively, which would injure the citizens of other States and kindle animosities among the States themselves. Subjects of foreign powers might suffer in the same way, and so the Union would be discredited and drawn into quarrels by the indiscretion of a single member. A power in the States to emit paper money is no less open to every one of these harms than a power to coin gold or silver. The power to make anything but gold and silver a tender in payment of debts is withdrawn from the States on the same principle as the power to issue a paper currency.

Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing the obligation of contracts violate the first principles of the social compact and every principle of sound legislation. The declarations prefixed to some of the State constitutions expressly forbid the first two, and the spirit and scope of these fundamental charters forbid all three. Our own experience has taught us, nevertheless, that we should not neglect to add further fences against these dangers. The Convention was entirely right, then, to add this constitutional bulwark for personal security and private rights. And I am much mistaken if, in doing so, they have not served the genuine feelings of their constituents as faithfully as their undoubted interests. The sober people of America are weary of the shifting policy that has guided the public councils. They have seen with regret and indignation that sudden changes and legislative interference in matters affecting personal rights become profitable schemes in the hands of enterprising and influential speculators, and snares for the more industrious and less informed part of the community. They have seen, too, that one legislative interference is only the first link in a long chain of repetitions, each later interference being naturally produced by the effects of the one before. They rightly infer that some thorough reform is needed, one that will end speculation on public measures, inspire general prudence and industry, and give the business of society a regular course. The prohibition on titles of nobility is copied from the Articles of Confederation and needs no comment.

2. "No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce of all duties and imposts laid by any State on imports or exports, shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress. No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

Every argument that proves trade must be regulated in the federal councils also supports the restraint on the States' power over imports and exports. There is therefore no need to say more on this point, except that the way the restraint is qualified seems well designed to do two things at once. It secures to the States a reasonable discretion in providing for the convenience of their imports and exports, and it gives the United States a reasonable check against abuse of that discretion. The remaining particulars of this clause fall under reasonings that are either so obvious or so fully developed already that they may be passed over without remark.
The SIXTH and last class consists of the various powers and provisions that give effect to all the rest.

1. The first of these is the "power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof."

Few parts of the Constitution have been attacked more intemperately than this one, yet on fair investigation no part appears more completely invulnerable. Without the SUBSTANCE of this power, the whole Constitution would be a dead letter. Those who object to the article can therefore only mean that the FORM of the provision is wrong. But have they considered whether a better form could have been found?

The Constitution might have dealt with this subject in four other ways. It might have copied the second article of the existing Confederation, which would have forbidden the exercise of any power not EXPRESSLY delegated. It might have tried to list positively the powers comprehended in the general terms "necessary and proper." It might have tried to list them negatively, by naming the powers excepted from the general definition. Or it might have said nothing at all, leaving these necessary and proper powers to construction and inference.

Suppose the Convention had taken the first course and adopted the second article of the Confederation. It is evident that the new Congress, like its predecessors, would constantly face a choice between two alternatives. It could read the word "EXPRESSLY" so strictly that the government was left with no real authority at all, or so loosely that the restriction lost all its force. It would be easy to show, if it were necessary, that Congress has never been able, and never will be able, to carry out any important power delegated by the Articles of Confederation without turning, more or less, to the doctrine of CONSTRUCTION or IMPLICATION. The powers delegated under the new system are more extensive, so the government administering it would be still more hard pressed by the alternative of betraying the public interests by doing nothing, or violating the Constitution by exercising powers that are indispensably necessary and proper but not EXPRESSLY granted.

Suppose the Convention had tried to list positively the powers necessary and proper for carrying their other powers into effect. The attempt would have required a complete digest of the laws on every subject the Constitution touches. And that digest would have had to fit not only the present state of things but every possible change the future may bring. For whenever a general power is newly applied, the PARTICULAR POWERS that serve as means to the OBJECT of the general power must always vary with that object. They must often properly be varied even while the object remains the same.

Suppose they had tried instead to list the particular powers or means that are not necessary or proper for carrying the general powers into execution. The task would have been no less chimerical, and open to a further objection: every gap in the list would have amounted to a positive grant of authority. To avoid this, they might have listed only some of the exceptions and described all the rest by the general words NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER. Then the list would have covered only a few of the excepted powers. These would be the ones least likely to be assumed or tolerated, because a list would naturally pick out those that are least necessary or proper. And the unnecessary and improper powers left in the unlisted remainder would be less firmly excepted than if no partial list had been made at all.

Had the Constitution said nothing on this head, there can be no doubt that all the particular powers needed as means of executing the general powers would have passed to the government by unavoidable implication. No axiom is more clearly established in law or in reason than this: wherever the end is required, the means are authorized, and wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary to do it is included. Had the Convention followed this last course, then, every objection now raised against their plan would remain as plausible as ever. And there would be a real drawback: a pretext would be left standing which can be seized on at critical moments to call into question the essential powers of the Union.

Someone may ask what will follow if Congress misconstrues this part of the Constitution and exercises powers its true meaning does not warrant. I answer that the result will be the same as if Congress misconstrued or enlarged any other power vested in it. It will be the same as if the general power had been broken down into particulars and one of those particulars were violated. In short, it will be the same as if the State legislatures should violate their own constitutional authorities. In the first case, whether the usurpation succeeds will depend on the executive and judiciary departments, which expound and give effect to the legislative acts. In the last resort, the remedy must come from the people, who can annul the acts of the usurpers by electing more faithful representatives. The truth is that we can rely on this ultimate redress more against unconstitutional acts of the federal legislature than against those of the State legislatures, for a plain reason. Every such federal act will invade the rights of the State legislatures, and they will always be ready to point out the innovation, to sound the alarm to the people, and to use their local influence to bring about a change of federal representatives. There is no such intermediate body, between the State legislatures and the people, with an interest in watching the conduct of the former. Violations of the State constitutions are therefore more likely to go unnoticed and unredressed.

2. "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land, and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

The indiscreet zeal of the Constitution's opponents has led them to attack this part of it as well, though without it the Constitution would plainly and radically be defective. To see this fully, we need only suppose for a moment that a clause saving the State constitutions had left their supremacy intact.

First, these constitutions give the State legislatures absolute sovereignty in all cases the existing Articles of Confederation do not except. Every authority in the proposed Constitution that goes beyond those listed in the Confederation would therefore have been nullified, and the new Congress would have been left as powerless as its predecessors.

Second, the constitutions of some of the States do not even expressly and fully recognize the existing powers of the Confederacy. In those States, an express saving of the supremacy of the State constitutions would have called into question every power in the proposed Constitution.

Third, the State constitutions differ greatly from one another. A treaty or national law of great and equal importance to all the States might therefore conflict with some constitutions and not with others. It would then be valid in some of the States and have no effect in others.

In short, the world would have seen, for the first time, a system of government founded on an inversion of the fundamental principles of all government. It would have seen the authority of the whole society everywhere subordinate to the authority of the parts. It would have seen a monster whose head took its orders from its limbs.

3. "The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution."

Some have asked why it was thought necessary to bind the State officials to support the federal Constitution, yet unnecessary to impose a like oath on the officers of the United States in favor of the State constitutions.

Several reasons might be given for the distinction. I will content myself with one, which is obvious and conclusive. The members of the federal government will have no part in putting the State constitutions into effect. The members and officers of the State governments, on the contrary, will play an essential part in putting the federal Constitution into effect. The election of the President and Senate will depend in every case on the legislatures of the individual States. The election of the House of Representatives will likewise depend on the same authority at first, and will probably always be conducted by State officers and under State laws.

4. Among the provisions for making the federal powers effective we might add those that belong to the executive and judiciary departments. But since these are reserved for particular examination elsewhere, I pass them over here.

We have now reviewed in detail all the articles that make up the sum of power the proposed Constitution delegates to the federal government. They bring us to this undeniable conclusion: no part of that power is unnecessary or improper for accomplishing the necessary objects of the Union. The question whether to grant this amount of power therefore comes down to another: whether to establish a government equal to the needs of the Union, or, in other words, whether the Union itself shall be preserved.

chapters.title: No. 45 — The Alleged Danger From the Powers of the Union to the State Governments. Considered For the Independent Journal. Saturday, January 26, 1788 (Madison)
paragraphs: I have shown that none of the powers transferred to the federal government is unnecessary or improper. The next question is whether the whole mass of them will endanger the portion of authority left to the individual States.

The opponents of the Convention's plan, instead of first asking how much power the federal government absolutely needs for its purposes, have exhausted themselves on a secondary question: what the proposed degree of power might do to the governments of the particular States. But consider what has been shown. The Union is essential to the security of the American people against foreign danger. It is essential to their security against quarrels and wars among the different States. It is essential to protect them from those violent and oppressive factions which embitter the blessings of liberty, and from those military establishments which must gradually poison liberty at its very fountain. In a word, the Union is essential to the happiness of the American people. Given all this, is it not preposterous to object to a government, one without which the objects of the Union cannot be attained, that it may diminish the importance of the governments of the individual States? Was the American Revolution fought, was the American Confederacy formed, was the precious blood of thousands shed and the hard-earned wealth of millions spent, so that the people of America might enjoy peace, liberty, and safety? Or was it so that the governments of the individual States, those particular municipal establishments, might hold a certain extent of power and be dressed in certain dignities and attributes of sovereignty? We have heard of the impious doctrine of the Old World that the people were made for kings, not kings for the people. Is the same doctrine now to be revived in the New World in another shape, so that the solid happiness of the people is to be sacrificed to the views of political institutions of a different form? It is too early for politicians to count on our having forgotten this: the public good, the real welfare of the great body of the people, is the supreme object to be pursued, and no form of government has any value except as it is fitted to attain that object. If the plan of the Convention were against the public happiness, my voice would be, Reject the plan. If the Union itself were inconsistent with the public happiness, it would be, Abolish the Union. In the same way, wherever the sovereignty of the States cannot be reconciled with the happiness of the people, the voice of every good citizen must be, Let the former be sacrificed to the latter. How far the sacrifice is necessary has been shown. How far what remains unsacrificed will be endangered is the question now before us.

In the course of these papers I have touched on several important considerations that count against the supposition that the federal government's operation will gradually prove fatal to the State governments. The more I turn the subject over, the more fully I am persuaded that the balance is much more likely to be upset by the State scale outweighing the federal one than the reverse.

In every example of ancient and modern confederacies, we have seen the members showing the strongest tendency to strip the general government of its authorities, while the general government was very ineffectual at defending itself against their encroachments. Most of these systems were so unlike the one before us that any inference from their fate to ours is greatly weakened. Still, the States will keep a very large share of active sovereignty under the proposed Constitution, so the inference should not be dismissed entirely. In the Achaean league, the federal head probably had a degree and kind of power that made it much like the government framed by the Convention. The Lycian Confederacy, as far as its principles and form have been handed down, must have resembled it more closely still. Yet history never tells us that either of them degenerated, or tended to degenerate, into a single consolidated government. We know, on the contrary, that one of them was ruined because the federal authority could not prevent the quarrels, and finally the disunion, of the subordinate authorities. These cases deserve our attention all the more because the outside pressures forcing the component parts together were far more numerous and powerful than in our case. Weaker bonds within would therefore have been enough to hold the members to the head and to each other.

The feudal system showed a similar tendency. The local sovereigns lacked the proper sympathy of the people in every instance, and in some instances the general sovereign had it. Even so, it usually happened that the local sovereigns won the rivalry in encroachments. If external dangers had not forced internal harmony and subordination, and especially if the local sovereigns had held the people's affections, the great kingdoms of Europe would today consist of as many independent princes as they once had feudal barons.

The State governments will have the advantage over the federal government by whatever measure we compare them: how directly the one depends on the other; how much personal influence each side will have; what powers each is given; which the people prefer and are likely to support; and how willing and able each is to resist and frustrate the other's measures.

The State governments can be regarded as constituent and essential parts of the federal government, while the federal government is in no way essential to the operation or organization of the State governments. Without the State legislatures, the President of the United States cannot be elected at all. They must have a great share in his appointment in every case, and in most cases will perhaps decide it themselves. The Senate will be elected absolutely and exclusively by the State legislatures. Even the House of Representatives, though drawn directly from the people, will be chosen very much under the influence of the class of men whose hold on the people wins them election to the State legislatures. Each of the principal branches of the federal government will thus owe its existence, more or less, to the favor of the State governments. It must therefore feel a dependence much more likely to breed a disposition that is too obsequious toward them than one that is too overbearing. On the other side, the component parts of the State governments will in no case owe their appointment to the direct action of the federal government, and very little, if at all, to the local influence of its members.

The number of individuals employed under the Constitution of the United States will be much smaller than the number employed under the particular States. There will accordingly be less personal influence on the federal side than on the State side. Think of the members of the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments of thirteen and more States; the justices of the peace; the militia officers; the ministerial officers of justice; and all the county, corporation, and town officers, serving over three million people. They are mingled with the people and personally acquainted with every class and circle. In number and in influence they must exceed, out of all proportion, every kind of officer who will be employed in administering the federal system. Compare the members of the three great departments of the thirteen States, leaving the justices of the peace out of the judiciary, with the members of the corresponding departments of the single government of the Union. Compare the militia officers of three million people with the military and naval officers of any establishment that is within the compass of probability, or, I may add, of possibility. From this view alone, we may pronounce the advantage of the States decisive. If the federal government has collectors of revenue, the State governments will have theirs too. The federal collectors will be mainly on the seacoast and not very numerous; the State collectors will be spread across the country and very numerous. From this view, too, the advantage lies on the same side. It is true that the Confederacy is to have, and may use, the power of collecting internal as well as external taxes throughout the States. But this power will probably be used only for supplemental purposes of revenue. The States will then probably be given the option of supplying their quotas by collections of their own made in advance. And any eventual collection under the Union's immediate authority will generally be made by officers, and under rules, appointed by the individual States. It is indeed extremely probable that in other matters as well, particularly in organizing the judicial power, the officers of the States will be given the corresponding authority of the Union. Suppose, however, that separate collectors of internal revenue are appointed under the federal government. The influence of the whole number could not stand comparison with that of the multitude of State officers on the other side. Within every district to which a federal collector would be assigned, there would be at least thirty or forty officers of different kinds, perhaps more, and many of them would be persons of character and weight whose influence would lie on the side of the State.

The powers the proposed Constitution delegates to the federal government are few and defined. Those that remain with the State governments are numerous and indefinite. The federal powers will be exercised mainly on external objects: war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce, with which last the power of taxation will for the most part be connected. The powers reserved to the individual States will reach all the objects that, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and properties of the people, and the internal order, improvement, and prosperity of the State.

The federal government's operations will be most extensive and important in times of war and danger; those of the State governments, in times of peace and security. Times of the first kind will probably be only a small share of the total, and so the State governments have another advantage here over the federal government. Indeed, the more adequate the federal powers are made for the national defense, the less often will there be those scenes of danger which might help the federal government rise over the governments of the particular States.

Examine the new Constitution accurately and fairly, and you will find that the change it proposes consists much less in adding NEW POWERS to the Union than in strengthening its ORIGINAL POWERS. The regulation of commerce, it is true, is a new power. But few oppose this addition, and no one fears anything from it. The powers concerning war and peace, armies and fleets, treaties and finance, and the other more considerable powers, are all vested in the existing Congress by the Articles of Confederation.
