The proposed change does not enlarge these powers; it only substitutes a more effective way of administering them. The change concerning taxation may be regarded as the most important. Yet the present Congress has as complete authority to REQUIRE indefinite supplies of money from the States, for the common defense and general welfare, as the future Congress will have to require them from individual citizens. And the citizens will be no more bound than the States themselves have been to pay the quotas assessed on each of them. Suppose the States had complied punctually with the Articles of Confederation, or suppose their compliance could have been enforced by means as peaceable as can be used successfully on single persons. Our past experience gives no support to the opinion that the State governments would then have lost their constitutional powers and gradually been entirely consolidated. To maintain that such a result would have followed would be to say outright that the existence of the State governments is incompatible with any system whatever that accomplishes the essential purposes of the Union.

chapters.title: No. 46 — The Influence of the State and Federal Governments Compared (Madison)
paragraphs: Resuming the subject of the last paper, I now ask whether the federal government or the State governments will have the advantage in winning the preference and support of the people. The two are appointed in different ways, but we must regard both as substantially dependent on the great body of the citizens of the United States. I take this to be true of the federal government and set it down here as a position, reserving the proofs for another place. The federal and State governments are in fact only different agents and trustees of the people, given different powers and designed for different purposes. The opponents of the Constitution seem to have lost sight of the people altogether when they reason on this subject. They appear to have viewed these different establishments not only as mutual rivals and enemies, but as free of any common superior in their efforts to usurp each other's authorities. These gentlemen must be reminded of their error here. They must be told that the ultimate authority, wherever the derivative authority may be found, resides in the people alone. Whether either government, or which of them, will manage to enlarge its sphere of jurisdiction at the expense of the other will not depend merely on how ambitious or skillful the governments are in comparison with each other. Truth, no less than decency, requires us to suppose that in every case the outcome will depend on the views and approval of their common constituents.

Many considerations, in addition to those suggested on a former occasion, seem to put it beyond doubt that the people's first and most natural attachment will be to the governments of their own States. More individuals will expect to rise into the administration of these governments. More offices, with the pay attached to them, will flow from their gift. Their watchful care will regulate and provide for all the more domestic and personal interests of the people. The people will know their affairs more familiarly and in more detail. And a greater share of the people will have ties of personal acquaintance and friendship, and of family and party attachment, with their members. The popular bias may well be expected to lean most strongly toward these governments.

Experience says the same. The federal administration has so far been very defective compared with what may be hoped for under a better system. Yet during the war, and especially while the independent fund of paper-money issues was in credit, it had as much activity and importance as it can well have in any future circumstances. It was also engaged in a course of measures aimed at protecting everything dear to the people at large and winning everything they could desire. It was nevertheless invariably found, once the passing enthusiasm for the early Congresses was over, that the people's attention and attachment turned back to their own particular governments. The federal council was never the idol of popular favor. And the side usually taken, against proposed enlargements of its powers and importance, was that of the men who wished to build their own political consequence on their fellow citizens' prepossessions.

Suppose, then, that the people should in future become more biased toward the federal government than toward the State governments, as has been remarked elsewhere. The change could only result from such manifest and irresistible proofs of better administration as would overcome all their earlier inclinations. In that case the people surely ought not to be barred from giving most of their confidence where they find it most deserved. And even then the State governments would have little to fear, because, by the nature of things, federal power can be administered to advantage only within a certain sphere.
The remaining points on which I propose to compare the federal and State governments are how disposed, and how able, each will be to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

It has already been proved that the members of the federal government will depend more on the members of the State governments than the latter will depend on the former. It has also appeared that the people, on whom both will depend, are more prepossessed in favor of the State governments than of the federal government. Insofar as each government's disposition toward the other may be influenced by these causes, the State governments clearly have the advantage. But from a separate and very important point of view, the advantage lies on the same side. The prepossessions the members themselves carry into the federal government will generally favor the States, whereas members of the State governments will rarely carry into the public councils a bias in favor of the general government. A local spirit will infallibly prevail much more among the members of Congress than a national spirit will prevail in the legislatures of the particular States. Everyone knows that a great proportion of the errors the State legislatures commit come from their members' willingness to sacrifice the comprehensive and permanent interest of the State to the particular and separate views of the counties or districts where they live. And if they do not broaden their policy enough to embrace the collective welfare of their own State, how can anyone imagine that they will make the aggregate prosperity of the Union, and the dignity and respectability of its government, the objects of their affections and deliberations? The State legislators are unlikely to attach themselves enough to national objects, and for the same reason the members of the federal legislature will be likely to attach themselves too much to local objects. The States will be to the members of Congress what counties and towns are to the members of the State legislatures. Measures will too often be decided by their probable effect, not on national prosperity and happiness, but on the prejudices, interests, and pursuits of the governments and people of the individual States. What has been the spirit that has generally marked the proceedings of Congress? Their journals, and the frank acknowledgments of those who have sat in that assembly, tell us that the members have far too often acted as partisans of their respective States rather than as impartial guardians of a common interest. For every occasion on which local considerations have been improperly sacrificed to the aggrandizement of the federal government, there have been a hundred on which the great interests of the nation have suffered from undue attention to the local prejudices, interests, and views of the particular States. By these reflections I do not mean to insinuate that the new federal government will fail to embrace a more enlarged plan of policy than the existing government has followed. Still less do I mean that its views will be as confined as those of the State legislatures. I mean only that it will share enough of the spirit of both to be disinclined to invade the rights of the individual States or the prerogatives of their governments. The motives of the State governments to increase their prerogatives by subtractions from the federal government will be overruled by no reciprocal predispositions in the members.

Suppose it were admitted, however, that the federal government may feel as much inclination as the State governments to extend its power beyond the due limits. The State governments would still have the advantage in the means of defeating such encroachments. Take an act of a particular State that is unfriendly to the national government but generally popular in that State, and does not too grossly violate the oaths of the State officers. It is executed at once and, of course, by means on the spot and dependent on the State alone. Opposition by the federal government, or interference by federal officers, would only inflame the zeal of every party on the side of the State. The evil could not be prevented or repaired, if at all, without means that must always be resorted to with reluctance and difficulty. On the other hand, suppose an unwarrantable measure of the federal government is unpopular in particular States, as would seldom fail to be the case. Or suppose even a warrantable measure is unpopular, as may sometimes happen. The means of opposing it are then powerful and at hand. The people's disquiet; their repugnance and, perhaps, refusal to cooperate with the officers of the Union; the frowns of the State's chief executive; the embarrassments created by legislative devices, which would often be added on such occasions: all of these would present difficulties in any State that are not to be despised. In a large State they would form very serious impediments. And where several adjoining States happened to be of one mind, they would present obstructions the federal government would hardly be willing to meet.

But ambitious encroachments by the federal government on the authority of the State governments would not raise opposition in a single State, or in a few States only. They would be signals of general alarm. Every government would take up the common cause. A correspondence would be opened. Plans of resistance would be concerted. One spirit would animate and guide the whole. In short, the same combinations would result from fear of a federal yoke as were produced by dread of a foreign one. And unless the projected innovations were voluntarily given up, the same appeal to a trial of force would be made in the one case as in the other. But what degree of madness could ever drive the federal government to such an extremity? In the contest with Great Britain, one part of the empire was set against the other. The more numerous part invaded the rights of the less numerous part. The attempt was unjust and unwise, but in theory it was not absolutely chimerical. But what would the contest be in the case we are supposing? Who would the parties be? A few representatives of the people would be set against the people themselves. Or rather, one set of representatives would be contending against thirteen sets of representatives, with the whole body of their common constituents on the side of the thirteen.

The only refuge left to those who prophesy the downfall of the State governments is the visionary supposition that the federal government may first build up a military force for the projects of ambition. The reasonings in these papers must have been employed to little purpose indeed if I must now disprove the reality of this danger. The people and the States would have to elect, for a long enough time, an unbroken succession of men ready to betray both. Throughout this time the traitors would have to pursue, uniformly and systematically, some fixed plan for extending the military establishment. And the governments and the people of the States would have to watch the gathering storm silently and patiently, and keep supplying the materials, until it was ready to burst on their own heads. To everyone this must seem more like the incoherent dreams of a delirious jealousy, or the misjudged exaggerations of a counterfeit zeal, than like the sober apprehensions of genuine patriotism. Extravagant as the supposition is, however, let it be made. Let a regular army fully equal to the resources of the country be formed, and let it be entirely at the devotion of the federal government. Even so, it would not be going too far to say that the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger. By the best computation, a standing army in any country cannot be raised above one hundredth part of the whole number of souls, or one twenty-fifth part of the number able to bear arms. In the United States that proportion would produce an army of no more than twenty-five or thirty thousand men. Against these would stand a militia of nearly half a million citizens with arms in their hands, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and led by governments that possess their affections and confidence. It may well be doubted whether a militia in such circumstances could ever be conquered by so small a proportion of regular troops. Those who know best how this country recently and successfully resisted the British arms will be the most inclined to deny the possibility. The Americans have the advantage of being armed, which they hold over the people of almost every other nation. Beyond that, there are the subordinate governments to which the people are attached and which appoint the militia officers. These form a barrier against the enterprises of ambition more insurmountable than any that a simple government of any form can offer. The several kingdoms of Europe carry their military establishments as far as the public resources will bear, and yet their governments are afraid to trust the people with arms. And it is not certain that, with arms alone, the people would fail to shake off their yokes. But suppose the people had the further advantages of local governments chosen by themselves, able to collect the national will and direct the national force, and of officers appointed out of the militia by these governments and attached both to them and to the militia. It may be affirmed with the greatest assurance that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would be quickly overturned in spite of the legions that surround it. Let us not insult the free and gallant citizens of America with the suspicion that they would be less able to defend the rights they actually possess than the debased subjects of arbitrary power would be to rescue theirs from their oppressors. Let us rather stop insulting them with the supposition that they can ever bring themselves to the necessity of making the experiment, through blind and tame submission to the long train of insidious measures that must precede and produce it.

The argument under this head can be put in a very short form, which appears altogether conclusive. Either the way the federal government is to be constructed will make it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not. On the first supposition, that dependence will restrain it from forming schemes obnoxious to its constituents. On the other, it will not have the confidence of the people, and its schemes of usurpation will be easily defeated by the State governments, which the people will support.

Adding up the considerations stated in this paper and the last, they seem to amount to the most convincing evidence that the powers proposed for the federal government are as little formidable to the powers reserved to the individual States as they are indispensably necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Union. And all the alarms that have been sounded about a meditated and consequent annihilation of the State governments must, on the most favorable interpretation, be put down to the chimerical fears of those who sounded them.

chapters.title: No. 47 — The Particular Structure of the New Government and the Distribution of Power Among Its Different Parts. (Madison)
paragraphs: We have reviewed the general form of the proposed government and the general mass of power allotted to it. Now I turn to the particular structure of this government and to the way that mass of power is divided among its constituent parts.

One of the main objections pressed by the more respectable opponents of the Constitution is that it supposedly violates the political maxim that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct. In building the federal government, they say, no heed seems to have been given to this essential precaution in favor of liberty. The separate departments of power are, they say, distributed and blended in a way that at once destroys all symmetry and beauty of form, and exposes some of the essential parts of the edifice to being crushed by the disproportionate weight of the others.

No political truth is certainly of greater intrinsic value, or bears the stamp of more enlightened champions of liberty, than the one on which this objection rests. When all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, are accumulated in the same hands, whether of one, of a few, or of many, and whether those hands are hereditary, self-appointed, or elected, we may justly call it the very definition of tyranny. If the federal Constitution were truly guilty of accumulating power in this way, or of mixing powers in a manner that dangerously tended toward such accumulation, no further argument would be needed to make everyone condemn the system. I am confident, however, that everyone will see that the charge cannot be supported, and that the maxim it relies on has been totally misunderstood and misapplied. To form correct ideas on this important subject, we should begin by investigating in what sense liberty requires the three great departments of power to be separate and distinct.

The oracle always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu. If he did not originate this invaluable precept of political science, he deserves at least the credit of having displayed it and urged it on mankind's attention more effectively than anyone else. Let us first try to establish what he meant on this point.

The British Constitution was to Montesquieu what Homer has been to the writers who teach the art of epic poetry. Those writers have taken the work of the immortal bard as the perfect model from which to draw the principles and rules of the epic art and by which to judge all similar works. In the same way, this great political critic appears to have treated the Constitution of England as the standard, or, in his own phrase, the mirror of political liberty, and to have set down the characteristic principles of that particular system as though they were elementary truths. To be sure we do not mistake his meaning, then, let us go back to the source from which the maxim was drawn.

The slightest look at the British Constitution shows that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments are by no means totally separate and distinct from each other. The chief executive is an integral part of the legislative authority. He alone has the prerogative of making treaties with foreign sovereigns, and these, once made, have under certain limits the force of legislative acts. He appoints every member of the judiciary department and can remove them on the address of the two Houses of Parliament, and when he chooses to consult them they form one of his constitutional councils. One branch of the legislative department likewise forms a great constitutional council to the executive head. On the other hand, it alone holds judicial power in cases of impeachment, and it has the supreme appellate jurisdiction in all other cases. The judges, for their part, are connected with the legislative department closely enough that they often attend and take part in its deliberations, though they are not admitted to a legislative vote.

The reasons on which Montesquieu bases his maxim show his meaning still further. "When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body," says he, "there can be no liberty, because apprehensions may arise lest THE SAME monarch or senate should ENACT tyrannical laws to EXECUTE them in a tyrannical manner." Again: "Were the power of judging joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control, for THE JUDGE would then be THE LEGISLATOR. Were it joined to the executive power, THE JUDGE might behave with all the violence of AN OPPRESSOR." Other passages explain some of these reasons more fully. Brief as they are here, they are enough to establish the meaning we have given to this celebrated maxim of this celebrated author.

Look at the constitutions of the individual States. The axiom has been laid down emphatically and, in some of them, in unqualified terms. Yet in not one State have the individual departments of power been kept absolutely separate and distinct. New Hampshire, whose constitution was the most recently formed, seems to have recognized fully that avoiding any mixture of these departments whatever is both impossible and unwise. She has qualified the doctrine by declaring "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT; OR AS IS CONSISTENT WITH THAT CHAIN OF CONNECTION THAT BINDS THE WHOLE FABRIC OF THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE INDISSOLUBLE BOND OF UNITY AND AMITY." Her constitution accordingly mixes the departments in several ways. The Senate, a branch of the legislative department, also sits as a judicial court to try impeachments. The President, who heads the executive department, also presides over the Senate, where he has an equal vote in all cases and a casting vote in a tie. The executive head is himself elected each year, in the final stage, by the legislative department, and his council is chosen each year by that department from among its own members. Several officers of state are also appointed by the legislature. And the members of the judiciary department are appointed by the executive department.

The constitution of Massachusetts has been sufficiently cautious, though less pointed, in stating this fundamental article of liberty. It declares "that the legislative department shall never exercise the executive and judicial powers, or either of them; the executive shall never exercise the legislative and judicial powers, or either of them; the judicial shall never exercise the legislative and executive powers, or either of them." This declaration corresponds exactly to Montesquieu's doctrine as we have explained it, and the plan of the Convention violates it at no point. It goes no further than to forbid any one of the entire departments from exercising the powers of another. Yet the very Constitution that carries this declaration admits a partial mixture of powers. The chief executive has a qualified negative on the legislative body. The Senate, which is part of the legislature, is a court of impeachment for members of both the executive and the judiciary departments. The members of the judiciary department can be appointed by the executive department, and removed by the same authority on the address of the two legislative branches. Finally, the legislative department appoints a number of the officers of government each year. Appointment to office, executive office in particular, is by its nature an executive function. So on this last point at least, the framers of that Constitution violated the rule they themselves set.

I pass over the constitutions of Rhode Island and Connecticut, because they were formed before the Revolution, and even before the principle we are examining had become a subject of political attention.

The constitution of New York contains no declaration on this subject, but it plainly appears to have been framed with an eye to the danger of improperly blending the different departments. It nevertheless gives the chief executive a partial control over the legislative department. More than that, it gives the judiciary department a like control, and it even blends the executive and judiciary departments in exercising it. In its council of appointment, members of the legislative department join the executive authority in appointing officers, executive and judiciary alike. And its court for the trial of impeachments and the correction of errors is to consist of one branch of the legislature and the principal members of the judiciary department.

The constitution of New Jersey blends the different powers of government more than any of those I have mentioned. The governor, the chief executive, is appointed by the legislature. He is chancellor and ordinary, or surrogate, of the State; he is a member of the Supreme Court of Appeals; and he presides, with a casting vote, over one of the legislative branches. That legislative branch also serves as the governor's executive council, and with him forms the Court of Appeals. The legislative department appoints the members of the judiciary department, and one branch of it can remove them on the impeachment of the other.

Under the constitution of Pennsylvania, the president, who heads the executive department, is elected each year by a vote in which the legislative department predominates. Together with an executive council, he appoints the members of the judiciary department, and he forms a court of impeachment to try all officers, judiciary as well as executive. The judges of the Supreme Court and the justices of the peace also appear to be removable by the legislature, and the executive power of pardon in certain cases appears to be referred to the same department. The members of the executive council are made EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace throughout the State.

In Delaware, the legislative department elects the chief executive each year. The speakers of the two legislative branches are vice-presidents in the executive department. The executive head, together with six others, three appointed by each of the legislative branches, forms the Supreme Court of Appeals, and he joins the legislative department in appointing the other judges. Throughout the States it appears that members of the legislature may at the same time serve as justices of the peace. In this State the members of one legislative branch are EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace, and so are the members of the executive council. The legislative department appoints the principal officers of the executive department, and one branch of it forms a court of impeachments. The legislature may remove any officer on its address.

Maryland has adopted the maxim in the most unqualified terms, declaring that the legislative, executive, and judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other. Yet her constitution lets the legislative department appoint the chief executive, and the executive department appoint the members of the judiciary.

Virginia's language on this subject is more pointed still. Her constitution declares, "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct; so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other; nor shall any person exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time, except that the justices of county courts shall be eligible to either House of Assembly." Yet we find more than this express exception for members of the inferior courts. The legislature also appoints the chief executive, together with his executive council. Two members of that council are displaced every three years at the legislature's pleasure. And the same department fills all the principal offices, executive and judiciary alike. The executive prerogative of pardon, too, is in one case vested in the legislative department.

The constitution of North Carolina declares "that the legislative, executive, and supreme judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other." At the same time, it assigns to the legislative department the appointment not only of the executive head but of all the principal officers within both the executive and the judiciary departments.

In South Carolina, the constitution makes the executive office elective by the legislative department. It also gives the legislative department the appointment of the members of the judiciary department, including even justices of the peace and sheriffs, and the appointment of officers in the executive department, down to captains in the army and navy of the State.

Georgia's constitution declares "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct, so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other." Yet we find that appointments by the legislature are to fill the executive department, and that the same authority is to exercise the executive prerogative of pardon in the end. Even justices of the peace are to be appointed by the legislature.

In citing these cases, where the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments have not been kept totally separate and distinct, I do not want to be taken as an advocate for the particular organizations of the individual State governments. I know well that, along with the many excellent principles they embody, they bear strong marks of the haste in which they were framed, and still stronger marks of the inexperience. It is all too plain that in some cases the fundamental principle under consideration has been violated by too great a mixture, and even an actual consolidation, of the different powers. And in no case has adequate provision been made for maintaining in practice the separation drawn on paper. What I have wished to show is that the charge against the proposed Constitution, that it violates the sacred maxim of free government, is warranted neither by the real meaning its author gave to the maxim nor by the sense in which it has so far been understood in America. This interesting subject will be resumed in the next paper.

chapters.title: No. 48 — These Departments Should Not Be So Far Separated as to Have No Constitutional Control Over Each Other. (Madison)
paragraphs: The last paper showed that the political saying examined there does not require the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments to be wholly unconnected with each other. Now I shall undertake to show that, unless these departments are connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional control over the others, the degree of separation that the maxim requires as essential to a free government can never in practice be properly maintained.

Everyone agrees that the powers properly belonging to one department ought not to be directly and completely administered by either of the others. It is equally clear that none of them ought to have, directly or indirectly, an overruling influence over the others in administering their respective powers. No one will deny that power is encroaching by nature and that it ought to be effectively held back from passing the limits assigned to it. Once we have distinguished in theory the several classes of power, according to whether their nature is legislative, executive, or judiciary, the next and hardest task is to provide some practical security for each against invasion by the others. What this security ought to be is the great problem to be solved.

Is it enough to mark the boundaries of these departments precisely in the constitution of the government, and to trust these parchment barriers against the encroaching spirit of power? The framers of most of the American constitutions appear to have relied chiefly on this security. But experience assures us that the effectiveness of the provision has been greatly overrated, and that the weaker members of the government indispensably need some more adequate defense against the stronger. The legislative department is everywhere extending the sphere of its activity and drawing all power into its impetuous vortex.

The founders of our republics deserve so much credit for their wisdom that no task could be less pleasing than pointing out the errors they have fallen into. Respect for truth, however, requires us to remark that they seem never for a moment to have taken their eyes off one danger to liberty: the overgrown and all-grasping prerogative of a hereditary monarch, supported and fortified by a hereditary branch of the legislative authority. They seem never to have remembered the danger from legislative usurpations. These, by gathering all power into the same hands, must lead to the same tyranny that executive usurpations threaten.

In a government where an hereditary monarch holds numerous and extensive prerogatives, the executive department is very justly regarded as the source of danger, and is watched with all the jealousy that zeal for liberty ought to inspire. In a democracy, a multitude of people exercise the legislative functions in person. Because they cannot deliberate regularly or act in concert, they are continually exposed to the ambitious intrigues of their chief executives, and tyranny may well be feared to spring up in that same quarter on some favorable occasion. But take a representative republic. There the executive office is carefully limited in both the extent and the duration of its power. The legislative power is exercised by an assembly which, from a supposed influence over the people, is filled with fearless confidence in its own strength. That assembly is numerous enough to feel all the passions that move a multitude, yet not so numerous as to be unable to pursue the objects of those passions by means that reason prescribes. It is against the enterprising ambition of this department that the people ought to turn all their jealousy and exhaust all their precautions.

The legislative department draws its superiority in our governments from other circumstances too. Its constitutional powers are at once more extensive and less capable of precise limits. It can therefore more easily mask, under complicated and indirect measures, the encroachments it makes on the coordinate departments. In legislative bodies it is often a question of real delicacy whether a particular measure's operation will or will not go beyond the legislative sphere. On the other side, the executive power is confined to a narrower compass and is simpler in nature, and the judiciary is marked out by landmarks still less uncertain. Any project of usurpation by either of these departments would therefore betray and defeat itself at once. Nor is this all. Only the legislative department has access to the pockets of the people. In some constitutions it has full discretion, and in all it has a prevailing influence, over the pay of those who fill the other departments. That creates a dependence in the other departments, and it gives the legislature still greater ease in encroaching on them.

I have appealed to our own experience for the truth of what I say on this subject. If this experience needed to be confirmed with particular proofs, they could be multiplied without end. I could find a witness in every citizen who has taken part in the course of public administrations, or paid attention to it. I could gather abundant testimony from the records and archives of every State in the Union. But I will offer evidence that is shorter and just as satisfactory: the example of two States, vouched for by two unexceptionable authorities.

The first example is Virginia, a State which, as we have seen, has expressly declared in its constitution that the three great departments ought not to be intermixed. The authority in support of it is Mr. Jefferson. Besides his other advantages for observing how the government works, he was himself its chief executive. To convey fully the ideas his experience gave him on this subject, I must quote a passage of some length from his very interesting Notes on the State of Virginia, p. 195. "All the powers of government, legislative, executive, and judiciary, result to the legislative body. The concentrating these in the same hands, is precisely the definition of despotic government. It will be no alleviation, that these powers will be exercised by a plurality of hands, and not by a single one. One hundred and seventy-three despots would surely be as oppressive as one. Let those who doubt it, turn their eyes on the republic of Venice. As little will it avail us, that they are chosen by ourselves. An ELECTIVE DESPOTISM was not the government we fought for; but one which should not only be founded on free principles, but in which the powers of government should be so divided and balanced among several bodies of magistracy, as that no one could transcend their legal limits, without being effectually checked and restrained by the others. For this reason, that convention which passed the ordinance of government, laid its foundation on this basis, that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct, so that no person should exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time. BUT NO BARRIER WAS PROVIDED BETWEEN THESE SEVERAL POWERS. The judiciary and the executive members were left dependent on the legislative for their subsistence in office, and some of them for their continuance in it. If, therefore, the legislature assumes executive and judiciary powers, no opposition is likely to be made; nor, if made, can be effectual; because in that case they may put their proceedings into the form of acts of Assembly, which will render them obligatory on the other branches. They have accordingly, IN MANY instances, DECIDED RIGHTS which should have been left to JUDICIARY CONTROVERSY, and THE DIRECTION OF THE EXECUTIVE, DURING THE WHOLE TIME OF THEIR SESSION, IS BECOMING HABITUAL AND FAMILIAR."

The other State I shall use as an example is Pennsylvania, and the other authority is the Council of Censors, which met in 1783 and 1784. Part of this body's duty, as the constitution laid it out, was "to inquire whether the constitution had been preserved inviolate in every part; and whether the legislative and executive branches of government had performed their duty as guardians of the people, or assumed to themselves, or exercised, other or greater powers than they are entitled to by the constitution." In carrying out this trust, the council had necessarily to compare the proceedings of both the legislature and the executive with these departments' constitutional powers. The facts the council set out were mostly accepted as true by both sides in it. It appears from them that the legislature had flagrantly violated the constitution in a variety of important instances.

A great many laws had been passed in violation of the rule that all bills of a public nature must first be printed for the people's consideration, and no apparent necessity excused the violation. Yet this is one of the precautions the constitution chiefly relies on against improper acts of the legislature.
The constitutional trial by jury had been violated, and powers had been taken that the constitution had not delegated.
Executive powers had been usurped.

The salaries of the judges, which the constitution expressly requires to be fixed, had at times been changed, and cases belonging to the judiciary department had often been pulled into legislative hearing and decision.

Anyone who wants to see the particulars under each of these heads may consult the council's journals, which are in print. It will be found that some of them may be blamed on peculiar circumstances connected with the war, but that most may be regarded as the spontaneous offshoots of an ill-constituted government.

It appears, also, that the executive department had not been innocent of frequent breaches of the constitution. Three observations ought to be made on this head, however. FIRST, a great proportion of the cases were either produced directly by the necessities of the war, or recommended by Congress or the commander-in-chief. SECOND, in most of the other cases, they conformed to the declared or known views of the legislative department. THIRD, the executive department of Pennsylvania differs from that of the other States in the number of members that make it up. In this respect it is as much like a legislative assembly as like an executive council. It is exempt at once from the restraint of individual responsibility for the acts of the body, and it draws confidence from mutual example and joint influence. Unauthorized measures would therefore, of course, be ventured more freely than where the executive department is administered by a single hand, or by a few hands.

The conclusion I am warranted in drawing from these observations is that merely marking the constitutional limits of the separate departments on parchment is not a sufficient guard against those encroachments which lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.

chapters.title: No. 49 — Method of Guarding Against the Encroachments of Any One Department of Government by Appealing to the People Through a Convention. (Madison)
paragraphs: The author of the "Notes on the State of Virginia," whom I quoted in the last paper, attached to that valuable work the draft of a constitution. It had been prepared to be laid before a convention that the legislature was expected to call in 1783 to establish a constitution for that commonwealth. The plan, like everything from the same pen, shows an original, comprehensive and accurate turn of mind. It deserves attention all the more because it displays both a fervent attachment to republican government and an enlightened view of the dangerous tendencies against which such a government ought to be guarded. One of the precautions he proposes, and the one on which he seems finally to rely as a safeguard for the weaker departments of power against invasions by the stronger, is perhaps entirely his own. Since it bears directly on the subject of our present inquiry, it should not be overlooked.

His proposal is "that whenever any two of the three branches of government shall concur in opinion, each by the voices of two thirds of their whole number, that a convention is necessary for altering the constitution, or CORRECTING BREACHES OF IT, a convention shall be called for the purpose."

The people are the only legitimate fountain of power, and the constitutional charter under which the separate branches of government hold their power is derived from them. It therefore seems entirely consistent with republican theory to return to that same original authority, not only whenever the powers of the government need to be enlarged, reduced or remodeled, but also whenever any one of the departments encroaches on the chartered authorities of the others. The separate departments are perfectly co-ordinate under the terms of their common commission. It is evident that none of them can claim an exclusive or superior right to settle the boundaries between their respective powers. How, then, are the encroachments of the stronger to be prevented, or the wrongs of the weaker to be redressed, without an appeal to the people themselves? As the grantors of the commissions, they alone can declare its true meaning and enforce its observance.

There is certainly great force in this reasoning. It must be granted to prove that a constitutional road to the decision of the people ought to be marked out and kept open for certain great and extraordinary occasions. But there appear to be insuperable objections to the proposed recourse to the people as a provision for keeping the separate departments of power within their constitutional limits in all cases.

In the first place, the provision does not reach the case of two of the departments combining against the third. The legislative authority has so many ways of working on the motives of the other departments. Suppose it should win over to its side either of the others, or even one third of the members of either. The remaining department could then derive no benefit from this remedy. I do not dwell on this objection, however, because it may be thought to count against the particular form of the principle rather than against the principle itself.

In the next place, there is an objection that may be considered inherent in the principle. Every appeal to the people would carry an implication that the government has some defect. Frequent appeals would therefore, to a great extent, deprive the government of the veneration that time bestows on everything, and without which even the wisest and freest governments would perhaps lack the stability they require. If it is true that all governments rest on opinion, it is no less true that the strength of opinion in each individual, and its practical influence on his conduct, depend greatly on the number of others he supposes to have held the same opinion. The reason of man, like man himself, is timid and cautious when left alone, and gains firmness and confidence in proportion to the number with which it is associated. When the examples that fortify opinion are ANCIENT as well as NUMEROUS, they are known to have a double effect. In a nation of philosophers this consideration ought to be disregarded, because the voice of enlightened reason would be enough to instill a reverence for the laws. But a nation of philosophers is as little to be expected as the philosophical race of kings that Plato wished for. And in every other nation, even the most rational government will find it no superfluous advantage to have the prejudices of the community on its side.

The danger of disturbing the public tranquillity by stirring the public passions too strongly is a still more serious objection to frequently referring constitutional questions to the decision of the whole society. Our established forms of government have been revised with success, which does much honor to the virtue and intelligence of the people of America. Even so, it must be admitted that such experiments are too delicate to be multiplied without need. We should remember that all the existing constitutions were formed in the midst of a danger that held down the passions most hostile to order and harmony. They were formed amid an enthusiastic confidence of the people in their patriotic leaders, which silenced the ordinary diversity of opinion on great national questions. They were formed amid a universal ardor for new and opposite forms, produced by a universal resentment and indignation against the old government. And they were formed at a time when no spirit of party, connected with the changes to be made or the abuses to be reformed, could mix its leaven into the work. The situations in which we must expect usually to find ourselves in the future offer no equivalent security against the danger that is feared.

But the greatest objection of all is that the decisions likely to result from such appeals would not serve the purpose of maintaining the constitutional equilibrium of the government. We have seen that the tendency of republican governments is for the legislative department to aggrandize itself at the expense of the others. The appeals to the people, therefore, would usually be made by the executive and judiciary departments. But whichever side made them, would each side have equal advantages in the trial? Let us look at their different situations. The members of the executive and judiciary departments are few in number and can be personally known to only a small part of the people. The judges, because of the way they are appointed and the nature and permanence of their tenure, are too far removed from the people to share much in their prepossessions. The executive officers are generally objects of jealousy, and their administration can always be distorted and made unpopular. The members of the legislative department, on the other hand, are numerous. They are scattered among the people at large and live among them. Their ties of blood, friendship and acquaintance reach a great proportion of the most influential part of society. The nature of their public trust implies a personal influence among the people and implies that they are more directly the trusted guardians of the rights and liberties of the people. With these advantages, it can hardly be supposed that the opposing party would have an equal chance of a favorable outcome.

But the legislative party would not only be able to plead its cause most successfully with the people. It would probably also be made the judge. The same influence that had won them election to the legislature would win them a seat in the convention. If this should not hold for all of them, it would probably hold for many, and quite certainly for those leading figures on whom everything depends in such bodies. In short, the convention would be composed chiefly of men who had been, who actually were, or who expected to be members of the department whose conduct was being charged. They would consequently be parties to the very question they were to decide.

It might happen, however, that appeals would sometimes be made under circumstances less unfavorable to the executive and judiciary departments. The usurpations of the legislature might be so flagrant and so sudden as to admit of no plausible disguise. A strong party within the legislature itself might take the side of the other branches. The executive power might be in the hands of a special favorite of the people. In such a state of things, the public decision might be less swayed by prepossessions in favor of the legislative party. But it could still never be expected to turn on the true merits of the question. It would inevitably be bound up with the spirit of already existing parties, or of parties springing out of the question itself. It would be bound up with persons of distinguished character and wide influence in the community. And it would be pronounced by the very men who had been agents in, or opponents of, the measures to which the decision would relate. The PASSIONS of the public, therefore, not its REASON, would sit in judgment. But it is the reason of the public alone that ought to control and regulate the government. The passions ought to be controlled and regulated by the government.

The last paper showed that mere declarations in a written constitution cannot hold the separate departments to their legal rights. This paper has shown that occasional appeals to the people would be neither a fitting nor an effective way to do it. I will not examine how well the other kinds of provision in the plan I quoted might work. Some of them rest, without question, on sound political principles, and all of them are drawn up with unusual ingenuity and precision.

chapters.title: No. 50 — Periodical Appeals to the People Considered (Madison)
paragraphs: It may perhaps be argued that, in place of OCCASIONAL appeals to the people, which are open to the objections urged against them, PERIODICAL appeals are the proper and adequate means of PREVENTING AND CORRECTING INFRACTIONS OF THE CONSTITUTION.

Note that in examining these expedients I confine myself to how well they would ENFORCE the Constitution by keeping the separate departments of power within their proper bounds. I am not considering them in particular as ways of ALTERING the Constitution itself. Looked at in the first way, appeals to the people at fixed periods seem almost as unsuitable as appeals on particular occasions, as these arise. Suppose the periods are separated by short intervals. Then the measures to be reviewed and corrected will be recent, and will be tangled up with all the circumstances that tend to corrupt and distort the result of occasional revisions. Suppose the periods are far apart. Then the same remark applies to all recent measures. And whatever advantage the distance of the older measures may give to a dispassionate review of them comes with drawbacks that seem to outweigh it. In the first place, a distant prospect of public censure would be a very feeble restraint on power when present motives drive it to excess. Can anyone imagine that a legislative assembly of a hundred or two hundred members, eagerly bent on some favorite object and breaking through the restraints of the Constitution to reach it, would be stopped by the thought that its conduct would be reviewed by a censorial body ten, fifteen or twenty years from now? In the next place, the abuses would often have done their harm before the remedy was applied. And in the last place, where that might not be so, the abuses would be of long standing, would have taken deep root, and would not easily be pulled out.

The scheme of revising the constitution, in order to correct recent breaches of it as well as for other purposes, has actually been tried in one of the States. One of the tasks of the Council of Censors that met in Pennsylvania in 1783 and 1784 was, as we have seen, to inquire "whether the constitution had been violated, and whether the legislative and executive departments had encroached upon each other." This important and novel experiment in politics deserves very particular attention from several points of view. In some respects, as a single experiment made under somewhat peculiar circumstances, it may perhaps be thought not absolutely conclusive. But as applied to the case under consideration, it involves some facts that I venture to say are a complete and satisfactory illustration of the reasoning I have used.

First. The names of the gentlemen who made up the council show that some of its most active members, at least, had also been active and leading figures in the parties that already existed in the State.

Second. The same active and leading members of the council had, it appears, been active and influential members of the legislative and executive branches during the very period under review. Some had even been patrons or opponents of the measures that were now to be tested against the constitution. Two of the members had been vice-presidents of the State, and several others members of the executive council, in the seven preceding years. One of them had been speaker, and a number of others distinguished members, of the legislative assembly in the same period.

Third. Every page of the council's proceedings shows what these circumstances did to the temper of its deliberations. For as long as the council lasted, it was split into two fixed and violent parties. The members themselves acknowledged and lamented the fact. Even if they had not, the record of their proceedings gives equally satisfactory proof. On every question, however unimportant in itself or unconnected with the others, the same names stand opposed in the opposite columns. Any unbiased observer may infer, without risk of mistake and without meaning to reflect on either party or on any individual in either, that, unfortunately, PASSION, not REASON, must have presided over their decisions. When men use their reason coolly and freely on a variety of distinct questions, they inevitably come to different opinions on some of them. When they are ruled by a common passion, their opinions, if they can be called that, will be the same.

Fourth. It is at least doubtful whether, in several instances, this body's decisions misconstrue the limits prescribed for the legislative and executive departments, rather than holding those departments to their constitutional places.

Fifth. As far as I have understood, the council's decisions on constitutional questions, whether rightly or wrongly reached, have had no effect in changing the practice that rests on legislative constructions. It even appears, if I am not mistaken, that in one instance the legislature of the day rejected the council's constructions and in fact won the contest.
This censorial body, therefore, proves at once, through its investigations, that the disease exists, and, through its own example, that the remedy is ineffective.

It cannot be argued against this conclusion that the State where the experiment was made was at that moment, and had long been, violently heated and torn by the rage of party. Are we to presume that at any future seven-year point the same State will be free from parties? Are we to presume that any other State, at that point or any other, will be exempt from them? Such a thing ought to be neither presumed nor desired, because the end of parties necessarily means either a universal alarm for the public safety or the complete end of liberty.

Suppose a precaution were taken to exclude from the assemblies elected by the people to review the previous administration of the government everyone who had had any connection with the government during the period in question. The difficulties would still not be removed. The important task would probably fall to men who, with lesser abilities, would be little better qualified in other respects. They might not have been personally involved in the administration, and so might not have been direct agents in the measures to be examined. But they would probably have been caught up in the parties tied to those measures, and would have been elected under their auspices.

chapters.title: No. 51 — The Structure of the Government Must Furnish the Proper Checks and Balances Between the Different Departments. (Madison)
paragraphs: What expedient, then, shall we finally turn to for keeping up in practice the necessary partition of power among the separate departments, as laid down in the Constitution? The only possible answer is this. All these external provisions have proved inadequate, so the gap must be filled by designing the interior structure of the government in such a way that its separate parts, through their relations with one another, serve to keep each other in their proper places. I will not presume to develop this important idea in full. But I will venture a few general observations that may perhaps put it in a clearer light and help us judge more accurately the principles and structure of the government the Convention has planned.

Everyone admits that, to a certain extent, a separate and distinct exercise of the different powers of government is essential to the preservation of liberty. To lay a proper foundation for that, each department plainly needs a will of its own. Each must therefore be constituted so that its members have as little part as possible in appointing the members of the others. Followed strictly, this principle would require that every appointment to the supreme executive, legislative and judiciary offices be drawn from the same fountain of authority, the people, through channels with no communication whatever between them. Perhaps such a plan for constructing the separate departments would be less difficult in practice than it may seem to be in contemplation. Still, some difficulties, and some added expense, would come with carrying it out. Some departures from the principle must therefore be allowed. In constituting the judiciary department in particular, it might be unwise to insist strictly on the principle. First, since peculiar qualifications are essential in its members, the main concern ought to be to choose the mode of selection that best secures those qualifications. Secondly, the permanent tenure by which judges hold their appointments must soon destroy any sense of dependence on the authority that conferred them.

It is equally evident that the members of each department should depend as little as possible on those of the others for the pay attached to their offices. If the chief executive or the judges did not stand independent of the legislature in this respect, their independence in every other would be only nominal.

But the great security against a gradual concentration of the several powers in one department is to give those who run each department the necessary constitutional means and the personal motives to resist encroachments by the others. Here, as everywhere, the provision for defense must be made proportionate to the danger of attack. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. The interest of the man must be tied to the constitutional rights of the place. It may be a reflection on human nature that such devices are needed to control the abuses of government. But what is government itself but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed, and then oblige it to control itself. A dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind that auxiliary precautions are necessary.

This policy of making up for the lack of better motives by setting opposite and rival interests against each other could be traced through the whole system of human affairs, private as well as public. We see it especially in all the lesser distributions of power, where the constant aim is to divide and arrange the various offices so that each is a check on the other, and the private interest of every individual stands as a sentinel over the public rights. These inventions of prudence are surely no less necessary in distributing the supreme powers of the State.

But it is impossible to give every department an equal power of self-defense. In republican government the legislative authority necessarily predominates. The remedy for this problem is to divide the legislature into different branches. These should be made as little connected with each other as the nature of their common functions and their common dependence on the society will permit, by giving them different modes of election and different principles of action. It may even be necessary to guard against dangerous encroachments with still further precautions. Just as the weight of the legislative authority requires that it be divided in this way, so the weakness of the executive may require, on the other hand, that it be strengthened. An absolute negative on the legislature appears, at first view, to be the natural defense with which to arm the chief executive. But perhaps it would be neither entirely safe nor sufficient by itself. On ordinary occasions it might not be used with the needed firmness, and on extraordinary occasions it might be treacherously abused. May not this lack of an absolute negative be made up by some qualified connection between this weaker department and the weaker branch of the stronger department, by which that branch may be led to support the constitutional rights of the executive without being too much detached from the rights of its own department?

I persuade myself that the principles behind these observations are just. If they are, and if they are used as a test for the individual State constitutions and for the federal Constitution, we will find that, even if the latter does not correspond perfectly with them, the former are infinitely less able to stand up to such a test.
There are, besides, two considerations that apply particularly to the federal system of America and that set it in a very interesting light.

First. In a single republic, all the power the people give up is placed under the administration of one government, and usurpations are guarded against by dividing that government into distinct and separate departments. In the compound republic of America, the power the people give up is first divided between two distinct governments, and then the portion given to each is subdivided among distinct and separate departments. Hence the rights of the people gain a double security. The different governments will control each other, at the same time that each will be controlled by itself.

Second. In a republic it matters greatly not only to guard the society against the oppression of its rulers but to guard one part of the society against the injustice of the other part. Different classes of citizens necessarily have different interests. If a majority is united by a common interest, the rights of the minority will be insecure. There are only two ways to provide against this evil. One is to create a will in the community that is independent of the majority, that is, independent of the society itself. The other is to include in the society so many separate kinds of citizens that an unjust combination of a majority of the whole becomes very improbable, if not impracticable. The first way is the one found in all governments that hold an hereditary or self-appointed authority. At best this is a precarious security, because a power independent of the society may as readily take up the unjust views of the majority as the rightful interests of the minority, and may even be turned against both parties. The second way will be exemplified in the federal republic of the United States. All authority in it will be derived from the society and dependent on it, while the society itself will be broken into so many parts, interests and classes of citizens that the rights of individuals, or of the minority, will be in little danger from self-interested combinations of the majority. In a free government the security for civil rights must be the same as that for religious rights. In the one case it consists in the multiplicity of interests, and in the other in the multiplicity of sects. In both cases the degree of security will depend on the number of interests and sects, and this may be presumed to depend on the extent of country and the number of people brought under the same government. This view of the subject must particularly recommend a proper federal system to all the sincere and thoughtful friends of republican government. It shows that to the exact degree that the territory of the Union may be formed into smaller Confederacies or States, oppressive combinations of a majority will be made easier. The best security that the republican forms offer for the rights of every class of citizens will then be weakened. And so the stability and independence of some member of the government, the only other security, must be increased in the same proportion. Justice is the end of government. It is the end of civil society. It always has been, and always will be, pursued until it is obtained, or until liberty is lost in the pursuit. Take a society organized in such a way that the stronger faction can readily unite and oppress the weaker. Anarchy may as truly be said to reign there as in a state of nature, where the weaker individual has no protection against the violence of the stronger. And in the state of nature even the stronger individuals are driven by the uncertainty of their condition to accept a government that can protect the weak as well as themselves. In the same way, in the former case the more powerful factions or parties will gradually be led by a like motive to want a government that will protect all parties, the weaker as well as the more powerful. It can hardly be doubted that if the State of Rhode Island were separated from the Confederacy and left to itself, the insecurity of rights under popular government within such narrow limits would be displayed by such repeated oppressions by factional majorities that some power altogether independent of the people would soon be called for by the voice of the very factions whose misrule had proved the need for it. In the extended republic of the United States, with the great variety of interests, parties and sects that it embraces, a coalition of a majority of the whole society could seldom form on any principles other than those of justice and the general good. And since a minority would thus have less to fear from the will of a majority, there would also be less pretext for providing for its security by bringing into the government a will not dependent on the majority, or, in other words, a will independent of the society itself. It is as certain as it is important, whatever contrary opinions have been held, that the larger the society, provided it lies within a practical sphere, the better able it will be to govern itself. And happily for the REPUBLICAN CAUSE, the practicable sphere may be carried to a very great extent by a judicious modification and mixture of the FEDERAL PRINCIPLE.

chapters.title: No. 52 — The House of Representatives (Madison)
paragraphs: The first thing to examine in this part of the government is the qualifications of the electors and of the elected. The electors are to have the same qualifications as those who elect the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. The definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government, so the Convention was bound to define and establish this right in the Constitution. To leave it open to occasional regulation by Congress would have been improper, for the reason just given. To leave it to the legislative discretion of the States would have been improper for the same reason. It would also have made too dependent on the State governments a branch of the federal government that ought to depend on the people alone. To reduce the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule would probably have displeased some of the States as much as it would have been difficult for the Convention. The provision the Convention made therefore appears to be the best of the choices open to it. It must satisfy every State, because it conforms to the standard that the State itself has already established, or may establish. It will be safe for the United States because, being fixed by the State constitutions, it cannot be altered by the State governments; and there is no reason to fear that the people of the States will alter this part of their constitutions so as to cut down the rights the federal Constitution secures to them.

The State constitutions define the qualifications of the elected less carefully and properly, and these qualifications are also better suited to uniformity. The Convention has therefore very properly considered and regulated them itself. A representative of the United States must be twenty-five years old, must have been a citizen of the United States for seven years, must be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent at the time of his election, and must hold no office under the United States while he serves. Under these reasonable limits, the door to this part of the federal government stands open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, young or old, poor or rich, and without regard to any particular profession of religious faith.

The term for which the representatives are to be elected comes under a second view of this branch. To decide whether this article is proper, two questions must be considered: first, whether biennial elections will be safe in this case; secondly, whether they are necessary or useful.

First. Liberty requires that the government in general have a common interest with the people, and it requires in particular that the branch we are considering depend directly on the people and feel close sympathy with them. Frequent elections are without question the only policy that can effectively secure this dependence and sympathy. But how frequent they must be to do it cannot, it seems, be calculated exactly, and depends on a variety of circumstances connected with the matter. Let us consult experience, the guide that ought always to be followed whenever it can be found.

Ancient forms of government knew the scheme of representation, as a substitute for a meeting of the citizens in person, only very imperfectly at best. We should therefore expect instructive examples only from more modern times. Even among these, to avoid a search too vague and sprawling, we should limit ourselves to the few examples that are best known and most closely resemble our own case. The first one that fits this description is the House of Commons in Great Britain. The history of this branch of the English Constitution before Magna Charta is too obscure to teach anything. Students of political antiquities have even questioned whether it existed. The earliest records from after that date show only that parliaments were to SIT every year, not that they were to be ELECTED every year. Even these annual sessions were left so much to the monarch's discretion that royal ambition, under various pretexts, often arranged very long and dangerous gaps between them. To remedy this grievance, a statute in the reign of Charles II provided that the gaps should not be stretched beyond three years. When William III came to the throne and a revolution took place in the government, the subject was taken up again, more seriously, and it was declared to be among the fundamental rights of the people that parliaments ought to be held FREQUENTLY. Another statute, passed a few years later in the same reign, gave the word "frequently," which had referred to the three-year period fixed under Charles II, a precise meaning: it expressly enacted that a new parliament must be called within three years after the end of the previous one. The last change, from three years to seven, is well known to have come fairly early in the present century, under an alarm for the Hanoverian succession. These facts show that the greatest frequency of elections ever thought necessary in that kingdom to bind the representatives to their constituents is no more than a return every three years. And if we may argue from the degree of liberty that survives even under septennial elections and all the other vicious ingredients in the parliamentary constitution, we cannot doubt that cutting the period from seven years to three, together with the other needed reforms, would extend the people's influence over their representatives enough to satisfy us that biennial elections under the federal system cannot possibly endanger the dependence the House of Representatives must have on its constituents.

Until recently, the crown regulated elections in Ireland entirely at its own discretion. They were seldom repeated except when a new prince acceded or some other chance event occurred. The parliament that began with George II lasted through his whole reign, about thirty-five years. The representatives depended on the people only in that the people could fill occasional vacancies by electing new members, and in the chance of some event that might bring on a general new election. The Irish parliament's ability to defend the rights of its constituents, so far as it was inclined to, was also badly shackled by the crown's control over the subjects it could deliberate on. Lately, if I am not mistaken, these shackles have been broken, and octennial parliaments have also been established. What effect this partial reform will have must be left to further experience. Seen in this light, then, the example of Ireland can throw little light on the subject. If any conclusion can be drawn from it, it can only be this: if the people of that country have managed, under all these disadvantages, to keep any liberty at all, then biennial elections would give them every degree of liberty that depends on a proper connection between their representatives and themselves.

Let us bring our inquiries closer to home. The example of these States when they were British colonies deserves particular attention, though it is so well known that little needs to be said about it. All of them had established the principle of representation, in one branch of the legislature at least. But the periods of election differed, varying from one year to seven. Do we have any reason to infer, from the spirit and conduct of the representatives of the people before the Revolution, that biennial elections would have endangered the public liberties? The spirit that appeared everywhere at the start of the struggle, and that overcame the obstacles to independence, is the best proof that a sufficient measure of liberty had been enjoyed everywhere to inspire both a sense of its worth and a zeal for properly enlarging it. This holds as true for the colonies with the least frequent elections as for those with the most frequent. Virginia was the colony that took the lead in resisting the parliamentary usurpations of Great Britain, and the first to adopt, by public act, the resolution of independence. Yet in Virginia, if I have not been misinformed, elections under the former government were septennial. I bring up this example not as proof of any special merit, since the priority in those instances was probably accidental. Still less do I offer it as proof of any advantage in SEPTENNIAL elections, which are unacceptable when compared with more frequent ones. I offer it merely as proof, and I think a very substantial proof, that the liberties of the people can be in no danger from BIENNIAL elections.

Three further circumstances considerably strengthen the conclusion these examples lead to. The first is that the federal legislature will hold only a part of the supreme legislative authority that is vested entirely in the British Parliament, and that the colonial assemblies and the Irish legislature, with a few exceptions, exercised. It is a received and well-founded maxim that, other things being equal, the greater the power, the shorter its duration ought to be; and conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely its duration may be extended. In the second place, it has been shown elsewhere that the federal legislature will be restrained by its dependence on its people, as other legislative bodies are, and will also be watched and controlled by the collateral legislatures of the individual States, which other legislative bodies are not. And in the third place, there is no comparison between the means the more permanent branches of the federal government will have to seduce the House of Representatives from its duty to the people, if they were disposed to try, and the means of influence over the popular branch that the other branches of the governments I have cited possessed. With less power to abuse, therefore, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.

chapters.title: No. 53 — The Same Subject Continued (The House of Representatives) (Madison)
paragraphs: I shall perhaps be reminded here of a common saying, "that where annual elections end, tyranny begins." It has often been remarked that sayings that become proverbs are generally founded in reason. It is no less true that, once they are established, they are often applied to cases the reason behind them does not reach. The case before us is proof enough. What is the reason this proverb is founded on? No one will expose himself to ridicule by pretending that there is any natural connection between the sun or the seasons and the length of time human virtue can stand up to the temptations of power. Happily for mankind, liberty is not tied to any single point of time in this respect. It lies between extremes that leave room for all the variations that the different situations and circumstances of civil society may require.
