The election of public officials might be daily, weekly or monthly, as well as annual, if that were found expedient; in some instances it actually has been. And if circumstances may call for a departure from the rule in one direction, why not in the other? Look at the periods established among ourselves for electing the most numerous branches of the State legislatures. They by no means coincide here, any more than in the elections of other civil officials. In Connecticut and Rhode Island the periods are half-yearly. In the other States, except South Carolina, they are annual. In South Carolina they are biennial, as is proposed for the federal government. That is a difference of four to one between the longest and shortest periods. Yet it would not be easy to show that Connecticut or Rhode Island is better governed, or enjoys more rational liberty, than South Carolina. Nor would it be easy to show that either of these States is distinguished in those respects, or by those causes, from the States whose elections differ from both.

I can find only one ground for this doctrine, and it is wholly inapplicable to our case. Americans understand well the important distinction between a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government, and a law established by the government and alterable by the government. In any other country this distinction seems to have been little understood and less observed. Wherever the supreme power of legislation has resided, people have supposed that it also held a full power to change the form of the government. Even in Great Britain, where the principles of political and civil liberty have been most discussed and where we hear most about the rights of the Constitution, it is maintained that the authority of Parliament is transcendent and uncontrollable, as much over the Constitution as over the ordinary objects of legislation. Parliament has accordingly, in several instances, changed some of the most fundamental articles of the government by legislative acts. In particular, it has several times changed the period of election. On the last occasion it not only brought in septennial elections in place of triennial ones, but in the same act extended its own term four years beyond what the people had elected it for. Attention to these dangerous practices has naturally alarmed the devotees of free government, of which frequent elections are the cornerstone, and has led them to look for some security for liberty against the danger it faces. Where no Constitution paramount to the government existed or could be had, no constitutional security like the one established in the United States could be tried. Some other security had to be found. What better security would the case allow than to pick some simple and familiar portion of time and appeal to it as a standard, by which to measure the danger of innovations, to fix the national feeling and to unite patriotic efforts? The simplest and most familiar portion of time suited to the purpose was a year. Hence a laudable zeal, seeking to put up some barrier against the gradual innovations of an unlimited government, has taught the doctrine that the approach of tyranny can be measured by how far one departs from the fixed point of annual elections. But what need is there to apply this expedient to a government limited, as the federal government will be, by the authority of a paramount Constitution? Or who will claim that the liberties of the people of America will not be more secure under biennial elections, unalterably fixed by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be where elections were annual, or even more frequent, but could be altered by the ordinary power of the government?
The second question stated is whether biennial elections are necessary or useful. Several very obvious considerations show that the answer should be yes.

No one can be a competent legislator unless, besides upright intentions and sound judgment, he has a certain amount of knowledge of the subjects he is to legislate on. Part of this knowledge can be gained from information available to men in private as well as public stations. Another part can only be gained, or at least thoroughly gained, through actual experience in the post that requires it. In all such cases, therefore, the period of service ought to bear some proportion to the amount of practical knowledge the service requires. In most of the States, as we have seen, the period of legislative service for the more numerous branch is one year. The question can then be put in this simple form: is the proportion of two years to the knowledge needed for federal legislation any greater than that of one year to the knowledge needed for State legislation? The mere statement of the question in this form suggests the answer it deserves.

In a single State, the knowledge needed concerns the existing laws, which are uniform throughout the State and with which all citizens are more or less familiar. It also concerns the general affairs of the State, which lie within a small compass, are not very varied, and take up much of the attention and conversation of every class of people. The great stage of the United States presents a very different scene. The laws are far from uniform; they differ in every State. The public affairs of the Union are scattered across a very large region and are made extremely varied by the local affairs bound up with them. They can hardly be learned correctly anywhere except in the central councils, where the representatives of every part of the empire will bring that knowledge. Yet the members from each State ought to have some knowledge of the affairs, and even the laws, of all the States. How can foreign trade be properly regulated by uniform laws without some acquaintance with the commerce, the ports, the usages and the regulations of the different States? How can trade between the different States be properly regulated without some knowledge of their relative situations in these and other respects? How can taxes be wisely imposed and effectively collected unless they are adapted to the different laws and local circumstances that bear on them in the different States? How can uniform regulations for the militia be properly provided without a similar knowledge of the many internal circumstances that set the States apart from each other? These are the principal objects of federal legislation, and they strongly suggest how much information the representatives must acquire. The other internal objects will call for a proportional amount of information about them.

It is true that all these difficulties will gradually be much reduced. The hardest task will be launching the government properly and forming the original federal code. Improvements on the first drafts will become both easier and fewer each year. Past transactions of the government will be a ready and accurate source of information for new members. The affairs of the Union will become more and more objects of curiosity and conversation among citizens at large. And the growing contact among citizens of different States will do much to spread knowledge of one another's affairs, which will in turn help bring their manners and laws into general likeness. But even after all these reductions, the business of federal legislation must continue to exceed the legislative business of a single State, in both novelty and difficulty, by enough to justify the longer period of service given to those who are to conduct it.

One branch of knowledge belongs among the acquirements of a federal representative and has not yet been mentioned: foreign affairs. In regulating our own commerce he ought to know not only the treaties between the United States and other nations but also the commercial policy and laws of those nations. He ought not to be altogether ignorant of the law of nations, since, so far as it is a proper object of municipal legislation, the federal government holds authority over it. And although the House of Representatives is not directly to take part in foreign negotiations and arrangements, the several branches of public affairs are necessarily connected. Those particular branches will therefore often deserve attention in the ordinary course of legislation, and will sometimes require specific legislative sanction and co-operation. Some of this knowledge may no doubt be gained in a man's study, but some can only come from public sources of information; and all of it will be gained to best effect by practical attention to the subject during actual service in the legislature.

There are other considerations, perhaps of less importance, but still worth noticing. Many of the representatives will have to travel a long way, and will have to make arrangements because of it. For suitable men this might be a much more serious objection to the service if it were limited to a single year than if it ran for two. Nothing can be argued on this point from the case of the delegates to the existing Congress. They are indeed elected annually, but the legislative assemblies treat their re-election almost as a matter of course. The people's election of the representatives would not follow the same principle.

A few of the members, as happens in all such assemblies, will have superior talents. Through frequent re-election they will become members of long standing and thorough masters of the public business, and perhaps not unwilling to use these advantages. The larger the proportion of new members, and the less information the bulk of the members have, the more easily they will fall into the snares laid for them. This remark applies just as much to the relation that will exist between the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Our frequent elections have advantages, even in single States, but mixed in with them is a drawback. Where the States are large and hold only one legislative session a year, spurious elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time for the decision to have its proper effect. If a man can get a return, no matter by what unlawful means, the irregular member takes his seat as a matter of course and is sure to hold it long enough to serve his purposes. Hence a very harmful encouragement is given to using unlawful means to get irregular returns. If elections for the federal legislature were annual, this practice might become a very serious abuse, particularly in the more distant States. Each house is, as it necessarily must be, the judge of the elections, qualifications and returns of its members. However many improvements experience may suggest for simplifying and speeding up the process in disputed cases, so large a part of a year would unavoidably pass before an illegitimate member could be removed from his seat that the prospect of it would do little to check unfair and illicit means of getting a seat.

Taken together, all these considerations warrant us in affirming that biennial elections will be as useful to the affairs of the public as we have seen that they will be safe for the liberty of the people.

chapters.title: No. 54 — The Apportionment of Members Among the States (Madison)
paragraphs: The next aspect of the House of Representatives I shall take up is the appointment of its members among the individual States, which is to be determined by the same rule as direct taxes.

No one argues that the number of people in each State should not be the standard for fixing the share of those who are to represent that State's people. Using the same rule for the appointment of taxes will probably be disputed just as little, though the rule rests on a different principle in this case. For representation, the rule is understood to refer to the personal rights of the people, with which numbers have a natural and universal connection. For taxation, it refers to the proportion of wealth, of which numbers are in no case a precise measure and in ordinary cases a very poor one. But the rule is imperfect as applied to the relative wealth and contributions of the States, and yet it is plainly the least objectionable of the rules that could be put into practice. America had also given it general approval too recently for the Convention not to prefer it readily.

All this is admitted, it will perhaps be said. But does it follow, from admitting numbers as the measure of representation, or slaves added to free citizens as a ratio of taxation, that slaves ought to be counted in the numerical rule of representation? Slaves are regarded as property, not as persons. They ought therefore to be counted in estimates of taxation, which rest on property, and left out of representation, which is regulated by a census of persons. This is the objection as I understand it, stated in its full force. I shall be just as fair in stating the reasoning that may be offered on the opposite side.

"We accept the doctrine," one of our Southern brethren might say, "that representation relates more directly to persons, and taxation more directly to property, and we join in applying this distinction to the case of our slaves. But we must deny that slaves are regarded merely as property and in no respect whatever as persons. The true state of the case is that they share in both qualities: our laws treat them in some respects as persons and in others as property. The slave is forced to labor, not for himself, but for a master. He can be sold by one master to another. He can be restrained in his liberty and chastised in his body at any time by the whim of another. In these respects the slave may seem to be degraded from the human rank and classed with those irrational animals that the law calls property. On the other hand, he is protected in his life and limbs against the violence of everyone else, even the master of his labor and his liberty, and he is himself punishable for any violence he commits against others. In these respects the slave is just as plainly regarded by the law as a member of the society, not as part of the irrational creation; as a moral person, not as a mere article of property. The federal Constitution therefore decides very properly on the case of our slaves when it views them in the mixed character of persons and property. This is in fact their true character. It is the character that the laws under which they live give them; and no one will deny that these laws are the proper test. For it is only on the pretext that the laws have turned the negroes into subjects of property that anyone disputes their place in the count of numbers. And it is admitted that if the laws were to restore the rights that have been taken away, the negroes could no longer be refused an equal share of representation with the other inhabitants.

"The question may be put in another light. Everyone agrees that numbers are the best scale of wealth and taxation, as they are the only proper scale of representation. Would the Convention have been impartial or consistent if it had left the slaves off the list of inhabitants when the shares of representation were calculated, and put them on the lists when the tariff of contributions was fixed? Could anyone reasonably expect the Southern States to join in a system that counted their slaves as men to some degree when burdens were to be imposed, but refused to count them the same way when advantages were to be handed out? Might there not also be some surprise that those who reproach the Southern States for the barbarous policy of treating a part of their human brethren as property should themselves argue that the government of which all the States are to be parties ought to treat this unfortunate race more fully in the unnatural light of property than the very laws they complain of?

"Perhaps it will be answered that slaves are not counted in the estimate of representatives in any of the States that have them. They do not vote themselves, nor do they add to the votes of their masters. On what principle, then, ought they to enter into the federal estimate of representation? In rejecting them altogether, the Constitution would in this respect have followed the very laws that have been appealed to as the proper guide.

"A single observation answers this objection. It is a fundamental principle of the proposed Constitution that the total number of representatives allotted to the individual States is to be fixed by a federal rule based on the total number of inhabitants. In the same way, the right to choose the number allotted to each State is to be exercised by whatever part of the inhabitants the State itself designates. The qualifications on which the right of suffrage depends are perhaps the same in no two States, and in some States the difference is very material. In every State, a certain proportion of inhabitants are deprived of this right by the State's constitution, yet they will be counted in the census by which the federal Constitution apportions the representatives. Seen this way, the Southern States could throw the complaint back. They could insist that the principle the Convention laid down required no regard to any State's policy toward its own inhabitants. It would follow that the slaves, as inhabitants, should have been admitted into the census at their full number, like other inhabitants whom the policy of other States does not admit to all the rights of citizens. But those who would gain from it give up insisting on this principle in all its rigor. All they ask is that the other side show equal moderation. Let the case of the slaves be treated as what it truly is, a peculiar one. Let both sides accept the compromising expedient of the Constitution, which regards the slaves as inhabitants, but as debased by servitude below the equal level of free inhabitants; which regards the SLAVE as stripped of two fifths of the MAN.

"After all, may we not take another ground on which this article of the Constitution can be defended still more easily? So far we have assumed that representation concerned persons only and not property at all. But is that assumption just? Government is instituted no less to protect the property of individuals than their persons. Property as well as persons, then, may be considered as represented by those who are charged with the government. On this principle, in several of the States, and particularly in the State of New York, one branch of the government is meant to be especially the guardian of property, and is elected accordingly by the part of the society most interested in that object of government. This policy does not prevail in the federal Constitution. The rights of property are placed in the same hands as the personal rights. Some attention ought therefore to be paid to property in choosing those hands.

"There is another reason why the votes the people of each State are allowed in the federal legislature ought to bear some proportion to the comparative wealth of the States. States do not, like individuals, have an influence over each other that comes from superior advantages of fortune. If the law gives a wealthy citizen only a single vote in choosing his representative, the respect and standing he gets from his fortunate situation very often steer the votes of others toward the objects of his choice. Through this imperceptible channel the rights of property are carried into the public representation. A State has no such influence over other States. It is not likely that the richest State in the Confederacy will ever sway the choice of a single representative in any other State. Nor will the representatives of the larger and richer States have any advantage in the federal legislature over the representatives of other States except what comes from their greater number alone. To whatever extent their greater wealth and weight may justly entitle them to an advantage, therefore, it ought to be secured to them by a larger share of representation. In this respect the new Constitution differs materially from the existing Confederation, and from that of the United Netherlands and other similar confederacies. In each of those, the effectiveness of the federal resolutions depends on the later and voluntary resolutions of the states that make up the union. Hence the states, though they hold an equal vote in the public councils, have an unequal influence, matching the unequal importance of these later and voluntary resolutions. Under the proposed Constitution, the federal acts will take effect without the individual States having to step in. They will depend merely on a majority of votes in the federal legislature. Consequently each vote will have equal weight and effect, whether it comes from a larger or smaller State, or from a State more or less wealthy or powerful. It will be just as with the votes individually cast in a State legislature by the representatives of unequal counties or other districts, which each have precisely equal value and effect. Or if there is any difference in the case, it comes from the difference in the personal character of the individual representative, rather than from any regard to the size of the district he comes from."

Such is the reasoning that an advocate for the Southern interests might use on this subject. It may seem a little strained at some points, yet on the whole I must confess that it fully reconciles me to the scale of representation the Convention has established.

In one respect, setting up a common measure for representation and taxation will have a very beneficial effect. The accuracy of the census Congress is to take will necessarily depend a good deal on the disposition, if not the co-operation, of the States. It is therefore very important that the States feel as little bias as possible toward inflating or shrinking their numbers. If the rule governed only their share of representation, they would have an interest in exaggerating their inhabitants. If it decided only their share of taxation, the opposite temptation would win out. By extending the rule to both objects, the States will have opposite interests that control and balance each other and produce the necessary impartiality.

chapters.title: No. 55 — The Total Number of the House of Representatives (Madison)
paragraphs: The number of members the House of Representatives is to have is another very interesting point from which to consider this branch of the federal legislature. Hardly any article in the whole Constitution seems to deserve more attention, given the weight of character and the apparent force of argument with which it has been attacked. The charges brought against it are these. First, that so small a number of representatives will be an unsafe guardian of the public interests. Secondly, that they will lack proper knowledge of the local circumstances of their many constituents. Thirdly, that they will be drawn from the class of citizens who will sympathize least with the feelings of the mass of the people, and who will be most likely to aim at lifting the few permanently up by pushing the many down. Fourthly, that however inadequate the number will be at the start, it will grow more and more out of proportion as the people multiply and as obstacles prevent a matching increase in the representatives.

As a general matter, no political problem can be solved less precisely than the question of what number is most convenient for a representative legislature. And on no point do the policies of the individual States differ more, whether we compare their legislative assemblies directly with each other or consider the proportions they bear to the numbers of their constituents. Leave aside the difference between the smallest and largest States, such as Delaware, whose most numerous branch has twenty-one representatives, and Massachusetts, where it has between three and four hundred. A very considerable difference can still be seen among States of nearly equal population. Pennsylvania has no more than one fifth as many representatives as the State just mentioned. New York, whose population is to that of South Carolina as six to five, has little more than one third as many representatives. Georgia differs just as widely from Delaware or Rhode Island. In Pennsylvania the representatives are no more numerous than one for every four or five thousand constituents. In Rhode Island the proportion is at least one for every thousand. And under the constitution of Georgia, the proportion may reach one for every ten electors, and must unavoidably far exceed the proportion in any of the other States.

Another general remark is that the ratio between the representatives and the people should not be the same where the people are very numerous as where they are very few. If Virginia's representatives were set by Rhode Island's standard, they would now come to between four and five hundred, and in twenty or thirty years to a thousand. On the other hand, applying Pennsylvania's ratio to the State of Delaware would cut the latter's representative assembly to seven or eight members. Nothing is more misleading than to build our political calculations on arithmetical principles. Sixty or seventy men may more properly be trusted with a given degree of power than six or seven. But it does not follow that six or seven hundred would be proportionately a better guardian of it. And if we carry the supposition up to six or seven thousand, the whole reasoning ought to be reversed. The truth is that in all cases at least a certain number seems necessary to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes. On the other side, the number ought at most to be held within a certain limit, so as to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude. In all very numerous assemblies, of whatever kind of people, passion never fails to wrest the scepter from reason. Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

We must also recall here what was said about biennial elections. The limited powers of Congress and the control of the State legislatures justify less frequent elections than the public safety might otherwise demand. For the same reason, the members of Congress need not be as numerous as they would have to be if they held the whole power of legislation and were under no restraints beyond those ordinarily placed on other legislative bodies.

With these general ideas in mind, let us weigh the objections raised against the number of members proposed for the House of Representatives. It is said, first, that so small a number cannot safely be trusted with so much power.

This branch of the legislature will have sixty-five members when the government begins. Within three years a census is to be taken, and then the number may be raised to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. The census is to be renewed within every following period of ten years, and increases may continue to be made under the same limit. It will not be thought an extravagant guess that the first census will raise the number of representatives, at the rate of one for every thirty thousand, to at least one hundred. If the negroes are counted at three fifths, there can hardly be any doubt that the population of the United States will by then amount to three millions, if it does not already. At the end of twenty-five years, at the computed rate of increase, the number of representatives will come to two hundred, and at the end of fifty years to four hundred. I presume this number will put an end to all fears arising from the smallness of the body. I take for granted here what I shall show later, in answering the fourth objection: that the number of representatives will be increased from time to time in the way the Constitution provides. On the opposite supposition, I should admit that the objection carries very great weight indeed.

The true question to be decided, then, is whether the smallness of the number, as a temporary regulation, endangers the public liberty. Is sixty-five members for a few years, and a hundred or two hundred for a few more, a safe guardian for a limited and well-guarded power of legislating for the United States? I must own that I could not answer no without first wiping out every impression I have received of the present character of the people of America, of the spirit that moves the State legislatures, and of the principles woven into the political character of every class of citizens. I cannot conceive that the people of America, in their present disposition, or under any circumstances that can soon arise, will choose, and every second year choose again, sixty-five or a hundred men who would be inclined to form and carry out a scheme of tyranny or treachery. I cannot conceive that the State legislatures, which must feel so many motives to watch the federal legislature and have so many means of counteracting it, would fail to detect or to defeat a conspiracy by the latter against the liberties of their common constituents. I am equally unable to conceive that there are now, or can be within any short time, in the United States any sixty-five or a hundred men able to win the choice of the people at large who would either wish or dare, in the short space of two years, to betray the solemn trust committed to them. What change of circumstances, time and a fuller population of our country may bring about would take a prophetic spirit to declare, and I make no claim to one. But judging from the circumstances now before us, and from their probable state within a moderate period of time, I must pronounce that the liberties of America cannot be unsafe in the number of hands the federal Constitution proposes.

Where can the danger come from? Are we afraid of foreign gold? If foreign gold could so easily corrupt our federal rulers and enable them to ensnare and betray their constituents, how is it that we are a free and independent nation today? The Congress that led us through the Revolution was a less numerous body than their successors will be. They were not chosen by their fellow citizens at large, nor answerable to them. Though they were appointed from year to year and could be recalled at pleasure, they were generally kept on for three years, and before the ratification of the federal articles for a still longer term. They always held their consultations in secrecy. They alone conducted our affairs with foreign nations. Throughout the whole course of the war they held the fate of their country more in their hands than it is to be hoped our future representatives ever will. And given the greatness of the prize at stake and the eagerness of the party that lost it, we may well suppose that means other than force would not have been scrupled. Yet we know from happy experience that the public trust was not betrayed, and the purity of our public councils in this respect has never suffered, even from the whispers of slander.

Is the danger feared from the other branches of the federal government? But where will the President, or the Senate, or both, find the means? Their pay for office, it is to be presumed, will not exceed what is needed for very different purposes, and without first corrupting the House of Representatives it cannot. Their private fortunes, since they must all be American citizens, cannot possibly be sources of danger. The only means they can have, then, lie in handing out appointments. Is it here that suspicion rests her charge? Sometimes we are told that the President is to use up this fund of corruption in subduing the virtue of the Senate. Now it is the fidelity of the other House that is to be the victim. The improbability of such a mercenary and treacherous combination among the several members of the government should alone quiet this fear. They stand on foundations as different as republican principles will well allow, and they are at the same time accountable to the society over which they are placed. But fortunately the Constitution has provided a still further safeguard. The members of Congress are made ineligible to any civil offices that may be created, or whose emoluments may be increased, during the term for which they were elected. No offices, therefore, can be handed out to the sitting members except those that fall vacant by ordinary chance. To suppose that these would be enough to buy the guardians of the people, chosen by the people themselves, is to give up every rule by which events ought to be calculated, and to put in its place an indiscriminate and unbounded jealousy, against which all reasoning must be useless. The sincere friends of liberty who surrender themselves to the extravagances of this passion do not realize the injury they do their own cause. There is a degree of depravity in mankind that calls for a certain degree of caution and distrust; but there are other qualities in human nature that justify a certain portion of esteem and confidence. Republican government presupposes these qualities in a higher degree than any other form does. If the pictures that the political jealousy of some among us has drawn were faithful likenesses of the human character, the inference would be that men do not have enough virtue for self-government, and that nothing less than the chains of despotism can keep them from destroying and devouring one another.

chapters.title: No. 56 — The Same Subject Continued (The Total Number of the House of Representatives) (Madison)
paragraphs: The second charge against the House of Representatives is that it will be too small to have a proper knowledge of the interests of its constituents.

This objection plainly comes from comparing the proposed number of representatives with the great extent of the United States, the number of its inhabitants and the diversity of their interests. It overlooks the circumstances that will distinguish Congress from other legislative bodies. The best answer I can give, then, is a brief explanation of those peculiarities.

It is a sound and important principle that a representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents. But this principle extends only to those circumstances and interests that fall within the authority and care of the representative. Ignorance of a great many minute and particular matters that lie outside the reach of legislation is consistent with every quality needed to carry out the legislative trust properly. To determine how much information is required for exercising a particular authority, we must therefore look to the objects that fall within that authority.
What are the objects of federal legislation? Those of greatest importance, and those that seem to require the most local knowledge, are commerce, taxation and the militia.

A proper regulation of commerce requires a great deal of information, as I have remarked elsewhere. But so far as that information concerns the laws and local situation of each individual State, a very few representatives would be quite sufficient to carry it to the federal councils.

Taxation will consist, in great measure, of duties that will be bound up with the regulation of commerce, and to that extent the preceding remark applies here as well. So far as taxation consists of internal collections, a more widespread knowledge of the circumstances of the State may be needed. But will not a very few intelligent men, elected from across the State, possess this knowledge in sufficient degree? Divide the largest State into ten or twelve districts, and you will find that no district has any peculiar local interests that the representative of that district will not know. Besides this source of information, the laws of the State, framed by representatives from every part of it, will be almost sufficient of themselves as a guide. In every State, regulations on this subject have been made, and must continue to be made, that will in many cases leave the federal legislature little more to do than review the different laws and combine them in one general act. A skillful individual in his study, with all the local codes before him, might draw up a law on some subjects of taxation for the whole Union without any help from oral information. And it may be expected that whenever internal taxes are necessary, and particularly in cases requiring uniformity throughout the States, the simpler objects will be preferred. To appreciate fully how much the State codes will ease this branch of federal legislation, we need only suppose for a moment that this State, or any other, were divided into a number of parts, each having and exercising within itself a power of local legislation. Is it not evident that the several volumes of their proceedings would hold a good deal of local information and preparatory labor, which would greatly shorten the work of the general legislature and make a much smaller number of members sufficient for it? The federal councils will gain a great advantage from another circumstance as well. The representatives of each State will bring with them not only a considerable knowledge of its laws and a local knowledge of their own districts. They will also probably in all cases have been members, and may even at that very time be members, of the State legislature, where all the local information and interests of the State are gathered, and from which they may easily be carried by a very few hands into the legislature of the United States.

(What I have said about taxation applies with even greater force to the militia. For however much the rules of discipline may differ among the States, they are the same throughout each particular State, and they depend on circumstances that can differ but little in different parts of the same State.)(E1)

(Regulating the militia hardly calls for local knowledge at all. The general lay of the land is almost the only consideration of that kind that can come up: whether the country is mountainous or level, and so better suited to infantry or to cavalry. The art of war teaches general principles of organization, movement and discipline, and these apply universally.)(E1)

The attentive reader will see that the reasoning used here to prove that a moderate number of representatives is sufficient does not in any way contradict what I argued on another occasion about the extensive information representatives ought to have and the time it may take to acquire it. Where this information concerns local objects, it is made necessary and difficult not by differences of laws and local circumstances within a single State, but by differences among different States. Taking each State by itself, its laws are the same and its interests are only slightly varied. A few men, therefore, will have all the knowledge needed to represent it properly. If the interests and affairs of each individual State were perfectly simple and uniform, knowing them in one part would mean knowing them in every other, and a single member taken from any part of the State could represent the whole of it competently. When we compare the different States with one another, we find great dissimilarity in their laws and in many other circumstances connected with the objects of federal legislation, all of which the federal representatives ought to know something about. So while a few representatives from each State may bring with them a proper knowledge of their own State, every representative will have much to learn about all the other States. The changes of time, as I remarked before, will have an assimilating effect on the comparative situation of the different States. The effect of time on the internal affairs of the States taken singly will be just the opposite. At present some of the States are little more than a society of farmers, and few of them have made much progress in those branches of industry that give variety and complexity to the affairs of a nation. These, however, will in every one of them be the fruits of a more advanced population, and will require a fuller representation on the part of each State. The foresight of the Convention has accordingly provided that the growth of population may be accompanied by a proper increase in the representative branch of the government.

The experience of Great Britain, which offers mankind so many political lessons, both warnings and examples, and which has often been consulted in the course of these inquiries, confirms the conclusion we have just reached. The number of inhabitants in the two kingdoms of England and Scotland cannot be put at less than eight million. The representatives of these eight million in the House of Commons number five hundred and fifty-eight. Of these, one ninth are elected by three hundred and sixty-four persons, and one half by five thousand seven hundred and twenty-three persons.(1) It cannot be supposed that the half thus elected, who do not even live among the people at large, can add anything either to the people's security against the government or to the legislative councils' knowledge of the people's circumstances and interests. On the contrary, it is notorious that they are more often the representatives and instruments of the executive than the guardians and advocates of the people's rights. They might therefore, with great propriety, be considered as something more than a mere deduction from the real representatives of the nation. We will, however, consider them in that light alone, and will not extend the deduction to a considerable number of others who do not live among their constituents, are only faintly connected with them and have very little particular knowledge of their affairs. With all these concessions, only two hundred and seventy-nine persons will be the depository of the safety, interest and happiness of eight million. That is to say, there will be only one representative to uphold the rights and explain the situation of TWENTY-EIGHT THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY constituents, in an assembly exposed to the whole force of executive influence, and extending its authority to every object of legislation in a nation whose affairs are in the highest degree diversified and complicated. Yet it is quite certain, not only that a valuable portion of liberty has been preserved under all these circumstances, but also that the defects in the British code can be blamed only in very small proportion on the legislature's ignorance of the circumstances of the people. Giving this case the weight it deserves, and comparing it with that of the House of Representatives as explained above, it seems to give the fullest assurance that one representative for every THIRTY THOUSAND INHABITANTS will make the House both a safe and a competent guardian of the interests that will be entrusted to it.
1. Burgh's "Political Disquisitions."
E1. Two versions of this paragraph appear in different editions.

chapters.title: No. 57 — The Alleged Tendency of the New Plan to Elevate the Few at the Expense of the Many Considered in Connection with Representation. (Madison)
paragraphs: The third charge against the House of Representatives is that its members will come from the class of citizens with the least sympathy for the mass of the people. That class, the charge says, is the one most likely to aim at ambitiously sacrificing the many to the aggrandizement of the few.

Of all the objections raised against the federal Constitution, this may be the most extraordinary. It is aimed at a supposed oligarchy, yet its principle attacks the very root of republican government.

Every political constitution has, or ought to have, two aims. The first is to obtain as rulers the men with the most wisdom to see, and the most virtue to pursue, the common good of society. The second is to take the most effective precautions to keep them virtuous for as long as they hold public trust. Choosing rulers by election is the characteristic policy of republican government. This form of government relies on many different means to prevent its rulers from degenerating, and the most effective is to limit the term of office so that rulers stay properly accountable to the people.

Let me now ask what feature of the House of Representatives violates the principles of republican government or helps the few rise on the ruins of the many. Is not every feature, on the contrary, strictly in line with those principles? Is not each one scrupulously fair to the rights and claims of every class and description of citizens?

Who will elect the federal representatives? Not the rich rather than the poor, not the learned rather than the ignorant, not the haughty heirs of distinguished names rather than the humble sons of obscurity and bad fortune. The electors will be the great body of the people of the United States. They will be the same people who, in every State, have the right to elect the corresponding branch of the State legislature.

Who may the people choose? Any citizen whose merit earns him the esteem and confidence of his country. No requirement of wealth, birth, religious faith or occupation is allowed to bind the people's judgment or thwart their inclination.

Consider the position of the men on whom the free votes of their fellow citizens may confer the representative trust. We shall find that it carries every security anyone could devise or desire for their faithfulness to their constituents.

In the first place, the preference of their fellow citizens will have set them apart. We may presume, then, that in general they will also be somewhat distinguished by the qualities that earn such a preference, and that promise a sincere and scrupulous respect for the commitments they take on.

In the second place, they will enter public service in circumstances that must produce, at least for a time, some affection for their constituents. Every heart is sensitive to marks of honor, favor, esteem and confidence, and apart from any thought of interest, that sensitivity is some pledge of grateful and kindly returns. People often speak bitterly of ingratitude as a failing of human nature, and I must admit that examples of it, in public and private life alike, are all too frequent and glaring. But the universal and extreme indignation it arouses is itself proof of how strong and widespread the opposite feeling is.

In the third place, motives of a more selfish kind strengthen the ties that bind a representative to his constituents. His pride and vanity attach him to a form of government that supports his claims and gives him a share in its honors and distinctions. A few aspiring characters may harbor hopes or schemes of their own. Still, a great proportion of men who owe their advancement to their influence with the people will generally have more to hope for from keeping that favor than from changes in the government that would destroy the people's authority.

All these securities, however, would prove very insufficient without the restraint of frequent elections. So, in the fourth place, the House of Representatives is built to keep its members constantly mindful that they depend on the people. The feelings left on their minds by the way they were raised to office will not have time to fade under the exercise of power. They will be forced to look ahead to the moment when their power ends, when their use of it will be reviewed, and when they must come down to the level from which they rose. There they will stay forever, unless faithful performance of their trust has earned them a renewal of it.

I will add a fifth circumstance that restrains the House of Representatives from oppressive measures: they can make no law that will not apply with full force to themselves and their friends as well as to the great mass of society. This has always been counted among the strongest bonds human policy can forge between rulers and people. It creates a community of interests and a sympathy of feelings between them, of which few governments have given examples, and without which every government degenerates into tyranny. Someone may ask what will stop the House of Representatives from passing laws that discriminate in favor of themselves and a particular class of society. I answer: the character of the whole system; the nature of just and constitutional laws; and above all, the vigilant and manly spirit that moves the people of America, a spirit that nourishes liberty and is nourished by it in return.
If that spirit is ever so degraded that the people tolerate a law not binding on the legislature as well as on themselves, they will be ready to tolerate anything but liberty.

Such will be the relation between the House of Representatives and its constituents. Duty, gratitude, interest and even ambition are the cords that will bind members to fidelity and sympathy with the great mass of the people. It is possible that all of these together may fail to control the caprice and wickedness of man. But are they not everything that government will allow, and everything human prudence can devise? Are they not the genuine and characteristic means by which republican government provides for the liberty and happiness of the people? Are they not the very means on which every State government in the Union relies to achieve these important ends? What, then, are we to make of the objection this paper has fought? What are we to say to men who profess the most flaming zeal for republican government and yet boldly attack its fundamental principle? They claim to champion the right and capacity of the people to choose their own rulers, and yet they maintain that the people will prefer only those who will immediately and infallibly betray the trust given them.

Imagine someone who had not seen the method the Constitution prescribes for choosing representatives reading this objection. He could suppose nothing less than one of three things. Perhaps an unreasonable property qualification was attached to the right to vote. Perhaps the right to be elected was limited to people of particular families or fortunes. Or at the least, perhaps the method set by the State constitutions had been grossly departed from in some way. We have seen how badly such a supposition would err on the first two points. It would be no less mistaken on the last. The only difference we can find between the two cases is this: each representative of the United States will be elected by five or six thousand citizens, while in the individual States a representative is elected by about as many hundreds. Will anyone pretend that this difference justifies an attachment to the State governments and an abhorrence of the federal government? If the objection turns on this point, it deserves examination.

Does REASON support it? That cannot be said without maintaining that five or six thousand citizens are less able to choose a fit representative, or more easily corrupted by an unfit one, than five or six hundred. Reason tells us the opposite. In so large a number a fit representative is more likely to be found, and the choice is less likely to be drawn away from him by the intrigues of the ambitious or the ambitious or the bribes of the rich.

Can we accept the CONSEQUENCE of this doctrine? Suppose we say that five or six hundred citizens are as many as can jointly exercise the right to vote. Then must we not deprive the people of direct choice of their public servants wherever the administration of government does not need as many servants as one for each such number of citizens?

Do FACTS warrant the doctrine? The last paper showed that real representation in the British House of Commons very little exceeds the proportion of one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. There are also many powerful causes there, absent here, that favor the claims of rank and wealth. No one can be a representative of a county unless he owns real estate with a clear value of six hundred pounds sterling a year, or of a city or borough unless he owns a like estate of half that yearly value. Besides this requirement for county representatives, there is another for county electors: the vote is restricted to persons with a freehold estate worth more than twenty pounds sterling a year, at the present value of money. Despite these unfavorable circumstances, and despite some very unequal laws in the British code, no one can say that the representatives of that nation have raised the few on the ruins of the many.

But we do not need to look to foreign experience on this subject. Our own is explicit and decisive. The districts in New Hampshire where the people directly choose senators are nearly as large as her congressional districts will need to be. Those in Massachusetts are larger than needed for that purpose, and those in New York larger still. In New York, the members of Assembly for the cities and counties of New York and Albany are elected by very nearly as many voters as will be entitled to a representative in Congress, if we calculate on sixty-five representatives only. It makes no difference that in these senatorial districts and counties each elector votes for several representatives at once. If the same electors can choose four or five representatives at one time, they cannot be unable to choose one. Pennsylvania is another example. Some of her counties, which elect her State representatives, are almost as large as the districts that will elect her federal representatives. The city of Philadelphia is believed to hold between fifty and sixty thousand souls, so it will make up nearly two districts for choosing federal representatives. Yet it forms only one county, in which every elector votes for each of its representatives in the State legislature. And what may seem still more to our purpose, the whole city actually elects a SINGLE MEMBER of the executive council. The same is true of all the other counties of the State.

Are these facts not the most satisfactory proof of the fallacy used against this branch of the federal government? Has experience shown that the senators of New Hampshire, Massachusetts and New York, or the executive council of Pennsylvania, or the members of the Assembly in the last two States, have displayed any special disposition to sacrifice the many to the few? Has it shown them any less worthy of their places than the representatives and public officials chosen in other States by very small divisions of the people?

But some cases are stronger than any I have yet quoted. One branch of the legislature of Connecticut is set up so that each of its members is elected by the whole State. So is the governor of that State, of Massachusetts and of this State, and so is the president of New Hampshire. I leave every man to decide whether the outcome of any of these experiments can be said to support a suspicion that a broad mode of choosing the people's representatives tends to raise up traitors and undermine public liberty.

chapters.title: No. 58 — Objection That The Number of Members Will Not Be Augmented as the Progress of Population Demands. Considered For the Independent Journal Wednesday, February 20, 1788. (Madison)
paragraphs: The last charge against the House of Representatives that I must examine rests on a supposition: that the number of members will not be increased from time to time as the growth of population may require.

It has been admitted that this objection would carry great weight if it were well supported. The following observations will show that, like most other objections to the Constitution, it can only come from an incomplete view of the subject, or from a jealousy that discolors and distorts everything it looks at.

1. Those who press the objection seem to have forgotten that the federal Constitution compares well with the State constitutions in the security it provides for a gradual increase in the number of representatives. The number that is to apply at first is declared temporary, and it lasts only three years.

A census of the inhabitants is to be repeated within every successive term of ten years. These regulations plainly have two objects. First, they readjust the apportionment of representatives to the number of inhabitants from time to time, with the single exception that each State shall have at least one representative. Second, they increase the number of representatives at the same intervals, with the sole limit that the whole number shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. If we review the constitutions of the individual States, we shall find that some contain no definite rules on this subject, that others correspond pretty much to the federal Constitution on this point, and that the most effective security in any of them comes down to a mere directory provision.

2. As far as experience goes on this subject, the gradual increase of representatives under the State constitutions has at least kept pace with the increase of constituents. It appears that the representatives have been as ready to agree to such measures as the constituents have been to demand them.

3. The federal Constitution has a peculiarity that ensures watchful attention, among a majority of both the people and their representatives, to a constitutional increase in the number of the latter. The peculiarity is that one branch of the legislature represents citizens and the other represents the States. In the former the larger States will therefore carry the most weight; in the latter the advantage will lie with the smaller States. From this we may infer with certainty that the larger States will strongly press for increasing the number and weight of the part of the legislature where their influence predominates. And it so happens that four of the largest States alone will hold a majority of all the votes in the House of Representatives. Suppose the representatives or people of the smaller States should at some point oppose a reasonable addition of members. A coalition of a very few States would be enough to overrule them. On ordinary occasions, rivalry and local prejudices might prevent such a coalition. But it would not fail to form when it was driven not merely by common interest but also justified by equity and the principles of the Constitution.

Perhaps it will be said that the Senate would be moved by similar motives to form an opposing coalition, and that since its agreement would be indispensable, the just and constitutional views of the other branch might be defeated. This is the difficulty that has probably caused the most serious apprehension among the jealous friends of a numerous representation. Fortunately it is one of those difficulties that exist only in appearance and vanish under close and accurate inspection. If I am not mistaken, the following reflections will be accepted as conclusive and satisfactory on this point.

The two houses will have equal authority on all legislative subjects except the origination of money bills. Even so, it cannot be doubted that the House has no small advantage in any question that turns on the relative firmness of the two houses. It has the larger number of members, it will be backed by the more powerful States, and it will speak the known and settled view of a majority of the people.

This advantage must be increased by the consciousness on one side of being supported in its demands by right, by reason and by the Constitution, and the consciousness on the other side of contending against the force of all these solemn considerations.

There is a further point. Between the smallest and the largest States there is a gradation, and several States in the middle will most likely, in general, line up with the smaller ones. Yet they are too little removed in size and population from the larger ones to back an opposition to the larger States' just and legitimate claims. Hence it is by no means certain that even in the Senate a majority of votes would be unfriendly to proper increases in the number of representatives.

It is not looking too far ahead to add that the senators from all the new States may be won over to the just views of the House of Representatives by an expedient too obvious to be overlooked. These States will grow in population with peculiar rapidity for a very long time, so they will have an interest in frequent reapportionments of representatives to the number of inhabitants. The large States, which will prevail in the House of Representatives, therefore need only make reapportionments and increases conditions of each other. The senators from all the fastest-growing States will then be bound to fight for the increases by the interest their States will feel in the reapportionments.

These considerations seem to give ample security on this subject, and ought alone to settle all the doubts and fears that have been indulged about it. Suppose, however, that they should all prove insufficient to overcome the unjust policy of the smaller States, or their predominant influence in the councils of the Senate. The larger States would still have a constitutional and infallible resource by which they could accomplish their just purposes at any time. The House of Representatives can not only refuse the supplies needed to support the government; it alone can propose them. In a word, they hold the purse. In the history of the British Constitution we see what a powerful instrument this is. By means of it an infant and humble representation of the people gradually enlarged the sphere of its activity and importance, and finally reduced, as far as it seems to have wished, all the overgrown prerogatives of the other branches of government. This power over the purse may in fact be regarded as the most complete and effective weapon that any constitution can put into the hands of the immediate representatives of the people, for obtaining redress of every grievance and carrying out every just and beneficial measure.

But will not the House of Representatives be as much interested as the Senate in keeping the government working as it should? Will it not therefore be unwilling to risk the government's existence or reputation on the Senate's giving way? Or, if such a test of firmness between the two branches were risked, would one not be as likely as the other to yield first? These questions will give no trouble to those who reflect that in every case, the smaller the number of men in power and the more lasting and conspicuous their position, the stronger the interest each of them will feel individually in whatever concerns the government. Those who represent the dignity of their country in the eyes of other nations will be especially aware of every prospect of public danger or of dishonorable stagnation in public affairs. We must ascribe to these causes the continual triumph of the British House of Commons over the other branches of the government whenever it has used the engine of a money bill. Absolute inflexibility on the part of those other branches would have thrown every department of the state into general confusion. It has neither been feared nor experienced. The greatest firmness the federal Senate or President can show will be no more than equal to a resistance in which they will be backed by constitutional and patriotic principles.

In this review of the make-up of the House of Representatives, I have passed over considerations of economy. In the present state of affairs these might have helped reduce the temporary number of representatives, and ignoring them would probably have been as rich a theme for denouncing the Constitution as the smallness of the proposed number has been. I also say nothing about the difficulty that might arise, under present circumstances, in engaging a large number of the kind of characters the people will probably elect to serve in the federal government. One observation, however, I must be allowed to add on this subject, because in my judgment it claims very serious attention. In all legislative assemblies, the greater the number of members, the fewer the men who in fact direct their proceedings. In the first place, the more numerous an assembly is, whatever characters compose it, the greater is the ascendancy of passion over reason, as is well known. In the next place, the larger the number, the greater the proportion of members with limited information and weak capacities. Now it is precisely on characters of this kind that the eloquence and skill of the few are known to work with all their force. In the ancient republics, where the whole body of the people assembled in person, a single orator or an artful statesman was generally seen to rule as completely as if a scepter had been placed in his hand alone. By the same principle, the more numerous a representative assembly is made, the more it shares the weaknesses of collective meetings of the people. Ignorance will be the dupe of cunning, and passion the slave of sophistry and declamation. The people can never make a greater mistake than to suppose that by multiplying their representatives beyond a certain limit they strengthen the barrier against government by a few. Experience will forever warn them of the opposite: AFTER SECURING A SUFFICIENT NUMBER FOR THE PURPOSES OF SAFETY, OF LOCAL INFORMATION, AND OF DIFFUSIVE SYMPATHY WITH THE WHOLE SOCIETY, they will defeat their own aims with every addition to their representatives. The face of the government may become more democratic, but the soul that animates it will be more oligarchic. The machine will be bigger, but the springs that move it will be fewer, and often more hidden.

Related to the objection about the number of representatives, and properly noted here, is another objection, about the number needed to conduct legislative business. It has been said that a quorum should have required more than a majority, and that in particular cases, if not in all, a decision should have required more than a majority of a quorum. It cannot be denied that such a precaution might have brought some advantages. It might have been an additional shield for some particular interests, and a further general obstacle to hasty and biased measures. But the drawbacks on the other side outweigh these considerations. Whenever justice or the general good might require new laws or active measures, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. The majority would no longer rule; power would pass to the minority. Suppose this protective privilege were limited to particular cases. A self-interested minority might use it to shield themselves from fair sacrifices for the general welfare, or, in particular emergencies, to extort unreasonable concessions. Lastly, it would make easy and encourage the harmful practice of secessions by members. This practice has appeared even in States where only a majority is required. It undermines every principle of order and regular government, and it leads more directly to public convulsions and the ruin of popular governments than any other practice yet seen among us.

chapters.title: No. 59 — Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The natural order of the subject now brings us to the provision of the Constitution that lets the national legislature regulate, in the last resort, the election of its own members. It reads: "The TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of holding elections for senators and representatives shall be prescribed in each State by the legislature thereof; but the Congress may, at any time, by law, make or alter SUCH REGULATIONS, except as to the PLACES of choosing senators."(1) Those who condemn the Constitution wholesale have denounced this provision. So have those who object with less sweep and more moderation. And in one instance a gentleman who has declared himself the advocate of every other part of the system has found it objectionable.

Nevertheless, I am greatly mistaken if any article in the whole plan is more completely defensible. Its propriety rests on the evidence of one plain proposition: EVERY GOVERNMENT OUGHT TO CONTAIN IN ITSELF THE MEANS OF ITS OWN PRESERVATION. Every just reasoner will approve, at first sight, of keeping to this rule in the work of the Convention. He will disapprove of every departure from it, unless it seems to have been forced by the need to include some particular ingredient that strict conformity with the rule would have ruled out. Even then he may accept the necessity, but he will still regard such a departure from so fundamental a principle as a portion of imperfection in the system, and regret it. It may prove the seed of future weakness, and perhaps of anarchy.

No one will claim that an election law could have been drafted and placed in the Constitution that would always fit every probable change in the country's situation. It will therefore not be denied that some discretionary power over elections must exist somewhere. I presume it will be as readily conceded that this power could reasonably have been arranged in only three ways. It had to be lodged wholly in the national legislature, or wholly in the State legislatures, or primarily in the latter and ultimately in the former. The Convention has, with reason, preferred the last. It has given the first regulation of elections for the federal government to the local administrations. In ordinary cases, and when no improper views prevail, they may be both more convenient and more satisfactory. But it has reserved to the national authority a right to step in whenever extraordinary circumstances might make this necessary for its safety.

Nothing is more evident than this: an exclusive power to regulate elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy. They could destroy it at any moment by neglecting to provide for choosing the persons who administer its affairs. It does little good to say that such neglect or omission would be unlikely. The constitutional possibility of it, with nothing to balance the risk, is an unanswerable objection. Nor has any satisfactory reason yet been given for taking that risk. The extravagant surmises of a distempered jealousy can never be called a reason. If we are in the mood to presume abuses of power, it is as fair to presume them from the State governments as from the general government. Sound theory says it is more fitting to trust the Union with the care of its own existence than to hand that care to anyone else. So if we must risk abuses of power on one side or the other, it is more rational to risk them where the power would naturally be placed than where it would be placed unnaturally.

Suppose the Constitution had included an article empowering the United States to regulate elections for the individual States. Would anyone have hesitated to condemn it, both as an unwarranted transfer of power and as a deliberate engine for destroying the State governments? The violation of principle in that case would have needed no comment. To an unbiased observer it is just as plain in a scheme that makes the national government's existence, in a similar respect, depend on the pleasure of the State governments. An impartial look at the matter cannot fail to convince us that each government, as far as possible, ought to depend on itself for its own preservation.

Here is an objection to this position. The make-up of the national Senate, it may be said, would carry in its full extent the very danger that an exclusive power in the State legislatures to regulate federal elections is supposed to bring. By declining to appoint senators, the State legislatures might at any time strike a fatal blow at the Union. From this it may be inferred that since the Union's existence would thus depend on them in so essential a point, there can be no objection to trusting them with it in the particular case under consideration. It may be added that each State's interest in keeping its representation in the national councils would be a complete security against abuse of the trust.

This argument looks plausible, but it will not prove sound on examination. It is certainly true that the State legislatures, by refusing to appoint senators, may destroy the national government. It does not follow that because they hold such a power in one instance, they ought to hold it in every other. There are cases in which the harmful tendency of such a power may be far more decisive, and in which no motive as compelling as the one that must have guided the Convention in forming the Senate recommends admitting it. Insofar as that arrangement exposes the Union to possible injury from the State legislatures, it is an evil. But it was an evil that could not have been avoided without shutting the States, in their political capacities, entirely out of the organization of the national government. Had that been done, it would doubtless have been read as a complete abandonment of the federal principle. It would also certainly have deprived the State governments of the absolute safeguard they will enjoy under this provision. However wise it may have been to accept a drawback in this instance to gain a necessary advantage or a greater good, nothing follows from it in favor of piling up the evil where no necessity urges it and no greater good invites it.

We can also easily see that the national government would run a much greater risk from a State legislative power over the elections of its House of Representatives than from the State power to appoint members of its Senate. Senators are to be chosen for six years. A rotation will empty and refill the seats of a third of them every two years. No State is to have more than two senators, and a quorum of the body is to be sixteen members. Together, these circumstances mean that a temporary combination of a few States to suspend the appointment of senators could neither end the body's existence nor impair its activity. And a general and permanent combination of the States is not something we have anything to fear from. The first might come from sinister designs in the leading members of a few State legislatures. The last would require a fixed and rooted disaffection in the great body of the people. Either that will never exist at all, or it will in all probability come from experience of the general government's inability to advance their happiness, and in that event no good citizen could want it to continue.

The federal House of Representatives is different. A general election of its members is intended once every two years. Suppose the State legislatures were given an exclusive power to regulate these elections. Then every election time would be a delicate crisis in the national situation. It might end in the dissolution of the Union, if the leaders of a few of the most important States had conspired beforehand to prevent an election.

I do not deny that there is some weight in the observation that each State's interest in being represented in the federal councils will protect against abuse of a power over its elections held by the State legislatures. But those who note an obvious distinction will not think the protection complete. The people have an interest in the public happiness; their local rulers have an interest in the power and importance of their offices. The people of America may be warmly attached to the government of the Union at times when the particular rulers of particular States may feel very differently. Those rulers are spurred by the natural rivalry of power and by hopes of personal aggrandizement, and each is supported by a strong faction in his State. This difference of feeling between a majority of the people and the individuals with the most credit in their councils is, in some of the States, visible at this very moment, on the present question. The scheme of separate confederacies, which will always multiply the chances of ambition, will be a never-failing bait to every influential character in the State administrations who is capable of preferring his own personal gain and advancement to the public welfare. Such men would hold a very effective weapon in the exclusive power to regulate elections for the national government. A combination of a few of them in a few of the most considerable States, where the temptation will always be strongest, might destroy the Union. They would only need to seize the opportunity of some casual dissatisfaction among the people (which perhaps they may themselves have stirred up) and stop choosing members for the federal House of Representatives. We should never forget that a firm union of this country under an effective government will probably be an increasing object of jealousy to more than one nation of Europe. Enterprises to subvert it will sometimes begin in the intrigues of foreign powers, and some of those powers will seldom fail to encourage and abet them. Wherever it can be avoided, then, its preservation ought not to be committed to the guardianship of anyone except those whose situation will always give them an immediate interest in the faithful and vigilant performance of the trust.
1. 1st clause, 4th section, of the 1st article.

chapters.title: No. 60 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: We have seen that an uncontrollable power over elections to the federal government could not safely be committed to the State legislatures. Now let us see what the danger would be on the other side: trusting the Union itself with the ultimate right to regulate its own elections. No one claims that this right would ever be used to shut any State out of its share in the representation. The interest of all would, in this respect at least, be the security of all. But it is alleged that the right might be used to promote the election of some favorite class of men and exclude others. The means would be to confine the places of election to particular districts, making it impracticable for citizens at large to take part in the choice. Of all fanciful suppositions, this seems the most fanciful. On the one hand, no rational calculation of probabilities would lead us to imagine that the national councils could ever harbor the disposition so violent and extraordinary a course would imply. On the other hand, we may conclude with certainty that if so improper a spirit ever did gain entry, it would show itself in a quite different and far more decisive form.

We can fairly infer how improbable the attempt is from this one reflection: it could never be made without causing an immediate revolt of the great body of the people, led and directed by the State governments. In certain turbulent and factional seasons, it is not hard to imagine this characteristic right of liberty being violated against a particular class of citizens by a victorious and overbearing majority. But it is altogether inconceivable and incredible that so fundamental a privilege, in a country so situated and so enlightened, would be invaded to the injury of the great mass of the people by the deliberate policy of the government without bringing on a popular revolution.

Beyond this general reflection, there are more precise considerations that rule out any apprehension on the subject. The elements that will compose the national government are unlike one another, and the manner in which they will be brought into action in its various branches is more unlike still. This must form a powerful obstacle to any concert of views on a biased scheme of elections. The people of the different parts of the Union differ enough in the state of property, and in character, manners and habits, to produce a material difference of disposition among their representatives toward the different ranks and conditions of society.
