Close contact under one government will promote some gradual assimilation in certain of these respects. Even so, there are causes, physical as well as moral, that may in greater or lesser degree permanently nourish different inclinations on this point. But the circumstance likely to have the greatest influence will be the different ways of constituting the separate parts of the government. The House of Representatives is to be elected directly by the people, the Senate by the State legislatures, and the President by electors chosen for that purpose by the people. There would be little chance of a common interest to cement these different branches in a preference for any particular class of electors.

As for the Senate, no regulation of "time and manner" can affect the spirit that will direct the choice of its members. And "time and manner" is all that is proposed to be submitted to the national government with respect to that body. The collective view of the State legislatures can never be swayed by extraneous circumstances of that sort. This consideration alone ought to satisfy us that the feared discrimination would never be attempted. What inducement could the Senate have to agree to a preference in which it would not itself be included? And to what purpose would such a preference be established for one branch of the legislature if it could not be extended to the other? The make-up of the one would in that case counteract that of the other. We can never suppose that it would reach the appointments to the Senate unless we also suppose the voluntary cooperation of the State legislatures. If we make that supposition, it becomes immaterial where the power in question is placed, whether in their hands or in those of the Union.

But what is to be the object of this arbitrary bias in the national councils? Will it discriminate between the different departments of industry, or between the different kinds of property, or between the different degrees of property? Will it lean toward the landed interest, or the moneyed interest, or the mercantile interest, or the manufacturing interest? Or, in the fashionable language of the Constitution's adversaries, will it seek the elevation of "the wealthy and the well-born" while excluding and debasing all the rest of society?

Suppose this bias is to be exercised in favor of those engaged in some particular kind of industry or property. I presume it will readily be admitted that the competition for it would lie between landed men and merchants. And I do not hesitate to say that it is infinitely less likely that either of them would gain the upper hand in the national councils than that one or the other would dominate all the local councils. The inference is that we have much less to fear from the former than from the latter in conduct that tends to give an undue preference to either.

The individual States are devoted in varying degrees to agriculture and commerce. In most of them, if not all, agriculture is predominant. In a few, however, commerce nearly shares its empire, and in most it has a considerable share of influence. Whichever prevails will be carried into the national representation in proportion to its strength. But this representation will come from a greater variety of interests, in much more varied proportions, than any single State contains. For that very reason it will be much less apt to embrace either interest with decided partiality than the representation of any single State.

In a country made up chiefly of cultivators of land, where equal representation prevails, the landed interest must on the whole preponderate in the government. As long as that interest prevails in most of the State legislatures, it must keep a matching superiority in the national Senate, which will generally be a faithful copy of the majorities of those assemblies. It cannot be presumed, then, that sacrificing the landed class to the mercantile class will ever be a favorite object of this branch of the federal legislature. In applying a general observation, suggested by the situation of the country, specifically to the Senate, I am guided by this consideration: the credulous devotees of State power cannot, on their own principles, suspect that the State legislatures would be warped from their duty by any outside influence. But in reality the same situation must have the same effect, in the original composition at least of the federal House of Representatives. We should expect an improper bias toward the mercantile class as little from that quarter as from the other.

Perhaps, to give the objection some countenance in any case, someone will ask whether there is a danger of an opposite bias in the national government, disposing it to try to secure a monopoly of the federal administration for the landed class. Those who would be directly injured by such a bias are unlikely to find the supposition terrifying, so I will dispense with a labored answer to this question. It is enough to remark, first, that for the reasons given elsewhere, it is less likely that any decided partiality will prevail in the councils of the Union than in those of any of its members. Second, there would be no temptation to violate the Constitution in favor of the landed class, because that class would in the natural course of things enjoy as great a preponderance as it could want. Third, men used to examining the sources of public prosperity on a large scale must be too well convinced of the usefulness of commerce to be inclined to wound it as deeply as they would by excluding altogether from the management of public affairs those who would best understand its interest. In terms of revenue alone, the importance of commerce must effectively protect it from the enmity of a body that would be continually pressed on its behalf by the urgent calls of public necessity.

I am the more inclined to be brief on the probability of a preference based on discrimination between different kinds of industry and property because, as far as I understand the objectors, they have a different kind of discrimination in mind. They appear to have in view, as the objects of the preference with which they try to alarm us, those they describe as "the wealthy and the well-born." These, it seems, are to be raised to an odious pre-eminence over the rest of their fellow citizens. At one time, however, their elevation is to follow necessarily from the smallness of the representative body; at another, it is to be brought about by depriving the people at large of the chance to exercise their right to vote in choosing that body.

But on what principle is the discrimination of the places of election to be made, so as to serve the purpose of the intended preference? Are "the wealthy and the well-born," as they are called, confined to particular spots in the individual States? Have they, by some miraculous instinct or foresight, set aside a common place of residence in each of them? Are they found only in the towns or cities? Or are they, on the contrary, scattered over the countryside, wherever greed or chance has happened to place them or their predecessors? If the latter is the case (as every intelligent man knows it to be,(1)) is it not evident that confining the places of election to particular districts would defeat its own aim, besides being objectionable on every other account? The truth is that there is no way of securing the feared preference to the rich except by prescribing property qualifications for those who may elect or be elected. But that forms no part of the power to be given to the national government. Its authority would be expressly restricted to regulating the TIMES, the PLACES and the MANNER of elections. The qualifications of those who may choose or be chosen, as has been remarked on other occasions, are defined and fixed in the Constitution, and the legislature cannot alter them.

Still, let it be admitted for the sake of argument that the suggested expedient might succeed. Let it be equally taken for granted that the national rulers overcame every scruple that a sense of duty, or fear of the danger of the experiment, might awaken in them. Even so, I imagine no one will claim that they could ever hope to carry out such an enterprise without a military force large enough to subdue the resistance of the great body of the people. Different parts of these papers have discussed and demonstrated how improbable it is that a force equal to that object will exist. But to show the futility of the objection in the strongest light, let us concede for a moment that such a force might exist and that the national government actually possessed it. What will follow? Suppose they had a disposition to invade the essential rights of the community, and the means of gratifying it. Is it likely that persons moved by that disposition would amuse themselves with the ridiculous task of fabricating election laws to secure a preference for a favorite class of men? Would they not prefer a course better suited to their own immediate aggrandizement? Would they not rather boldly resolve to perpetuate themselves in office by one decisive act of usurpation than rely on precarious expedients? Such expedients, despite all the precautions that might accompany them, might end in the dismissal, disgrace and ruin of their authors. Would they not fear that citizens, as tenacious of their rights as they are aware of them, would flock from the remote ends of their States to the places of election to overthrow their tyrants and put in their place men disposed to avenge the violated majesty of the people?
1. Particularly in the Southern States and in this State.

chapters.title: No. 61 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the Power of Congress to Regulate the Election of Members) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The fairer opponents of the provision on elections in the plan of the Convention will sometimes, when pressed in argument, grant that it is proper. They qualify this, however: it ought to have come with a declaration that all elections must be held in the counties where the electors live. This, they say, was a necessary precaution against abuse of the power. Such a declaration would certainly have done no harm, and to the extent that it quieted apprehensions it might not have been undesirable. But it would in fact have added little or no security against the danger feared. An impartial and judicious examiner will never count its absence as a serious objection to the plan, much less an insuperable one. The views taken of the subject in the two preceding papers must be enough to convince all dispassionate and discerning men of this. If public liberty is ever sacrificed to the ambition of the national rulers, the power under examination, at least, will not be to blame.

Some people are inclined to follow only their jealousy. If they would use it to inspect the individual State constitutions carefully, they would find little less cause for uneasiness and alarm in the latitude most of those constitutions allow on elections than in the latitude proposed for the national government. A review of the State constitutions on this point would go a long way toward removing any ill impressions that remain. But such a review would lead into long and tedious details, so I shall content myself with one example, the State in which I write. The constitution of New York makes no other provision for the LOCALITY of elections than that members of the Assembly shall be elected in the COUNTIES and those of the Senate in the great districts into which the State is or may be divided. There are four such districts at present, each including from two to six counties. It is easy to see that it would be no harder for the legislature of New York to defeat the votes of New York's citizens by confining elections to particular places than for the legislature of the United States to defeat the votes of the citizens of the Union by the same expedient. Suppose, for instance, that the city of Albany were named the sole place of election for the county and district it belongs to. Would not the inhabitants of that city soon become the only electors of the members of both the Senate and the Assembly for that county and district? Can we imagine that electors living in the remote parts of the counties of Albany, Saratoga, Cambridge and so on, or anywhere in the county of Montgomery, would take the trouble to come to Albany to vote for members of the Assembly or Senate sooner than they would go to the city of New York to take part in choosing members of the federal House of Representatives? The alarming indifference we see in the use of so invaluable a privilege under the existing laws, which make every facility available, gives a ready answer. And even apart from any experience, we can have no trouble seeing that when the place of election is at an INCONVENIENT DISTANCE from the elector, the effect on his conduct will be the same whether that distance is twenty miles or twenty thousand miles. Hence it must be clear that objections to the particular form of the federal power to regulate elections apply, in substance, with equal force to the form of the like power in the constitution of this State. For this reason it will be impossible to acquit the one and condemn the other. A similar comparison would lead to the same conclusion about the constitutions of most of the other States.

Someone may say that defects in the State constitutions are no excuse for those in the proposed plan. I answer as follows. No one has ever accused the State constitutions of neglecting the security of liberty. So where the charges thrown at the plan can be shown to apply to them also, the presumption is that those charges are petty quibbles from a predetermined opposition rather than well-founded inferences from a fair search for truth. Some people are willing to treat as innocent omissions in the State constitutions what they regard as unpardonable blemishes in the plan of the Convention. Nothing can be said to them. At most they can be asked to give some substantial reason why the representatives of the people of a single State should be more proof against the lust of power or other sinister motives than the representatives of the people of the United States. If they cannot, they ought at least to prove to us that it is easier to subvert the liberties of three million people, who have local governments to lead their opposition, than those of two hundred thousand people who lack that advantage. And on the point immediately under consideration, they ought to convince us of something else. They must show that it is less probable for a predominant faction in a single State to lean toward a preference for a particular class of electors, in order to maintain its superiority, than for a similar spirit to take hold of the representatives of thirteen States. Those States are spread over a vast region and set apart from each other in several respects by a diversity of local circumstances, prejudices and interests.

So far my observations have aimed only at defending the provision in question on three grounds: theoretical propriety, the danger of placing the power elsewhere, and the safety of placing it as proposed. But I must mention one more thing, a positive advantage that will result from this arrangement and that could not as well have been obtained from any other. I mean the uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives. It is more than possible that experience will prove this uniformity of great importance to the public welfare. It may prove important both as a security against the perpetuation of the same spirit in the body and as a cure for the diseases of faction. If each State may choose its own time of election, there may be at least as many different times as there are months in the year. The times of election in the individual States, as now fixed for local purposes, range between extremes as far apart as March and November. The result of this diversity would be that the body could never be entirely dissolved or renewed at one time. If an improper spirit of any kind happened to prevail in it, that spirit would tend to pass itself on to the new members as they arrived in succession. The mass would probably stay nearly the same, constantly absorbing its gradual additions into itself. There is a contagion in example that few men have the strength of mind to resist. I am inclined to think that three times the term in office, on condition that the whole body is dissolved at once, might be less dangerous to liberty than one third of that term with gradual and successive changes.
Uniformity in the time of elections seems no less necessary for carrying out the idea of regular rotation in the Senate, and for conveniently assembling the legislature at a fixed time each year.

It may be asked why a time could not have been fixed in the Constitution. The most zealous adversaries of the plan of the Convention in this State are, in general, no less zealous admirers of the State constitution. So the question may be turned back on them: why was no time fixed for the same purpose in the constitution of this State? The best answer is that it was a matter that could safely be left to legislative discretion, and that a time once appointed might, on trial, have proved less convenient than some other. The same answer serves for the question put on the other side. It may be added that the supposed danger of a gradual change is merely speculative. It would hardly have been advisable, on the strength of such speculation, to establish as a fundamental point something that would deprive several States of the convenience of holding the elections for their own governments and for the national government at the same times.

chapters.title: No. 62 — The Senate (Madison)
paragraphs: Having examined the makeup of the House of Representatives, and answered those objections against it that seemed to deserve notice, I turn next to the Senate. This part of the government may be considered under five heads: I. The qualifications of senators; II. Their appointment by the State legislatures; III. The equality of representation in the Senate; IV. The number of senators and the term for which they are to be elected; V. The powers vested in the Senate.

I. The qualifications proposed for senators differ from those of representatives in requiring greater age and a longer period of citizenship. A senator must be at least thirty years old, while a representative must be twenty-five. The senator must also have been a citizen for nine years, where seven are required of the representative. The reason for these distinctions lies in the nature of the senatorial trust. That trust calls for a greater range of information and a steadier character, and so calls for a senator who has reached the time of life most likely to supply these qualities. It also involves a direct part in dealings with foreign nations, and so ought to be exercised only by those who have been thoroughly weaned from the prejudices and habits that come with foreign birth and education. The term of nine years seems a prudent middle course. At one extreme is a total exclusion of adopted citizens, whose merits and talents may deserve a share of the public confidence. At the other is a hasty and indiscriminate admission of them, which might open a channel for foreign influence in the national councils.

II. It is equally unnecessary to dwell on the appointment of senators by the State legislatures. Of the various ways in which this branch of the government might have been constituted, the one proposed by the Convention is probably the most agreeable to public opinion. It has a double advantage to recommend it. It favors a select appointment, and it gives the State governments such a part in forming the federal government as must secure their authority, and may serve as a convenient link between the two systems.

III. The equality of representation in the Senate is another point that does not call for much discussion, since it was plainly the result of a compromise between the opposing claims of the large and the small States. It may indeed be right that among a people thoroughly merged into one nation, every district should have a PROPORTIONAL share in the government. It may also be right that among independent and sovereign States bound together only by a simple league, the parties, however unequal in size, should have an EQUAL share in the common councils. If both are right, then it does not seem to be without some reason that in a compound republic, which partakes of both the national and the federal character, the government should be founded on a mixture of proportional and equal representation. But it is pointless to test by the standard of theory a part of the Constitution that everyone admits to be the result, not of theory, but "of a spirit of amity, and that mutual deference and concession which the peculiarity of our political situation rendered indispensable." The voice of America, and still more loudly her political situation, calls for a common government with powers equal to its objects. The smaller States are not likely to grant a government founded on principles more agreeable to the wishes of the larger States. The only choice for the larger States, then, lies between the proposed government and one that is still more objectionable. Given this alternative, prudence advises embracing the lesser evil. Instead of fruitlessly anticipating the harms that may follow, we should consider the advantages that may offset the sacrifice.

In that spirit, note that the equal vote given to each State does two things. It is a constitutional acknowledgment of the share of sovereignty that the individual States still retain, and it is a means of preserving that share. On this score the equality ought to be just as acceptable to the large States as to the small, because the large States are equally anxious to guard, by every possible means, against an improper consolidation of the States into one simple republic.

Another advantage that comes from this ingredient in the makeup of the Senate is the additional obstacle it will place against improper acts of legislation. No law or resolution can now be passed without the agreement, first, of a majority of the people, and then of a majority of the States. It must be acknowledged that this complicated check on legislation may in some instances be harmful as well as beneficial. It must also be acknowledged that the special protection it gives the smaller States would be more reasonable if some interests common to them, and distinct from those of the other States, would otherwise be exposed to particular danger. But the larger States will always be able, through their power over the supplies, to defeat any unreasonable use of this prerogative of the lesser States. And the ease and excess of law-making seem to be the diseases to which our governments are most liable. So it is not impossible that this part of the Constitution may prove more convenient in practice than it appears to many in theory.

IV. The number of senators and the duration of their appointment come next to be considered. To form an accurate judgment on both points, it is proper to inquire into the purposes a senate is meant to serve. To determine these, it is necessary to review the problems a republic must suffer for lack of such an institution.

First. It is a misfortune that comes with republican government, though in a smaller degree than with other governments, that those who administer it may forget their obligations to their constituents and prove unfaithful to their important trust. From this point of view, a senate, as a second branch of the legislative assembly, distinct from the first and dividing power with it, must in all cases be a beneficial check on the government. It doubles the security of the people, by requiring the agreement of two distinct bodies in schemes of usurpation or betrayal, where the ambition or corruption of one would otherwise be enough. This precaution rests on such clear principles, and is now so well understood in the United States, that it would be more than superfluous to enlarge on it. I will only remark that the unlikelihood of sinister combinations will be in proportion to the difference in character between the two bodies. It must therefore be wise to distinguish them from each other in every respect consistent with due harmony in all proper measures and with the genuine principles of republican government.

Second. The necessity of a senate is just as clearly shown by the tendency of all single and numerous assemblies to yield to sudden and violent passions, and to be led by factional leaders into intemperate and destructive resolutions. Examples could be cited without number, both from proceedings within the United States and from the history of other nations. But a position that will not be contradicted need not be proved. All that needs to be remarked is that a body meant to correct this weakness ought itself to be free from it, and so ought to be less numerous. It ought, moreover, to have great firmness, and so ought to hold its authority for a considerable length of time.

Third. Another defect that a senate can supply is a lack of due acquaintance with the objects and principles of legislation. An assembly of men drawn for the most part from private pursuits, kept in office for a short time, and led by no lasting motive to spend the intervals between public duties studying the laws, the affairs and the broad interests of their country, cannot, if left wholly to themselves, escape a variety of serious errors in exercising their legislative trust. It may be affirmed, on the best grounds, that no small share of the present troubles of America is to be blamed on the blunders of our governments, and that these have come from the heads rather than the hearts of most of their authors. What indeed are all the repealing, explaining and amending laws that fill and disgrace our voluminous codes, but so many monuments of deficient wisdom? They are so many charges brought by each session against the one before it, and so many warnings to the people of the value of the help that may be expected from a well-constituted senate.

A good government implies two things: first, fidelity to the object of government, which is the happiness of the people; second, knowledge of the means by which that object can best be attained. Some governments are deficient in both of these qualities; most governments are deficient in the first. I do not hesitate to assert that American governments have paid too little attention to the second. The federal Constitution avoids this error. And what deserves particular notice is that it provides for the second in a way that increases the security for the first.

Fourth. The instability in the public councils that comes from a rapid succession of new members, however well qualified they may be, shows in the strongest way the need for some stable institution in the government. Every new election in the States is found to change one half of the representatives. From this change of men must come a change of opinions, and from a change of opinions, a change of measures. But continual change, even of good measures, is inconsistent with every rule of prudence and every prospect of success. The remark holds true in private life, and it becomes both more just and more important in national affairs.
To trace the harmful effects of an unstable government would fill a volume. I will point out only a few, each of which will be seen to be the source of countless others.

In the first place, it forfeits the respect and confidence of other nations, and all the advantages that go with a national character. An individual who is seen to be inconstant in his plans, or perhaps to conduct his affairs with no plan at all, is marked at once by all prudent people as a speedy victim of his own unsteadiness and folly. His more friendly neighbors may pity him, but all will decline to link their fortunes with his, and not a few will seize the chance to make their own fortunes out of his. One nation is to another what one individual is to another, with this melancholy difference perhaps: nations have fewer benevolent feelings than individuals, and are also under fewer restraints from taking undue advantage of each other's indiscretions. Every nation, therefore, whose affairs betray a lack of wisdom and stability may expect to suffer every loss that the more systematic policy of its wiser neighbors can inflict. But the best lesson on this subject is, unhappily, given to America by the example of her own situation. She finds that she is held in no respect by her friends, that she is the derision of her enemies, and that she is a prey to every nation that has an interest in speculating on her fluctuating councils and embarrassed affairs.

The internal effects of an unstable policy are still more calamitous. It poisons the blessing of liberty itself. It will do the people little good that the laws are made by men of their own choice, if the laws are so voluminous that they cannot be read, or so incoherent that they cannot be understood; if they are repealed or revised before they are published, or undergo such incessant changes that no one who knows what the law is today can guess what it will be tomorrow. Law is defined as a rule of action. But how can something be a rule when it is little known and even less fixed?

Public instability has another effect: it gives the shrewd, the enterprising and the moneyed few an unreasonable advantage over the industrious and uninformed mass of the people. Every new regulation of commerce or revenue, or any rule that changes the value of the various kinds of property, offers a fresh harvest to those who watch for the change and can foresee its consequences. It is a harvest they did not raise themselves; it was raised by the toil and care of the great body of their fellow citizens. In such a state of things it may be said with some truth that laws are made for the FEW, not for the MANY.

From another point of view, an unstable government does great injury. The lack of confidence in the public councils discourages every useful undertaking whose success and profit may depend on existing arrangements continuing. What prudent merchant will risk his fortune in any new branch of commerce when he cannot be sure that his plans will not be made unlawful before they can be carried out? What farmer or manufacturer will organize his work around the encouragement given to some particular crop or enterprise, when he can have no assurance that his preparatory labor and outlay will not make him a victim of an inconstant government? In a word, no great improvement or praiseworthy enterprise can go forward that requires the backing of a steady system of national policy.

But the most deplorable effect of all is the decline of attachment and reverence that steals into the hearts of the people toward a political system that shows so many marks of weakness and disappoints so many of their flattering hopes. No government, any more than an individual, will long be respected without being truly respectable, and it cannot be truly respectable without a certain measure of order and stability.

chapters.title: No. 63 — The Senate Continued (Madison)
paragraphs: A FIFTH need, which shows the usefulness of a senate, is a due sense of national character. Without a select and stable part of the government, the esteem of foreign powers will be forfeited by an uninformed and changeable policy arising from the causes already mentioned. In addition, the national councils will lack that sensitivity to the opinion of the world, which is perhaps as necessary to deserve the world's respect and confidence as it is to obtain them.

Attention to the judgment of other nations is important to every government for two reasons. The first is that, whatever the merits of a particular plan or measure, it is desirable on various grounds that it appear to other nations to be the product of a wise and honorable policy. The second is that in doubtful cases, particularly where the national councils may be bent by some strong passion or momentary interest, the presumed or known opinion of the impartial world may be the best guide to follow. What has America not lost for want of a character with foreign nations? And how many errors and follies would she have avoided, if the justice and propriety of her measures had in every instance first been tested by the light in which they would probably appear to the unbiased part of mankind?

Yet however necessary a sense of national character may be, it is plain that a numerous and changeable body can never have enough of it. It can be found only in a number so small that each individual receives a real share of the praise and blame for public measures, or in an assembly so durably invested with public trust that the pride and importance of its members are bound up with the reputation and prosperity of the community. The half-yearly representatives of Rhode Island would probably have been little affected, in their deliberations on the unjust measures of that State, by arguments drawn from how such measures would look to foreign nations, or even to the sister States. Yet it can hardly be doubted that if the agreement of a select and stable body had been required, regard for national character alone would have prevented the calamities under which that misguided people is now suffering.

I add, as a SIXTH defect, the lack in some important cases of proper responsibility of the government to the people. This comes from the very frequency of elections which in other cases produces such responsibility. This remark will perhaps seem not only new but paradoxical. Yet when explained, it must be acknowledged to be as undeniable as it is important.

To be reasonable, responsibility must be limited to matters within the power of the party held responsible. To be effective, it must relate to operations of that power on which the constituents can readily form a proper judgment. The objects of government may be divided into two general classes. One depends on measures that each have an immediate and noticeable effect. The other depends on a succession of well-chosen and well-connected measures, whose effect is gradual and perhaps unobserved. The importance of the second kind to the collective and lasting welfare of every country needs no explanation. And yet it is clear that an assembly elected for so short a term that it can provide only one or two links in a chain of measures on which the general welfare may essentially depend ought not to answer for the final result. A steward or tenant engaged for one year could not justly be made to answer for estates or improvements that could not be completed in less than half a dozen years. Nor can the people estimate the SHARE of influence that their annual assemblies may each have had on events resulting from the mixed transactions of several years. It is difficult enough to keep the members of a NUMEROUS body personally responsible even for those acts of the body that have an immediate, separate and obvious effect on its constituents.

The proper remedy for this defect must be an additional body in the legislative department. Having enough permanence to provide for objects that require continued attention and a train of measures, it can be justly and effectively held answerable for achieving those objects.

So far I have considered the circumstances that show the need for a well-constructed Senate only as they relate to the representatives of the people. To a people as little blinded by prejudice or corrupted by flattery as those I address, I do not hesitate to add that such an institution may sometimes be necessary as a defense of the people against their own temporary errors and delusions. The calm and deliberate judgment of the community ought, in all governments, and actually will, in all free governments, prevail in the end over the views of its rulers. Even so, there are particular moments in public affairs when the people, stirred up by some irregular passion or some illicit advantage, or misled by the artful misrepresentations of interested men, may call for measures that they themselves will afterward be the first to lament and condemn. In these critical moments, how beneficial will be the interference of some temperate and respectable body of citizens, to check the misguided course and to hold back the blow the people are aiming at themselves, until reason, justice and truth can regain their authority over the public mind! What bitter anguish the people of Athens might often have escaped, if their government had contained so provident a safeguard against the tyranny of their own passions! Popular liberty might then have escaped the lasting reproach of decreeing hemlock to the same citizens one day and statues the next.

It may be suggested that a people spread over a wide region cannot, like the crowded inhabitants of a small district, be subject to the infection of violent passions or to the danger of uniting in pursuit of unjust measures. I am far from denying that this is a distinction of special importance. On the contrary, I tried in an earlier paper to show that it is one of the principal recommendations of a confederated republic. At the same time, this advantage should not be taken to make additional precautions unnecessary. It may even be remarked that the same wide situation that will spare the people of America some of the dangers of smaller republics will expose them to a different problem: they may stay for a longer time under the influence of those misrepresentations that the combined effort of interested men may succeed in spreading among them.

It adds considerable weight to all these considerations to recall that history shows no long-lived republic that did not have a senate. Sparta, Rome and Carthage are in fact the only states to which that description applies. In each of the first two there was a senate for life. The constitution of the senate in the last is less well known. Circumstantial evidence makes it probable that it did not differ in this respect from the other two. It is at least certain that it had some quality or other that made it an anchor against popular fluctuations, and that a smaller council drawn from the senate was appointed for life and filled its own vacancies. These examples are as unfit for imitation as they are repugnant to the character of America. Nevertheless, when compared with the short and turbulent existence of other ancient republics, they are very instructive proofs of the need for some institution that will blend stability with liberty. I am not unaware of the circumstances that distinguish the American government from other popular governments, ancient as well as modern, and that make extreme caution necessary in reasoning from one case to the other. But after giving this consideration its due weight, it can still be maintained that there are many points of likeness that make these examples worth our attention. Many of the defects that, as we have seen, can be supplied only by a senatorial institution are common to a numerous assembly frequently elected by the people and to the people themselves. There are others peculiar to the assembly, which require the control of such an institution. The people can never willfully betray their own interests, but they may possibly be betrayed by the representatives of the people. And the danger will plainly be greater where the whole legislative trust is lodged in the hands of one body of men than where the agreement of separate and dissimilar bodies is required for every public act.

The difference most relied on between the American republic and other republics lies in the principle of representation. It is the pivot on which the American government turns, and it is supposed to have been unknown to the others, or at least to the ancient ones. The use made of this difference in the reasoning of former papers will have shown that I am disposed neither to deny that it exists nor to undervalue its importance. I feel the less restraint, therefore, in observing that the position that the ancient governments were ignorant of representation is by no means exactly true in the broad sense commonly given to it. Without entering into a discussion that would be out of place here, I will point to a few known facts in support of what I say.

Even in the purest democracies of Greece, the people did not carry out many of the executive functions themselves. Those functions were performed by officers elected by the people and REPRESENTING the people in their EXECUTIVE capacity.

Before the reform of Solon, Athens was governed by nine Archons, annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE AT LARGE. How much power was delegated to them seems to be left in great obscurity. After that period we find an assembly, first of four, and afterward of six hundred members, annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE. It PARTIALLY represented them in their LEGISLATIVE capacity, since its members were not only associated with the people in the function of making laws but also had the exclusive right of originating legislative proposals to the people. The senate of Carthage, too, whatever its power or the length of its appointment, appears to have been ELECTIVE, by the votes of the people. Similar instances might be found in most, if not all, of the popular governments of antiquity.

Lastly, in Sparta we meet the Ephori, and in Rome the Tribunes: two bodies, small in numbers, but annually ELECTED BY THE WHOLE BODY OF THE PEOPLE and regarded as the REPRESENTATIVES of the people, almost in a PLENIPOTENTIARY capacity. The Cosmi of Crete were also annually ELECTED BY THE PEOPLE. Some authors have considered them an institution analogous to those of Sparta and Rome, with this difference only: in electing that representative body, the right to vote was given to only a part of the people.

In answer to all these arguments, suggested by reason, illustrated by examples and backed by our own experience, the suspicious opponent of the Constitution will probably be content to repeat that a senate not appointed directly by the people, and serving a term of six years, must gradually gain a dangerous preeminence in the government and finally transform it into a tyrannical aristocracy.

The general answer to this should be enough: liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as by the abuses of power; there are numerous instances of the former as well as of the latter; and it is the former, rather than the latter, that the United States apparently has most to fear. But a more particular reply can be given.

Before such a revolution could be brought about, the Senate, it should be observed, would have to corrupt itself first. It would next have to corrupt the State legislatures, then the House of Representatives, and finally the people at large. It is evident that the Senate must be corrupted first before it can attempt to establish tyranny. It cannot carry on the attempt without corrupting the State legislatures, because the periodic change of members would otherwise renew the whole body. Unless it used the means of corruption with equal success on the House of Representatives, the opposition of that coequal branch of the government would inevitably defeat the attempt. And unless it corrupted the people themselves, a succession of new representatives would soon restore everything to its original order. Can anyone seriously persuade himself that the proposed Senate could, by any means within the reach of human skill, arrive at the goal of a lawless ambition through all these obstacles?

If reason condemns the suspicion, experience pronounces the same verdict. The constitution of Maryland furnishes the most fitting example. The Senate of that State is elected, as the federal Senate will be, indirectly by the people, and for a term only one year shorter than that of the federal Senate. It is also distinguished by the remarkable prerogative of filling its own vacancies within the term of its appointment, and it is not subject to any rotation like the one provided for the federal Senate. There are some other lesser differences that would expose the Maryland Senate to plausible objections that do not apply to the federal one. If the federal Senate really contained the danger that has been so loudly proclaimed, then some symptoms at least of a like danger ought by this time to have shown themselves in the Senate of Maryland. No such symptoms have appeared. On the contrary, the suspicions first held by men of the same description as those who view the corresponding part of the federal Constitution with terror have been gradually put to rest by the progress of the experiment. And the Maryland constitution is daily gaining, from the beneficial working of this part of it, a reputation that probably no other State in the Union will rival.

If anything could silence these suspicions, it ought to be the British example. The Senate there is not elected for six years and is not open to people of any family or fortune; it is a hereditary assembly of wealthy nobles. The House of Representatives there is not elected for two years by the whole body of the people; it is elected for seven years, and in very great proportion by a very small proportion of the people. Here, beyond question, we ought to see in full display the aristocratic usurpations and tyranny that are supposed to be played out in the United States at some future time. Unfortunately for the anti-federal argument, however, British history tells us that this hereditary assembly has been unable to defend itself against the continual encroachments of the House of Representatives, and that as soon as it lost the support of the monarch, it was actually crushed by the weight of the popular branch.

To the extent that antiquity can teach us anything on this subject, its examples support our reasoning. In Sparta the Ephori, the annual representatives of the people, proved more than a match for the senate for life; they gained on its authority continually and finally drew all power into their own hands. The Tribunes of Rome, who were the representatives of the people, prevailed, as is well known, in almost every contest with the senate for life, and in the end gained the most complete triumph over it. The fact is the more remarkable because the Tribunes had to be unanimous in every act, even after their number was increased to ten. It proves the irresistible force of that branch of a free government which has the people on its side. To these examples might be added that of Carthage. According to the testimony of Polybius, its senate, far from drawing all power into its vortex, had by the beginning of the second Punic War lost almost the whole of its original share.

These facts together are conclusive evidence that the federal Senate will never be able to turn itself, by gradual usurpations, into an independent and aristocratic body. But we are warranted in believing something more. Suppose such a revolution should ever happen, from causes that human foresight cannot guard against. Then the House of Representatives, with the people on their side, will always be able to restore the Constitution to its original form and principles. Against the force of the people's immediate representatives, nothing will be able to maintain even the constitutional authority of the Senate, except a display of enlightened policy and devotion to the public good that wins for it, alongside that branch of the legislature, the affection and support of the entire body of the people themselves.

chapters.title: No. 64 — The Powers of the Senate (Jay)
paragraphs: It is a just observation, and not a new one, that enemies of particular persons and opponents of particular measures seldom confine their criticism to what actually deserves blame in either. Only on this principle is it easy to explain the motives of those who condemn the proposed Constitution as a whole and treat with severity some of its most unobjectionable articles.
The second section gives power to the President, "BY AND WITH THE ADVICE AND CONSENT OF THE SENATE, TO MAKE TREATIES, PROVIDED TWO THIRDS OF THE SENATORS PRESENT CONCUR."

The power of making treaties is an important one, especially as it bears on war, peace and commerce. It should be delegated only in a way, and with such precautions, as will give the highest security that it will be exercised by the men best qualified for it, and in the manner most conducive to the public good. The Convention appears to have attended to both points. It has directed that the President be chosen by select bodies of electors, appointed by the people for that express purpose, and it has committed the appointment of senators to the State legislatures. In such cases this method has a vast advantage over elections by the people in their collective capacity. In those elections the activity of party zeal, taking advantage of the indifference, the ignorance, and the hopes and fears of the unwary and the interested, often puts men in office by the votes of a small proportion of the electors.

The select assemblies that choose the President, like the State legislatures that appoint the senators, will in general be composed of the most enlightened and respectable citizens. There is reason to presume, therefore, that they will direct their attention and their votes only to those men who have become most distinguished for their abilities and virtue, and in whom the people see just grounds for confidence. The Constitution shows very particular attention to this object. It excludes men under thirty-five from the first office and those under thirty from the second. In this way it confines the electors to men of whom the people have had time to form a judgment, and with respect to whom they will not be liable to be deceived by those brilliant displays of talent and patriotism which, like passing meteors, sometimes mislead as well as dazzle. If it is well founded to say that wise kings will always be served by able ministers, it is fair to argue that an assembly of select electors has, in a greater degree than kings, the means of broad and accurate information about men and characters, and so their appointments will show at least equal discretion and discernment. The natural inference from these considerations is that the President and senators so chosen will always be among those who best understand our national interests, whether in relation to the individual States or to foreign nations; who are best able to promote those interests; and whose reputation for integrity inspires and deserves confidence. With such men the power of making treaties may safely be lodged.

The absolute necessity of system in the conduct of any business is universally known and acknowledged. Yet its great importance in national affairs has not yet been sufficiently impressed on the public mind. Those who wish to commit the power under consideration to a popular assembly, made up of members constantly coming and going in quick succession, seem not to recall that such a body must be inadequate to attaining the great objects that need to be kept steadily in view in all their relations and circumstances. Those objects can be approached and achieved only by measures that require not only talents but also exact information, and often much time, to plan and to carry out. It was wise, therefore, for the Convention to provide not only that the power of making treaties should be committed to able and honest men, but also that they should stay in place long enough to become perfectly acquainted with our national concerns, and to form and introduce a system for managing them. The term prescribed is such as will give them an opportunity to greatly extend their political information, and to make their accumulating experience more and more beneficial to their country. The Convention has shown no less prudence in providing for the frequent election of senators in a way that avoids the problem of periodically handing these great affairs over entirely to new men. By leaving a considerable remainder of the old ones in place, it preserves uniformity and order, as well as a constant succession of official information.

Few will deny that trade and navigation should be governed by a system that is carefully designed and steadily followed, and that our treaties and our laws alike should fit that system and be made to advance it. It matters greatly that this fit be carefully maintained. Anyone who grants the point will see and admit that it is well secured by making the agreement of the Senate necessary to both treaties and laws.

It seldom happens in negotiating treaties, of whatever kind, that perfect SECRECY and immediate DISPATCH are not sometimes required. These are cases where the most useful intelligence may be obtained, if the persons who possess it can be relieved of the fear of discovery. That fear will affect those persons whether they act from mercenary or from friendly motives, and there are doubtless many of both kinds who would rely on the secrecy of the President but would not trust that of the Senate, and still less that of a large popular assembly. The Convention has done well, therefore, in arranging the power of making treaties so that, although the President must act by the advice and consent of the Senate in forming them, he will be able to manage the business of intelligence as prudence may suggest.

Those who have turned their attention to the affairs of men must have noticed that there are tides in them: tides very irregular in their duration, strength and direction, and seldom found to run twice in exactly the same manner or measure. To discern these tides in national affairs and profit by them is the business of those who preside over those affairs. Those who have had much experience in this field tell us that there are often occasions when days, indeed even hours, are precious. The loss of a battle, the death of a prince, the removal of a minister, or other circumstances that change the present posture and look of affairs may turn the most favorable tide into a course opposite to our wishes. As in the field, so in the cabinet, there are moments to be seized as they pass, and those who preside in either should be left able to make use of them. So often and so seriously have we suffered in the past from lack of secrecy and dispatch that the Constitution would have been inexcusably defective if it had paid no attention to those objects. The matters that usually require the most secrecy and the most dispatch in negotiations are the preparatory and auxiliary measures, which matter from the national point of view only because they help to reach the objects of the negotiation. For these the President will have no difficulty making provision. And should any circumstance arise that requires the advice and consent of the Senate, he may convene them at any time. Thus we see that the Constitution provides for our negotiations of treaties to have every advantage that can be drawn from talents, information, integrity and deliberate investigation on the one hand, and from secrecy and dispatch on the other.
But to this plan, as to most others that have ever appeared, objections are devised and pressed.

Some are unhappy with it, not because they find any error or defect in it, but because treaties, once made, are to have the force of laws, and so, they say, should be made only by men who hold legislative authority. These gentlemen seem not to consider that the judgments of our courts, and the commissions our governor constitutionally issues, are as valid, and as binding on all the persons they concern, as the laws passed by our legislature. All constitutional acts of power, whether in the executive or in the judicial department, have as much legal validity and obligation as if they came from the legislature. Therefore, whatever name is given to the power of making treaties, and however binding treaties may be when made, it is certain that the people may with much propriety commit that power to a body distinct from the legislative, the executive or the judicial. It surely does not follow that because they have given the power of making laws to the legislature, they should likewise give it the power to do every other act of sovereignty by which the citizens are to be bound and affected.

Others, though content that treaties should be made in the way proposed, object to their being the SUPREME laws of the land. They insist, and profess to believe, that treaties, like acts of assembly, should be repealable at pleasure. This idea seems to be new and peculiar to this country, but new errors, as well as new truths, often appear. These gentlemen would do well to reflect that a treaty is only another name for a bargain. It would be impossible to find a nation that would make any bargain with us that bound it ABSOLUTELY but bound us only so long and so far as we might think proper. Those who make laws may, without doubt, amend or repeal them, and it will not be disputed that those who make treaties may alter or cancel them. But let us not forget that treaties are made, not by only one of the contracting parties, but by both. Consequently, just as the consent of both was essential to their formation at first, so it must always be afterward for altering or canceling them. The proposed Constitution, therefore, has not in the least extended the obligation of treaties. They are just as binding, and just as far beyond the lawful reach of legislative acts, now as they will be at any future time or under any form of government.

However useful jealousy may be in republics, when it abounds too much in the body politic, like bile in the natural body, the eyes of both become very liable to be deceived by the false appearances that this malady casts on surrounding objects. This is probably the source of the fears and suspicions of some, that the President and Senate may make treaties without an equal eye to the interests of all the States. Others suspect that two thirds will oppress the remaining third. They ask whether these gentlemen are made sufficiently responsible for their conduct; whether, if they act corruptly, they can be punished; and, if they make disadvantageous treaties, how we are to get rid of those treaties.

All the States are equally represented in the Senate, and by men who are the most able and the most willing to promote the interests of their constituents. They will therefore all have an equal degree of influence in that body, especially while they continue to take care in appointing proper persons and to insist on their punctual attendance. In proportion as the United States take on a national form and a national character, the good of the whole will be more and more an object of attention. A government would have to be weak indeed to forget that the good of the whole can be promoted only by advancing the good of each of the parts or members that make up the whole. It will not be in the power of the President and Senate to make any treaties by which they and their families and estates will not be bound and affected equally with the rest of the community. And since they have no private interests distinct from that of the nation, they will be under no temptation to neglect the latter.

As for corruption, we cannot even suppose it. Anyone who thinks it likely that the President and two thirds of the Senate will ever be capable of such unworthy conduct must have been very unlucky in his dealings with the world, or have a heart all too ready to believe the worst. The idea is too gross and too odious to be entertained. But in such a case, if it should ever happen, the treaty so obtained from us would, like all other fraudulent contracts, be null and void by the law of nations.

As for their responsibility, it is hard to see how it could be increased. Every consideration that can influence the human mind affords security for their fidelity: honor, oaths, reputation, conscience, love of country, and family affections and attachments. In short, the Constitution has taken the utmost care that they shall be men of talents and integrity. So we have reason to be persuaded that the treaties they make will be as advantageous as, all circumstances considered, could be made. And as far as the fear of punishment and disgrace can operate, that motive to good behavior is amply provided by the article on impeachments.

chapters.title: No. 65 — The Powers of the Senate Continued (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The remaining powers that the Convention's plan gives the Senate in a distinct capacity are two: its share with the executive in appointments to office, and its judicial character as a court for trying impeachments. In the business of appointments the executive will be the principal agent, so the provisions on that subject are best discussed when we examine that department. We will therefore conclude this head with a look at the judicial character of the Senate.

A well-constituted court for trying impeachments is as hard to obtain as it is to be desired, in a government that is wholly elective. The matters within its jurisdiction are those offenses that come from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust. They are of a kind that may with particular propriety be called POLITICAL, since they relate chiefly to injuries done directly to society itself. For this reason their prosecution will seldom fail to stir the passions of the whole community and to divide it into parties more or less friendly or hostile to the accused. In many cases it will attach itself to existing factions and will enlist all their animosities, biases, influence and interest on one side or the other. In such cases there will always be the greatest danger that the decision will be governed more by the relative strength of the parties than by the real proofs of innocence or guilt.

The delicacy and magnitude of a trust that so deeply concerns the political reputation and existence of every man engaged in the administration of public affairs speak for themselves. The difficulty of placing it rightly, in a government resting entirely on periodic elections, will be as readily seen when we consider this: the most conspicuous figures in such a government will, for that very reason, too often be the leaders or the tools of the most cunning or the most numerous faction. For this reason they can hardly be expected to have the neutrality required toward those whose conduct may be under scrutiny.

The Convention, it appears, judged the Senate the fittest keeper of this important trust. Those who can best see the inherent difficulty of the matter will be the slowest to condemn that opinion, and the most inclined to give due weight to the arguments that may be supposed to have produced it.

What, it may be asked, is the true spirit of the institution itself? Is it not designed as a method of NATIONAL INQUEST into the conduct of public men? If that is its design, who can be so proper to act as inquisitors for the nation as the representatives of the nation themselves? It is not disputed that the power to begin the inquiry, or in other words to bring the impeachment, ought to be placed in the hands of one branch of the legislative body. Will not the reasons that show the propriety of this arrangement argue strongly for admitting the other branch of that body to a share in the inquiry? The model from which the idea of this institution was borrowed pointed out that course to the Convention. In Great Britain it is the province of the House of Commons to bring the impeachment and of the House of Lords to decide it. Several of the State constitutions have followed the example. Both the latter and the former seem to have regarded impeachment as a bridle in the hands of the legislative body upon the executive servants of the government. Is not this the true light in which it ought to be regarded?

Where else but in the Senate could a court have been found that is sufficiently dignified or sufficiently independent? What other body would be likely to feel CONFIDENCE ENOUGH IN ITS OWN SITUATION to keep, unawed and uninfluenced, the necessary impartiality between an INDIVIDUAL accused and the REPRESENTATIVES OF THE PEOPLE, HIS ACCUSERS?

Could the Supreme Court have been relied on to meet this description? It is much to be doubted whether the members of that court would at all times have so eminent a portion of fortitude as so difficult a task would demand. It is still more doubtful whether they would have the degree of credit and authority that might on certain occasions be indispensable for reconciling the people to a decision that happened to clash with an accusation brought by their immediate representatives. A deficiency in the first would be fatal to the accused; in the second, dangerous to public tranquillity. The risk in both respects could be avoided, if at all, only by making that court more numerous than would be consistent with reasonable attention to economy. The nature of the proceeding equally requires a numerous court for trying impeachments. This proceeding can never be tied down by such strict rules, either in how the prosecutors define the offense or in how the judges construe it, as in ordinary cases serve to limit the discretion of courts in favor of personal security. There will be no jury to stand between the judges who are to pronounce the sentence of the law and the party who is to receive or suffer it. The awesome discretion that a court of impeachments must necessarily have, to doom to honor or to infamy the most trusted and most distinguished characters in the community, forbids committing the trust to a small number of persons.

These considerations alone seem enough to justify the conclusion that the Supreme Court would have been an improper substitute for the Senate as a court of impeachments. There is a further consideration that will do much to strengthen this conclusion. It is this: the punishment that may follow conviction on impeachment is not to end the offender's chastisement. After being sentenced to a perpetual banishment from the esteem and confidence, and the honors and pay, of his country, he will still be liable to prosecution and punishment in the ordinary course of law. Would it be proper that the persons who had disposed of his reputation and his most valuable rights as a citizen in one trial should, in another trial for the same offense, also dispose of his life and his fortune? Would there not be the greatest reason to fear that error in the first sentence would be the parent of error in the second? That the strong bias of one decision would be apt to overrule the influence of any new lights that might be brought to change the complexion of another decision? Those who know anything of human nature will not hesitate to answer these questions in the affirmative. They will have no trouble seeing that by making the same persons judges in both cases, those who happened to be the objects of prosecution would be largely deprived of the double security a double trial was meant to give them. The loss of life and estate would often be virtually included in a sentence that, in its terms, meant nothing more than dismissal from a present office and disqualification for a future one. It may be said that bringing in a jury in the second case would remove the danger. But juries are often influenced by the opinions of judges. They are sometimes induced to return special verdicts, which refer the main question to the decision of the court. Who would be willing to stake his life and his estate on the verdict of a jury acting under the auspices of judges who had already decided he was guilty?

Would it have improved the plan to unite the Supreme Court with the Senate in forming the court of impeachments? This union would certainly have had several advantages. But would they not have been outweighed by the serious disadvantage already stated, which arises from the same judges' taking part in the double prosecution to which the offender would be liable? To a certain extent the benefits of that union will be obtained by making the chief justice of the Supreme Court the president of the court of impeachments, as the Convention's plan proposes. At the same time the problems of fully merging the former into the latter will be substantially avoided. This was perhaps the prudent middle course. I refrain from remarking on the additional pretext for clamor against the judiciary that so considerable an increase of its authority would have given.

Would it have been desirable to compose the court for the trial of impeachments of persons wholly distinct from the other departments of the government? There are weighty arguments both against and in favor of such a plan. To some minds it will not seem a trivial objection that it would tend to increase the complexity of the political machine and to add a new spring to the government, the usefulness of which would at best be questionable. But there is an objection that no one will think unworthy of attention: a court formed on such a plan would either entail heavy expense or might in practice be subject to a variety of mishaps and problems. It must consist either of permanent officers, stationed at the seat of government and therefore entitled to fixed and regular salaries, or of certain officers of the State governments, to be called on whenever an impeachment was actually pending. It will not be easy to imagine any third method, materially different, that could reasonably be proposed. As the court ought to be numerous, for reasons already given, the first scheme will be condemned by every man who can compare the extent of the public needs with the means of meeting them. The second will be adopted only with caution by those who seriously consider several things: the difficulty of gathering men scattered over the whole Union; the injury to the innocent from the long delay in deciding the charges that might be brought against them; the advantage to the guilty from the opportunities that delay would give for intrigue and corruption; and in some cases the damage to the State from the prolonged inaction of men whose firm and faithful performance of their duty might have exposed them to the persecution of an intemperate or scheming majority in the House of Representatives. This last supposition may seem harsh, and might not often be borne out, yet it should not be forgotten that the demon of faction will at certain seasons extend his scepter over all numerous bodies of men.

But suppose one or the other of the substitutes we have examined, or some other that might be devised, were thought preferable in this respect to the plan reported by the Convention. It would not follow that the Constitution ought for that reason to be rejected. If mankind were to resolve to agree on no institution of government until every part of it had been adjusted to the most exact standard of perfection, society would soon become a general scene of anarchy and the world a desert. Where is the standard of perfection to be found? Who will undertake to bring the clashing opinions of a whole community to the same judgment of it, and to persuade one conceited projector to give up his INFALLIBLE criterion for the FALLIBLE criterion of his more CONCEITED NEIGHBOR? To serve the purpose of the adversaries of the Constitution, they ought to prove, not merely that particular provisions in it are not the best that could have been imagined, but that the plan on the whole is bad and destructive.

chapters.title: No. 66 — Objections to the Power of the Senate To Set as a Court for Impeachments Further Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: A review of the principal objections that have been raised against the proposed court for the trial of impeachments will quite possibly uproot whatever remnants of unfavorable impressions may still linger on this subject.

The FIRST of these objections is that the provision in question mixes legislative and judicial authority in the same body, in violation of the important and well-established maxim that requires a separation between the different departments of power. The true meaning of this maxim has been discussed and settled elsewhere, and was shown to be entirely compatible with a partial intermixture of those departments for special purposes, so long as they are kept, in the main, distinct and unconnected. This partial intermixture is even, in some cases, not only proper but necessary for the mutual defense of the separate members of the government against each other. The ablest masters of political science admit that an absolute or qualified veto by the executive on the acts of the legislative body is an indispensable barrier against the legislature's encroachments on the executive. It may perhaps be argued with no less reason that the powers relating to impeachments are, as I suggested before, an essential check in the legislature's hands against the encroachments of the executive. These powers are divided between the two branches of the legislature, one given the right of accusing and the other the right of judging. This division avoids the problem of making the same persons both accusers and judges, and it guards against the danger of persecution from a factional spirit prevailing in either branch. Since two thirds of the Senate will be required for a conviction, the security this adds for innocence will be as complete as innocence itself could desire.

It is curious to see how vehemently this part of the plan is attacked, on the principle just noted, by men who profess to admire without exception the constitution of this State. That constitution makes the Senate, together with the chancellor and the judges of the Supreme Court, not only a court of impeachments but the highest court in the State in all cases, civil and criminal. The chancellor and judges are so few in number compared with the senators that the final judicial authority of New York may truly be said to reside in its Senate. If the Convention's plan is chargeable in this respect with a departure from the celebrated maxim that has been so often mentioned and seems to be so little understood, how much more blameworthy must the constitution of New York be?(1)

A SECOND objection to the Senate as a court of impeachments is that it contributes to an undue accumulation of power in that body, tending to give the government too aristocratic an appearance. The Senate, it is observed, is to have concurrent authority with the Executive in making treaties and in appointing to offices. If, say the objectors, the power of deciding all cases of impeachment is added to these prerogatives, it will give senatorial influence a decided predominance. To an objection so imprecise in itself, it is not easy to give a very precise answer. Where is the measure or standard to which we can appeal in deciding what will give the Senate too much influence, too little, or barely the proper amount? Would it not be both safer and simpler to dismiss such vague and uncertain calculations, to examine each power by itself, and to decide on general principles where it may be placed with the most advantage and the least drawback?

If we take this course, it will lead to a more intelligible, if not a more certain, result. The arrangement of the power of making treaties adopted in the Convention's plan will then, if I am not mistaken, appear fully justified by the considerations stated in a former number and by others that will come up under the next head of our inquiries. The expediency of joining the Senate with the Executive in the power of appointing to offices will, I trust, be shown in an equally satisfactory light in the discussions under that same head. And I flatter myself that the observations in my last paper must have gone a considerable way toward proving that it was not easy, if possible, to find a more fitting place for the power of deciding impeachments than the one that has been chosen. If this is truly the case, the hypothetical dread of too great a weight in the Senate ought to be dropped from our reasoning.

But this hypothesis, such as it is, has already been refuted in the remarks on the length of office prescribed for senators. There it was shown, both from historical examples and from the reason of the thing, that the most POPULAR branch of every government that has a republican character, because it is generally the favorite of the people, will be as generally a full match, if not an overmatch, for every other part of the government.

But apart from this most active and effective principle for securing the balance of the national House of Representatives, the Convention's plan has provided in its favor several important counterweights to the additional powers to be conferred on the Senate. The exclusive privilege of originating money bills will belong to the House of Representatives. The same house will have the sole right of bringing impeachments. Is this not a complete counterbalance to the Senate's right to decide them? The same house will be the umpire in all elections of the President that do not unite the votes of a majority of the whole number of electors, a case that, it cannot be doubted, will sometimes, if not often, occur. The constant possibility of this must be a rich source of influence for that body. The more it is considered, the more important this ultimate though contingent power will appear: that of deciding the competition among the most illustrious citizens of the Union for the first office in it. It would perhaps not be rash to predict that as a means of influence it will prove to outweigh all the peculiar powers of the Senate.

A THIRD objection to the Senate as a court of impeachments is drawn from the part it will have in appointments to office. It is imagined that the senators would be too lenient as judges of the conduct of men in whose official creation they had taken part. The principle of this objection would condemn a practice found in all the State governments, if not in all the governments we know of: that of making those who hold office during pleasure depend on the pleasure of those who appoint them. With equal plausibility it might be alleged in this case that the favoritism of the appointers would always be a refuge for the misbehavior of the appointed. But that practice, in contradiction to this principle, rests on a presumption. Those who appoint are responsible for the fitness and competence of the persons they choose, and they have an interest in a respectable and prosperous administration of affairs. The presumption is that these motives will give them enough disposition to remove from a share in the administration all those who by their conduct have proved themselves unworthy of the confidence placed in them. Facts may not always match this presumption. But if it is in the main just, it must destroy the supposition that the Senate, which will merely approve the choice of the Executive, would feel a bias toward the objects of that choice strong enough to blind its members to evidence of guilt so extraordinary as to have led the representatives of the nation to become the accusers.

If any further arguments were needed to show how unlikely such a bias is, they might be found in the nature of the Senate's part in appointments.
