It will be the office of the President to NOMINATE and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to APPOINT. There will, of course, be no exercise of CHOICE on the part of the Senate. The senators may defeat one choice of the Executive and oblige him to make another, but they cannot themselves CHOOSE; they can only approve or reject the President's choice. They might even prefer some other person at the very moment they were assenting to the one proposed, because there might be no positive ground for opposing him. And if they withheld their assent, they could not be sure that the next nomination would fall on their own favorite, or on any other person they judged more deserving than the one rejected. Thus it could hardly happen that a majority of the Senate would feel any warmth toward the object of an appointment beyond what the appearance of merit might inspire and proofs of its absence would destroy.

A FOURTH objection to the Senate in the capacity of a court of impeachments is derived from its union with the Executive in the power of making treaties. This, it has been said, would make the senators their own judges in every case of a corrupt or treacherous exercise of that trust. After joining with the Executive in betraying the interests of the nation in a ruinous treaty, what prospect would there be, it is asked, of making them suffer the punishment they would deserve, when they were themselves to decide on the accusation brought against them for the treachery they had committed?

This objection has been spread with more zeal, and with a better appearance of reason, than any other raised against this part of the plan. And yet unless I am deceived, it rests on a mistaken foundation.

The security the Constitution essentially intends against corruption and treachery in making treaties is to be sought in the numbers and characters of those who are to make them. The JOINT AGENCY of the chief executive of the Union and of two thirds of the members of a body selected by the collective wisdom of the legislatures of the individual States is designed to be the pledge for the fidelity of the national councils in this matter. The Convention might properly have intended the punishment of the Executive for departing from the instructions of the Senate, or for lack of integrity in conducting the negotiations entrusted to him. It might also have had in view the punishment of a few leading individuals in the Senate who had prostituted their influence in that body as the mercenary instruments of foreign corruption. But it could not, with more or even equal propriety, have contemplated the impeachment and punishment of two thirds of the Senate for consenting to an improper treaty, any more than of a majority of that branch or of the other branch of the national legislature for consenting to a harmful or unconstitutional law. That is a principle which, I believe, has never been admitted into any government. How, in fact, could a majority in the House of Representatives impeach themselves? Not better, it is evident, than two thirds of the Senate could try themselves. And yet what reason is there that a majority of the House of Representatives, sacrificing the interests of society by an unjust and tyrannical act of legislation, should escape with impunity any more than two thirds of the Senate, sacrificing the same interests in an injurious treaty with a foreign power? The truth is that in all such cases it is essential to the freedom and the necessary independence of the body's deliberations that its members be exempt from punishment for acts done in a collective capacity. The security of society must depend on the care taken to place the trust in proper hands, to make it their interest to execute it faithfully, and to make it as difficult as possible for them to combine in any interest opposed to the public good.

As far as the misbehavior of the Executive is concerned, in perverting the instructions or going against the views of the Senate, we need not fear that the Senate will lack the disposition to punish the abuse of its confidence or to vindicate its own authority. We may count this far on its pride, if not on its virtue. And as far as the corruption of leading members is concerned, by whose arts and influence the majority may have been tricked into measures odious to the community, the usual tendency of human nature warrants the conclusion that, if the proofs of that corruption were satisfactory, the body would commonly show no lack of inclination to turn public resentment away from itself by readily sacrificing the authors of its mismanagement and disgrace.

1. In that of New Jersey, also, the final judicial authority is in a branch of the legislature. In New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and South Carolina, one branch of the legislature is the court for the trial of impeachments.

chapters.title: No. 67 — The Executive Department (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The next subject that demands our attention is how the executive department of the proposed government is constituted.
Hardly any part of the system could have been harder to arrange than this one. And hardly any part has been attacked with so little fairness or criticized with so little judgment.

Here the writers against the Constitution seem to have made a point of displaying their talent for misrepresentation. Counting on the people's dislike of monarchy, they have tried to recruit all of the public's jealousies and fears against the intended President of the United States. They present him not merely as the embryo of that detested parent but as its full-grown offspring. To prove the supposed family resemblance, they have not hesitated to borrow even from the world of fiction. The powers of a chief executive, in a few respects greater and in others less than those of the governor of New York, have been blown up into more than royal prerogatives. He has been dressed in attributes that surpass in dignity and splendor those of a king of Great Britain. We have been shown him with the diadem sparkling on his brow and the imperial purple trailing behind him. We have seen him on a throne, surrounded by favorites and mistresses, receiving the envoys of foreign rulers with all the haughty pomp of majesty. The images of Asiatic despotism and sensual indulgence have scarcely been left out to crown this exaggerated scene. We have been taught to tremble at the terrifying faces of murderous janizaries and to blush at the unveiled mysteries of a future seraglio.

Attempts this extravagant to disfigure the object, or rather, one might say, to turn it into something else, make it necessary to look carefully at its real nature and form. We need to establish its true appearance, and we need as well to unmask the dishonesty and expose the falsity of the counterfeit likenesses that have been spread so cunningly and so busily.

In doing this, no one could easily look with moderation, or treat seriously, the devices, no less weak than wicked, that have been contrived to twist public opinion on the subject. They go so far beyond the usual license of party trickery, unjustifiable as that is, that even the most fair-minded and tolerant person must set aside the views that incline him to a generous reading of his political adversaries' conduct, and give way to open and unreserved indignation. It is impossible not to charge deliberate imposture and deceit against the gross pretense that a king of Great Britain resembles an executive of the character marked out for the President of the United States. It is still more impossible to withhold that charge from the rash and barefaced expedients used to make the imposition succeed.

I cite one instance as a sample of the general spirit. Here the recklessness has gone so far as to give the President of the United States a power that the proposed instrument EXPRESSLY assigns to the Executives of the individual States. I mean the power of filling casual vacancies in the Senate.

This bold experiment on the discernment of his countrymen was tried by a writer who (whatever his real merit may be) has had no small share of his party's applause,(1) and who has built a whole series of observations on this false and groundless claim, themselves equally false and groundless. Let him now be confronted with the evidence, and let him, if he can, justify or excuse the shameful outrage he has committed against the dictates of truth and the rules of fair dealing.

The second clause of the second section of the second article empowers the President of the United States "to nominate, and by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other OFFICERS of United States whose appointments are NOT in the Constitution OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR, and WHICH SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." Right after this clause comes another in these words: "The President shall have power to fill up all VACANCIES that may happen DURING THE RECESS OF THE SENATE, by granting commissions which shall EXPIRE AT THE END OF THEIR NEXT SESSION." It is from this last provision that the alleged power of the President to fill vacancies in the Senate has been drawn. Only a little attention to how the clauses connect, and to the plain meaning of their terms, is needed to see that the deduction does not even look valid.

The first of these two clauses, it is plain, merely supplies a way of appointing officers "whose appointments are NOT OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution, and which SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." It cannot, of course, reach the appointment of senators. Their appointments are OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution,(2) they are ESTABLISHED BY THE CONSTITUTION, and they will not need to be established later by law. Hardly anyone will dispute this.

The last of these two clauses, it is equally plain, cannot be read to cover the filling of vacancies in the Senate, for the following reasons. First. The way that clause stands in relation to the other, which gives the general method of appointing officers of the United States, shows that it is only a supplement, establishing an auxiliary method of appointment for cases the general method could not handle. The ordinary power of appointment belongs to the President and Senate JOINTLY, and so can be used only while the Senate is in session. But it would have been improper to require this body to sit continuously just to make appointments, and vacancies might arise IN THEIR RECESS that the public service could require to be filled without delay. The next clause is evidently meant to authorize the President, SINGLY, to make temporary appointments "during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session." Second. If this clause is a supplement to the one before it, then the VACANCIES it mentions must be understood to concern the "officers" described in that preceding clause; and we have seen that its description leaves out the members of the Senate. Third. The period in which the power is to operate, "during the recess of the Senate," and the length of the appointments, "to the end of the next session" of that body, both point toward the meaning of the provision. Had senators been intended, the clause would naturally have tied the temporary power to the recess of the State legislatures, which make the permanent appointments, and not to the recess of the national Senate, which has no part in those appointments. It would also have let the temporary senators serve until the next session of the legislature of the State whose representation had the vacancy, instead of having them expire at the end of the next session of the national Senate. The situation of the body that makes the permanent appointments would naturally have shaped any power over temporary ones. But the national Senate is the only body whose situation the clause takes into account, and so the vacancies it refers to can only be those among officers in whose appointment that body shares authority with the President. Finally, the first and second clauses of the third section of the first article not only remove every possibility of doubt but destroy any pretext of misunderstanding. The first provides that "the Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen BY THE LEGISLATURE THEREOF for six years"; and the second directs that "if vacancies in that body should happen by resignation or otherwise, DURING THE RECESS OF THE LEGISLATURE OF ANY STATE, the Executive THEREOF may make temporary appointments until the NEXT MEETING OF THE LEGISLATURE, which shall then fill such vacancies." Here, in clear and unambiguous terms, is an express power given to the State Executives to fill casual vacancies in the Senate by temporary appointments. This does more than disprove the notion that the clause considered before could have been meant to give that power to the President of the United States. It shows that the notion, which lacks even the merit of being plausible, must have come from an intention to deceive the people that is too obvious to be hidden by sophistry and too outrageous to be excused by hypocrisy.

I have taken pains to choose this instance of misrepresentation and to set it in a clear and strong light, as unmistakable proof of the unwarrantable arts being practiced to prevent a fair and impartial judgment of the real merits of the Constitution now submitted to the people. In so flagrant a case, I have not hesitated to allow myself a severity of criticism that sits poorly with the general spirit of these papers. I am ready to submit to any fair and honest opponent of the proposed government the question whether language can supply any epithets too harsh for so shameless and so mercenary an attempt to impose on the citizens of America.
1. See CATO, No. V.
2. Article I, section 3, clause 1.

chapters.title: No. 68 — The Mode of Electing the President (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The way the chief executive of the United States is to be chosen is almost the only important part of the system that has escaped harsh criticism, or has earned any word of approval from its opponents. The most plausible of them to appear in print has even condescended to admit that the election of the President is fairly well guarded.(1) I venture to go further, and I do not hesitate to say that if the method is not perfect, it is at least excellent. It combines, to an eminent degree, all the advantages that one could have wished to see combined.(E1)

It was desirable that the sense of the people should have a part in choosing the person to whom so important a trust would be given. This is achieved by giving the right of choice not to any body that already exists, but to men whom the people select for that special purpose and at that particular moment.

It was equally desirable that the immediate choice should be made by men best able to weigh the qualities suited to the office, and acting in circumstances that favor deliberation and a sound weighing of all the reasons and inducements that should govern their decision. A small number of persons, picked by their fellow citizens from the general mass, are the most likely to have the information and discernment that such complicated investigations require.

It was also especially desirable to give tumult and disorder as little opportunity as possible. This evil was not the least to be feared in choosing an official who would have so important a part in running the government as the President of the United States. But the precautions so happily devised in the system before us promise effective security against this harm. The choice of SEVERAL persons, forming an intermediate body of electors, is much less likely to throw the community into extraordinary or violent upheaval than the choice of ONE, who would himself be the final object of the public's wishes. And because the electors chosen in each State are to meet and vote in that State, their scattered and divided situation will expose them much less to the heats and ferments that could pass from them to the people than if they all had to be gathered at one time in one place.

Nothing was more to be desired than that every practicable obstacle be set against cabal, intrigue and corruption. These deadliest enemies of republican government might naturally be expected to approach from more than one direction, but chiefly from the desire of foreign powers to gain an improper influence in our councils. How could they better satisfy that desire than by raising one of their own creatures to the chief executive office of the Union? But the Convention has guarded against every danger of this kind with the most farsighted and judicious care. It has not made the appointment of the President depend on any bodies of men already in existence, who might be tampered with in advance and induced to sell their votes. It has instead referred the appointment in the first instance to a direct act of the people of America, to be used in choosing persons whose temporary and sole purpose is to make the appointment. And it has excluded from eligibility all those who, by their position, might be suspected of too much devotion to the President in office. No senator, representative or other person holding a place of trust or profit under the United States can be among the electors. In this way, without corrupting the body of the people, the immediate agents in the election will at least begin their task free of any sinister bias. Their short existence and their scattered situation, already noted, give good reason to expect that they will stay free of it to the end. Corruption on so large a scale, reaching so many men, takes time as well as money. Nor would it be easy to enlist them quickly, spread out as they would be over thirteen States, in any combination founded on motives that, though not properly called corrupt, might still mislead them from their duty.

Another desideratum, no less important, was that the Executive should depend for his continuance in office on no one but the people themselves. Otherwise he might be tempted to give up his duty out of eagerness to please those whose favor he needed to keep his official standing. This advantage too is secured, by making his re-election depend on a special body of representatives, appointed by the society for the single purpose of making this important choice.

All these advantages will happily come together in the plan devised by the Convention. The people of each State are to choose a number of electors equal to the number of senators and representatives that State has in the national government. These electors are to meet within the State and vote for some fit person as President. Their votes are then to be sent to the seat of the national government, and the person who happens to have a majority of the whole number of votes will be the President. But a majority might not always center on one man, and it might be unsafe to let anything less than a majority decide the matter. So it is provided that in such a case the House of Representatives shall choose, from the candidates with the five highest numbers of votes, the man who in their opinion is best qualified for the office.

The process of election gives a moral certainty that the office of President will never fall to anyone who does not possess, in an eminent degree, the necessary qualifications. Talents for low intrigue and the petty arts of popularity may be enough to lift a man to the first honors in a single State. It will take other talents, and a different kind of merit, to establish him in the esteem and confidence of the whole Union, or of so large a part of it as a successful candidate for the distinguished office of President of the United States would need. It will not be too strong to say that there will be a constant likelihood of seeing the office filled by characters of outstanding ability and virtue. Those who can appreciate how much the executive in any government shapes its good or bad administration will count this no small recommendation of the Constitution. We cannot accept the political heresy of the poet who says:

"For forms of government let fools contest—That which is best administered is best." Yet we may safely declare that the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration.

The Vice-President is to be chosen in the same way as the President, with this difference: the Senate is to do, in the case of the Vice-President, what the House of Representatives is to do in the case of the President.

Some have objected that appointing a separate person as Vice-President is superfluous, if not harmful. They allege that it would have been better to authorize the Senate to elect an officer of that description from among its own members. But two considerations seem to justify the Convention's view. The first is that, to make certain the body can always reach a definite decision, its presiding officer must have only a casting vote. To take a State's senator out of his seat as senator and make him President of the Senate would be to trade, for the State he came from, a constant vote for a contingent one. The second is that the Vice-President may occasionally take the President's place in the supreme executive office, and so all the reasons that recommend the manner of election prescribed for the one apply with great, if not equal, force to the manner of appointing the other. It is remarkable that here, as in most other instances, the objection raised would lie equally against the constitution of this State. We have a Lieutenant-Governor, chosen by the people at large, who presides in the Senate and is the constitutional substitute for the Governor in emergencies like those that would authorize the Vice-President to exercise the authorities and discharge the duties of the President.

chapters.title: No. 69 — The Real Character of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: I now proceed to trace the real character of the proposed Executive as the Convention's plan marks it out. This will show in a strong light how unfair the representations made about it have been.

The first thing that strikes us is that the executive authority, with few exceptions, is to be placed in a single chief executive. Yet this can hardly be treated as a basis for comparison. If in this respect there is a resemblance to the king of Great Britain, there is just as much resemblance to the Grand Seignior, to the khan of Tartary, to the Man of the Seven Mountains, or to the governor of New York.

This chief executive is to be elected for four years, and he may be re-elected as often as the people of the United States think him worthy of their confidence. In these respects he is wholly unlike a king of Great Britain, who is a hereditary monarch and holds the crown as a family property that passes to his heirs forever. But he is closely like a governor of New York, who is elected for three years and may be re-elected without limit or interruption. Consider how much less time it would take to build up a dangerous influence in a single State than to build up the same influence across the United States. We must conclude that a four-year term for the chief executive of the Union is a degree of permanence far less to be feared in that office than a three-year term for the corresponding office in a single State.

The President of the United States could be impeached and tried. If convicted of treason, bribery or other high crimes or misdemeanors, he would be removed from office, and afterward he could still be prosecuted and punished in the ordinary course of law. The person of the king of Great Britain is sacred and inviolable. There is no constitutional court to which he answers, and no punishment can be inflicted on him without bringing on the crisis of a national revolution. On this delicate and important matter of personal responsibility, the President of Confederated America would stand on no better ground than a governor of New York, and on worse ground than the governors of Maryland and Delaware.

The President is to have the power to send back for reconsideration a bill that has passed both branches of the legislature, and the bill so returned becomes law if, on reconsideration, two thirds of both houses approve it. The king of Great Britain, for his part, holds an absolute negative on the acts of the two houses of Parliament. That this power has not been used for a considerable time does not change the fact that it exists. The reason is wholly that the crown has found a way to substitute influence for authority, that is, the art of winning a majority in one or the other house, in place of exercising a prerogative that could seldom be used without risking some degree of national disturbance. The President's qualified negative differs widely from the British sovereign's absolute one, and matches exactly the power of revision held by the council of revision of this State, of which the governor is one member. In this respect the President's power would exceed that of the governor of New York, because the President would hold alone what the governor shares with the chancellor and judges. But it would be precisely the same as that of the governor of Massachusetts, whose constitution, on this point, seems to have been the model the Convention copied.

The President is to be the "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States. He is to have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment; to recommend to the consideration of Congress such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient; to convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses of the legislature, or either of them, and, in case of disagreement between them with respect to the time of adjournment, to adjourn them to such time as he shall think proper; to take care that the laws be faithfully executed; and to commission all officers of the United States." In most of these respects the President's power will resemble equally that of the king of Great Britain and that of the governor of New York. The most important points of difference are these. First. The President will have only occasional command of that part of the nation's militia which legislative provision may call into the actual service of the Union. The king of Great Britain and the governor of New York have at all times full command of all the militia within their separate jurisdictions. On this point, therefore, the President's power would be inferior to that of either the monarch or the governor. Second. The President is to be commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States. In this respect his authority would be the same as the British king's in name, but much less in substance. It would amount to no more than the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy. The British king's authority extends to declaring war and to raising and regulating fleets and armies, all of which, under the Constitution now before us, would belong to the legislature.(1) The governor of New York, on the other hand, is given by the State constitution only the command of its militia and navy. But the constitutions of several of the States expressly declare their governors commanders-in-chief of the army as well as the navy, and it may well be a question whether those of New Hampshire and Massachusetts in particular do not give their governors larger powers on this point than a President of the United States could claim. Third. The President's power over pardons would extend to all cases except impeachment. The governor of New York may pardon in all cases, even impeachment, except treason and murder. Is not the governor's power on this point, reckoned by its political consequences, greater than the President's? All conspiracies and plots against the government that have not ripened into actual treason may be shielded from any punishment by the interposition of the pardoning prerogative. If a governor of New York, then, were at the head of such a conspiracy, he could guarantee his accomplices and followers complete impunity until the design had ripened into actual hostility. A President of the Union, on the other hand, though he may even pardon treason when it is prosecuted in the ordinary course of law, could not shelter any offender, in any degree, from the effects of impeachment and conviction. Would not the prospect of total immunity for all the preliminary steps be a greater temptation to start and persist in an enterprise against public liberty than the mere prospect of escaping death and confiscation if the final execution of the design should fail in an actual appeal to arms? Would this last expectation have any influence at all, once one calculated the probability that the person who was to grant the exemption might himself be caught up in the consequences of the scheme, and might be made unable, by his own part in it, to give the impunity desired? To judge this matter better, we must recall that under the proposed Constitution the offense of treason is limited "to levying war upon the United States, and adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort," and that under the laws of New York it is confined within similar bounds. Fourth. The President can adjourn the national legislature only in the single case of disagreement about the time of adjournment. The British monarch may prorogue Parliament or even dissolve it. The governor of New York may also prorogue the legislature of this State for a limited time, a power that in certain situations may be used for very important purposes.

The President is to have the power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur. The king of Great Britain is the sole and absolute representative of the nation in all foreign dealings. He can make treaties of peace, commerce, alliance and every other kind entirely on his own. It has been hinted that his authority here is not final, and that his agreements with foreign powers are subject to the review of Parliament and need its ratification. But I believe this doctrine was never heard of until it was brought up on the present occasion. Every jurist(2) of that kingdom, and every other man acquainted with its Constitution, knows as an established fact that the prerogative of making treaties exists in the crown in its fullest extent, and that compacts made by royal authority have complete legal validity and perfection, independent of any other sanction. Parliament, it is true, is sometimes seen altering existing laws to bring them into line with the terms of a new treaty, and this may have given rise to the idea that its cooperation was necessary to make the treaty binding. But this parliamentary intervention has a different cause. It comes from the need to fit a highly artificial and intricate system of revenue and commercial laws to the changes the treaty makes in them, and to adapt new provisions and precautions to the new state of things, so as to keep the machine from running into disorder. In this respect, then, there is no comparison between the intended power of the President and the actual power of the British sovereign. The one can do alone what the other can do only with the concurrence of a branch of the legislature. It must be admitted that in this instance the power of the federal Executive would exceed that of any State Executive. But this follows naturally from the sovereign power that relates to treaties. If the Confederacy were dissolved, it would become a question whether the Executives of the individual States would not alone be invested with that delicate and important prerogative.

The President is also to be authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers. This has been a rich theme of declamation, but it is more a matter of dignity than of authority. It will have no consequence in the administration of the government, and it was far more convenient to arrange things this way than to make it necessary to convene the legislature, or one of its branches, at every arrival of a foreign minister, even if only to fill the place of a predecessor who had left.

The President is to nominate and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and in general all officers of the United States who are established by law and whose appointments the Constitution does not otherwise provide for. The king of Great Britain is emphatically and truly called the fountain of honor. He not only appoints to all offices but can create offices. He can confer titles of nobility at will, and he has the disposal of an immense number of church positions. The President's power in this respect is plainly far inferior to the British king's. Nor is it equal to that of the governor of New York, if we judge the meaning of the State's constitution by the practice that has grown up under it. The power of appointment among us is lodged in a council made up of the governor and four members of the Senate, chosen by the Assembly. The governor claims, and has often exercised, the right of nomination, and he is entitled to a casting vote in the appointment. If he really has the right of nominating, his authority here equals the President's and exceeds it in the matter of the casting vote. In the national government, if the Senate should be divided, no appointment could be made. In the government of New York, if the council should be divided, the governor can turn the scale and confirm his own nomination.(3) Compare the publicity that must necessarily attend the President's appointments, made with an entire branch of the national legislature, to the privacy of the governor of New York's, who sits closeted in a secret room with at most four people, and often with only two. At the same time, consider how much easier it must be to influence the small number that a council of appointment consists of than the considerable number that the national Senate would consist of. We cannot hesitate to conclude that the power of this State's chief executive in handing out offices must, in practice, be greatly superior to that of the chief executive of the Union.

It appears from all this that, apart from the President's shared authority in the matter of treaties, it would be hard to say whether that official would, taken as a whole, hold more or less power than the Governor of New York. And it appears still more clearly that the parallel attempted between him and the king of Great Britain has no basis at all. But to make the contrast in this respect still more striking, it may be useful to bring the principal points of difference together in a closer group.

The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for four years; the king of Great Britain is a perpetual and hereditary prince. The one would be liable to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable. The one would have a qualified negative on the acts of the legislative body; the other has an absolute negative. The one would have the right to command the military and naval forces of the nation; the other has this right and in addition holds that of declaring war and of raising and regulating fleets and armies by his own authority. The one would share with a branch of the legislature the power of making treaties; the other is the sole holder of that power. The one would share in the same way in appointing to offices; the other is the sole source of all appointments. The one can grant no privileges whatever; the other can make denizens of aliens (foreigners granted residence and some of the rights of citizens) and noblemen of commoners, and can create corporations with all the rights that belong to corporate bodies. The one can set no rules about the nation's commerce or currency; the other is in several respects the arbiter of commerce, and in that capacity can establish markets and fairs, regulate weights and measures, lay embargoes for a limited time, coin money, and authorize or prohibit the circulation of foreign coin. The one has not a particle of spiritual jurisdiction; the other is the supreme head and governor of the national church! What answer shall we give to those who would persuade us that things so unlike resemble each other? The same answer that ought to be given to those who tell us that a government whose entire power would be in the hands of the elected servants of the people, who are chosen at regular intervals, is an aristocracy, a monarchy and a despotism.

1. A writer in a Pennsylvania paper, under the signature of TAMONY, has asserted that the king of Great Britain owes his prerogative as commander-in-chief to an annual mutiny bill. The truth is, on the contrary, that his prerogative in this respect is immemorial, and was disputed only, "contrary to all reason and precedent," as Blackstone vol. i., page 262, puts it, by the Long Parliament of Charles I. But by the statute of the 13th of Charles II., chap. 6, it was declared to be in the king alone, because the sole supreme government and command of the militia within his Majesty's realms and dominions, and of all forces by sea and land, and of all forts and places of strength, EVER WAS AND IS the undoubted right of his Majesty and his royal predecessors, kings and queens of England, and both or either house of Parliament cannot nor ought to pretend to the same.
2. Vide Blackstone's Commentaries, Vol I., p. 257.

3. Honesty requires me to admit, however, that I do not think the governor's claim to a right of nomination is well founded. Still, it is always fair to reason from how a government actually operates, until that practice has been challenged on constitutional grounds. And even setting this claim aside, if we weigh the other considerations and follow them out to all their consequences, we shall be inclined to reach much the same conclusion.

chapters.title: No. 70 — The Executive Department Further Considered (Hamilton)
paragraphs: There is an idea, not without its advocates, that a vigorous Executive is inconsistent with the character of republican government. The enlightened friends of this kind of government must at least hope that the supposition has no foundation, since they could never admit it to be true without also condemning their own principles. Energy in the Executive is a leading feature in the definition of good government. It is essential to protecting the community against foreign attacks. It is no less essential to the steady administration of the laws, and to protecting property against those irregular and high-handed combinations that sometimes interrupt the ordinary course of justice. It is essential as well to securing liberty against the enterprises and assaults of ambition, of faction and of anarchy. Anyone with the slightest knowledge of Roman history knows how often that republic had to take refuge in the absolute power of a single man, under the formidable title of Dictator. It did so against the intrigues of ambitious individuals who aspired to tyranny, and against the seditions of whole classes of the community whose conduct threatened the existence of all government, as well as against the invasions of foreign enemies who threatened to conquer and destroy Rome.

There is no need, however, to pile up more arguments or examples on this point. A feeble Executive means a feeble execution of the government. A feeble execution is only another way of saying a bad execution. And a government that is badly executed, whatever it may be in theory, must be a bad government in practice.

Taking it for granted, then, that all sensible men will agree on the necessity of an energetic Executive, it remains only to ask what ingredients make up this energy. How far can they be combined with the other ingredients that make up safety in the republican sense? And how far does that combination mark the plan reported by the Convention?
The ingredients that make up energy in the Executive are, first, unity; second, duration; third, an adequate provision for its support; fourth, competent powers.
The ingredients that make up safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people; second, a due responsibility.

The politicians and statesmen most celebrated for the soundness of their principles and the justice of their views have declared in favor of a single Executive and a numerous legislature. They have rightly regarded energy as the most necessary quality of the former, and have held that it is best found in power placed in a single hand. With equal justice they have regarded the latter as best suited to deliberation and wisdom, and best fitted to win the confidence of the people and secure their rights and interests.

No one will dispute that unity promotes energy. Decision, activity, secrecy and dispatch will generally mark the proceedings of one man far more strongly than those of any larger number, and as the number grows, these qualities will diminish.

This unity may be destroyed in two ways. One is by vesting the power in two or more chief executives of equal dignity and authority. The other is by vesting it ostensibly in one man who is subject, wholly or in part, to the control and cooperation of others serving as his counselors. The two Consuls of Rome may serve as an example of the first. Examples of the second we shall find in the constitutions of several of the States. New York and New Jersey, if I remember rightly, are the only States that have entrusted the executive authority wholly to single men.(1) Both these ways of destroying the unity of the Executive have their partisans, but the supporters of an executive council are the more numerous. Both are open to similar objections, if not equal ones, and may in most respects be examined together.

The experience of other nations will teach us little on this subject. Insofar as it teaches anything, however, it teaches us not to be fond of plurality in the Executive. We have seen that the Achaeans, after trying two Praetors, were led to abolish one. Roman history records many instances of harm to the republic from quarrels between the Consuls, and between the military Tribunes who were at times substituted for the Consuls. But it gives us no example of any particular advantage the state gained from having several of these officials. That their quarrels were not more frequent or more fatal is a matter of astonishment, until we notice the unusual position in which the republic was almost continually placed, and the prudent policy that circumstances pointed out and the Consuls followed, of dividing the government between them. The patricians were engaged in a perpetual struggle with the plebeians to preserve their ancient authorities and dignities. The Consuls, who were generally chosen from the former body, were commonly united by their personal interest in defending the privileges of their order. Beyond this motive for unity, after the arms of the republic had greatly widened the bounds of its empire, it became the established custom for the Consuls to divide the administration between themselves by lot. One of them stayed at Rome to govern the city and its surroundings, and the other took command in the more distant provinces. This expedient must, no doubt, have done much to prevent the collisions and rivalries that might otherwise have disturbed the peace of the republic.

But if we leave the dim light of historical research and rely purely on the dictates of reason and good sense, we shall find much greater cause to reject than to approve the idea of plurality in the Executive, in any form whatever.

Wherever two or more persons are engaged in a common undertaking or pursuit, there is always a danger of differences of opinion. If it is a public trust or office, in which they are clothed with equal dignity and authority, there is a special danger of personal rivalry and even hostility. From either of these causes, and especially from all of them together, the bitterest quarrels are likely to spring. Whenever they occur, they lower the respect given to those they divide, weaken their authority, and distract their plans and actions. If they should unfortunately strike the supreme executive office of a country that consists of several persons, they might block or defeat the most important measures of the government in the most critical emergencies of the state. And what is still worse, they might split the community into the most violent and irreconcilable factions, attached in different ways to the different individuals who made up the executive.

Men often oppose a thing merely because they had no hand in planning it, or because it was planned by people they dislike. But if they were consulted and happened to disapprove, opposition then becomes, in their eyes, an indispensable duty of self-love. They seem to think themselves bound in honor, and by every motive of personal infallibility, to defeat whatever has been resolved contrary to their views. Men of upright and benevolent temperament have too many occasions to observe, with horror, to what desperate lengths this disposition is sometimes carried, and how often the great interests of society are sacrificed to the vanity, the conceit and the obstinacy of individuals who have enough credit to make their passions and whims matter to the public. Perhaps the question now before the public may in its consequences furnish melancholy proofs of the effects of this contemptible weakness, or rather detestable vice, in human character.

On the principles of a free government, drawbacks from the source just mentioned must necessarily be accepted in forming the legislature. But it is unnecessary, and therefore unwise, to introduce them into the constitution of the Executive. It is here, too, that they may do the most harm. In the legislature, quickness of decision is oftener an evil than a benefit. The differences of opinion and the wrangling of parties in that department, though they may sometimes obstruct beneficial plans, often promote deliberation and caution and help to check excesses by the majority. Moreover, once a resolution has been taken, the opposition must end. That resolution is a law, and resistance to it is punishable. But no favorable circumstance softens or makes up for the disadvantages of dissension in the executive department. Here they are pure and unmixed. There is no point at which they cease to operate. They embarrass and weaken the carrying out of the plan or measure they relate to, from the first step to the last. They constantly work against those qualities of the Executive that are the most necessary ingredients in its composition, vigor and expedition, and this without any compensating good. In the conduct of war, in which the energy of the Executive is the bulwark of national security, everything would be to be feared from its plurality.

It must be confessed that these observations apply with the greatest weight to the first case supposed, that is, to a plurality of chief executives of equal dignity and authority, a scheme whose advocates are not likely to form a numerous sect. But they apply, though not with equal weight, still with considerable weight, to the project of a council whose concurrence is made constitutionally necessary to the operations of the ostensible Executive. A scheming cabal in that council would be able to distract and enervate the whole system of administration. If no such cabal should exist, the mere diversity of views and opinions would be enough to tinge the exercise of executive authority with a spirit of habitual feebleness and delay.

(Yet among the weightiest objections to a plurality in the Executive, an objection that holds as much against the council plan as against the first, is that it tends to hide faults and destroy responsibility. Responsibility is of two kinds, to censure and to punishment. The first is the more important of the two, especially in an elective office. A man in public trust will much more often act in a way that makes him unworthy of being trusted any longer than in a way that makes him liable to legal punishment. But multiplying the Executive makes detection harder in either case. Amid mutual accusations it often becomes impossible to decide on whom the blame or the punishment for a harmful measure, or series of harmful measures, should really fall. It is shifted from one to another with so much skill, and under such plausible appearances, that public opinion is left in suspense about the real author. The circumstances that may have led to a national failure or misfortune are sometimes so complicated that, where a number of actors may have had different degrees and kinds of involvement, we may clearly see on the whole that there has been mismanagement and yet find it impossible to say to whose account the resulting evil is truly chargeable.)(E1)

(Yet among the weightiest objections to a plurality in the Executive, an objection that holds as much against the council plan as against the first, is that it tends to hide faults and destroy responsibility.

Responsibility is of two kinds, to censure and to punishment. The first is the more important of the two, especially in an elective office. A man in public trust will much more often act in a way that makes him unworthy of being trusted any longer than in a way that makes him liable to legal punishment. But multiplying the Executive makes detection harder in either case. Amid mutual accusations it often becomes impossible to decide on whom the blame or the punishment for a harmful measure, or series of harmful measures, should really fall. It is shifted from one to another with so much skill, and under such plausible appearances, that public opinion is left in suspense about the real author. The circumstances that may have led to a national failure or misfortune are sometimes so complicated that, where a number of actors may have had different degrees and kinds of involvement, we may clearly see on the whole that there has been mismanagement and yet find it impossible to say to whose account the resulting evil is truly chargeable.)(E1)

"I was overruled by my council. The council were so divided in their opinions that it was impossible to obtain any better resolution on the point." These and similar excuses are constantly at hand, whether true or false. And who will take the trouble, or bear the ill will, of a strict inquiry into the secret springs of the transaction? Suppose a citizen is found zealous enough to undertake the unpromising task. If the parties concerned happen to be in collusion, it is easy for them to wrap the circumstances in so much ambiguity that no one can tell what any of them precisely did.

In the one case where the governor of this State is joined with a council, that is, in appointing to offices, we have seen the harms of it from the point of view now under consideration. Scandalous appointments to important offices have been made. Some cases, indeed, have been so flagrant that ALL PARTIES have agreed the thing was improper. When inquiry has been made, the governor has put the blame on the members of the council, who in turn have charged it to his nomination, while the people remain altogether at a loss to say whose influence put their interests into hands so unqualified and so obviously improper. Out of tenderness to individuals, I refrain from going into particulars.

It is evident from these considerations that a plurality in the Executive tends to deprive the people of the two greatest securities they can have for the faithful exercise of any delegated power. The first is the restraint of public opinion, which loses its effectiveness, both because the censure that attends bad measures is divided among a number of people and because it is uncertain on whom it ought to fall. The second is the opportunity to discover easily and clearly the misconduct of the persons they trust, so as either to remove them from office or, in cases that allow it, to punish them.

In England the king is a perpetual chief executive, and for the sake of public peace it has become an accepted maxim that he is not accountable for his administration and that his person is sacred. Nothing, therefore, can be wiser in that kingdom than to attach to the king a constitutional council, who may be responsible to the nation for the advice they give. Without this there would be no responsibility whatever in the executive department, an idea not to be admitted in a free government. But even there the king is not bound by the resolutions of his council, though they are answerable for the advice they give. He is the absolute master of his own conduct in the exercise of his office, and may follow or disregard the counsel given him at his sole discretion.

But in a republic, where every public official ought to be personally responsible for his conduct in office, the reason that in the British Constitution makes a council proper not only ceases to apply but turns against the institution. In the monarchy of Great Britain, the council serves as a substitute for the forbidden responsibility of the chief executive, and to some degree as a hostage to national justice for his good behavior. In the American republic, it would serve to destroy, or greatly reduce, the intended and necessary responsibility of the chief executive himself.

The idea of a council to the Executive, which has so generally been adopted in the State constitutions, was drawn from that maxim of republican jealousy which holds power to be safer in the hands of a number of men than of a single man. Even if the maxim were admitted to apply to this case, I would maintain that the advantage on that side would not outweigh the many disadvantages on the other. But I do not think the rule applies to the executive power at all. In this I clearly agree with a writer whom the celebrated Junius pronounces to be "deep, solid, and ingenious," who holds that "the executive power is more easily confined when it is ONE";(2) that it is far safer for the people's jealousy and watchfulness to have a single object; and, in a word, that every multiplication of the Executive is more dangerous than friendly to liberty.

A little consideration will satisfy us that the kind of security sought through multiplying the Executive cannot be had. The numbers must be so large as to make combination difficult, or else they are a source of danger rather than security. The united credit and influence of several individuals must be more formidable to liberty than the credit and influence of any one of them alone. When power is placed in the hands of so small a number of men that their interests and views can easily be combined in a common enterprise by a skillful leader, it becomes more liable to abuse, and more dangerous when abused, than if it were lodged in one man. Such a man, by the very fact of being alone, will be more closely watched and more readily suspected, and cannot gather so great a mass of influence as when he is associated with others. The Decemvirs of Rome, whose name denotes their number,(3) were more to be dreaded in their usurpation than any ONE of them would have been. No one would think of proposing an Executive much more numerous than that body; from six to a dozen have been suggested as the size of the council. Even the largest of these numbers is not too large for an easy combination, and from such a combination America would have more to fear than from the ambition of any single individual. A council to a chief executive who is himself responsible for what he does is generally nothing better than a clog on his good intentions, is often the instrument and accomplice of his bad ones, and is almost always a cloak for his faults.

I refrain from dwelling on the subject of expense. Yet it is evident that if the council were numerous enough to serve the principal end the institution aims at, the salaries of its members, who would have to be drawn from their homes to live at the seat of government, would make an item among the public expenditures too serious to be incurred for an object of doubtful usefulness. I will only add that before the Constitution appeared, I seldom met an intelligent man from any of the States who did not admit, as a result of experience, that the UNITY of the executive of this State was one of the best distinguishing features of our constitution.

1. New York has no council except for the single purpose of appointing to offices; New Jersey has a council whom the governor may consult. But I think, from the terms of the constitution, their resolutions do not bind him.
2. De Lolme.
E1. Two versions of these paragraphs appear in different editions.

chapters.title: No. 71 — The Duration in Office of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Duration in office has been named as the second requisite of energy in the executive authority. It bears on two things: the personal firmness of the chief executive in using his constitutional powers, and the stability of the system of administration adopted under his leadership. As to the first, it must be evident that the longer the term in office, the greater the probability of gaining so important an advantage. It is a general principle of human nature that a man takes an interest in whatever he possesses in proportion to how secure or precarious his hold on it is. He will be less attached to what he holds by a momentary or uncertain title than to what he enjoys by a lasting and certain one, and he will naturally be willing to risk more for the one than for the other. This remark applies no less to a political privilege, honor or trust than to any ordinary article of property. The inference is that a man acting as chief executive, aware that in a very short time he MUST give up his office, will be apt to feel too little interest in it to risk any serious censure or difficulty by exerting his powers independently. He will not want to face the ill humors, however passing, that may prevail in a considerable part of society itself, or even in a dominant faction of the legislative body. Suppose instead that he MIGHT give up the office unless he is continued by a new choice, and that he wishes to be continued. Then his wishes, joining with his fears, would corrupt his integrity or debase his courage still more powerfully. In either case, feebleness and irresolution must be the marks of the office.

Some would be inclined to count the Executive's servile yielding to whatever current prevails, in the community or in the legislature, as its best recommendation. But such men hold very crude notions both of the purposes for which government was instituted and of the true means of promoting the public happiness. The republican principle demands that the deliberate sense of the community should govern the conduct of those to whom it entrusts the management of its affairs. It does not require unqualified compliance with every sudden breeze of passion, or with every passing impulse the people may receive from the arts of men who flatter their prejudices in order to betray their interests. It is a fair observation that the people commonly INTEND the PUBLIC GOOD. This is often true even of their errors. But their good sense would despise the flatterer who pretended that they always REASON RIGHT about the MEANS of promoting it. They know from experience that they sometimes err, and the wonder is that they err so seldom, constantly beset as they are by the wiles of parasites and sycophants, by the snares of the ambitious, the greedy and the desperate, and by the artifices of men who possess their confidence more than they deserve it, and of those who seek to possess it rather than deserve it. When occasions arise in which the interests of the people are at odds with their inclinations, it is the duty of the persons they have appointed as guardians of those interests to withstand the temporary delusion, so as to give the people time and opportunity for calmer and more sober reflection. Instances might be cited in which conduct of this kind has saved the people from the very fatal consequences of their own mistakes, and has won lasting monuments of their gratitude for the men who had the courage and magnanimity to serve them at the risk of their displeasure.

But however inclined we might be to insist on unbounded compliance in the Executive with the inclinations of the people, we cannot with any propriety insist on the same compliance with the whims of the legislature. The latter may sometimes stand in opposition to the former, and at other times the people may be entirely neutral. In either case it is certainly desirable that the Executive should be in a position to dare to act on his own opinion, with vigor and decision.

The same rule that teaches the propriety of a partition between the different branches of power also teaches that the partition should be arranged so as to make each independent of the others. What is the point of separating the executive or the judiciary from the legislative if both the executive and the judiciary are so constituted as to be at the absolute disposal of the legislative? Such a separation must be merely nominal, and unable to achieve the ends for which it was established. It is one thing to be subordinate to the laws and another to be dependent on the legislative body. The first is consistent with the fundamental principles of good government; the last violates them and, whatever the forms of the Constitution may be, unites all power in the same hands. The tendency of the legislative authority to absorb every other has been fully shown, with examples, in some earlier numbers. In governments that are purely republican, this tendency is almost irresistible. The representatives of the people in a popular assembly sometimes seem to fancy that they are the people themselves, and show strong signs of impatience and disgust at the least sign of opposition from any other quarter, as if the exercise of its rights by either the executive or the judiciary were a breach of their privilege and an outrage to their dignity. They often appear disposed to exert an imperious control over the other departments. And since they commonly have the people on their side, they always act with such momentum that it is very hard for the other members of the government to maintain the balance of the Constitution.

It may perhaps be asked how a short term in office can affect the independence of the Executive from the legislature, unless the one holds the power of appointing or removing the other. One answer to this question can be drawn from the principle already noted, namely the slight interest a man tends to take in a short-lived advantage, and the little inducement it gives him to expose himself to any considerable inconvenience or danger on its account. Another answer, perhaps more obvious though no more conclusive, comes from considering the influence of the legislative body over the people. That influence might be used to prevent the re-election of a man who, by honestly resisting some sinister project of that body, had made himself the target of its resentment.

It may also be asked whether a term of four years would serve the end proposed. If it would not, would a shorter period, which would at least be recommended by greater security against ambitious designs, not be preferable, for that reason, to a longer one that was still too short to inspire the firmness and independence wanted in the chief executive?

It cannot be asserted that a term of four years, or any other limited term, would completely serve the end proposed. But it would contribute toward it in a degree that would have a material influence on the spirit and character of the government. Between the beginning and the end of such a period there would always be a considerable interval in which the prospect of losing office would be far enough away not to affect improperly the conduct of a man with a fair share of fortitude. In that interval he might reasonably expect that there would be time enough, before the end arrived, to make the community aware of the propriety of the measures he was inclined to pursue. It is probable that as he approached the moment when the public were to express their judgment of his conduct by a new election, his confidence, and with it his firmness, would decline. Even so, both would draw support from the opportunities his earlier time in the office had given him to establish himself in the esteem and goodwill of his constituents. He could then take risks safely, in proportion to the proofs he had given of his wisdom and integrity, and to the claim he had earned to the respect and attachment of his fellow citizens. On the one hand, then, a term of four years will contribute enough to the firmness of the Executive to make it a very valuable ingredient in the composition. On the other hand, it is not enough to justify any alarm for public liberty. Consider the British House of Commons. From the most feeble beginnings, FROM THE MERE POWER OF ASSENTING OR DISAGREEING TO THE IMPOSITION OF A NEW TAX, it has by rapid strides reduced the prerogatives of the crown and the privileges of the nobility to the limits it judged compatible with the principles of a free government, while raising itself to the rank and consequence of a coequal branch of the legislature. In one instance it has been able to abolish both the royalty and the aristocracy and to overturn all the ancient establishments, in Church as well as State. On a recent occasion it has been able to make the monarch tremble at the prospect of an innovation(1) it attempted. If all this is so, what would be to be feared from an elective chief executive with a four-year term and the confined authorities of a President of the United States? Only that he might be unequal to the task the Constitution assigns him. I shall add only this: if his term is such as to leave a doubt about his firmness, that doubt is inconsistent with a jealousy of his encroachments.
1. This was the case with respect to Mr. Fox's India bill, which was carried in the House of Commons, and rejected in the House of Lords, to the entire satisfaction, as it is said, of the people.

chapters.title: No. 72 — The Same Subject Continued, and Re-Eligibility of the Executive Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: In its broadest sense, the administration of government covers every operation of the body politic, whether legislative, executive, or judiciary. In its most common sense, and perhaps its most exact one, though, it means only executive details and belongs especially to the executive department. The actual conduct of foreign negotiations, the preparatory plans of finance, the use and spending of public money in keeping with the general appropriations of the legislature, the organization of the army and navy, and the direction of the operations of war: these and other matters of a similar nature make up what seems most properly to be understood by the administration of government. The persons, therefore, to whose immediate management these different matters are entrusted ought to be regarded as the assistants or deputies of the chief executive. For that reason they ought to receive their offices from his appointment, or at least from his nomination, and ought to be subject to his supervision. This view of the subject at once shows us how closely the length of time the chief executive remains in office is connected with the stability of the system of administration. A successor very often regards reversing and undoing what his predecessor has done as the best proof he can give of his own ability and worth. In addition to this inclination, where the change has come about by public choice, the person put in the place of another is justified in supposing that the dismissal of his predecessor came from a dislike of that man's measures, and that the less he resembles him, the more he will recommend himself to the favor of his constituents. These considerations, together with the influence of personal trust and attachment, would be likely to lead every new President to promote a change of men to fill the subordinate positions. And these causes together could not fail to produce a disgraceful and ruinous instability in the administration of the government.

I pair a term of considerable length with eligibility for reelection. The long term is needed so that the officer himself has the inclination and resolve to do his part well, and so that the community has time and leisure to watch where his measures lead and to judge their merits from experience. Reelection is needed so that the people, when they see reason to approve of his conduct, can keep him in his post. That prolongs the usefulness of his talents and virtues, and it gives the government the benefit of permanence in a wise system of administration.

Nothing appears more plausible at first sight, or more ill-founded on close inspection, than a scheme that has had some respectable advocates on the present point. I mean the scheme of keeping the chief executive in office for a certain time and then excluding him from it, either for a limited period or forever after. This exclusion, whether temporary or permanent, would have nearly the same effects, and those effects would for the most part be harmful rather than beneficial.

One bad effect of the exclusion would be a reduction of the inducements to good behavior. There are few men who would not feel much less zeal in the discharge of a duty when they knew that the advantages of the position connected with it must be given up at a fixed time, than when they were allowed to hope to earn a continuance of those advantages by deserving it. This point will not be disputed, so long as it is admitted that the desire of reward is one of the strongest incentives of human conduct, or that the best security for the fidelity of mankind is to make their interests coincide with their duty. Even the love of fame, the ruling passion of the noblest minds, would be affected in such a case. If a man could flatter himself with the prospect of being allowed to finish what he had begun, that passion would prompt him to plan and undertake extensive and arduous enterprises for the public benefit, enterprises requiring considerable time to mature and perfect. But when he foresaw that he must leave the scene before he could accomplish the work, and must commit it, together with his own reputation, to hands that might be unequal or unfriendly to the task, that same passion would deter him from the undertaking. The most that can be expected from the generality of men in such a situation is the negative merit of doing no harm, in place of the positive merit of doing good.

Another bad effect of the exclusion would be the temptation to sordid aims, to embezzlement, and, in some instances, to usurpation. An avaricious man who happened to hold the office would look ahead to a time when he must in any event give up the pay he enjoyed. He would feel an inclination, not easy for such a man to resist, to make the best use of his opportunity while it lasted, and he might not hesitate to resort to the most corrupt expedients to make the harvest as abundant as it was brief. The same man, with a different prospect before him, might probably content himself with the regular perquisites of his position, and might even be unwilling to risk the consequences of abusing his opportunities. His avarice might be a guard upon his avarice. Add to this that the same man might be vain or ambitious, as well as avaricious. If he could expect to prolong his honors by his good conduct, he might hesitate to sacrifice his appetite for them to his appetite for gain. But with the prospect before him of approaching and inevitable extinction, his avarice would be likely to defeat his caution, his vanity, or his ambition.

An ambitious man, too, would find himself seated on the summit of his country's honors. He would look ahead to the time when he must descend forever from that exalted height, and would reflect that no exertion of merit on his part could save him from the unwelcome reversal. Such a man, in such a situation, would be much more strongly tempted to seize a favorable opportunity to attempt to prolong his power, at every personal risk, than if he had a reasonable prospect of reaching the same end by doing his duty.

Would it promote the peace of the community, or the stability of the government, to have half a dozen men who had enjoyed enough credit to be raised to the seat of the highest executive office wandering among the people like discontented ghosts, sighing for a place they were destined never to possess again?

A third bad effect of the exclusion would be to deprive the community of the benefit of the experience the chief executive has gained in the exercise of his office. That experience is the parent of wisdom is a saying whose truth the wisest and the simplest of mankind alike recognize. What is more desirable or more essential than this quality in the governors of nations? Where is it more desirable or more essential than in the chief executive of a nation? Can it be wise to put this desirable and essential quality under the ban of the Constitution, and to declare that the moment it is acquired, its possessor shall be forced to abandon the position in which he acquired it and to which it is suited? Yet this is the precise meaning of all those regulations that exclude men from serving their country, by the choice of their fellow citizens, after they have fitted themselves, through a course of service, to do so with greater usefulness.

A fourth bad effect of the exclusion would be the banishing of men from positions in which, in certain emergencies of the state, their presence might be of the greatest importance to the public interest or safety. There is no nation that has not, at one time or another, found an absolute necessity for the services of particular men in particular situations. Perhaps it would not be too strong to say that this necessity has extended to the preservation of its political existence. How unwise, therefore, must be every such self-denying ordinance as forbids a nation to use its own citizens in the manner best suited to its needs and circumstances! Even without supposing that any one man is personally indispensable, it is evident that a change of chief executive, at the outbreak of a war or in any similar crisis, would at all times harm the community, even if the replacement were a man of equal merit. It would put inexperience in the place of experience, and would tend to unsettle and throw into confusion the already established course of the administration.

A fifth bad effect of the exclusion would be that it would operate as a constitutional prohibition of stability in the administration. By making a change of men in the first office of the nation necessary, it would make a change of measures necessary. It is not generally to be expected that men will change and measures remain the same. The contrary is the usual course of things. And we need not fear that there will be too much stability while the option of changing still exists. Nor need we wish to forbid the people from continuing their confidence where they think it may safely be placed, and where, by their constancy, they may avoid the fatal problems of shifting councils and a changeable policy.

These are some of the disadvantages that would flow from the principle of exclusion. They apply most forcibly to the scheme of permanent exclusion. But when we consider that even a partial exclusion would always make the person's readmission a remote and uncertain prospect, the observations that have been made will apply almost as fully to one case as to the other.

What advantages are promised to offset these disadvantages? They are represented to be: first, greater independence in the chief executive; second, greater security to the people. Unless the exclusion is permanent, there will be no pretense for inferring the first advantage. But even in that case, may he not have some object beyond his present position, to which he may sacrifice his independence? May he not have connections and friends for whom he may sacrifice it? May he not be less willing to make personal enemies by firm conduct, when he acts under the impression that a time is fast approaching when he not only MAY, but MUST, be exposed to their resentment, on an equal footing with them, or perhaps an inferior one? It is not an easy point to determine whether his independence would be more promoted or more impaired by such an arrangement.

As to the second supposed advantage, there is still greater reason to doubt it. If the exclusion were permanent, a man of irregular ambition, the only kind of man about whom there could be reason in any case to feel apprehension, would yield with infinite reluctance to the necessity of taking leave forever of a post in which his passion for power and pre-eminence had grown into habit. And if he had been fortunate or skillful enough to win the good will of the people, he might induce them to regard as a very odious and unjustifiable restraint upon themselves a provision designed to deprive them of the right to give a fresh proof of their attachment to a favorite. Circumstances can be imagined in which this disgust of the people, backing the thwarted ambition of such a favorite, might produce greater danger to liberty than could ever reasonably be feared from the possibility of a continuation in office, by the voluntary votes of the community exercising a constitutional privilege.

There is an excess of refinement in the idea of depriving the people of the ability to keep in office men who had earned, in the people's own opinion, their approval and confidence. The advantages of this idea are at best speculative and doubtful, and are outweighed by disadvantages far more certain and decisive.

chapters.title: No. 73 — The Provision For The Support of the Executive, and the Veto Power (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The third ingredient in the vigor of the executive authority is adequate provision for its support. Without proper attention to this matter, it is clear, the separation of the executive from the legislative department would be merely nominal and worthless. If the legislature had discretionary power over the salary and pay of the chief executive, it could make him as submissive to its will as it chose. In most cases it could either starve him into compliance or tempt him with gifts, and so make him hand over his judgment to its inclinations whenever it liked. Taken in the full breadth of their terms, these expressions would no doubt say more than I intend. There are men who could be neither distressed nor won into sacrificing their duty. But this stern virtue grows in few soils, and on the whole it will be found that power over a man's support is power over his will. If so plain a truth needed confirming with facts, examples would not be lacking, even in this country, of an Executive intimidated or seduced by the threats or the enticements of the legislative body's money arrangements.

It is hard, therefore, to praise too highly the sound attention this subject has received in the proposed Constitution.
