It provides there that "The President of the United States shall, at stated times, receive for his services a compensation which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period for which he shall have been elected; and he shall not receive within that period any other emolument from the United States, or any of them." No provision could be imagined that would be more desirable. When a President is appointed, the legislature is to declare once and for all what his compensation will be for the term of his election. After that, it will have no power to change it, up or down, until a new term begins with a new election. It can neither weaken his firmness by working on his needs nor corrupt his integrity by appealing to his greed. Neither the Union nor any of its members will be free to give, and he will not be free to receive, any pay other than what the first act determined. He can therefore have no money motive to give up or abandon the independence the Constitution intends for him.
The last of the requisites to energy that were listed is adequate powers. Let us now consider the ones proposed to be vested in the President of the United States.

The first thing to claim our attention is the President's qualified negative on the acts or resolutions of the two houses of the legislature. Put another way, he has the power to return any bill with his objections, and this prevents it from becoming law unless two thirds of the members of each house afterward approve it.

I have already suggested, and repeated, that the legislative department tends to intrude on the rights of the other departments and to absorb their powers. I have also remarked that a mere description of each one's boundaries on parchment is not enough, and I have concluded and proved that each must be given constitutional arms for its own defense. From these clear and undeniable principles it follows that the Executive should have a negative, whether absolute or qualified, on the acts of the legislative branches. Without one or the other, the Executive would be utterly unable to defend himself against the legislature's plundering. Resolution by resolution he might gradually be stripped of his authorities, or he might be wiped out by a single vote. Either way, the legislative and executive powers might soon come to be blended in the same hands. And even if the legislative body had never shown the slightest tendency to invade the rights of the Executive, sound reasoning and theoretical propriety would still teach us that the one ought not to be left at the mercy of the other, but ought to have a constitutional and effective power of self-defense.

But the power in question has a further use. It is not only a shield for the Executive; it is also an additional security against the passing of improper laws. It sets up a beneficial check on the legislative body, meant to protect the community from the effects of faction, of haste, or of any impulse hostile to the public good that may happen to sway a majority of that body.

Some have opposed a negative with the remark that we cannot presume a single man to have more virtue and wisdom than a number of men, and that unless we presume this, it would be improper to give the chief executive any kind of control over the legislative body.

But on examination this remark will prove more specious than solid. The propriety of the negative does not rest on supposing the Executive to have superior wisdom or virtue. It rests on supposing that the legislature will not be infallible: that its love of power may sometimes betray it into a disposition to encroach on the rights of other parts of the government; that a spirit of faction may sometimes distort its deliberations; and that the impressions of the moment may sometimes rush it into measures that it would itself condemn on calmer reflection. The primary reason for giving the Executive this power is to enable him to defend himself. The secondary reason is to improve the community's chances against the passing of bad laws, whether through haste, carelessness, or design. The more often a measure is brought up for examination, and the more varied the situations of those who examine it, the smaller must be the danger of errors that come from a lack of proper deliberation, or of missteps that come from the contagion of some shared passion or interest. It is far less probable that blameworthy views of any kind would infect every part of the government at the same moment and on the same object than that they would take control of each part in turn and mislead it.

Perhaps it will be said that the power of preventing bad laws includes that of preventing good ones, and may be used for the one purpose as readily as for the other. But this objection will carry little weight with those who can properly judge the harms of that inconstancy and instability in the laws which are the greatest blemish on the character and spirit of our governments. They will regard any institution meant to restrain excessive law-making, and to keep things in whatever state they happen to be in at a given time, as far more likely to do good than harm, because it favors greater stability in the system of legislation. The damage that may possibly be done by defeating a few good laws will be more than made up by the advantage of blocking a number of bad ones.

Nor is this all. In a free government the legislative body has superior weight and influence, and the Executive risks much in a trial of strength with it. This gives satisfactory security that the negative would generally be used with great caution, and that there would more often be grounds to charge the Executive with timidity than with rashness in using it. Even a king of Great Britain, with all his train of sovereign attributes and all the influence he draws from a thousand sources, would today hesitate to put a negative on the joint resolutions of the two houses of Parliament. He would not fail to use the utmost resources of that influence to smother a measure he disliked on its way to the throne, so as to avoid the dilemma of either letting it take effect or risking the nation's displeasure by opposing the sense of the legislative body. Nor is it likely that he would in the end venture to use his prerogatives except in a case of manifest propriety or extreme necessity. All well-informed men in that kingdom will grant that this remark is just. A very long time has passed since the crown last exercised its negative.

If an official as powerful and as well fortified as a British monarch would have scruples about using the power under consideration, how much greater caution can reasonably be expected from a President of the United States, who is clothed with the executive authority for only four years, in a government wholly and purely republican?

Plainly, there would be greater danger that he would fail to use his power when necessary than that he would use it too often or too much. An argument against its expediency has indeed been drawn from this very point. On this ground it has been called a power that is odious in appearance and useless in practice. But it does not follow that because it might rarely be used, it would never be used. In the case it is chiefly designed for, an immediate attack on the constitutional rights of the Executive, or a case in which the public good was clearly and plainly being sacrificed, a man of reasonable firmness would use his constitutional means of defense and would heed the warnings of duty and responsibility. In the first case, his firmness would be spurred by his direct interest in the power of his office. In the second, it would be spurred by the likelihood that his constituents would approve. In a doubtful case they would naturally lean toward the legislative body, but they would hardly let their bias deceive them in a very plain one. I am speaking now with a chief executive in view who has only an ordinary share of firmness. There are men who, in any circumstances, will have the courage to do their duty whatever the risk.

But the Convention has taken a middle course in this business. It will make it easier for the chief executive to use the power vested in him here, and it makes the power's effectiveness depend on the view of a considerable part of the legislative body. In place of an absolute negative, it proposes to give the Executive the qualified negative already described. This power would be much more readily used than the other. A man who might be afraid to defeat a law by his single VETO might not hesitate to return it for reconsideration, knowing that it can be finally rejected only if more than one third of each house agree that his objections were sufficient. He would be encouraged by the thought that if his opposition should prevail, a very respectable share of the legislative body would be in it with him, and their influence would join his in defending the propriety of his conduct before public opinion. A direct and categorical negative looks harsher, and is more likely to irritate, than the mere offering of reasoned objections to be approved or rejected by those they are addressed to. To the degree that it would give less offense, it would be more likely to be used, and for that very reason it may be found in practice to be more effective. It is to be hoped that improper views will seldom control as many as two thirds of both branches of the legislature at once, and this despite the counterweight of the Executive. It is in any case far less probable that this would happen than that such views would taint the resolutions and conduct of a bare majority. A power of this kind in the Executive will often work silently and unnoticed, though forcefully. When men engaged in unjustifiable pursuits know that an obstruction may come from a quarter they cannot control, the mere fear of opposition will often restrain them from doing what they would eagerly rush into if no such outside obstacles were to be feared.

As I have remarked elsewhere, this qualified negative is, in this State, vested in a council made up of the governor, the chancellor, and the judges of the Supreme Court, or any two of them. It has been freely used on a variety of occasions, and often with success. Its usefulness has become so apparent that persons who fiercely opposed it when the Constitution was being drawn up have, through experience, become its avowed admirers.(1)

I have remarked in another place that in shaping this part of its plan the Convention departed from the model of this State's constitution and followed that of Massachusetts instead. Two strong reasons for this preference can be imagined. One is that the judges, who are to be the interpreters of the law, might pick up an improper bias from having already given an opinion in their revisionary capacities. The other is that, through frequent association with the Executive, they might be led too far into the political views of that chief executive, and so a dangerous combination might gradually be cemented between the executive and judiciary departments. The judges cannot be kept too separate from every occupation but that of expounding the laws. It is especially dangerous to put them in a position where the Executive could corrupt or influence them.
1. Mr. Abraham Yates, a warm opponent of the plan of the Convention, is one of these.

chapters.title: No. 74 — The Command of the Military and Naval Forces, and the Pardoning Power of the Executive. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The President of the United States is to be "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States when called into the actual service of the United States." This provision is so obviously proper in itself, and so closely follows the precedents of the State constitutions generally, that it hardly needs explaining or defending. Even the State constitutions that elsewhere give the chief executive a council have, for the most part, placed military authority in him alone. Of all the tasks of government, directing a war calls most especially for the qualities that mark power exercised by a single hand. To direct a war is to direct the common strength, and the power to direct and employ the common strength is a usual and essential part of what we mean by the executive authority.

"The President may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive departments, upon any subject relating to the duties of their respective officers." In my view this is merely redundant in the plan, because the office would carry that right with it automatically.

He is also to be authorized to grant "reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment." Humanity and sound policy join in dictating that the merciful prerogative of pardoning should be as little restricted or hampered as possible. The criminal code of every country has so much necessary severity in it that, without easy access to exceptions in favor of unfortunate guilt, justice would wear a face too bloody and cruel. The sense of responsibility is always strongest in proportion as it is undivided. It may therefore be inferred that a single man would be most ready to attend to the force of those motives that might plead for a softening of the rigor of the law, and least likely to yield to considerations meant to shelter a fit object of its vengeance. The thought that the fate of a fellow creature depended on his sole decision would naturally inspire scrupulousness and caution. The dread of being accused of weakness or connivance would produce an equal circumspection, though of a different kind. On the other hand, since men generally draw confidence from their numbers, they might often encourage one another in an act of hardness, and might be less affected by the fear of suspicion or censure for an unwise or affected clemency. For these reasons, one man appears to be a better dispenser of the mercy of government than a body of men.

The expediency of vesting the power of pardoning in the President has, if I am not mistaken, been contested only in relation to the crime of treason. It has been urged that this power ought to have depended on the assent of one, or both, of the branches of the legislative body. I shall not deny that there are strong reasons for requiring, in this particular case, the concurrence of that body or of a part of it. Treason is a crime aimed at the very existence of the society. Once the laws have established the offender's guilt, there seems a fitness in referring the question whether an act of mercy toward him is advisable to the judgment of the legislature. This ought the more to be the case because the possibility that the chief executive himself might connive ought not to be entirely excluded. But there are also strong objections to such a plan. It is not to be doubted that a single man of prudence and good sense is better fitted, in delicate situations, to weigh the motives that may plead for and against the remission of the punishment than any numerous body whatever. It deserves particular attention that treason will often be connected with seditions that involve a large proportion of the community, as lately happened in Massachusetts. In every such case, we might expect to see the representation of the people tainted with the same spirit that had given birth to the offense. And when the parties were fairly evenly matched, the secret sympathy of the friends and supporters of the condemned person, taking advantage of the good nature and weakness of others, might frequently grant impunity where the terror of an example was necessary. On the other hand, when the sedition had arisen from causes that had inflamed the resentments of the larger party, they might often be found obstinate and unyielding when policy demanded forbearance and clemency. But the principal argument for placing the power of pardoning in this case in the chief executive is this: in times of insurrection or rebellion, there are often critical moments when a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquillity of the commonwealth, and which, if allowed to pass unused, it may never be possible to recall afterward. The slow process of convening the legislature, or one of its branches, to obtain its sanction for the measure would frequently cause the golden opportunity to slip away. The loss of a week, a day, an hour, may sometimes be fatal. If it should be observed that a discretionary power, with a view to such contingencies, might be conferred on the President occasionally, the answer is, in the first place, that it is questionable whether, in a limited Constitution, that power could be delegated by law; and in the second place, that it would generally be unwise to take beforehand any step that might hold out the prospect of impunity. A proceeding of this kind, outside the usual course, would be likely to be read as a sign of timidity or weakness, and would tend to embolden guilt.

chapters.title: No. 75 — The Treaty-Making Power of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The President is to have power, "by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur." This provision has been attacked on various grounds, and often with considerable vehemence. Even so, I do not hesitate to declare my firm conviction that it is one of the best-conceived and least objectionable parts of the plan. One ground of objection is the stale topic of the intermixture of powers. Some argue that the President alone ought to have the power of making treaties; others, that it should have been placed exclusively in the Senate. Another objection arises from the small number of persons by whom a treaty may be made. Some who press this objection think the House of Representatives ought to have been brought into the business. Others seem to think it would have been enough to require two thirds of all the members of the Senate instead of two thirds of the members present. I flatter myself that the observations made in a preceding number on this part of the plan must have been enough to show it, to a discerning eye, in a very favorable light. So I shall content myself here with offering a few supplementary remarks, mainly aimed at the objections I have just stated.

On the intermixture of powers, I shall rely on the explanations already given elsewhere of the true meaning of the rule on which that objection rests. I shall take it for granted, as an inference from them, that joining the Executive with the Senate in the matter of treaties breaks no such rule. I venture to add that the particular nature of the power of making treaties shows a special propriety in that union. Several writers on government place that power among the executive authorities, but this is plainly an arbitrary classification, for if we look carefully at how it operates, it will be found to have more of the legislative character than of the executive, although it does not seem to fall strictly within the definition of either. The essence of legislative authority is to enact laws, that is, to prescribe rules for regulating the society. The execution of the laws, and the use of the common strength for that purpose or for the common defense, seem to make up all the functions of the chief executive. The power of making treaties is plainly neither of these. It has nothing to do with executing the existing laws, or with enacting new ones, and still less with exerting the common strength. Its objects are CONTRACTS with foreign nations, which have the force of law but get that force from the obligations of good faith. They are not rules laid down by the sovereign for the subject, but agreements between sovereign and sovereign. The power in question therefore seems to form a distinct department, belonging properly neither to the legislative nor to the executive. The qualities I detailed elsewhere as indispensable in managing foreign negotiations point to the Executive as the fittest agent in those transactions. Yet the vast importance of the trust, and the fact that treaties operate as laws, argue strongly for the participation of the whole legislative body, or a part of it, in the business of making them.

It may be proper and safe, in governments where the chief executive is an hereditary monarch, to commit the entire power of making treaties to him. But it would be utterly unsafe and improper to entrust that power to an elected chief executive who serves four years. It has been remarked on another occasion, and the remark is unquestionably just, that an hereditary monarch, though often the oppressor of his people, has too great a personal stake in the government to be in any real danger of being corrupted by foreign powers. But consider a man raised from private life to the rank of chief executive, with a moderate or slender fortune, who looks ahead to a time not far off when he will probably have to return to the station he came from. Such a man might at times face temptations to sacrifice his duty to his interest that only exceptional virtue could resist. An avaricious man might be tempted to betray the interests of the state in order to acquire wealth. An ambitious man might make his own advancement, with the help of a foreign power, the price of his treachery to his constituents. The record of human conduct gives no warrant for so lofty an opinion of human virtue as would make it wise for a nation to commit interests as delicate and weighty as those of its dealings with the rest of the world to the sole disposal of an executive created and situated as a President of the United States would be.

Entrusting the power of making treaties to the Senate alone would have meant giving up the benefit of the President's constitutional agency in conducting foreign negotiations. True, the Senate would then be free to employ him in that role, but it would be equally free to leave him out, and pique or intrigue might lead it to choose the second course rather than the first. Besides this, the Senate's own subordinate agent could not be expected to enjoy the confidence and respect of foreign powers to the same degree as the constitutional representatives of the nation, and so could not act with the same weight or effectiveness. On this account the Union would lose a considerable advantage in managing its external concerns, and the people would lose the added security that would come from the Executive's cooperation. It would be imprudent to confide so important a trust to him alone, but there can be no doubt that his participation would materially add to the safety of the society. It must indeed be clear to a demonstration that the joint possession of the power in question by the President and the Senate would offer better prospects of security than possession by either of them separately. And anyone who has carefully weighed the circumstances that must come together in the appointment of a President will be satisfied that the office will always be likely to be filled by men whose character makes their concurrence in the making of treaties especially desirable, for their wisdom as well as their integrity.

The remarks made in a former number, alluded to in another part of this paper, apply with conclusive force against giving the House of Representatives a share in the making of treaties. Its membership changes constantly, and, once its future growth is taken into account, it will be a large body. We cannot expect in it the qualities essential to the proper execution of such a trust. Accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics, steady and systematic adherence to the same views, a delicate and uniform sensitivity to national character, and decision, secrecy, and dispatch are all incompatible with the character of so variable and so numerous a body. The very complication of the business, by requiring the agreement of so many different bodies, would be a solid objection in itself. The House of Representatives would have to be called on more often, and would often have to be kept together longer once assembled, in order to obtain its sanction at each stage of a treaty. That would be a source of so much trouble and expense that it alone ought to condemn the project.

The only objection left to be examined is the one that would substitute two thirds of all the members of the Senate for two thirds of the members present. It has been shown, under the second head of our inquiries, that every provision requiring more than a majority of any body for its resolutions directly tends to hamper the operations of the government and indirectly tends to subject the sense of the majority to that of the minority. This consideration seems enough to settle our opinion that the Convention has gone as far as it could in seeking the advantage of numbers in the making of treaties, consistent with the activity of the public councils and with a reasonable regard for the prevailing sense of the community. Had two thirds of the whole membership been required, then in many cases, because some members were absent, it would in practice amount to requiring unanimity. And the history of every political establishment in which this principle has prevailed is a history of impotence, perplexity, and disorder. I could offer proofs of this from the Roman Tribuneship, the Polish Diet, and the States-General of the Netherlands, if an example at home did not make foreign precedents unnecessary.

Requiring a fixed proportion of the whole body would probably do no more for the advantages of a numerous agency than merely requiring a proportion of the members attending. The former makes a fixed number necessary for every resolution, and so weakens the motives to punctual attendance. The latter makes the body's capacity to act depend on a proportion that the absence or presence of a single member can change, and so has the opposite effect. Because it promotes punctuality and so tends to keep the body complete, there is great likelihood that in this case its resolutions would generally be made by as many members as in the other, while there would be far fewer occasions of delay. It ought not to be forgotten that under the existing Confederation two members may represent a State, and usually do. Hence Congress, which now alone holds all the powers of the Union, rarely consists of more persons than would make up the intended Senate. Add to this that the members vote by States, and that when only one member from a State is present, his vote is lost. This justifies supposing that the active voices in the Senate, where the members are to vote individually, would rarely be fewer than the active voices in the existing Congress. When we also take into view the cooperation of the President, we shall not hesitate to infer that the people of America would have greater security against an improper use of the power of making treaties under the new Constitution than they now enjoy under the Confederation. And if we go one step further and look ahead to the probable enlargement of the Senate by the creation of new States, we shall not only find ample ground for confidence in the sufficiency of the members to whom that power will be entrusted, but shall probably conclude that a body more numerous than the Senate is likely to become would be very poorly fitted to discharge the trust properly.

chapters.title: No. 76 — The Appointing Power of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The President is "to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution. But the Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior officers as they think proper, in the President alone, or in the courts of law, or in the heads of departments. The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session."

I observed in an earlier paper that "the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration." If that observation is just, then the method of appointing the officers of the United States set out in the clauses above must, once examined, be admitted to deserve particular praise. It is hard to imagine a plan better designed than this one to promote a sound choice of men to fill the offices of the Union, and it needs no proof that the character of the Union's administration must depend essentially on this point.

Everyone will agree that the power of appointment, in ordinary cases, ought to take one of three forms. It ought to be placed either in a single man, or in a select assembly of moderate size, or in a single man acting with the concurrence of such an assembly. That the people at large should exercise it will readily be admitted to be impractical, if only because, setting aside every other consideration, it would leave them little time for anything else. So when I speak of an assembly or body of men in the reasoning that follows, it must be understood to mean a select body or assembly of the kind just described. The people as a whole, because of their numbers and their scattered situation, cannot be guided in their movements by that systematic spirit of cabal and intrigue which will be urged as the chief objection to placing the power in question in a body of men.

Those who have thought about this subject themselves, or who have attended to the observations made elsewhere in these papers on the appointment of the President, will, I presume, agree that there would always be a strong probability of the office being filled by a man of at least respectable abilities. Taking this as given, I go on to lay down a rule: one man of discernment is better suited to analyze and judge the particular qualities fitted to particular offices than a body of men of equal, or perhaps even greater, discernment.

The sole and undivided responsibility of one man will naturally produce a livelier sense of duty and a more exact regard for reputation. For that reason he will feel himself under stronger obligations, and will have more reason to investigate carefully the qualities needed in the positions to be filled and to prefer, impartially, the persons with the fairest claims to them. He will have fewer personal attachments to gratify than a body of men, each of whom may be supposed to have as many, and so he will be that much less liable to be misled by feelings of friendship and affection. A single well-directed man, with a single understanding, cannot be distracted and twisted by that diversity of views, feelings, and interests which frequently distracts and twists the resolutions of a collective body. Nothing so readily stirs the passions of mankind as personal considerations, whether they concern ourselves or others who are to be the objects of our choice or preference. Hence, whenever an assembly of men exercises the power of appointing to offices, we must expect a full display of all the private and party likings and dislikes, biases and antipathies, attachments and animosities, felt by those who make up the assembly. A choice made under such circumstances will naturally be the result either of a victory won by one party over the other or of a compromise between the parties. In either case, the real merit of the candidate will too often be lost from sight. In the first case, the qualifications best suited to unite the votes of the party will be weighed more heavily than those that fit the person for the position. In the second, the coalition will commonly turn on some self-interested exchange: "Give us the man we wish for this office, and you shall have the one you wish for that." This will be the usual condition of the bargain. And it will rarely happen that the advancement of the public service is the primary object either of party victories or of party negotiations.

The truth of the principles advanced here seems to have been felt by the most intelligent of those who have found fault with the provision the Convention has made on this point. They contend that the President alone ought to have been authorized to make the appointments under the federal government. But it is easy to show that every advantage to be expected from such an arrangement would, in substance, come from the power of nomination that is proposed to be given him, while several disadvantages that might accompany the absolute power of appointment in the hands of that officer would be avoided. In the act of nomination his judgment alone would be exercised. Since it would be his sole duty to point out the man who, with the approval of the Senate, should fill an office, his responsibility would be as complete as if he were to make the final appointment. From this point of view there can be no difference between nominating and appointing. The same motives that would lead him to do his duty properly in one case would exist in the other. And since no man could be appointed except on his prior nomination, every man who might be appointed would in fact be his choice.

But might not his nomination be overruled? I grant that it might, yet this could only make room for another nomination by himself. The person finally appointed must be the object of his preference, though perhaps not his first preference. It is also not very probable that his nominations would often be overruled. The Senate could not be tempted, by a preference for someone else, to reject the person proposed, because they could not be sure that the person they wished for would be brought forward by a second nomination or by any later one. They could not even be certain that a future nomination would present a candidate in any degree more acceptable to them. And since their refusal might cast a kind of stigma on the person rejected, and might look like a reflection on the judgment of the chief executive, it is not likely that they would often withhold their approval unless there were special and strong reasons for doing so.

To what purpose, then, require the cooperation of the Senate? I answer that the necessity of their concurrence would have a powerful, though generally silent, effect. It would be an excellent check on a spirit of favoritism in the President, and would do much to prevent the appointment of unfit persons out of State prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or a view to popularity. In addition, it would be an effective source of stability in the administration.

It is easy to see that a man who had the sole disposal of offices would be governed much more by his private inclinations and interests than when he was required to submit the propriety of his choice to the discussion and decision of a different and independent body, and that body an entire branch of the legislature. The possibility of rejection would be a strong motive to care in making proposals. The danger to his own reputation, and, in the case of an elected chief executive, to his political existence, from displaying a spirit of favoritism or an unbecoming pursuit of popularity before a body whose opinion would carry great weight in forming the public's, could not fail to work as a barrier against both. He would be both ashamed and afraid to bring forward, for the most distinguished or lucrative positions, candidates whose only merit was coming from the same State he himself belonged to, or being in some way personally allied to him, or having the necessary insignificance and pliancy to make them the servile instruments of his pleasure.

It has been objected to this reasoning that the President, through the influence of the power of nomination, may secure the compliance of the Senate with his views. To suppose universal venality in human nature is hardly less an error in political reasoning than to suppose universal rectitude. The institution of delegated power implies that there is a portion of virtue and honor among mankind that may be a reasonable foundation for confidence, and experience bears out the theory. It has been found to exist in the most corrupt periods of the most corrupt governments. The venality of the British House of Commons has long been a topic of accusation against that body, in its own country as well as in this one, and it cannot be doubted that the charge is, to a considerable extent, well founded. But it is just as little to be doubted that a large proportion of that body always consists of independent and public-spirited men who carry real weight in the councils of the nation. Hence it is (the present reign not excepted) that the sense of that body is often seen to control the inclinations of the monarch, with regard both to men and to measures. So although it might be allowable to suppose that the Executive might occasionally influence some individuals in the Senate, the supposition that he could in general buy the integrity of the whole body would be forced and improbable. A man disposed to view human nature as it is, neither flattering its virtues nor exaggerating its vices, will see sufficient ground for confidence in the honesty of the Senate. He will rest satisfied not only that it will be impracticable for the Executive to corrupt or seduce a majority of its members, but also that the necessity of its cooperation in the business of appointments will be a considerable and beneficial restraint on the conduct of that officer. Nor is the integrity of the Senate the only thing we can rely on. The Constitution has provided some important guards against the danger of executive influence on the legislative body. It declares that "No senator or representative shall during the time for which he was elected, be appointed to any civil office under the United States, which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person, holding any office under the United States, shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office."

chapters.title: No. 77 — The Appointing Power Continued and Other Powers of the Executive Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: One of the advantages expected from the Senate's cooperation in the business of appointments, it has been mentioned, is that it would contribute to the stability of the administration. The consent of that body would be necessary to remove officers as well as to appoint them. A change of chief executive, therefore, would not cause so violent or so general an upheaval among the officers of the government as might be expected if he were the sole disposer of offices. Where a man in any position had given satisfactory evidence of his fitness for it, a new President would be held back from trying to replace him with a person more agreeable to himself, by the fear that the Senate's disapproval might defeat the attempt and bring some discredit on himself. Those who best understand the value of a steady administration will be most inclined to prize a provision that ties the official existence of public men to the approval or disapproval of that body, which, because its own membership is more permanent, will in all probability be less subject to inconstancy than any other part of the government.

Of this union of the Senate with the President in the matter of appointments, it has been suggested in some quarters that it would give the President an undue influence over the Senate, and in others that it would have the opposite tendency. That is strong proof that neither suggestion is true.

To state the first in its proper form is to refute it. It amounts to this: the President would have an improper influence over the Senate because the Senate would have the power to restrain him. This is an absurdity in terms. There can be no doubt that the entire power of appointment would enable him far more effectively to establish a dangerous domination over that body than a mere power of nomination subject to their control.

Let us look at the converse of the proposition: "the Senate would influence the Executive." As I have had occasion to remark in several other instances, the vagueness of the objection forbids a precise answer. In what manner is this influence to be exerted? Over what objects? The power of influencing a person, in the sense used here, must imply a power of conferring a benefit on him. How could the Senate confer a benefit on the President by the way it used its right of negative on his nominations? If it is said that they might sometimes please him by going along with a favorite choice when public motives might dictate a different course, I answer that the cases in which the President could have a personal interest in the result would be too few for him to be materially affected by the Senate's compliance. The POWER that can originate the disposal of honors and pay is more likely to attract than to be attracted by the POWER that can merely obstruct their course. If by influencing the President is meant restraining him, this is precisely what must have been intended. And it has been shown that the restraint would be beneficial, while not destroying a single advantage to be looked for from the uncontrolled agency of that officer. The right of nomination would produce all the (good, without the ill.)(E1) (good of that of appointment, and would in a great measure avoid its evils.)(E1)

Compare the plan for appointing the officers of the proposed government with the one established by the constitution of this State, and the former must clearly be preferred. Under that plan the power of nomination is unequivocally vested in the Executive. And since each nomination would have to be submitted to the judgment of an entire branch of the legislature, the circumstances of an appointment would, from the way it is conducted, naturally become public knowledge, and the public would have no difficulty determining what part each of the actors had played. The blame for a bad nomination would fall on the President alone and entirely. The censure for rejecting a good one would lie wholly at the door of the Senate, made worse by the fact that they had thwarted the good intentions of the Executive. If a bad appointment were made, the Executive for nominating and the Senate for approving would share, though in different degrees, in the disgrace.

The reverse of all this characterizes the manner of appointment in this State. The council of appointment consists of from three to five persons, of whom the governor is always one. This small body, shut up in a private room, closed to the public eye, goes about carrying out the trust committed to it. It is known that the governor claims the right of nomination, on the strength of some ambiguous expressions in the constitution. But it is not known to what extent or in what manner he exercises it, nor on what occasions he is contradicted or opposed. The censure of a bad appointment, because its author is uncertain and there is no definite object for it, has neither sting nor staying power. And while an unbounded field for cabal and intrigue lies open, every idea of responsibility is lost. The most the public can know is that the governor claims the right of nomination; that two out of the small number of four men can too often be managed without much difficulty; that if some members of a particular council should happen to be uncooperative, it is frequently not impossible to get rid of their opposition by arranging the meeting times so that attendance is inconvenient for them; and that, from whatever cause, a great number of very improper appointments are made from time to time. Whether a governor of this State uses the ascendancy he must necessarily have in this delicate and important part of the administration to promote to offices the men best qualified for them, or whether he prostitutes that advantage to advance persons whose chief merit is their unquestioning devotion to his will, and to support a despicable and dangerous system of personal influence, are questions that, unfortunately for the community, can only be matters of speculation and conjecture.

Every mere council of appointment, however constituted, will be a conclave in which cabal and intrigue will have full scope. Without an unwarranted increase of expense, its numbers cannot be large enough to rule out easy combination. And since each member will have friends and connections to provide for, the desire for mutual favors will produce a scandalous trading of votes and bargaining for places. The private attachments of one man might easily be satisfied, but to satisfy the private attachments of a dozen, or of twenty men, would cause a monopoly of all the principal employments of the government in a few families, and would lead more directly to an aristocracy or an oligarchy than any measure that could be devised. If, to avoid an accumulation of offices, there were frequent changes in the persons who made up the council, this would bring the harms of a changeable administration in their full extent. Such a council would also be more open to executive influence than the Senate, because it would have fewer members and would act less directly under the public eye. In short, such a council, as a substitute for the plan of the Convention, would bring an increase of expense, a multiplication of the evils that spring from favoritism and intrigue in the distribution of public honors, a decrease of stability in the administration of the government, and a reduction of the security against undue influence by the Executive. And yet such a council has been warmly urged as an essential amendment to the proposed Constitution.

I could not properly close my remarks on appointments without noticing one more scheme, which has found a few advocates, though only a few: that of giving the House of Representatives a share in making them. I shall do little more than mention it, because I cannot imagine that any considerable part of the community is likely to support it. A body that is both so changeable and so numerous can never be considered fit to exercise that power. Its unfitness will be obvious to everyone once we recall that within half a century it may have three or four hundred members. This union would destroy all the benefits of stability, in the Executive and in the Senate alike, and would cause endless delays and embarrassments. Most of the States, in their own constitutions, set an example that encourages us to reject the idea.

The only remaining powers of the Executive are these. He gives Congress information on the state of the Union and recommends to its consideration the measures he judges expedient. He may convene Congress, or either house, on extraordinary occasions, and he may adjourn them when they cannot agree among themselves on a time. He receives ambassadors and other public ministers, sees that the laws are faithfully executed, and commissions all the officers of the United States.

No one has objected to this class of authorities, apart from some quibbling over the power to convene either house of the legislature and the power to receive ambassadors, and in truth they could not possibly support any objection. It took an insatiable appetite for censure to invent exceptions to the very parts that have been excepted to. On the power to convene either house, I shall only remark that, at least for the Senate, a good reason for it is easy to see. The Senate shares power with the Executive over treaties, so it might often be necessary to call it together for that purpose at a time when it would be unnecessary and improper to convene the House of Representatives. As for the reception of ambassadors, what I said in a former paper gives a sufficient answer.

We have now finished surveying the structure and powers of the executive department. I have tried to show that it combines, as far as republican principles allow, every requisite to energy. The question that remains is whether it also combines the requisites to safety in a republican sense, which are a due dependence on the people and a due responsibility. We have already anticipated the answer in examining its other characteristics, and it can be drawn satisfactorily from these facts. The President is elected once every four years, by persons whom the people choose directly for that purpose. And he is at all times liable to impeachment, trial, removal from office, disqualification from holding any other, and loss of life and estate through later prosecution in the ordinary course of law. But great as these precautions are, they are not the only ones the plan of the Convention has provided for the public security. In the only cases where abuse of the executive authority was seriously to be feared, the chief executive of the United States would, under that plan, be subject to the control of a branch of the legislative body. What more could an enlightened and reasonable people ask?
E1. These two alternate endings of this sentence appear in different editions.

chapters.title: No. 78 — The Judiciary Department (Hamilton)
paragraphs: We now proceed to examine the judiciary department of the proposed government.

In setting out the defects of the existing Confederation, the usefulness and necessity of a federal judiciary were clearly pointed out. I need not review the considerations urged there, because no one disputes that the institution is proper in principle. The only questions raised concern how it is to be constituted and how far its authority is to extend. Our observations will therefore be confined to those two points.

The question of how the judiciary is to be constituted seems to include these separate matters: 1st. The way the judges are appointed. 2d. The terms on which they hold their places. 3d. The division of judicial authority among different courts, and the relations of those courts to each other.

First. As to how the judges are appointed: this is the same as the way the other officers of the Union are appointed, and it was discussed so fully in the last two numbers that anything I said here would be useless repetition.
Second. As to the terms on which the judges hold their places: this chiefly concerns how long they stay in office, the provisions for their support, and the precautions for holding them responsible.

Under the plan of the Convention, all judges appointed by the United States are to hold their offices during good behavior. This is in accordance with the best of the State constitutions, including that of this State. That the adversaries of the plan have questioned the provision is no small sign of the rage for objection that disorders their imaginations and their judgment. The standard of good behavior for keeping judicial office is certainly one of the most valuable of the modern improvements in the practice of government. In a monarchy it is an excellent barrier against the despotism of the prince; in a republic it is an equally excellent barrier against the encroachments and oppressions of the representative body. And it is the best means that can be devised, in any government, of securing a steady, upright and impartial administration of the laws.

Anyone who carefully considers the different departments of power must see that in a government where they are kept separate from one another, the judiciary, by the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution, because it will be the least able to annoy or injure them. The Executive not only dispenses the honors but holds the sword of the community. The legislature not only controls the purse but prescribes the rules by which the duties and rights of every citizen are to be regulated. The judiciary, by contrast, has no influence over either the sword or the purse; it has no direction of the strength or of the wealth of the society, and can take no active resolution whatever. It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment; and in the end it must depend on the aid of the executive arm even for the effectiveness of its judgments.

This simple view of the matter suggests several important consequences. It proves beyond question that the judiciary is by far the weakest of the three departments of power(1); that it can never successfully attack either of the other two; and that every possible care is needed to enable it to defend itself against their attacks. It proves equally that although individual oppression may now and then come from the courts of justice, the general liberty of the people can never be endangered from that quarter. I mean this so long as the judiciary remains truly distinct from both the legislature and the Executive. For I agree that "there is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers."(2) And it proves, finally, the following. Liberty can have nothing to fear from the judiciary alone, but would have everything to fear from its union with either of the other departments. All the effects of such a union must follow from a dependence of the judiciary on one of the others, despite a nominal and apparent separation. From its natural feebleness the judiciary is in continual danger of being overpowered, awed or influenced by its co-ordinate branches. And nothing can contribute so much to its firmness and independence as permanency in office. This quality may therefore be justly regarded as an indispensable ingredient in its constitution, and in a great measure as the citadel of the public justice and the public security.

The complete independence of the courts of justice is especially essential in a limited Constitution. By a limited Constitution I mean one that sets out certain specific exceptions to the legislative authority; for instance, that the legislature may pass no bills of attainder and no ex post facto laws, and so on. In practice, such limitations can be kept only through courts of justice, whose duty it must be to declare all acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution void. Without this, every reservation of particular rights or privileges would come to nothing.

Some perplexity about the right of the courts to pronounce legislative acts void because they are contrary to the Constitution has arisen from the notion that this doctrine would imply a superiority of the judiciary to the legislative power. It is argued that the authority that can declare the acts of another void must necessarily be superior to the authority whose acts may be declared void. Since this doctrine is of great importance in all the American constitutions, a brief discussion of the ground it rests on cannot be unwelcome.

No position rests on clearer principles than this: any act of a delegated authority that is contrary to the terms of the commission under which it acts is void. So no legislative act contrary to the Constitution can be valid. To deny this would be to say that the deputy is greater than his principal, that the servant is above his master, that the representatives of the people are superior to the people themselves, and that men acting under granted powers may do not only what those powers do not authorize but even what they forbid.

Suppose it is said that the legislative body is itself the constitutional judge of its own powers, and that its interpretation of them is binding on the other departments. The answer is that this cannot be the natural presumption where no particular provision of the Constitution points to it. Otherwise we cannot suppose that the Constitution meant to enable the representatives of the people to substitute their will for that of their constituents. It is far more reasonable to suppose that the courts were designed to be an intermediate body between the people and the legislature, in order, among other things, to keep the legislature within the limits assigned to its authority. Interpreting the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts. A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges as, a fundamental law. It therefore belongs to them to determine its meaning, as well as the meaning of any particular act coming from the legislative body. If an irreconcilable conflict should arise between the two, the one with the superior obligation and validity ought of course to be preferred. In other words, the Constitution ought to be preferred to the statute, the intention of the people to the intention of their agents.

Nor does this conclusion in any way suppose that the judicial power is superior to the legislative. It supposes only that the power of the people is superior to both. Where the will of the legislature, declared in its statutes, stands in opposition to that of the people, declared in the Constitution, the judges ought to be governed by the latter rather than the former. They ought to base their decisions on the fundamental laws rather than on those that are not fundamental.

A familiar instance shows this exercise of judicial discretion in choosing between two contradictory laws. It not uncommonly happens that two statutes exist at the same time, clashing in whole or in part, and neither contains any repealing clause or expression. In such a case it is the province of the courts to settle and fix their meaning and operation. As far as they can be reconciled by any fair construction, reason and law together dictate that this should be done. Where that is impracticable, it becomes necessary to give effect to one and exclude the other. The rule the courts have adopted for deciding their relative validity is that the last in order of time shall be preferred to the first. But this is a mere rule of construction. It is derived not from any positive law but from the nature and reason of the thing. It is a rule not imposed on the courts by the legislature, but adopted by the courts themselves as consonant with truth and propriety, to direct their conduct as interpreters of the law. They thought it reasonable that, between the conflicting acts of an EQUAL authority, the one that was the last expression of its will should be preferred.

But where the conflicting acts come from a superior and a subordinate authority, an original and a derivative power, the nature and reason of the thing point to the reverse of that rule. They teach us that the earlier act of a superior ought to be preferred to the later act of an inferior and subordinate authority. Accordingly, whenever a particular statute contravenes the Constitution, it will be the duty of the courts to adhere to the Constitution and disregard the statute.

It carries no weight to say that the courts, on the pretense of a conflict, may substitute their own pleasure for the constitutional intentions of the legislature. This might just as well happen with two contradictory statutes, or in every judgment on any single statute. The courts must declare the sense of the law; and if they were disposed to exercise WILL instead of JUDGMENT, the result would equally be that their pleasure was substituted for that of the legislative body. If this observation proves anything, it proves that there ought to be no judges distinct from that body.

If, then, the courts of justice are to be considered the bulwarks of a limited Constitution against legislative encroachments, this strongly supports permanent tenure for judicial offices, since nothing will contribute so much as that tenure to the independent spirit in the judges which is essential to the faithful performance of so arduous a duty.

This independence of the judges is equally necessary to guard the Constitution and the rights of individuals from the effects of those ill humors that the arts of designing men, or the influence of particular conjunctures, sometimes spread among the people themselves. Though these give way quickly to better information and more deliberate reflection, in the meantime they tend to produce dangerous innovations in the government and serious oppressions of the minority in the community. I trust the friends of the proposed Constitution will never join its enemies(3) in questioning that fundamental principle of republican government, which admits the right of the people to alter or abolish the established Constitution whenever they find it inconsistent with their happiness. Yet it does not follow from this principle that the representatives of the people would be justified in violating the provisions of the existing Constitution whenever a momentary inclination, incompatible with those provisions, takes hold of a majority of their constituents. Nor does it follow that the courts would be under a greater obligation to connive at infractions of that kind than at infractions that came wholly from the cabals of the representative body. Until the people have, by some solemn and authoritative act, annulled or changed the established form, it is binding on them collectively as well as individually. No presumption, or even knowledge, of their views can warrant their representatives in departing from it before such an act. But it is easy to see that it would take an uncommon degree of fortitude in the judges to do their duty as faithful guardians of the Constitution where legislative invasions of it had been instigated by the majority voice of the community.

But it is not only with a view to infractions of the Constitution that the independence of the judges may be an essential safeguard against the effects of occasional ill humors in society. These sometimes go no further than injuring the private rights of particular classes of citizens through unjust and biased laws. Here also the firmness of the judges is of vast importance in softening the severity of such laws and confining their operation. It not only serves to moderate the immediate harms of those that may have been passed, but it acts as a check on the legislative body in passing them. Legislators who see that the scruples of the courts will obstruct the success of an unjust intention are in a manner compelled, by the very motives of the injustice they plan, to moderate their attempts. This circumstance is likely to have more influence on the character of our governments than few may realize. The benefits of the integrity and moderation of the judiciary have already been felt in more than one State. Though they may have displeased those whose improper expectations they disappointed, they must have earned the esteem and applause of all the virtuous and disinterested. Thoughtful men of every description ought to value whatever tends to produce or strengthen that disposition in the courts, since no one can be sure that he will not be the victim tomorrow of a spirit of injustice by which he may be a gainer today. And everyone must now feel that the inevitable tendency of such a spirit is to undermine the foundations of public and private confidence, and to put universal distrust and distress in their place.

That inflexible and uniform adherence to the rights of the Constitution and of individuals, which we see to be indispensable in the courts of justice, certainly cannot be expected from judges who hold their offices by a temporary commission. Periodical appointments, however regulated and by whomever made, would in one way or another be fatal to their necessary independence. If the power of making them were committed to the Executive or the legislature, there would be danger of improper compliance toward the branch that held it. If it were committed to both, the judges would be unwilling to risk the displeasure of either. If it were committed to the people, or to persons chosen by them for the purpose, there would be too great a disposition to consult popularity, so that we could not rely on the judges to consult nothing but the Constitution and the laws.

There is a further and weightier reason for permanency in judicial offices, which follows from the nature of the qualifications they require. It has often been remarked, and with great justice, that a voluminous code of laws is one of the drawbacks that necessarily go with the advantages of a free government. To avoid arbitrary discretion in the courts, it is indispensable that they be bound by strict rules and precedents, which define and point out their duty in every particular case that comes before them. It is easy to see, given the variety of controversies that grow out of the folly and wickedness of mankind, that the records of those precedents must inevitably swell to a considerable bulk, and that acquiring a competent knowledge of them demands long and laborious study. Hence few men in the society will have enough skill in the laws to qualify them to be judges. And after making the proper deductions for the ordinary depravity of human nature, the number is smaller still of those who unite the requisite integrity with the requisite knowledge. These considerations show that the government can have no great choice among fit characters. A temporary term in office would naturally discourage such characters from leaving a lucrative practice to take a seat on the bench, and would tend to put the administration of justice into hands less able and less well qualified to conduct it with usefulness and dignity. In the present circumstances of this country, and in those in which it is likely to be for a long time to come, the disadvantages on this score would be greater than they may at first appear. But it must be admitted that they are far less than those that present themselves under the other aspects of the subject.

Upon the whole, there can be no room to doubt that the Convention acted wisely in following the models of those constitutions that have established good behavior as the tenure of their judicial offices, as regards duration. Far from being blamable on this account, their plan would have been inexcusably defective if it had lacked this important feature of good government. The experience of Great Britain offers an illustrious commentary on the excellence of the institution.
1. The celebrated Montesquieu, speaking of them, says: "Of the three powers above mentioned, the judiciary is next to nothing."—Spirit of Laws. Vol. I, page 186.
2. Idem, page 181.
3. Vide Protest of the Minority of the Convention of Pennsylvania, Martin's Speech, etc.

chapters.title: No. 79 — The Judiciary Continued (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Next to permanency in office, nothing can do more for the independence of the judges than a fixed provision for their support. The remark I made about the President applies equally here. In the general course of human nature, power over a man's subsistence amounts to power over his will. We can never hope to see the judicial power completely separated from the legislative in practice under any system that leaves the former dependent for its financial resources on the occasional grants of the latter. The enlightened friends of good government in every State have had reason to lament the lack of precise and explicit precautions on this point in the State constitutions. Some of them, it is true, have declared that permanent(1) salaries shall be established for the judges. But experience has shown, in some instances, that such expressions are not definite enough to prevent legislative evasions. Something still more positive and unequivocal has proved to be necessary. The plan of the Convention accordingly provides that the judges of the United States "shall at stated times receive for their services a compensation which shall not be diminished during their continuance in office."

All things considered, this is the best provision that could have been devised. It is easy to understand that fluctuations in the value of money and in the state of society made it inadmissible to fix a rate of compensation in the Constitution. What might be extravagant today might in half a century become meager and inadequate. It was therefore necessary to leave it to the discretion of the legislature to vary the provisions as circumstances vary, yet under such restrictions as to put it out of that body's power to make any individual's condition worse. A man may then be sure of the ground he stands on, and can never be deterred from his duty by fear of being placed in a less favorable situation. The clause I have quoted combines both advantages. The salaries of judicial officers may be altered from time to time as occasion requires, but never so as to reduce the allowance with which any particular judge comes into office, as far as he is concerned. It will be noticed that the Convention made a difference between the compensation of the President and that of the judges. The President's can be neither increased nor diminished; the judges' can only not be diminished. This probably arose from the difference in the length of the two offices. Since the President is to be elected for no more than four years, it can rarely happen that a salary adequate at the beginning of that period will fail to remain so to its end. But the judges, if they behave properly, will be secure in their places for life. It may well happen, especially in the early stages of the government, that a stipend quite sufficient when they are first appointed would become too small as their service goes on.

This provision for the judges' support shows every mark of prudence and effectiveness. We can say with confidence that, together with their permanent tenure, it gives them a better prospect of independence than the constitution of any State gives its own judges.

Their responsibility is secured by the article on impeachments. For misconduct they may be impeached by the House of Representatives and tried by the Senate; if convicted, they may be removed from office and barred from holding any other. This is the only provision on the point that is consistent with the necessary independence of the judicial character, and it is the only one in our own Constitution regarding our own judges.

Critics have complained that there is no provision for removing judges for inability. But all thoughtful men will recognize that such a provision would either go unused or be more open to abuse than able to serve any good end. Measuring the faculties of the mind has, I believe, no place among the known arts. An attempt to draw the line between ability and inability would far more often give room to personal and party attachments and enmities than serve justice or the public good. Except in cases of insanity, the result must mostly be arbitrary; and insanity, without any formal or express provision, may safely be pronounced a virtual disqualification.

The constitution of New York, to avoid investigations that must forever be vague and dangerous, has taken a particular age as the test of inability: no man can be a judge beyond sixty. I believe there are few at present who do not disapprove of this provision. There is no station for which it is less suitable than that of a judge. The deliberating and comparing faculties generally keep their strength well beyond that age in men who live past it. Consider this together with how few outlive the season of intellectual vigor, and how unlikely it is that any considerable part of the bench, whether larger or smaller, would be in that condition at the same time. We shall then be ready to conclude that limitations of this sort have little to recommend them. In a republic, where fortunes are not affluent and pensions not expedient, the dismissal of men from stations in which they have long and usefully served their country needs a better excuse to humanity than the imaginary danger of a superannuated bench. Such men depend on their posts for subsistence, and it will be too late for them to turn to any other occupation for a livelihood.
1. Vide Constitution of Massachusetts, Chapter 2, Section 1, Article 13.

chapters.title: No. 80 — The Powers of the Judiciary (Hamilton)
paragraphs: To judge accurately the proper extent of the federal judiciary, it will be necessary first to consider what its proper objects are.

It seems hardly open to dispute that the judicial authority of the Union ought to extend to these several kinds of cases: 1st, all those that arise out of the laws of the United States, passed in accordance with their just and constitutional powers of legislation; 2d, all those that concern the execution of the provisions expressly contained in the articles of Union; 3d, all those in which the United States are a party; 4th, all those that involve the PEACE of the CONFEDERACY, whether they concern the dealings between the United States and foreign nations or those between the States themselves; 5th, all those that originate on the high seas and fall under admiralty or maritime jurisdiction; and lastly, all those in which the State courts cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased.

The first point rests on this obvious consideration: there ought always to be a constitutional method of giving effect to constitutional provisions. What, for instance, would restrictions on the authority of the State legislatures be worth without some constitutional means of enforcing them? Under the plan of the Convention the States are forbidden to do a variety of things, some of which are incompatible with the interests of the Union and others with the principles of good government. Imposing duties on imported articles and issuing paper money are examples of each kind. No sensible man will believe that such prohibitions would be scrupulously respected unless the government had some effective power to restrain or correct violations of them. This power must be either a direct negative on the State laws, or an authority in the federal courts to overrule those that were in manifest contravention of the articles of Union. I can imagine no third course. The Convention appears to have thought the latter preferable to the former, and, I presume, the latter will be more agreeable to the States.

As to the second point, no argument or comment can make it clearer than it is in itself. If there are such things as political axioms, the principle that the judicial power of a government should be coextensive with its legislative may be ranked among them. The mere need for uniformity in interpreting the national laws settles the question. Thirteen independent courts of final jurisdiction over the same causes, arising upon the same laws, would be a hydra in government, from which nothing but contradiction and confusion can come.

Still less need be said about the third point. Controversies between the nation and its members or citizens can properly be referred only to the national courts. Any other plan would be contrary to reason, to precedent and to decorum.

The fourth point rests on this plain proposition: the peace of the WHOLE ought not to be left at the disposal of a PART. The Union will undoubtedly be answerable to foreign powers for the conduct of its members. And responsibility for an injury ought always to come with the ability to prevent it. The denial or perversion of justice by the sentences of courts, like any other denial or perversion of it, is rightly classed among the just causes of war. It follows that the federal judiciary ought to have jurisdiction over all cases in which the citizens of other countries are concerned. This is no less essential to preserving the public faith than to securing the public tranquillity. A distinction may perhaps be imagined between cases arising under treaties and the laws of nations and those that rest merely on municipal law. The former kind may be thought proper for federal jurisdiction, the latter for that of the States. But it is at least doubtful whether an unjust sentence against a foreigner, in a controversy that was wholly a matter of the lex loci, would not, if left unredressed, be an aggression against his sovereign, as well as a violation of the stipulations of a treaty or of the general law of nations. And there would be a still greater objection to the distinction, in the immense difficulty, if not impossibility, of telling in practice the cases of one kind from those of the other. So large a proportion of the cases in which foreigners are parties involve national questions that it is by far the safest and most expedient course to refer all of them to the national courts.

The power of deciding causes between two States, between one State and the citizens of another, and between the citizens of different States is perhaps no less essential to the peace of the Union than the power just examined. History gives us a horrid picture of the dissensions and private wars that distracted and desolated Germany before Maximilian, toward the close of the fifteenth century, established the Imperial Chamber. It tells us at the same time of the vast influence of that institution in calming the disorders and establishing the tranquillity of the empire. This was a court invested with authority to decide finally all differences among the members of the Germanic body.

A method of ending territorial disputes between the States, under the authority of the federal head, was not overlooked even in the imperfect system by which they have been held together until now. But there are many other sources, besides conflicting claims of boundary, from which quarrels and animosities may arise among the members of the Union. We have witnessed some of these in our past experience. It will readily be guessed that I allude to the fraudulent laws passed in too many of the States. And though the proposed Constitution establishes particular safeguards against a repetition of the instances that have appeared before, it is reasonable to fear that the spirit that produced them will take new shapes, which could not be foreseen or specifically provided against. Whatever practices tend to disturb the harmony between the States are proper objects of federal superintendence and control.

It may be considered the basis of the Union that "the citizens of each State shall be entitled to all the privileges and immunities of citizens of the several States." And if it is a sound principle that every government ought to have the means of executing its own provisions by its own authority, it follows that, in order to maintain inviolably the equality of privileges and immunities to which the citizens of the Union will be entitled, the national judiciary ought to preside in all cases in which one State or its citizens are opposed to another State or its citizens. To secure the full effect of so fundamental a provision against all evasion and subterfuge, its interpretation must be committed to that court which, having no local attachments, is likely to be impartial between the different States and their citizens, and which, owing its official existence to the Union, will never be likely to feel any bias unfavorable to the principles on which the Union is founded.

The fifth point will call for little comment. The most bigoted worshipers of State authority have not so far shown any disposition to deny the national judiciary jurisdiction over maritime causes. These so generally depend on the laws of nations, and so commonly affect the rights of foreigners, that they fall within the considerations that concern the public peace. The most important of them are, under the present Confederation, submitted to federal jurisdiction.

That the national courts should act where the State courts cannot be presumed impartial is self-evident.
