No one should be judge in his own cause, or in any cause in which he has the slightest interest or bias. This principle weighs heavily in making the federal courts the proper courts for controversies between different States and their citizens. It should apply as well to some cases between citizens of one State. Claims to land under grants from different States, resting on opposing claims about boundaries, are of this kind. The courts of neither granting State could be expected to be unbiased. The laws may even have prejudged the question and bound the courts to rule for the grants of their own State. And even where that had not been done, the judges, being men, would naturally lean strongly toward the claims of their own government.

Having set out and discussed the principles that should shape the federal judiciary, we will now use them to test the particular powers that, under the plan of the Convention, make it up. It is to comprehend "all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties made, or which shall be made, under their authority; to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls; to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction; to controversies to which the United States shall be a party; to controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States; between citizens of the same State claiming lands and grants of different States; and between a State or the citizens thereof and foreign states, citizens, and subjects." This is the whole body of the Union's judicial authority. Let us now go through it item by item. It is, then, to extend:

First. To all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution and the laws of the United States. This corresponds with the first two classes of causes that I listed as proper for the jurisdiction of the United States. It has been asked what is meant by "cases arising under the Constitution," as distinguished from those "arising under the laws of the United States." The difference has already been explained. All the restrictions on the authority of the State legislatures furnish examples of it. The States are not, for instance, to issue paper money; but that prohibition comes from the Constitution and will have no connection with any law of the United States. Should paper money be issued notwithstanding, the controversies about it would be cases arising under the Constitution and not under the laws of the United States, in the ordinary meaning of those terms. This may serve as a sample of the whole.

It has also been asked why the word "equity" is needed. What equitable causes can grow out of the Constitution and laws of the United States? Hardly any lawsuit between individuals fails to involve some element of fraud, accident, trust or hardship that would make it a matter for equitable rather than legal jurisdiction, as the distinction is known and established in several of the States. For instance, it is the special province of a court of equity to give relief against what are called hard bargains. These are contracts in which there may have been no direct fraud or deceit sufficient to void them in a court of law, yet one party took some undue and unconscionable advantage of the other's needs or misfortunes, which a court of equity will not tolerate. In such cases, where foreigners were involved on either side, the federal courts could not do justice without equitable as well as legal jurisdiction. Agreements to convey lands claimed under grants from different States may supply another example of why the federal courts need equitable jurisdiction. This argument may be less obvious in those States where the formal and technical distinction between LAW and EQUITY is not kept up, as it is in this State, where every day's practice shows it.
The judicial authority of the Union is to extend:

Second. Treaties made, or to be made, under the authority of the United States, and all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls. These fall under the fourth class of cases I listed, because of their evident link to preserving the national peace.
Third. To cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction. Together these form the fifth of the classes of causes I listed as proper for the jurisdiction of the national courts.
Fourth. To controversies to which the United States shall be a party. These make up the third of those classes.

Fifth. Controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States. These fall under the fourth of those classes and, to some degree, share the nature of the last.

Sixth. Cases between citizens of the same State claiming lands under grants from different States. These come within the last class, and they are the only instances in which the proposed Constitution directly provides for jurisdiction over disputes between citizens of one State.

Seventh. To cases between a State or its citizens and foreign states, citizens or subjects. These have already been explained as belonging to the fourth of the classes I listed, and have been shown to be, in a special way, proper subjects for the national judiciary.

This review of the particular powers of the federal judiciary, as marked out in the Constitution, shows that they all conform to the principles that ought to have governed the structure of that department, and that were necessary to the perfection of the system. If some particular problems should appear to be connected with including any of them in the plan, we should remember that the national legislature will have ample authority to make such exceptions, and to prescribe such regulations, as are calculated to prevent or remove those problems. A well-informed mind can never regard the possibility of particular harms as a solid objection to a general principle that is meant to avoid general harms and to obtain general advantages.

chapters.title: No. 81 — The Judiciary Continued, and the Distribution of the Judicial Authority. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Let us now return to the division of judicial authority among different courts, and their relations to each other.

"The judicial power of the United States is" (by the plan of the Convention) "to be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as the Congress may, from time to time, ordain and establish."(1)

That there ought to be one court of supreme and final jurisdiction is a proposition not likely to be contested. The reasons for it have been given elsewhere and are too obvious to need repeating. The only question that seems to have been raised about it is whether it ought to be a distinct body or a branch of the legislature. Here we see the same contradiction that has been noticed in several other cases. The very men who object to the Senate as a court of impeachments, on the ground of an improper mixing of powers, argue, by implication at least, that the final decision of all causes should be vested in the whole or a part of the legislative body.

The arguments, or rather suggestions, on which this charge is founded run to this effect: "The authority of the proposed Supreme Court of the United States, which is to be a separate and independent body, will be superior to that of the legislature. The power of construing the laws according to the spirit of the Constitution will enable that court to mould them into whatever shape it may think proper; especially as its decisions will not be in any manner subject to the revision or correction of the legislative body. This is as unprecedented as it is dangerous. In Britain, the judicial power, in the last resort, resides in the House of Lords, which is a branch of the legislature; and this part of the British government has been imitated in the State constitutions in general. The Parliament of Great Britain, and the legislatures of the several States, can at any time rectify, by law, the exceptionable decisions of their respective courts. But the errors and usurpations of the Supreme Court of the United States will be uncontrollable and remediless." On examination, this will be found to consist entirely of false reasoning from a misunderstood fact.

In the first place, there is not a syllable in the plan under consideration that directly empowers the national courts to construe the laws according to the spirit of the Constitution, or that gives them any greater latitude in this respect than the courts of every State can claim. I admit, however, that the Constitution ought to be the standard for construing the laws, and that wherever there is an evident conflict, the laws ought to give way to the Constitution. But this doctrine does not follow from anything peculiar to the plan of the Convention. It follows from the general theory of a limited Constitution, and as far as it is true, it applies equally to most, if not all, of the State governments. There can be no objection on this account, therefore, to the federal judiciary that would not also lie against the local courts in general, and that would not serve to condemn every constitution that tries to set bounds to legislative discretion.

But perhaps the force of the objection may be thought to lie in the particular organization of the Supreme Court: in its being made up of a distinct body of judges, instead of being a branch of the legislature, as in the government of Great Britain and that of this State. To insist on this point, the authors of the objection must give up the meaning they have labored to attach to the celebrated maxim requiring a separation of the departments of power. Nevertheless, I will concede to them, in keeping with the interpretation given to that maxim in these papers, that it is not violated by vesting the ultimate power of judging in a PART of the legislative body. But though this is not an absolute violation of that excellent rule, it comes so close to one that on this account alone it is less desirable than the mode the Convention preferred. From a body that had even a partial hand in passing bad laws, we could rarely expect a disposition to temper and moderate them in application. The same spirit that had acted in making them would be too apt to act in interpreting them; and still less could we expect men who had infringed the Constitution as legislators to be disposed to repair the breach as judges. Nor is this all. Every reason that recommends the tenure of good behavior for judicial offices argues against placing the judicial power, in the last resort, in a body of men chosen for a limited period. It is absurd to refer the determination of causes in the first instance to judges of permanent standing and in the last instance to judges of a temporary and changing makeup. It is more absurd still to subject the decisions of men selected for their knowledge of the laws, acquired by long and laborious study, to the revision and control of men who, lacking the same advantage, cannot but be deficient in that knowledge. The members of the legislature will rarely be chosen with a view to the qualifications that fit men to be judges. So, just as there will be great reason to fear all the ill consequences of defective information, there will be no less reason, from the natural tendency of such bodies to divide into parties, to fear that the pestilential breath of faction may poison the fountains of justice. The habit of being continually marshaled on opposite sides will be too apt to stifle the voice both of law and of equity.

These considerations teach us to applaud the wisdom of those States that have committed the judicial power, in the last resort, not to a part of the legislature but to distinct and independent bodies of men. Contrary to the supposition of those who have described the plan of the Convention in this respect as novel and unprecedented, it is only a copy of the constitutions of New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. The preference given to those models deserves high praise.

In the second place, it is not true that the Parliament of Great Britain, or the legislatures of the individual States, can rectify the exceptionable decisions of their respective courts in any sense other than one in which a future legislature of the United States could do the same. Neither the British constitution nor the State constitutions in theory authorizes a legislative act to revise a judicial sentence. Nor is there anything in the proposed Constitution, any more than in either of them, that forbids it. In the former as well as the latter, the sole obstacle is the impropriety of the thing on the general principles of law and reason. A legislature, without exceeding its province, cannot reverse a determination once made in a particular case, though it may prescribe a new rule for future cases. This is the principle, and it applies, with all its consequences, in exactly the same manner and extent to the State governments as to the national government now under consideration. Not the least difference can be pointed out in any view of the subject.

It may finally be observed that the supposed danger of judicial encroachments on the legislative authority, which has been repeated on many occasions, is in reality a phantom. Particular misconstructions and contraventions of the will of the legislature may now and then happen, but they can never be so extensive as to amount to a problem, or in any noticeable degree to affect the order of the political system. This may be inferred with certainty from the general nature of the judicial power, from the objects to which it relates, from the manner in which it is exercised, from its comparative weakness, and from its total incapacity to support its usurpations by force. And the inference is greatly strengthened by considering the important constitutional check that the legislative body would have over the members of the judicial department, through the power of instituting impeachments in one part of it and of deciding on them in the other. This alone is a complete security. There can never be danger that the judges, by a series of deliberate usurpations on the authority of the legislature, would risk the united resentment of the body entrusted with that authority, while that body had the means of punishing their presumption by removing them from their stations. While this ought to remove all apprehensions on the subject, it also supplies a cogent argument for making the Senate a court for the trial of impeachments.

Having now examined, and, I trust, removed the objections to the distinct and independent organization of the Supreme Court, I proceed to consider whether it is proper to have the power of constituting inferior courts,(2) and what relations will exist between these and the Supreme Court.

The power of constituting inferior courts is plainly meant to spare us from having to resort to the Supreme Court in every case of federal jurisdiction. It is intended to enable the national government to institute or authorize, in each State or district of the United States, a court competent to decide matters of national jurisdiction within its limits.

But why, it is asked, could the same purpose not have been accomplished through the State courts? This admits of different answers. Even if the fitness and competence of those courts is allowed in the fullest measure, the substance of the power in question may still be regarded as a necessary part of the plan, if only to empower the national legislature to commit to them the jurisdiction of causes arising out of the national Constitution. To confer the power of deciding such causes on the existing courts of the individual States would perhaps be as much "to constitute tribunals" as to create new courts with the same power. But ought not a more direct and explicit provision to have been made in favor of the State courts? There are, in my opinion, substantial reasons against such a provision. The most discerning cannot foresee how far a local spirit may prevail and disqualify the local courts for jurisdiction over national causes; while everyone can see that courts constituted like those of some of the States would be improper channels for the judicial authority of the Union. State judges who hold their offices at pleasure, or from year to year, will be too little independent to be relied on for an inflexible execution of the national laws. And if it were necessary to entrust original jurisdiction over causes arising under those laws to them, it would be equally necessary to leave the door of appeal as wide as possible. The ease or difficulty of appeals ought to be proportioned to the grounds for confidence or distrust in the subordinate courts. I am well satisfied that the appellate jurisdiction is proper in the separate classes of causes to which the plan of the Convention extends it. Still, I should consider anything calculated to give appeals an unrestrained course in practice as a source of public and private problems.

I am not sure that it will not prove highly expedient and useful to divide the United States into four, five or half a dozen districts, and to institute a federal court in each district, in place of one in every State. The judges of these courts, with the aid of the State judges, may hold circuits for the trial of causes in the separate parts of their respective districts. Through them justice may be administered with ease and dispatch, and appeals may safely be confined within a narrow compass. This plan appears to me at present the best of any that could be adopted; and for it to be possible, the power of constituting inferior courts must exist in the full extent in which it is found in the proposed Constitution.

These reasons should satisfy any open mind that lacking such a power would have been a serious defect in the plan. Let us now see how the judicial authority is to be divided between the supreme and inferior courts of the Union.

The Supreme Court is to have original jurisdiction only "in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls, and those in which A STATE shall be a party." Public ministers of every class are the immediate representatives of their sovereigns. All questions in which they are concerned are so directly connected with the public peace that, both to preserve it and out of respect to the sovereignties they represent, it is expedient and proper for such questions to be submitted in the first instance to the highest court of the nation. Consuls do not strictly have a diplomatic character, but since they are the public agents of the nations to which they belong, the same observation applies to them in great measure. In cases in which a State might be a party, it would ill suit its dignity to be turned over to an inferior court.

This may be something of a digression from the subject of this paper, but I will take the occasion to mention a supposition that has caused some alarm on very mistaken grounds. It has been suggested that if the public securities of one State were assigned to the citizens of another, those citizens could sue that State in the federal courts for the amount of the securities. The following considerations prove this suggestion to be without foundation.

It is inherent in the nature of sovereignty not to be subject to suit by an individual without its consent. This is the general sense and the general practice of mankind, and the exemption, as one of the attributes of sovereignty, is now enjoyed by the government of every State in the Union. Unless the plan of the Convention surrenders this immunity, therefore, it will remain with the States, and the danger suggested must be merely imaginary. The circumstances necessary to bring about a transfer of State sovereignty were discussed in considering the article on taxation and need not be repeated here. Returning to the principles established there will satisfy us that there is no color for pretending that the State governments would, by adopting that plan, lose the privilege of paying their own debts in their own way, free from every constraint except that which flows from the obligations of good faith. Contracts between a nation and individuals are binding only on the conscience of the sovereign, and have no pretensions to compulsive force. They confer no right of action independent of the sovereign will. What would be the point of authorizing suits against States for the debts they owe? How could recoveries be enforced? Clearly it could not be done without waging war against the contracting State. To ascribe to the federal courts, by mere implication and in destruction of a pre-existing right of the State governments, a power that would involve such a consequence would be altogether forced and unwarrantable.

Let us pick up the thread again. We have seen that the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court would be limited to two kinds of causes, and those of a kind that seldom occur. In every other case of federal jurisdiction, original jurisdiction would belong to the inferior courts, and the Supreme Court would have only appellate jurisdiction, "with such exceptions and under such regulations as the Congress shall make."

Hardly anyone has questioned the propriety of this appellate jurisdiction in matters of law, but loud clamors have been raised against it in matters of fact. Some well-intentioned men in this State, taking their notions from the language and forms of our own courts, have come to see it as an implied replacement of trial by jury with the civil-law mode of trial used in our courts of admiralty, probate and chancery. They give the term "appellate" a technical sense, because in our legal usage it generally refers to appeals in the civil-law course. But if I am rightly informed, it would not carry that meaning anywhere in New England. There an appeal from one jury to another is familiar in both language and practice, and is even automatic until there have been two verdicts on one side. So the word "appellate" will not be understood the same way in New England as in New York, which shows how wrong it is to adopt a technical reading drawn from the law of any one State. Taken in the abstract, the expression means no more than the power of one court to review the proceedings of another, on the law or the fact or both. How it is done may depend on ancient custom or legislative provision (in a new government it must depend on the latter), and it may be done with or without a jury, as is thought advisable. If, therefore, the Constitution should in any case permit a fact once determined by a jury to be re-examined, it may be regulated so that a second jury does it, either by sending the cause back to the court below for a second trial of the fact, or by directing an issue straight out of the Supreme Court.

But it does not follow that the Supreme Court will be permitted to re-examine a fact once established by a jury. Why may it not be said, with the strictest propriety, when a writ of error is brought from an inferior to a superior court of law in this State, that the latter has jurisdiction of the fact as well as the law? It is true that it cannot begin a new inquiry into the fact, but it takes notice of the fact as it appears on the record and pronounces the law arising from it.(3) This is jurisdiction of both fact and law, and it is not even possible to separate them. Though the common-law courts of this State establish disputed facts by a jury, they undoubtedly have jurisdiction of both fact and law. Accordingly, when the facts are agreed on in the pleadings, they do not resort to a jury but proceed at once to judgment. On this ground, therefore, I contend that the expressions "appellate jurisdiction, both as to law and fact" do not necessarily imply a re-examination in the Supreme Court of facts decided by juries in the inferior courts.

We may well imagine that the following train of thought influenced the Convention in framing this particular provision. The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (it may have been argued) will extend to causes decided in different modes, some in the course of the COMMON LAW, others in the course of the CIVIL LAW. In the former, generally speaking, the proper province of the Supreme Court will be to revise only the law. In the latter, re-examination of the fact is customary, and in some cases, of which prize causes are an example, might be essential to preserving the public peace. It is therefore necessary that the appellate jurisdiction should, in certain cases, extend in the broadest sense to matters of fact. It will not do to make an express exception of cases that were originally tried by a jury, because in the courts of some of the States all causes are tried in this mode(4), and such an exception would preclude the revision of matters of fact where it might be proper as well as where it might be improper. To avoid all problems, it will be safest to declare in general terms that the Supreme Court shall have appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact, and that this jurisdiction shall be subject to such exceptions and regulations as the national legislature may prescribe. This will enable the government to shape it in the manner that will best serve the ends of public justice and security.

This view of the matter, at any rate, puts it beyond all doubt that the supposed abolition of trial by jury through this provision is false and untrue. The legislature of the United States would certainly have full power to provide that in appeals to the Supreme Court there should be no re-examination of facts that had been tried by juries in the original causes. This would certainly be an authorized exception. If, for the reason I have already suggested, it should be thought too broad, it might be qualified by confining it to those causes only that are decided at common law by that mode of trial.

The sum of the observations made so far on the authority of the judicial department is this. It has been carefully restricted to those causes that are plainly proper for the jurisdiction of the national judiciary. In the division of this authority, a very small portion of original jurisdiction has been kept for the Supreme Court and the rest assigned to the subordinate courts. The Supreme Court will have appellate jurisdiction, both as to law and fact, in all the cases referred to it, subject in both respects to any exceptions and regulations that may be thought advisable. This appellate jurisdiction in no case abolishes trial by jury. And an ordinary degree of prudence and integrity in the national councils will secure for us solid advantages from the establishment of the proposed judiciary, without exposing us to any of the problems that have been predicted from that source.
1. Article 3, Sec. 1.

2. This power has been absurdly represented as intended to abolish all the county courts in the individual States, which are commonly called inferior courts. But the expressions of the Constitution are, to constitute "tribunals INFERIOR TO THE SUPREME COURT"; and the evident design of the provision is to enable the institution of local courts, subordinate to the Supreme, either in States or larger districts. It is ridiculous to imagine that county courts were in contemplation.
3. This word is composed of JUS and DICTIO, juris dictio or a speaking and pronouncing of the law.
4. I hold that the States will have concurrent jurisdiction with the subordinate federal courts in many cases of federal jurisdiction, as will be explained in my next paper.

chapters.title: No. 82 — The Judiciary Continued. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The creation of a new government, however much care or wisdom marks the work, cannot fail to raise questions of intricacy and nicety. These may be expected to arise in a special way from establishing a constitution founded on the total or partial incorporation of a number of distinct sovereignties. Only time can mature and perfect so compound a system, settle the meaning of all its parts, and adjust them to one another in a harmonious and consistent WHOLE.

Such questions have accordingly arisen on the plan proposed by the Convention, particularly concerning the judiciary department. The principal ones concern the position of the State courts with respect to those causes that are to be submitted to federal jurisdiction. Is this jurisdiction to be exclusive, or are those courts to have a concurrent jurisdiction? If the latter, what relation will they have to the national courts? These are inquiries we hear from men of sense, and they certainly deserve attention.

The principles established in an earlier paper(1) teach us that the States will keep all pre-existing authorities that are not exclusively delegated to the federal head, and that exclusive delegation can exist only in one of three cases. The first is where an exclusive authority is granted to the Union in express terms. The second is where a particular authority is granted to the Union and the exercise of a like authority is forbidden to the States. The third is where an authority is granted to the Union with which a similar authority in the States would be utterly incompatible. These principles may not apply with the same force to the judiciary as to the legislative power. Still, I am inclined to think they are, in the main, just with respect to the former as well as the latter. With this in mind, I shall lay it down as a rule that the State courts will keep the jurisdiction they now have, unless it appears to be taken away in one of the ways I have listed.

The only thing in the proposed Constitution that has the appearance of confining causes of federal jurisdiction to the federal courts is this passage: "THE JUDICIAL POWER of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as the Congress shall from time to time ordain and establish." This might be construed to mean that the supreme and subordinate courts of the Union alone should have the power of deciding those causes to which their authority is to extend. Or it might simply denote that the organs of the national judiciary should be one Supreme Court and as many subordinate courts as Congress should think proper to appoint. In other words, the United States would exercise the judicial power with which they are to be invested through one supreme court and a certain number of inferior ones, to be instituted by them. The first construction excludes the concurrent jurisdiction of the State courts; the last admits it. And since the first would amount to a transfer of State power by implication, the last appears to me the most natural and the most defensible construction.

But this doctrine of concurrent jurisdiction clearly applies only to those kinds of causes of which the State courts have previous jurisdiction. It is not equally evident in relation to cases that may grow out of, and be peculiar to, the Constitution to be established; for denying the State courts jurisdiction in such cases can hardly be considered a curtailment of a pre-existing authority. I do not mean to contend, therefore, that the United States, in legislating on the objects entrusted to their direction, may not commit the decision of causes arising under a particular regulation solely to the federal courts, if such a measure should be thought expedient. But I hold that the State courts will lose no part of their original jurisdiction, except as it may relate to an appeal; and I am even of the opinion that in every case in which they are not expressly excluded by future acts of the national legislature, they will of course take jurisdiction of the causes to which those acts may give birth. I infer this from the nature of judicial power and from the general character of the system. The judicial power of every government looks beyond its own local or municipal laws, and in civil cases takes hold of all subjects of litigation between parties within its jurisdiction, though the causes of dispute relate to the laws of the most distant part of the globe. Those of Japan, no less than those of New York, may furnish matters of legal discussion to our courts. When in addition we consider the State governments and the national government as they truly are, as kindred systems and as parts of ONE WHOLE, the inference seems conclusive that the State courts would have a concurrent jurisdiction in all cases arising under the laws of the Union, where it was not expressly prohibited.

Here another question arises: what relation would exist between the national and State courts in these instances of concurrent jurisdiction? I answer that an appeal would certainly lie from the latter to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Constitution in direct terms gives the Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction in all the listed cases of federal jurisdiction in which it is not to have original jurisdiction, without a single expression to confine this to the inferior federal courts. Only the objects of appeal are contemplated, not the courts from which the appeal is to be made. From this circumstance, and from the reason of the thing, the provision ought to be construed to extend to the State courts. Either this must be the case, or the local courts must be excluded from concurrent jurisdiction in matters of national concern; otherwise the judicial authority of the Union may be evaded at the pleasure of every plaintiff or prosecutor. Neither of these consequences ought to be accepted without evident necessity. The latter would be entirely inadmissible, as it would defeat some of the most important and avowed purposes of the proposed government and would seriously hamper its measures. Nor do I see any foundation for such a supposition. As I have already remarked, the national and State systems are to be regarded as ONE WHOLE. The courts of the latter will naturally be auxiliaries in executing the laws of the Union, and an appeal from them will as naturally lie to the court that is destined to unite and bring into line the principles of national justice and the rules of national decisions. The evident aim of the plan of the Convention is that all the causes of the specified classes shall, for weighty public reasons, receive their original or final determination in the courts of the Union. To confine the general expressions giving appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court to appeals from the subordinate federal courts, instead of allowing them to extend to the State courts, would be to narrow the breadth of the terms and defeat their intent, contrary to every sound rule of interpretation.

But could an appeal lie from the State courts to the subordinate federal courts? This is another question that has been raised, and a harder one than the last. The following considerations favor the affirmative. First, the plan of the Convention authorizes the national legislature "to constitute tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court."(2) Next, it declares that "the JUDICIAL POWER of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as Congress shall ordain and establish"; and it then lists the cases to which this judicial power shall extend. It afterwards divides the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court into original and appellate, but defines nothing for the subordinate courts. The only outlines drawn for them are that they shall be "inferior to the Supreme Court" and that they shall not go beyond the specified limits of the federal judiciary. Whether their authority is to be original or appellate, or both, is not stated. All of this seems to be left to the discretion of the legislature. That being so, I see at present no obstacle to establishing an appeal from the State courts to the subordinate national courts, and many advantages of having that power can be imagined. It would lessen the motive to multiply federal courts and would allow arrangements to narrow the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. The State courts could then be left with fuller charge of federal causes; and appeals, in most cases where they are thought proper, instead of going to the Supreme Court, could lie from the State courts to district courts of the Union.
2. Sec. 8, Art. 1.

chapters.title: No. 83 — The Judiciary Continued in Relation to Trial by Jury (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The objection to the plan of the Convention that has had the most success in this State, and perhaps in several of the other States, is that the Constitution makes no provision for trial by jury in civil cases. The dishonest way in which this objection is usually stated has been pointed out and exposed more than once, but the opponents of the plan keep pressing it in all their conversations and writings. The mere silence of the Constitution about civil cases is presented as an abolition of trial by jury. The speeches for which this silence has served as a pretext are cleverly designed to persuade people that the supposed abolition is complete and universal, reaching not only every kind of civil case but even criminal cases. To argue about the criminal cases, however, would be as vain and fruitless as to attempt a serious proof that matter exists, or to demonstrate any of those propositions that carry conviction by their own evidence once they are put in language that conveys their meaning.

With regard to civil cases, subtleties almost too contemptible to refute have been used to support the notion that a thing which is merely not provided for has been entirely abolished. Every discerning person must see at once the wide difference between silence and abolition. But the inventors of this fallacy have tried to support it with certain legal maxims of interpretation, which they have twisted away from their true meaning, so it may not be wholly useless to examine the ground they have taken.

The maxims they rely on are of this kind: "A specification of particulars is an exclusion of generals"; or, "The expression of one thing is the exclusion of another." From these, they say, it follows that because the Constitution has established trial by jury in criminal cases and is silent about civil cases, this silence is an implied prohibition of trial by jury in the latter.

The rules of legal interpretation are rules of common sense, adopted by the courts in construing the laws. The true test of whether they are applied justly, therefore, is whether the application conforms to the source from which they come. This being so, let me ask whether it is consistent with common sense to suppose that a provision obliging the legislative power to commit the trial of criminal cases to juries takes away its right to authorize or permit that mode of trial in other cases. Is it natural to suppose that a command to do one thing is a prohibition against doing another, which the legislature already had the power to do and which is not incompatible with the thing commanded? If such a supposition would be unnatural and unreasonable, it cannot be rational to maintain that a requirement of trial by jury in certain cases forbids it in others.

A power to establish courts is a power to prescribe the mode of trial. Consequently, if the Constitution had said nothing on the subject of juries, the legislature would be free either to adopt that institution or to leave it alone. In criminal cases this discretion is limited by the express requirement of trial by jury in all such cases; but in civil cases, of course, it is left unrestricted, since there is total silence on that point. Specifying an obligation to try all criminal cases in a particular mode does exclude any obligation or necessity of using the same mode in civil cases, but it does not limit the legislature's power to use that mode if it thinks proper. The pretense, therefore, that the national legislature would not be at full liberty to submit all the civil cases of federal cognizance to the decision of juries is a pretense with no just foundation.

We have now seen that the maxims cannot support the use made of them. Let us try to establish what their proper use and true meaning are. Examples will do this best. The plan of the Convention states that the power of Congress, in other words of the national legislature, is to reach certain listed cases. Listing particulars in this way plainly rules out any claim to a general legislative authority, since it would be absurd and pointless to grant special powers affirmatively if a general authority was intended.

In the same way, the Constitution declares that the judicial authority of the federal courts comprehends certain particularly specified cases. The listing of those cases marks the precise limits beyond which the federal courts cannot extend their jurisdiction. Since the objects of their cognizance are enumerated, the specification would be meaningless if it did not exclude any idea of a more extensive authority.

These examples are enough to explain the maxims that have been mentioned and to show the way in which they should be used. But so that there may be no misunderstanding on this subject, I shall add one more case, to demonstrate the proper use of these maxims and the abuse that has been made of them.

Let us suppose that under the laws of this State a married woman was incapable of conveying her estate, and that the legislature, considering this an evil, should enact that she might dispose of her property by a deed executed in the presence of a public official. In such a case there can be no doubt that the specification would amount to an exclusion of any other mode of conveyance, because the woman had no previous power to transfer her property, and the specification determines the particular mode she is to use for that purpose. But let us further suppose that in a later part of the same act it should be declared that no woman may dispose of any estate of a given value without the consent of three of her nearest relations, shown by their signing the deed. Could anyone infer from this regulation that a married woman might not obtain her relations' approval of a deed conveying property of lesser value? The position is too absurd to merit a refutation, and yet this is precisely the position that must be established by those who contend that trial by jury in civil cases is abolished because it is expressly provided for in criminal cases.

The friends and the adversaries of the plan of the Convention, if they agree in nothing else, at least agree in the value they set upon trial by jury. If there is any difference between them, it is this: the former regard it as a valuable safeguard of liberty, while the latter call it the very palladium of free government. For my own part, the more I have seen of how the institution operates, the more reason I have found to hold it in high esteem. It would be altogether superfluous to examine how far it deserves to be thought useful or essential in a representative republic, or how much more merit it may have as a defense against the oppressions of a hereditary monarch than as a barrier against the tyranny of popular public officials in a popular government. Discussions of this kind would be more curious than beneficial, since everyone is satisfied of the usefulness of the institution and of its friendly aspect toward liberty. But I must acknowledge that I cannot readily see the inseparable connection between the existence of liberty and trial by jury in civil cases. Arbitrary impeachments, arbitrary methods of prosecuting pretended offenses, and arbitrary punishments following arbitrary convictions have always appeared to me the great engines of judicial despotism, and these all relate to criminal proceedings. Trial by jury in criminal cases, aided by the habeas corpus act, therefore seems to be the only thing concerned in the question. And both of these are provided for, in the most ample manner, in the plan of the Convention.
Some have said that trial by jury protects against oppressive use of the power of taxation. This claim deserves a closer look.

Plainly, trial by jury cannot affect the legislature's decisions about how much tax to lay, what to tax, or by what rule to apportion it. If it can have any effect at all, therefore, the effect must be on how taxes are collected and on how the officers charged with enforcing the revenue laws behave.

As for the manner of collection in this State under our own Constitution, trial by jury is in most cases not used. Taxes are usually raised by the quicker procedure of seizing and selling property, as is done for rent. Everyone acknowledges that this is essential if the revenue laws are to be effective. A slow lawsuit to recover the taxes owed by each individual would suit neither the needs of the public nor the convenience of the citizens. It would often pile up costs heavier than the tax originally due.

And as for the behavior of the revenue officers, the provision for trial by jury in criminal cases will give the security that is wanted. Deliberate abuses of public authority that oppress the subject, and every form of extortion by officials, are offenses against the government. Those who commit them may be indicted and punished as the circumstances of the case require.

The excellence of trial by jury in civil cases appears to depend on circumstances unrelated to the preservation of liberty. The strongest argument in its favor is that it is a security against corruption. There is always more time and better opportunity to tamper with a standing body of judges than with a jury summoned for the occasion, so there is reason to suppose that a corrupt influence would find its way more easily to the former than to the latter. The force of this consideration is, however, reduced by others. The sheriff, who summons ordinary juries, and the clerks of the courts, who nominate special juries, are themselves standing officers, and, acting individually, may be supposed more open to the touch of corruption than the judges, who are a collective body. It is not difficult to see that those officers would have the power to select jurors who would serve the purpose of the party as well as a corrupted bench. In the next place, it may fairly be supposed that there would be less difficulty in gaining over some of the jurors taken at random from the public at large than in gaining over men chosen by the government for their integrity and good character. But even after making every deduction for these considerations, trial by jury must still be a valuable check upon corruption. It greatly multiplies the obstacles to its success. As matters now stand, it would be necessary to corrupt both court and jury; for where the jury have gone clearly wrong, the court will generally grant a new trial, and it would in most cases be of little use to work on the jury unless the court could be gained as well. Here then is a double security, and it will readily be seen that this combined arrangement tends to preserve the purity of both institutions. By increasing the obstacles to success, it discourages attempts to seduce the integrity of either. The temptations to prostitute themselves that the judges might have to resist must certainly be much fewer, while the cooperation of a jury is necessary, than they would be if the judges had the exclusive determination of all cases.

Notwithstanding the doubts I have expressed as to whether trial by jury in civil cases is essential to liberty, therefore, I admit that in most cases, under proper regulations, it is an excellent method of deciding questions of property. On that account alone it would deserve a constitutional provision in its favor, if it were possible to fix the limits within which it ought to be confined. There is, however, great difficulty in this in all cases; and men not blinded by enthusiasm must be aware that in a federal government, which is a composition of societies whose ideas and institutions on the matter differ materially from one another, that difficulty must be not a little increased. For my own part, every time I look at the subject anew, I become more convinced of the reality of the obstacles which, we are authoritatively informed, prevented the insertion of a provision on this head in the plan of the Convention.

Few people understand how greatly the limits of jury trial differ from State to State. Because this bears considerably on the judgment we should pass on the omission complained of, I need to explain it. Of all the States, ours has judicial establishments that most closely resemble those of Great Britain. We have courts of common law, courts of probates (analogous in certain matters to the spiritual courts in England), a court of admiralty and a court of chancery. In the courts of common law only does trial by jury prevail, and even there with some exceptions. In all the others a single judge presides and proceeds in general according to the course of the canon or civil law, without the aid of a jury.(1) In New Jersey there is a court of chancery which proceeds like ours, but there are neither courts of admiralty nor of probates in the sense in which these last are established with us. In that State the courts of common law have cognizance of those cases which with us are decided in the courts of admiralty and of probates, and of course jury trial is more extensive in New Jersey than in New York. In Pennsylvania this is perhaps still more the case, for there is no court of chancery in that State, and its common-law courts have equity jurisdiction. It has a court of admiralty, but none of probates, at least on the plan of ours. Delaware has in these respects imitated Pennsylvania. Maryland comes closer to New York, as does Virginia, except that the latter has more than one chancellor. North Carolina has most in common with Pennsylvania, South Carolina with Virginia. I believe, however, that in some of those States which have separate courts of admiralty, the cases pending in them are tried by juries. In Georgia there are none but common-law courts, and an appeal of course lies from the verdict of one jury to another, which is called a special jury, and for which a particular mode of appointment is set out. In Connecticut they have no separate courts of either chancery or admiralty, and their courts of probates have no jurisdiction over cases. Their common-law courts have admiralty jurisdiction and, to a certain extent, equity jurisdiction. In cases of importance their General Assembly is the only court of chancery. In Connecticut, therefore, trial by jury extends in practice further than in any other State yet mentioned. Rhode Island is, I believe, in this respect much in the situation of Connecticut. Massachusetts and New Hampshire are in a similar position as regards the blending of law, equity and admiralty jurisdictions. In the four Eastern States trial by jury not only stands on a broader foundation than in the other States, but is attended with a peculiarity unknown, in its full extent, to any of them. There is an appeal of course from one jury to another, until there have been two verdicts out of three on one side.

From this sketch it appears that there is a material diversity, in the form as well as in the extent of the institution of trial by jury in civil cases, among the individual States. Two obvious reflections follow from this fact. First, the Convention could not have fixed upon any general rule that would have suited the circumstances of all the States. Second, more, or at least as much, might have been risked by taking the system of any one State as a standard than by omitting a provision altogether and leaving the matter, as has been done, to legislative regulation.

The proposals made to fill the gap have illustrated the difficulty more than they have removed it. The minority of Pennsylvania has proposed these words for the purpose—"Trial by jury shall be as heretofore"—and this, I maintain, would be senseless and meaningless. The United States, in their united or collective capacity, are the OBJECT to which all general provisions in the Constitution must necessarily be taken to refer. Now it is evident that although trial by jury, with various limitations, is known in each State individually, in the United States as such it is at this time altogether unknown, because the present federal government has no judiciary power whatever; and consequently there is no proper antecedent or previous establishment to which the word heretofore could relate. It would therefore lack a precise meaning and, from its uncertainty, would have no effect.

Just as the form of the provision would not fulfill the intent of its proposers, so, if I understand that intent rightly, the provision would on the other hand be inexpedient in itself. I presume the intent to be that cases in the federal courts should be tried by jury if, in the State where the court sat, that mode of trial would be used in a similar case in the State courts; that is to say, admiralty cases would be tried by a jury in Connecticut and without one in New York. The capricious operation of so dissimilar a method of trial in the same cases, under the same government, is by itself enough to turn every well-regulated judgment against it. Whether a case should be tried with or without a jury would depend, in a great number of cases, on the accidental location of the court and the parties.

But in my judgment this is not the greatest objection. I am deeply and deliberately convinced that there are many cases for which trial by jury is unsuitable. I think this especially true of cases that affect the public peace with foreign nations—that is, most cases in which the question turns wholly on the laws of nations. Among others, all prize cases are of this kind. Juries cannot be supposed competent to inquiries that demand a thorough knowledge of the laws and usages of nations. They will also sometimes be swayed by impressions that keep them from giving enough weight to the considerations of public policy that ought to guide their inquiries. There would therefore always be a danger that their decisions would violate the rights of other nations and so give occasion for reprisals and war. It is true that the proper province of juries is to decide matters of fact, but in most cases the legal consequences are so tangled up with the facts that the two cannot be separated.

It will add great weight to this remark about prize cases to mention that the method of deciding them has been thought worthy of particular regulation in various treaties between different powers of Europe, and that, under such treaties, they are decided in Great Britain, in the last resort, before the king himself in his privy council, where the facts as well as the law are re-examined. This alone demonstrates the unwisdom of inserting in the Constitution a fundamental provision that would make the State systems a standard for the national government in the article under consideration. It also shows the danger of burdening the government with any constitutional provisions whose propriety is not beyond dispute.

My convictions are equally strong that great advantages result from separating the equity jurisdiction from the law jurisdiction, and that the cases belonging to the former would be improperly committed to juries. The great and primary use of a court of equity is to give relief in extraordinary cases, which are exceptions(2) to general rules. To unite the jurisdiction over such cases with the ordinary jurisdiction must tend to unsettle the general rules and to subject every case that arises to a special determination. Separating the one from the other has the opposite effect: it makes one a sentinel over the other and keeps each within its proper limits. Besides this, the circumstances that make cases proper for courts of equity are in many instances so delicate and intricate that they are incompatible with the character of trials by jury. They often require such long, deliberate and critical investigation as would be impracticable for men called from their occupations and obliged to decide before they were permitted to return to them. The simplicity and speed that distinguish this mode of trial require that the matter to be decided be reduced to some single and obvious point, while the litigation usual in chancery frequently comprehends a long train of minute and independent particulars.

It is true that separating the equity jurisdiction from the legal jurisdiction is peculiar to the English system of jurisprudence, which several of the States have taken as their model. But it is equally true that wherever the two have been united, trial by jury has been unknown. And the separation is essential if that institution is to be kept in its original purity. A court of equity can readily extend its jurisdiction to matters of law. But there is considerable reason to suspect that extending the jurisdiction of the courts of law to matters of equity would not only fail to bring the advantages that courts of chancery can give on the plan on which they are established in this State. It would also tend, little by little, to change the nature of the courts of law and to undermine trial by jury, by bringing in questions too complicated to be decided in that mode.

These appear to be conclusive reasons against building the systems of all the States into the national judiciary, which is what the Pennsylvania minority may be guessed to have been attempting. Let us now examine how far the Massachusetts proposal is likely to cure the supposed defect.

It is in this form: "In civil actions between citizens of different States, every issue of fact, arising in actions at common law, may be tried by a jury if the parties, or either of them, request it."

This, at best, is a proposal confined to one kind of case. The fair inference is either that the Massachusetts convention considered this the only class of federal cases in which trial by jury would be proper, or that, if it desired a more extensive provision, it found it impracticable to devise one that would properly serve the purpose. If the first, the omission of a regulation concerning so limited an object can never be considered a material imperfection in the system. If the last, it strongly confirms the extreme difficulty of the thing.

But this is not all. If we recall the observations already made about the courts that exist in the individual States of the Union and the different powers exercised by them, it will appear that no expressions are more vague and indeterminate than those used to describe the kind of cases that are meant to be entitled to trial by jury. In this State the boundaries between actions at common law and actions of equitable jurisdiction are fixed in accordance with the rules that prevail in England on that subject. In many of the other States the boundaries are less precise. In some of them every case is to be tried in a court of common law, and on that footing every action may be considered an action at common law, to be decided by a jury if the parties, or either of them, choose it. Hence the same irregularity and confusion that I have already noticed as resulting from the regulation proposed by the Pennsylvania minority would be introduced by complying with this proposal. In one State a case would be decided by a jury if the parties, or either of them, requested it; but in another State a case exactly similar to the first must be decided without a jury, because the State courts differed as to common-law jurisdiction.

Clearly, then, the Massachusetts proposal cannot work as a general rule until the different States adopt some uniform plan for the limits between common-law and equitable jurisdictions. Devising such a plan is hard in itself and would take much time and thought to perfect. It would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to suggest any general regulation that all the States in the Union would accept, or that would fit exactly with the institutions of every individual State.

It may be asked, why could not a reference have been made to the constitution of this State, taking that, which I allow to be a good one, as a standard for the United States? I answer that it is not very probable that the other States would think of our institutions as we do ourselves. It is natural to suppose that they are so far more attached to their own, and that each would struggle for the preference. If the plan of taking one State as a model for the whole had been thought of in the Convention, it is to be presumed that adopting it in that body would have been made difficult by each delegation's preference for its own government; and it must be uncertain which of the States would have been taken as the model. It has been shown that many of them would be improper ones. And I leave it to conjecture whether, all things considered, it is most likely that New York or some other State would have been preferred. But suppose that a judicious selection could have been made in the Convention. There would still have been great danger of jealousy and disgust in the other States at the bias shown toward the institutions of one. The enemies of the plan would have been furnished with a fine pretext for raising a host of local prejudices against it, which might perhaps have endangered, in no small degree, its final establishment.

To avoid the difficulties of defining the cases that trial by jury ought to embrace, men of enthusiastic temper sometimes suggest that a provision might have been inserted establishing it in all cases whatsoever. For this, I believe, no precedent is to be found in any member of the Union; and the considerations that have been stated in discussing the proposal of the minority of Pennsylvania must satisfy every sober mind that establishing trial by jury in all cases would have been an unpardonable error in the plan.

In short, the more the matter is considered, the more difficult will appear the task of shaping a provision in such a form that it does not say too little to serve the purpose or too much to be advisable, and that it does not open other sources of opposition to the great and essential object of introducing a firm national government.

On the other hand, I cannot help believing that the different lights in which the subject has been placed in these observations will go far toward removing the apprehensions that open-minded persons may have felt about it. They have tended to show that the security of liberty is materially at stake only in trial by jury in criminal cases, which the plan of the Convention provides for in the most ample manner. They have also tended to show that, in by far the greatest proportion of civil cases, and in those that concern the great body of the community, that mode of trial will stay in full force as established by the State constitutions, untouched and unaffected by the plan of the Convention. They have further tended to show that the plan abolishes it(3) in no case, and that there are great, if not insurmountable, difficulties in the way of making any precise and proper provision for it in a Constitution for the United States.

The best judges of the matter will be the least anxious to have trial by jury in civil cases established in the Constitution. They will be the most ready to admit that the constant changes in the affairs of society may make a different way of deciding questions of property preferable in many of the cases where trial by jury now prevails. For my part, I acknowledge that I am convinced that even in this State it could usefully be extended to some cases to which it does not now apply, and could just as usefully be restricted in others. All reasonable men concede that it ought not to apply in all cases. Innovations that narrow its ancient limits, in these States as well as in Great Britain, strongly suggest that its former extent has been found inconvenient, and leave room to suppose that future experience may show the wisdom and usefulness of other exceptions. I suspect that, by the nature of the thing, it is impossible to fix the beneficial point at which the institution ought to stop operating, and to me this is a strong argument for leaving the matter to the discretion of the legislature.

This is now clearly understood to be the case in Great Britain, and it is equally so in the State of Connecticut. Yet it can safely be affirmed that more encroachments on trial by jury have been made in this State since the Revolution, although a positive article of our constitution provides for it, than in the same time in either Connecticut or Great Britain. It may be added that these encroachments have generally begun with the men who try to persuade the people that they are the warmest defenders of popular liberty, but who have seldom allowed constitutional obstacles to stop them in a favorite course. The truth is that the general CHARACTER of a government is all that can be substantially relied upon for lasting effects. Particular provisions, though not altogether useless, have far less virtue and effectiveness than are commonly ascribed to them; and the want of them will never be, with men of sound discernment, a decisive objection to any plan that shows the leading characters of a good government.

It certainly sounds more than a little harsh and extraordinary to claim that a Constitution offers no security for liberty, though it expressly establishes trial by jury in criminal cases, merely because it does not do so in civil cases too. Meanwhile it is notorious that Connecticut, always regarded as the most popular State in the Union, can boast of no constitutional provision for either.

1. It has been wrongly suggested that the court of chancery generally tries disputed facts by a jury. The truth is that such references to a jury seldom occur in that court, and in no case are they necessary except where the validity of a devise of land is in question.

2. It is true that the principles governing that relief have now been reduced to a regular system; but it is no less true that they apply, in the main, to SPECIAL circumstances, which form exceptions to general rules.
3. See No. 81, in which the supposition that it is abolished by vesting the appellate jurisdiction in matters of fact in the Supreme Court is examined and refuted.

chapters.title: No. 84 — Certain General and Miscellaneous Objections to the Constitution Considered and Answered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: In the preceding review of the Constitution, I have noted most of the objections that have been raised against it and have tried to answer them. A few remain, however, that either did not fall naturally under any particular head or were forgotten in their proper places. I will take them up now. Since this subject has already been drawn out to great length, I will keep to brevity by putting all my observations on these miscellaneous points into a single paper.

The most considerable of the remaining objections is that the plan of the Convention contains no bill of rights. Among the other answers given to this, it has been pointed out on various occasions that the constitutions of several of the States are in the same position. I add that New York is one of them. Yet the opponents of the new system in this State, who profess unlimited admiration for its constitution, are among the most intemperate champions of a bill of rights. To justify their zeal, they allege two things. One is that, although the constitution of New York has no bill of rights placed at its head, it contains in the body of the document various provisions in favor of particular privileges and rights, which in substance amount to the same thing. The other is that the constitution adopts the common law and statute law of Great Britain in their full extent, and that these equally secure many other rights that it does not state.
To the first, I answer that the Constitution proposed by the Convention contains a number of such provisions, just as the constitution of this State does.

Apart from those that concern the structure of the government, we find the following. Article 1, section 3, clause 7—"Judgment in cases of impeachment shall not extend further than to removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States; but the party convicted shall, nevertheless, be liable and subject to indictment, trial, judgment, and punishment according to law." Section 9 of the same article, clause 2—"The privilege of the writ of habeas corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in cases of rebellion or invasion the public safety may require it." Clause 3—"No bill of attainder or ex-post-facto law shall be passed." Clause 7—"No title of nobility shall be granted by the United States; and no person holding any office of profit or trust under them, shall, without the consent of the Congress, accept of any present, emolument, office, or title of any kind whatever, from any king, prince, or foreign state." Article 3, section 2, clause 3—"The trial of all crimes, except in cases of impeachment, shall be by jury; and such trial shall be held in the State where the said crimes shall have been committed; but when not committed within any State, the trial shall be at such place or places as the Congress may by law have directed." Section 3 of the same article—"Treason against the United States shall consist only in levying war against them, or in adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort. No person shall be convicted of treason, unless on the testimony of two witnesses to the same overt act, or on confession in open court." And clause 3 of the same section—"The Congress shall have power to declare the punishment of treason; but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attainted."

It may well be asked whether, on the whole, these provisions are not as important as any in the constitution of this State. Establishing the writ of habeas corpus and prohibiting ex post facto laws and TITLES OF NOBILITY, for which our own constitution has no corresponding provision, are perhaps greater securities for liberty and republicanism than anything it contains. Creating crimes after the act was committed, which means punishing men for things that were breaches of no law when they were done, and the practice of arbitrary imprisonment have in every age been tyranny's favorite and most formidable instruments. The remarks of the judicious Blackstone(1) on the latter are well worth repeating: "To bereave a man of life, (says he) or by violence to confiscate his estate, without accusation or trial, would be so gross and notorious an act of despotism, as must at once convey the alarm of tyranny throughout the whole nation; but confinement of the person, by secretly hurrying him to jail, where his sufferings are unknown or forgotten, is a less public, a less striking, and therefore a more dangerous engine of arbitrary government." And as a remedy for this fatal evil he speaks everywhere with particular emphasis in praise of the habeas corpus act, which in one place he calls "the BULWARK of the British Constitution."(2)

I need not argue for the importance of banning titles of nobility. It may fairly be called the cornerstone of republican government, because as long as such titles are excluded, there can be no serious danger that the government will be anything but the people's own.

To the second, that is, to the pretended establishment of the common law and state law by the Constitution, I answer that they are expressly made subject "to such alterations and provisions as the legislature shall from time to time make concerning the same." They are therefore liable at any moment to repeal by the ordinary legislative power, and so have no constitutional sanction. The only purpose of the declaration was to recognize the ancient law and to remove doubts that the Revolution might have caused. It can therefore be considered no part of a declaration of rights, which under our constitutions must be meant as limitations on the power of the government itself.

It has been truly remarked several times that bills of rights were originally agreements between kings and their subjects: curtailments of prerogative in favor of privilege, reservations of rights not surrendered to the prince. Such was MAGNA CHARTA, which the barons obtained from King John with sword in hand. Such were the later confirmations of that charter by succeeding princes. Such was the Petition of Right, to which Charles I. assented at the beginning of his reign. Such also was the Declaration of Right that the Lords and Commons presented to the Prince of Orange in 1688, and which was afterward put into the form of an act of parliament called the Bill of Rights. It is evident, therefore, that in their original meaning they have no application to constitutions that are openly founded on the power of the people and carried out by their immediate representatives and servants. Here, strictly speaking, the people surrender nothing; and since they retain everything, they have no need of particular reservations. "WE, THE PEOPLE of the United States, to secure the blessings of liberty to ourselves and our posterity, do ordain and establish this Constitution for the United States of America." Here is a better recognition of popular rights than volumes of those maxims which fill the principal place in several of our State bills of rights, and which would sound much better in a treatise on ethics than in a constitution of government.

But a minute listing of particular rights is certainly far less suited to a Constitution like this one, which is intended merely to regulate the general political interests of the nation, than to a constitution that regulates every kind of personal and private concern. If the loud clamors against the plan of the Convention on this score are well founded, therefore, no word of condemnation will be too strong for the constitution of this State. But the truth is that both of them contain everything that, in relation to their objects, can reasonably be wished.

I will go further and say that bills of rights, in the sense and to the extent demanded, are not merely unnecessary in the proposed Constitution but would even be dangerous. They would list exceptions to powers that are not granted, and for that very reason would hand people a plausible excuse to claim more power than was granted. Why declare that things shall not be done when no power exists to do them? Why, for instance, say that the liberty of the press shall not be restrained, when no power is given that could impose restrictions? I do not contend that such a provision would confer a power to regulate. But it is evident that it would give men inclined to usurp power a plausible pretense for claiming it. They could argue, with some show of reason, that the Constitution should not be charged with the absurdity of guarding against the abuse of an authority that was never given, and that a provision against restraining the liberty of the press clearly implied that the national government was meant to hold a power to prescribe proper regulations for it. This is one sample of the many handles that an ill-judged zeal for bills of rights would give to the doctrine of constructive powers.

On the subject of the liberty of the press, much as has been said about it, I cannot refrain from adding a remark or two. In the first place, I observe that there is not a syllable about it in the constitution of this State. In the next place, I contend that whatever has been said about it in the constitution of any other State amounts to nothing. What does a declaration that "the liberty of the press shall be inviolably preserved" signify? What is the liberty of the press? Who can give it any definition that would not leave the utmost room for evasion? I hold this to be impracticable; and from this I infer that its security, whatever fine declarations may be inserted in any constitution respecting it, must depend altogether on public opinion and on the general spirit of the people and of the government.(3) And here, after all, as I suggested on another occasion, we must look for the only solid basis of all our rights.

One other way of looking at this matter remains, and it will conclude the point. The truth is, after all the speeches we have heard, that the Constitution is itself, in every rational sense and for every useful purpose, A BILL OF RIGHTS. The various bills of rights in Great Britain make up its Constitution, and conversely the constitution of each State is its bill of rights. And the proposed Constitution, if adopted, will be the bill of rights of the Union. Is it one object of a bill of rights to declare and specify the political privileges of the citizens in the structure and administration of the government? This is done in the most ample and precise manner in the plan of the Convention, which includes various precautions for the public security that are not to be found in any of the State constitutions. Is another object of a bill of rights to define certain immunities and modes of proceeding that relate to personal and private concerns? We have seen that this too has been attended to, in a variety of cases, in the same plan. Considering, therefore, the substantial meaning of a bill of rights, it is absurd to allege that none is to be found in the work of the Convention. It may be said that it does not go far enough, though it will not be easy to make this appear; but it cannot properly be argued that there is no such thing. It must certainly be immaterial in what order the rights of the citizens are declared, as long as they are to be found somewhere in the instrument that establishes the government. It must therefore be apparent that much of what has been said on this subject rests merely on distinctions of word and name that have nothing to do with the substance of the thing.

Another objection has been made, and from the frequency with which it is repeated it may be presumed to be relied on. It is of this kind: "It is improper (say the objectors) to confer such large powers, as are proposed, upon the national government, because the seat of that government must of necessity be too remote from many of the States to admit of a proper knowledge on the part of the constituent, of the conduct of the representative body." This argument, if it proves anything, proves that there ought to be no general government at all. For the powers that all sides seem to agree ought to be vested in the Union cannot safely be entrusted to a body that is not under every necessary control. But there are satisfactory reasons to show that the objection is in reality not well founded. Most of the arguments about distance rest on a palpable illusion of the imagination. What are the sources of information by which the people of Montgomery County must form their judgment of the conduct of their representatives in the State legislature? They can have no benefit of personal observation, which is confined to the citizens on the spot. They must therefore depend on the information of intelligent men whom they trust; and how must these men get their information? Evidently from the character of public measures, from the public newspapers, and from correspondence with their representatives and with other persons who live at the place where the legislature deliberates. This applies not to Montgomery County only but to all the counties at any considerable distance from the seat of government.
